Harvard.text: A chemical that changes the sex hormone testosterone into a substance called dihydrotestosterone. This hormone can cause the prostate gland to grow abnormally.

LLM.text: An enzyme that converts testosterone to dihydrotestosterone, a hormone involved in prostate growth and male sexual development.

Harvard.text: A flat sheet of muscles on the front of the abdomen, between the ribcage and the pelvis.

LLM.text: The muscles forming the front and sides of the abdominal wall. They support the trunk, help with posture and breathing, and increase intra-abdominal pressure during coughing, lifting, and defecation.

Harvard.text: A procedure to remove excess abdominal skin and tighten the underlying stomach muscles. Also known as a tummy tuck.

LLM.text: A surgical procedure that removes excess abdominal skin and may tighten the abdominal wall. It is commonly called a tummy tuck.

Harvard.text: Movement of a body part, such as an arm or leg, away from the center of the body.

LLM.text: Movement of a limb or other body part away from the median plane of the body.

Harvard.text: A form of treatment that uses electrical energy, heat, cold, alcohol, or other modalities to destroy a small section of damaged tissue.

LLM.text: Destruction or removal of a small area of abnormal tissue using methods such as heat, cold, chemicals, or electrical energy.

Harvard.text: A scraping or rubbing away of the skin or other surface.

LLM.text: Superficial loss of tissue caused by friction or scraping. In dentistry, it commonly refers to mechanical loss of tooth structure from external forces.

Harvard.text: Pus that collects in a pocket of swollen, red tissue. Often occurs on the surface of the skin.

LLM.text: A localized collection of pus within a tissue, organ, or cavity, typically caused by bacterial infection. Abscesses form when bacteria (most commonly Staphylococcus aureus including MRSA) invade tissue, triggering an intense inflammatory response with neutrophil accumulation and tissue necrosis.

Harvard.text: A tooth or implant to which a fixed prosthesis is anchored.

LLM.text: A tooth or implant that supports and anchors a dental prosthesis.

Harvard.text: Psychotherapy techniques that use mindfulness to help a person recognize and accept thoughts and feelings but not be controlled by them.

LLM.text: Psychotherapeutic approaches that help a person notice and accept thoughts, feelings, or bodily sensations while reducing unhelpful attempts to control or avoid them.

Harvard.text: The eye's ability to focus on objects that are close.

LLM.text: The ability of the eye to change the shape of its lens so that near objects can be focused clearly.

Harvard.text: Abbreviation for angiotensin-converting enzyme, an enzyme that converts the inactive form of the protein angiotensin (angiotensin I) to its active form—angiotensin II.

LLM.text: An enzyme that converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II and breaks down bradykinin; it helps regulate blood pressure and fluid balance.

Harvard.text: Abbreviation of angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor, a drug used to treat high blood pressure and congestive heart failure.

LLM.text: A drug that inhibits angiotensin-converting enzyme, reducing formation of angiotensin II and degradation of bradykinin.

Harvard.text: A curved, bowl-shaped depression in the outer part of the hipbone. The ball-shaped portion at the top of the thighbone fits into this space to form the hip joint.

LLM.text: The cup-shaped socket of the hip formed by the fused ilium, ischium, and pubis. It articulates with the femoral head and is deepened by the acetabular labrum.

Harvard.text: The main breakdown product of alcohol metabolism; accumulation of it in the bloodstream may produce flushing (a feeling of heat in the face or chest) and vomiting.

LLM.text: A chemical produced when the body metabolizes alcohol. Accumulation may contribute to flushing, nausea, and vomiting.

Harvard.text: A common, over-the-counter drug used to reduce fever and relieve mild to moderate pain, but which does not reduce redness or swelling (inflammation).

LLM.text: Acetaminophen is a medicine, biologic, or pharmacologic term; its use, dose, interactions, and adverse effects depend on the specific clinical indication.

Harvard.text: A neurotransmitter (a chemical messenger that sends signals between brain cells) that plays roles in attention, learning, and memory.

LLM.text: A major neurotransmitter in both the central and peripheral nervous systems. In the peripheral nervous system, it is released at the neuromuscular junction (nicotinic receptors) to excite skeletal muscle, at all autonomic ganglia (nicotinic receptors), and at parasympathetic postganglionic terminals (muscarinic receptors).

Harvard.text: A band of connective tissue that connects the calf muscle to the heel bone. This tissue is prone to swelling and/or rupture.

LLM.text: The strong tendon connecting the calf muscles to the heel bone; it transmits force for plantar flexion and is commonly affected by tendinopathy or rupture.

Harvard.text: A condition in which the stomach produces little or no acid. This can affect digestion, cause stomach pain, and keep the body from absorbing vitamins and nutrients.

LLM.text: Absence of hydrochloric acid in gastric secretions. It may result from autoimmune gastritis, long-term acid suppression, or loss of acid-producing stomach cells.

Harvard.text: An inflammatory disease resulting from excess sebum production, follicle plugging, and increased bacterial production.

LLM.text: A chronic inflammatory disorder of hair follicles and sebaceous glands. It causes comedones, papules, pustules, or nodules, most often on the face, chest, and back.

Harvard.text: Usually abbreviated as AIDS. This is the most advanced stage of infection with the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), which can severely weaken the immune system. People with AIDS get many infections, often from diseases that don’t affect people with healthy immune systems.

LLM.text: Alternate Mayo Clinic label; see HIV/AIDS.

Harvard.text: The term given to the brain's absorption of new information to begin creating a memory.

LLM.text: The process by which new information or a skill is learned and initially encoded, especially in discussions of memory and learning.

Harvard.text: A shoulder joint that connects the clavicle to the scapula.

LLM.text: A plane synovial joint between the acromion of the scapula and the lateral end of the clavicle. It permits gliding movements and is stabilized primarily by the acromioclavicular and coracoclavicular ligaments.

Harvard.text: One of the proteins that allows cells to move and muscles to contract.

LLM.text: A structural and contractile protein found in many cells. In muscle, actin interacts with myosin to produce contraction; in other cells, it supports shape, movement, and intracellular transport.

Harvard.text: Scaly pink or red-brown raised spots or patches on the skin caused by overexposure to the sun. Actinic keratosis may be a precursor to skin cancer.

LLM.text: A rough, scaly skin lesion caused by chronic ultraviolet exposure, usually on sun-exposed skin. It can progress to squamous-cell carcinoma, so persistent, thickened, or changing lesions require clinical assessment.

Harvard.text: A strategy for managing early prostate cancer in which a man has regular checkups but does not undergo treatment until the disease shows signs of worsening.

LLM.text: Close, structured monitoring of a cancer or precancerous condition without immediate treatment. It includes scheduled examinations, laboratory tests, imaging, or biopsies, with treatment started if evidence of progression develops.

Harvard.text: Using the thumb or fingers to apply pressure to particular spots, or pressure points, on the body in order to relieve pain.

LLM.text: Application of pressure to selected body points, usually to relieve symptoms such as pain or nausea.

Harvard.text: A treatment based on Chinese medicine. Thin needles are inserted into the skin at specific points on the body. This therapy is used to treat pain and various health problems and to reduce stress.

LLM.text: A treatment in which thin needles are inserted into selected points of the body.

Harvard.text: A condition that comes on suddenly, often with severe, but short-lived symptoms.

LLM.text: Beginning suddenly or developing over a short period. The term may describe symptoms, illnesses, or complications.

Harvard.text: Severe pain that occurs suddenly and usually lasts a short while.

LLM.text: Pain that begins suddenly and usually lasts for a limited period, often because of injury, illness, or a procedure.

Harvard.text: A sudden inability to empty the bladder. Causes include an enlarged prostate gland (in men) or bladder muscle problems.

LLM.text: Sudden inability to empty the bladder, often causing painful lower-abdominal distension and requiring urgent assessment.

Harvard.text: The ability of the body to learn to fight specific infections after being exposed to the germs that cause them.

LLM.text: Antigen-specific immunity mediated principally by B and T lymphocytes. It develops after antigen exposure, generates immunologic memory, and includes humoral responses from B-cell antibodies and cellular responses from T cells.

Harvard.text: Loss of control over indulging in a substance or performing an action or behavior, and continued craving for it despite negative consequences.

LLM.text: A chronic, relapsing brain disorder characterized by compulsive substance use or behavior despite harmful consequences. It involves changes in brain reward, motivation, and memory circuits, leading to impaired control over the behavior. Treatment often combines medication, behavioral therapy, and social support.

Harvard.text: Movement of a body part toward or across the midline.

LLM.text: Movement of a body part toward the body's midline.

Harvard.text: A type of cancer that grows in the layer of tissue known as the epithelium. This tissue lines organs and structures in the body, protecting or enclosing them.

LLM.text: A malignant tumor arising from glandular epithelial tissue, forming gland-like structures. The most common type of carcinoma, occurring in organs such as the colon, breast, lung, pancreas, and prostate.

Harvard.text: A benign growth found in the layer of cells that lines certain organs (epithelial cells).

LLM.text: A benign tumour arising from glandular or gland-like epithelial tissue. Some adenomas, particularly certain colorectal adenomas, can develop dysplasia and progress to carcinoma.

Harvard.text: An energy-storing molecule that is found in all human cells. Usually abbreviated as ATP.

LLM.text: A molecule that stores and transfers energy within cells. It is commonly abbreviated ATP.

Harvard.text: An estimate of the amount of a nutrient needed by healthy people. The Adequate Intake is used when there isn’t enough information to set a recommended dietary allowance (RDA).

LLM.text: A recommended average daily nutrient intake based on observed or experimentally determined levels in healthy people when evidence is insufficient to establish a recommended dietary allowance.

Harvard.text: A band of scar-like tissue that forms between two surfaces inside the body, connecting tissues or organs which are not normally connected.

LLM.text: A band of scar-like tissue that abnormally connects surfaces or organs inside the body.

Harvard.text: Fat-filled tissue.

LLM.text: A specialized connective tissue composed mainly of adipocytes that store energy as triglycerides. It provides thermal insulation, cushioning for organs, and endocrine regulation through hormones and signaling molecules such as leptin and adiponectin.

Harvard.text: Extra therapy given after a primary treatment, to increase the effectiveness of the primary treatment. For example, using chemotherapy after surgery or radiation treatment for cancer.

LLM.text: Additional treatment after primary treatment to reduce recurrence risk. Examples: chemotherapy after surgery.

Harvard.text: Glands that sit on top of each kidney and secrete stress hormones.

LLM.text: Adrenal glands sit above the kidneys and produce cortisol, aldosterone, adrenal androgens, and catecholamines that regulate stress, blood pressure, salt balance, and metabolism.

Harvard.text: Stress hormone that puts the body on high alert. Changes include faster heartbeat, more rapid breathing, greater energy, and higher blood pressure. Also called epinephrine.

LLM.text: Epinephrine, a hormone and neurotransmitter released during stress that increases heart rate and contractility, constricts some blood vessels, and relaxes bronchial muscle.

Harvard.text: Centers providing daytime services to adults who need supervision, social support, or assistance with daily activities.

LLM.text: Community-based daytime programs providing supervision, social activities, health-related support, or assistance with daily activities for adults who cannot safely remain alone throughout the day.

Harvard.text: An ingredient in a medicinal product (herb, supplement, or prescription drug), which dilutes the purity of the product and does not contribute to its therapeutic effects.

LLM.text: A substance added to a drug, specimen, food, or other product that is not an intended component and may alter its quality, safety, composition, or test results.

terms.term: Advance Care Directive (Or Advance Medical Directive)

Harvard.text: A legal document that describes the kind of medical care a person want if an accident or illness leaves him or her unable to make or communicate decisions.

LLM.text: A document in which a person records treatment preferences or appoints a decision-maker for a time when they cannot communicate or make medical decisions.

terms.normalized_term: advance care directive (or advance medical directive)

Harvard.text: A pattern of falling asleep and waking up earlier than wanted that worsens progressively over time.

LLM.text: A circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorder in which a person becomes sleepy and wakes earlier than desired, with otherwise normal sleep when following the advanced schedule.

Harvard.text: Any process that requires oxygen. Often used to describe a form of exercise, aerobic exercise.

LLM.text: Requiring or involving molecular oxygen. In microbiology, aerobic organisms use oxygen for growth or energy production, either obligatorily or as one option among several; in physiology, aerobic metabolism uses oxidative phosphorylation in mitochondria to generate ATP from nutrients.

Harvard.text: Physical activity that speeds breathing, improves heart and lung function, and offers many other health benefits. Examples include brisk walking, running, or cycling.

LLM.text: Physical activity that uses sustained oxygen-dependent energy production, such as walking or cycling.

Harvard.text: Excessive swallowing of air.

LLM.text: Excessive swallowing of air, which may cause belching, abdominal bloating, distention, or increased intestinal gas.

Harvard.text: Licensed skin care professional who performs procedures such as deep cleansing, low-grade chemical peels, microdermabrasion, and postsurgical skin care.

LLM.text: A trained skin-care professional who provides nonmedical cosmetic skin treatments, such as cleansing, superficial exfoliation, and selected skin-care procedures within the scope of local regulation.

Harvard.text: Clouding of the lens of the eye that can occur months or years after cataract surgery.

LLM.text: Clouding of the posterior lens capsule that develops after cataract surgery and may cause blurred or hazy vision. It is also called posterior capsule opacification.

Harvard.text: The slight loss of memory and slowing of the brain’s information processing that occurs with normal aging.

LLM.text: A modest, age-associated change in memory, processing speed, or other cognitive abilities that does not necessarily interfere substantially with independent daily functioning.

Harvard.text: A potentially blinding condition that destroys sharp central vision.

LLM.text: A degenerative disorder of the macula that can impair central vision in older adults. The dry form involves retinal and pigment-cell changes and may progress gradually; the neovascular form involves abnormal blood-vessel growth and may cause more rapid vision loss. Risk is influenced by age, smoking, family history, and other factors.

Harvard.text: A rare disease in which a person can’t recognize objects, shapes, or people. Often due to a brain or neurological condition.

LLM.text: A higher-order neurological deficit characterized by the inability to recognize or process sensory stimuli (visual, auditory, tactile) despite intact primary sensory organs and pathways. Caused by focal lesions in specific cortical association areas (parietal, temporal, or occipital lobes).

Harvard.text: 1) A substance that triggers a physiological response when it combines with a receptor. 2) A muscle whose contraction is opposed by another muscle.

LLM.text: A substance that binds to a receptor and activates it, producing a biological response. A full agonist can produce the receptor's maximum response, whereas a partial agonist produces a lower maximum response even when it occupies all available receptors.

Harvard.text: Fear and avoidance of public places and open spaces.

LLM.text: Anxiety disorder characterized by fear and avoidance of situations where escape might be difficult or help unavailable during a panic-like episode. Common feared situations include public transportation, open spaces, enclosed spaces, standing in line, being in crowds, and being outside the home alone.

Harvard.text: abbreviation for acquired immunodeficiency syndrome, the most advanced stage of infection with the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV).

LLM.text: Acquired immunodeficiency syndrome: the advanced stage of HIV infection, defined by CD4 count <200 cells/µL or the presence of AIDS-defining illnesses.

Harvard.text: A loss of brain function that occurs rapidly in some AIDS patients; marked by forgetfulness, difficulty thinking, and trouble focusing.

LLM.text: A disorder of thinking, memory, behavior, or movement caused by advanced HIV-related disease affecting the brain.

Harvard.text: A group of inherited conditions that typically appear as a reduction or absence of melanin pigments in the skin, hair, and eyes.

LLM.text: An inherited condition involving reduced or absent melanin production, affecting the skin, hair, and eyes.

Harvard.text: A protein made by the liver. Abnormal levels of this substance may indicate liver or kidney disease.

LLM.text: The main protein in blood plasma, produced by the liver. It helps maintain oncotic pressure and transports various substances, including hormones, fatty acids, and medications.

Harvard.text: High amounts of albumin (a protein made by the liver) in the urine, possibly indicating kidney dysfunction.

LLM.text: Abnormally increased excretion of albumin in the urine, indicating disruption of the glomerular filtration barrier or another form of kidney disease. It is commonly detected with a urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio and classified as moderately or severely increased according to the quantity and persistence of excretion.

Harvard.text: Continuing consumption of alcohol despite alcohol-related social or interpersonal problems.

LLM.text: A nonpreferred older term for a pattern of alcohol use that causes recurrent problems or harm. Current clinical classification generally uses alcohol use disorder and specifies its severity.

Harvard.text: A liver enzyme that metabolizes alcohol into a substance called acetaldehyde, which is toxic. Sometimes referred to as ADH.

LLM.text: An enzyme, found mainly in the liver, that catalyzes the first major step in ethanol metabolism by converting alcohol to acetaldehyde.

Harvard.text: A chronic, progressive disease characterized by excessive and often compulsive drinking, impaired control over drinking, use of alcohol despite adverse consequences, and withdrawal symptoms when alcohol use is discontinued. Also known as alcoholism.

LLM.text: A pattern of alcohol use characterized by impaired control, compulsive use, tolerance, withdrawal, and continued drinking despite harm. In current terminology, it is generally classified under alcohol use disorder.

Harvard.text: Another term for alcohol dependence: A chronic, progressive disease characterized by excessive and often compulsive drinking, impaired control over drinking, use of alcohol despite adverse consequences, and withdrawal symptoms when alcohol use is discontinued. Also known as alcoholism.

LLM.text: A chronic disorder characterized by impaired control over alcohol use and continued use despite harm.

Harvard.text: A hormone secreted by the adrenal glands that helps regulate blood pressure by controlling sodium and potassium levels in the body.

LLM.text: A mineralocorticoid hormone produced by the zona glomerulosa of the adrenal cortex, the final effector of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS).

Harvard.text: A drug used to treat and prevent osteoporosis by slowing bone loss.

LLM.text: A bisphosphonate that reduces bone resorption and is used to treat or prevent osteoporosis and selected other disorders of excessive bone turnover.

Harvard.text: Another term for the gastrointestinal, or digestive, tract.

LLM.text: The continuous muscular tube from the mouth to the anus through which food passes; it includes the pharynx, esophagus, stomach, small intestine, and large intestine.

Harvard.text: One of two or more versions of a gene. Different alleles produce variations in inherited characteristics, such as eye color.

LLM.text: Alternative form of a gene at a particular locus. Individuals inherit two alleles for each gene (one from each parent). Alleles can be dominant, recessive, or codominant.

Harvard.text: A substance such as fur, pollen, or dust that produces an allergic reaction.

LLM.text: A substance capable of causing an allergic immune response in a susceptible person. Common allergens include proteins in foods, pollens, medicines, animal dander, insect venom, and natural rubber.

Harvard.text: Having a sensitivity to one or more normally harmless substances.

LLM.text: Describing an immune-mediated hypersensitivity response to a normally harmless substance, such as a food, medicine, or environmental allergen.

Harvard.text: A seasonal or year-round allergic condition marked by sneezing, runny nose, and congestion. The most common type of allergy, it is caused by an IgE-mediated immune response to inhaled airborne allergens.

LLM.text: An IgE-mediated inflammatory response of the nasal mucosa to inhaled allergens, causing sneezing, nasal congestion, clear rhinorrhea, nasal itching, and often conjunctival symptoms. Management may include allergen avoidance, intranasal corticosteroids, antihistamines, and allergen immunotherapy when indicated.

Harvard.text: An immune system reaction (for example, rash, fever, sneezing, or headaches) to something that is normally harmless.

LLM.text: An allergy is an inappropriate immune response to a normally harmless substance such as pollen, food, medicine, insect venom, or animal proteins. Symptoms range from localized rhinitis or hives to life-threatening anaphylaxis.

Harvard.text: Pain resulting from something not normally painful, such as a light touch.

LLM.text: Pain caused by a stimulus that is normally not painful, such as light touch or gentle pressure. It may occur with neuropathic, nociplastic, or other pain conditions.

Harvard.text: An autoimmune condition that appears as patchy hair loss on the scalp that may result in permanent hair loss.

LLM.text: A common, autoimmune, non-scarring hair loss disorder affecting approximately 1 to 2 percent of the population worldwide, with a lifetime risk of 2 percent, occurring equally across sexes and ethnicities, with peak onset between 15 and 29 years.

Harvard.text: Hair loss that involves the entire scalp.

LLM.text: Complete loss of hair from the scalp, usually caused by an autoimmune disorder.

Harvard.text: Hair loss that involves the entire body.

LLM.text: Loss of hair from the entire body, including the scalp, eyebrows, eyelashes, and other hair-bearing areas.

Harvard.text: A group of drugs that lower blood pressure by blocking the effects of adrenaline or adrenaline-like substances on cells' alpha receptors. Also used to treat some prostate gland problems. Alpha blockers are also known as alpha-adrenergic antagonists, alpha-adrenergic blocking agents, and alpha-adrenergic blockers.

LLM.text: Medicines that block alpha-adrenergic receptors and may lower blood pressure or improve urine flow in prostate enlargement.

common_names: alpha-adrenergic antagonists, alpha-adrenergic blocking agents, and alpha-adrenergic blockers

Harvard.text: Cells in the pancreas that produce the hormone glucagon.

LLM.text: Endocrine cells in the pancreatic islets that produce and release glucagon, a hormone that raises blood glucose during fasting or low-glucose states.

Harvard.text: Fruit-derived acids used in creams and lotions to act as exfoliants.

LLM.text: A group of organic acids used in dermatology and cosmetics to exfoliate the outer skin layer and improve texture or pigmentation. Examples include glycolic and lactic acid.

Harvard.text: A type of brain wave generated when a person is relaxed, awake, and receiving no visual input (eyes closed or in the dark).

LLM.text: Rhythmic electroencephalographic waves, typically around 8--13 Hz, most prominent when a relaxed, awake person has the eyes closed.

Harvard.text: Abnormal deep sleep; also called non-restorative sleep.

LLM.text: A sleep pattern in which alpha-frequency activity intrudes into delta-wave deep sleep and may be associated with nonrestorative sleep or chronic pain.

Harvard.text: A drug used to treat Type 2 diabetes.

LLM.text: An oral diabetes medicine that slows intestinal carbohydrate digestion and absorption, reducing the rise in blood glucose after meals.

Harvard.text: The part of the jawbone that supports the teeth.

LLM.text: Bone surrounding and supporting tooth roots. Resorbs with tooth loss. Maintained by function. Bone grafting may be needed for implants.

Harvard.text: Tiny air sacs in the lung. They are where oxygen enters and carbon dioxide leaves the bloodstream.

LLM.text: Microscopic air sacs in the lungs where oxygen enters the blood and carbon dioxide leaves it.

Harvard.text: A progressive brain disease that causes memory loss, impaired thinking, and personality changes.

LLM.text: A progressive brain disorder causing deterioration of memory, thinking, behavior, and the ability to perform daily activities.

Harvard.text: Able to walk; not confined to a bed.

LLM.text: Able to walk or move about; in healthcare, ambulatory care refers to assessment or treatment that does not require an overnight hospital stay.

Harvard.text: Unusual memory loss or forgetfulness.

LLM.text: Loss or impairment of memory that is greater than ordinary forgetting. It may affect the ability to form new memories (anterograde amnesia), recall past events (retrograde amnesia), or both.

Harvard.text: The surgical removal of a limb or other body part.

LLM.text: Surgical removal of a limb or part of a limb. The level may involve a digit, foot, lower leg, thigh, or hip, or a corresponding part of the upper limb. The level is selected according to tissue viability, function, and potential for rehabilitation.

Harvard.text: A tool used to check for vision problems, particularly macular degeneration. The grid looks like graph paper with a dot in the center.

LLM.text: A simple chart used to detect or monitor distortions and missing areas in central vision, especially in macular disease.

Harvard.text: Part of the brain involved in memory and emotion.

LLM.text: Almond-shaped nucleus cluster in the anterior medial temporal lobe, part of the limbic system, primarily processing emotions (especially fear/anxiety). Receives thalamic/cortical sensory input; projects to hypothalamus, brainstem, and cortex for autonomic/behavioral fear responses.

Harvard.text: An enzyme secreted by the pancreas that breaks starch into sugar.

LLM.text: An enzyme that breaks down starch and is produced mainly by the salivary glands and pancreas. Blood levels may rise in several conditions, including some pancreatic disorders.

Harvard.text: A protein that collects in tissues when certain diseases, including Alzheimer’s disease, are present.

LLM.text: An abnormal protein that can accumulate in tissues and impair their function in several diseases.

Harvard.text: Any process that doesn’t require oxygen. Often refers to a form of short, high intensity exercise, known as anaerobic exercise.

LLM.text: Able to live, grow, or function without oxygen.

Harvard.text: Exercise that improves the efficiency of energy-producing systems that do not rely on oxygen. Examples include sprinting and weight lifting.

LLM.text: Physical activity performed at an intensity that relies substantially on energy pathways that do not require immediate oxygen delivery, such as sprinting or heavy resistance exercise.

Harvard.text: The active growth phase of the hair-growth cycle.

LLM.text: The active growth phase of the hair cycle.

Harvard.text: The last inch of the large intestine, leading to the anal opening.

LLM.text: The terminal 3-4 cm of the gastrointestinal tract, extending from the anorectal junction (puborectalis/pectinate line) to the anal verge. Above the pectinate line: lined by columnar epithelium, innervated by autonomic nerves, draining to portal system, supplied by superior rectal artery.

Harvard.text: Absence of pain.

LLM.text: Absence or reduction of pain without necessarily causing loss of consciousness.

Harvard.text: A drug or other substance such as aspirin, acetaminophen, or morphine that is used to relieve pain.

LLM.text: A drug that relieves pain without producing loss of consciousness.

Harvard.text: Differences in how a test is done, for example how a sample is prepared, which can affect test outcomes.

LLM.text: Variation in a laboratory result caused by the measurement method, instrument, reagents, calibration, or specimen processing rather than by a true change in the patient.

Harvard.text: A severe allergic reaction, causing symptoms spanning from itching and swelling to trouble breathing, convulsions, shock, and coma.

LLM.text: A severe, potentially life-threatening systemic hypersensitivity reaction characterized by rapid onset of multisystem involvement, primarily affecting the skin, respiratory tract, cardiovascular system, and gastrointestinal tract.

Harvard.text: Any of a group of male sex hormones, including testosterone, that controls male characteristics such as beard growth.

LLM.text: A sex hormone, such as testosterone, that contributes to male reproductive development and other body functions.

Harvard.text: Female- and male-pattern baldness. The condition appears to involve a heightened response by the hair follicle to androgen levels in the body.

LLM.text: The most common cause of hair loss, caused by progressive miniaturization of genetically susceptible hair follicles under androgen influence. Male pattern commonly affects the frontal hairline and vertex; female pattern commonly causes diffuse crown thinning with relative preservation of the frontal hairline.

Harvard.text: Prostate cancer that no longer responds to hormone therapy.

LLM.text: Prostate cancer that continues to grow despite suppression of androgen production or blockade of the androgen receptor; it is also called castration-resistant prostate cancer.

Harvard.text: Having a lower than normal amount of red blood cells or hemoglobin (an oxygen-carrying protein inside red blood cells), leading to low energy, weakness, and other symptoms.

LLM.text: A reduction in the oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood, defined by a hemoglobin concentration below the normal range for age and sex: less than 13.5 g/dL in adult males, less than 12.0 g/dL in adult females.

Harvard.text: A birth defect in which an infant is born without most of the brain or without the skull bones covering the brain.

LLM.text: A fatal neural tube defect where the cerebral hemispheres and cranial vault fail to develop due to failed closure of the rostral neuropore during the fourth week of gestation. The brainstem and spinal cord are present, and reflex movements may occur, but there is no cognitive function.

Harvard.text: Temporarily blocking sensation, especially the feeling of pain.

LLM.text: The use of medications to prevent sensation, particularly pain, during medical procedures or surgery.

Harvard.text: A bulge or swelling on a portion of a blood vessel, due to weakness in the wall of that vessel.

LLM.text: A localized weakening and enlargement of a blood vessel. Aneurysms may occur in arteries or, rarely, veins and may rupture, dissect, or form emboli depending on their location and cause.

Harvard.text: Temporary chest pain that occurs when the heart isn’t getting enough oxygen and blood, usually occurring in response to physical activity or stress.

LLM.text: Chest discomfort caused by myocardial ischemia without infarction. Stable angina occurs predictably with exertion and resolves with rest. Unstable angina occurs at rest or with minimal exertion and is an acute coronary syndrome. Prinzmetal (variant) angina occurs at rest due to coronary vasospasm.

Harvard.text: The formation of new blood vessels.

LLM.text: Formation of new blood vessels. Tumors induce angiogenesis for growth. Targeted by anti-angiogenic drugs (bevacizumab).

Harvard.text: A test that shows how blood moves through the blood vessels and heart. It uses x-rays and the injection of a fluid called a contrast agent that can be seen on the x-rays.

LLM.text: Invasive imaging of blood vessels by injecting contrast material under fluoroscopy. Coronary angiography (cardiac catheterization): assesses coronary artery stenosis, guides PCI. Cerebral angiography: evaluates aneurysms, AVMs, and vasculitis. Peripheral angiography: evaluates PAD and guides intervention.

Harvard.text: A procedure used to open blocked or narrowed arteries, most commonly by inserting a thin tube, or catheter, into the affected artery and inflating a balloon.

LLM.text: A procedure that widens a narrowed blood vessel, usually with a balloon and sometimes a stent. It is used most often for coronary or peripheral arterial disease.

Harvard.text: A protein that raises blood pressure by narrowing blood vessels and causing the kidneys to store more sodium and water.

LLM.text: A family of peptides in the renin--angiotensin system that regulate blood pressure and fluid balance, with angiotensin II causing vasoconstriction and stimulating aldosterone release.

Harvard.text: An inactive form of the protein angiotensin. It is the precursor to the active form, angiotensin II.

LLM.text: An inactive precursor that is converted to angiotensin II in the renin-angiotensin system.

Harvard.text: The active form of the protein angiotensin, which raises blood pressure by narrowing blood vessels and causing the kidneys to store more sodium and water.

LLM.text: A hormone that narrows blood vessels and promotes sodium retention, thereby increasing blood pressure.

Harvard.text: A class of drugs that blocks the effects of angiotensin. Like ACE inhibitors, they keep coronary arteries open, lower blood pressure, and reduce the heart's workload.

LLM.text: Medicines that block angiotensin II type 1 receptors, lowering vasoconstriction and aldosterone effects to treat hypertension, heart failure, and some kidney disease.

Harvard.text: An enzyme that converts the inactive form of the protein angiotensin (angiotensin I) to its active form—angiotensin II. Usually abbreviated as ACE.

LLM.text: An enzyme that converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II and breaks down bradykinin; it helps regulate blood pressure and fluid balance.

Harvard.text: A drug used to treat high blood pressure and congestive heart failure. These drugs stop the production of angiotensin II. This lowers blood pressure and reduces the heart's workload. Usually abbreviated as ACE inhibitor.

LLM.text: A medicine that blocks angiotensin-converting enzyme, reducing angiotensin II formation and aldosterone release; it is used for hypertension, heart failure, and kidney protection in selected patients.

Harvard.text: A test that compares blood pressure at the ankle with blood pressure at the elbow. A difference between the two indicates the presence of peripheral artery disease.

LLM.text: The ratio of ankle systolic blood pressure to brachial systolic blood pressure. A low result supports peripheral arterial disease, while a very high result may indicate noncompressible arteries.

Harvard.text: Means crooked or bent; refers to stiffening of a joint.

LLM.text: A combining form meaning stiff, bent, or fused, as in ankylosis or ankylosing spondylitis.

Harvard.text: A disease that leads to swelling between the disks of the spine and in the joints where the pelvis and spine meet. Causes back pain and stiffness and can limit movement.

LLM.text: A long-term form of arthritis that mainly affects the joints between the spine and pelvis and the spine itself. It causes back pain and stiffness. Over time, new bone may form around the spine, causing some spinal bones to join together and making the back less flexible. It can also affect other joints, the eyes, skin, or bowel.

Harvard.text: Term used to describe ring or circle shaped objects or body parts.

LLM.text: A ring-shaped structure or band; examples include the annulus fibrosus around an intervertebral disk and the fibrous rings around heart valves.

Harvard.text: The tough outer covering of the discs in the spine.

LLM.text: The tough outer ring of fibrocartilage surrounding the nucleus pulposus of an intervertebral disc.

Harvard.text: Abnormal functioning of the anus and rectum, causing constipation or the inability to control bowel movements.

LLM.text: Impaired function of the anus or rectum affecting continence, evacuation, sensation, or coordination; causes include structural disease, nerve injury, and pelvic-floor disorders.

Harvard.text: An eating disorder in which a person has an intense fear of gaining weight and severely limits calories to the point of near starvation.

LLM.text: Loss of appetite, distinct from anorexia nervosa (the eating disorder).

Harvard.text: The muscle opposing the major muscle required to do a task. It works to help balance movement and ward off injury.

LLM.text: A substance, drug, muscle, or other factor that opposes or blocks the action of another; a receptor antagonist binds without activating the receptor.

Harvard.text: A heart attack affecting the front of the heart.

LLM.text: A myocardial infarction involving the anterior wall of the left ventricle, usually because of obstruction in the left anterior descending coronary artery.

Harvard.text: A drug that blocks or interferes with the activity of male sex hormones.

LLM.text: A medicine or other substance that reduces androgen production or blocks androgen action at its receptor.

Harvard.text: A substance that kills or slows the growth of bacteria.

LLM.text: A substance that kills or slows the growth of bacteria.

Harvard.text: A protein made by the immune system to protect the body from harmful substances, called antigens.

LLM.text: A protein produced by the immune system that specifically binds to a foreign or abnormal substance.

Harvard.text: A substance that helps prevent blood from clotting.

LLM.text: A medicine or substance that reduces the blood's ability to form clots.

Harvard.text: Drugs that diminish the blood's ability to clot. Anticoagulants are sometimes called blood thinners even though they do not thin the blood. Commonly used anticoagulant drugs include heparin and warfarin.

LLM.text: Medicines that reduce blood clot formation by inhibiting one or more steps in the coagulation cascade.

common_names: blood thinners even though they do not thin the blood

Harvard.text: Drugs used to treat seizures.

LLM.text: Medications used to prevent or control seizures in epilepsy and other seizure disorders.

Harvard.text: An antibody used to help diagnose rheumatoid arthritis.

LLM.text: An autoantibody directed against citrullinated proteins and used, with clinical findings and other tests, to support the diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis.

Harvard.text: A psychiatric drug used to treat mood disorders, such as depression.

LLM.text: A medicine used to treat depressive disorders and some other conditions involving mood, anxiety, pain, or sleep.

Harvard.text: A drug that prevents nausea and vomiting.

LLM.text: A medication that prevents or treats nausea and vomiting.

Harvard.text: Any substance that the body sees as harmful or foreign, causing the immune system to form antibodies in defense.

LLM.text: A molecule or molecular structure specifically recognized by an antibody, B-cell receptor, or T-cell receptor. An immunogen is an antigen capable of inducing an immune response; antigenicity and immunogenicity are related but not synonymous properties.

Harvard.text: Specialized white blood cells that detect harmful substances in the body and then signal other immune system defenders (known as T-cells) to mount a defense.

LLM.text: Specialized immune cells that process protein antigens and display peptide fragments bound to Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC) molecules on their surface for recognition by T-cell receptors. Professional APCs: dendritic cells (most potent for naive T cells), macrophages, and B cells.

Harvard.text: Medications that treat allergies and reduce symptoms such as sneezing and itching by blocking histamine, the substance in the body which causes these symptoms.

LLM.text: A drug that blocks histamine receptors. H1 antihistamines treat allergic rhinitis, urticaria, pruritus, and (older sedating agents) insomnia and motion sickness. First-generation (diphenhydramine, chlorpheniramine): CNS-penetrant—sedating, anticholinergic (dry mouth, urinary retention, confusion in elderly).

Harvard.text: Medications used to lower and control high blood pressure.

LLM.text: Medicines used to lower persistently elevated blood pressure and reduce the risk of cardiovascular, cerebrovascular, and kidney complications.

Harvard.text: A type of asthma medication that reduces swelling in airways and prevents muscles near the airways from tightening.

LLM.text: A drug class that blocks leukotriene-mediated airway inflammation or bronchoconstriction and is used in selected allergic or respiratory conditions.

Harvard.text: A general term for antibiotics and other drugs that fight microscopic organisms in the body, such as bacteria, viruses, fungi, and parasites.

LLM.text: A general term for antibiotics and other drugs that fight microscopic organisms in the body, such as bacteria, viruses, fungi, and parasites.

Harvard.text: Substances that protect the body from molecules that damage cells (free radicals); examples include beta carotene, vitamin C, vitamin A, and vitamin E.

LLM.text: A substance that limits oxidation by reacting with oxidizing molecules or free radicals.

Harvard.text: Medications or other substances that prevent blood cells called platelets from clustering and forming blood clots.

LLM.text: Medicines that reduce platelet activation or aggregation and thereby lower the risk of some blood clots.

Harvard.text: A drug used to treat schizophrenia and other severe mental health disorders; relieves symptoms such as delusions and hallucinations.

LLM.text: A drug used to treat psychotic disorders (schizophrenia, schizoaffective disorder, psychosis in bipolar/manic states and delirium). Typical (first-generation): haloperidol, chlorpromazine—D2 blockade, high EPS/tardive dyskinesia risk, hyperprolactinemia.

Harvard.text: Substances used on wounds to prevent or treat infection; they kill or slow the growth of disease-causing organisms, such as bacteria, on the surface of the body.

LLM.text: Substances used on wounds to prevent or treat infection; they kill or slow the growth of diseasecausing organisms, such as bacteria, on the surface of the body.

Harvard.text: Drug that relieves cramps and muscle spasms.

LLM.text: Medicines that reduce smooth-muscle spasm or cramping in selected gastrointestinal, urinary, biliary, or other conditions. Choice and use depend on the cause and clinical context.

Harvard.text: Drugs used to treat an overactive thyroid.

LLM.text: Medicines that reduce thyroid hormone production or availability and are used mainly to treat hyperthyroidism.

Harvard.text: The external opening at the end of digestive tract where feces are expelled.

LLM.text: The terminal opening of the gastrointestinal tract through which feces are expelled. It is surrounded by the internal smooth-muscle sphincter and external skeletal-muscle sphincter.

Harvard.text: The large artery emerging from the heart's left ventricle that distributes blood to the body.

LLM.text: Largest artery, from the left ventricle distributing oxygenated blood systemically. Approximately 30 cm long, 2.5 cm diameter. Four segments: ascending aorta, aortic arch (brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid, left subclavian), descending thoracic aorta, descending abdominal aorta (bifurcating into common iliacs at L4).

Harvard.text: A valve on the left side of the heart that acts as a one-way gate, opening to allow blood to leave the left ventricle and closing to prevent blood from leaking back into that ventricle.

LLM.text: A semilunar valve between the left ventricle and aorta, normally composed of right, left, and noncoronary cusps. It opens during systole and closes during diastole to direct blood flow. Each cusp forms a sinus of Valsalva from which coronary arteries originate. Opens during systole; closes during diastole.

Harvard.text: Difficulty speaking or comprehending language; a common occurrence after a stroke affecting the left hemisphere of the brain, where language is processed.

LLM.text: Impairment of language comprehension or production resulting from brain damage, most commonly from stroke affecting the left hemisphere (dominant) language areas.

Harvard.text: A temporary pause in breathing during sleep that can be very brief or can last so long that the amount of oxygen in the blood drops dangerously low.

LLM.text: Temporary cessation of breathing. Clinically important apnea may cause low oxygen, carbon-dioxide retention, or bradycardia.

Harvard.text: Proteins that combine with cholesterol and triglyceride to form lipoproteins.

LLM.text: Proteins associated with lipids in the blood that help transport and metabolize cholesterol and triglycerides.

Harvard.text: A process of programmed cell death in which redundant or flawed cells destroy themselves.

LLM.text: Programmed cell death. Dysregulated in cancer (avoiding death). Pro-apoptotic genes: BAX, P53. Anti-apoptotic: BCL-2.

Harvard.text: A normal brain protein that under certain circumstances produces beta amyloid, abnormal protein deposited in the brain in Alzheimer’s disease. Usually abbreviated as APP.

LLM.text: A normal transmembrane protein that can be processed into amyloid-beta peptides, which may accumulate in the brain in Alzheimer disease.

Harvard.text: A brain disorder in which a person cannot perform certain actions, such as combing hair, picking up a pencil, or speaking, even though they want to and have the physical ability to do so.

LLM.text: Inability to perform learned, skilled motor movements despite intact motor function, sensation, coordination, and comprehension.

Harvard.text: Clear fluid that fills the front part of the eye.

LLM.text: A clear, watery fluid that fills the anterior and posterior chambers of the eye, maintaining intraocular pressure and providing nutrients and oxygen to the avascular cornea and lens while removing metabolic waste products.

Harvard.text: Abbreviation for angiotensin II receptor blockers, a class of drugs that blocks the effects of angiotensin. Like ACE inhibitors, they keep coronary arteries open, lower blood pressure, and reduce the heart's workload.

LLM.text: A medicine that blocks angiotensin II type 1 receptors and is used to treat hypertension, heart failure, and selected kidney disorders.

Harvard.text: A virus transmitted by mosquitoes or other member of the arthropod phylum.

LLM.text: A virus transmitted by mosquitoes or other member of the arthropod phylum.

Harvard.text: The state of being awake or reactive to stimuli through one or more of the five senses.

LLM.text: A state of physiological and mental activation that supports alertness and responsiveness; abnormal arousal may occur in sleep disorders, delirium, brain injury, or psychiatric illness.

Harvard.text: The small muscle associated with an individual hair follicle that enables hair to stand on end.

LLM.text: A small involuntary smooth muscle attached to a hair follicle that contracts to raise the hair and produce gooseflesh.

Harvard.text: An abnormal heart rhythm caused by a disturbance in the heart’s electrical system.

LLM.text: Any abnormality of cardiac rate, rhythm, or site of impulse origin, arising through enhanced automaticity, reentry, or triggered activity. Classified by rate as tachyarrhythmia or bradyarrhythmia and by site as supraventricular or ventricular. Diagnosis rests on the 12-lead ECG and ambulatory monitoring when intermittent.

Harvard.text: The pressure that the artery walls exert on blood flow; in general, the less elastic the arteries, the greater the arterial resistance and the higher the blood pressure.

LLM.text: The opposition to blood flow produced mainly by the diameter and tone of small arteries and arterioles. It contributes to systemic vascular resistance and blood pressure.

Harvard.text: A test that uses x-rays and a special dye to see inside arteries.

LLM.text: An imaging procedure that shows arteries after contrast material is injected, usually using x-ray fluoroscopy or computed tomography, to identify narrowing, blockage, aneurysm, or malformation.

Harvard.text: Small, muscular branches of arteries.

LLM.text: Small branches of arteries that regulate blood flow into capillary beds through contraction and relaxation of their smooth muscle.

Harvard.text: A term encompassing a variety of conditions in which artery walls thicken and become less flexible. Sometimes called hardening of the arteries. Arteriosclerosis occurs when cholesterol-rich plaque forms on the inner lining of arteries (atherosclerosis), when artery walls become calcified, or when high blood pressure thickens the muscular wall of arteries.

LLM.text: Chronic inflammatory disease of medium and large arteries characterized by accumulation of lipids, inflammatory cells, and fibrous tissue within the arterial wall, forming atherosclerotic plaques. See Atherosclerosis.

Harvard.text: Abnormal connections between veins and arteries, usually caused by a birth defect.

LLM.text: Abnormal connection between artery and vein without capillary bed. Can bleed or cause symptoms.

Harvard.text: A blood vessel that carries blood away from the heart and to various parts of the body.

LLM.text: A blood vessel that carries oxygenated blood away from the heart to the tissues, except for the pulmonary arteries which carry deoxygenated blood to the lungs. Arteries have thick, elastic, muscular walls that withstand high pressure and distribute blood throughout the body. The aorta is the largest artery.

Harvard.text: A prefix meaning "joint.''

LLM.text: A combining form referring to a joint, as in arthritis, arthralgia, and arthroscopy.

Harvard.text: A condition in which joints are inflamed, causing pain, stiffness, swelling, and sometimes loss of movement.

LLM.text: Inflammation of one or more joints, characterized by joint pain, swelling, warmth, and stiffness.

Harvard.text: A procedure to drain fluid from a joint using a syringe.

LLM.text: Aspiration of joint fluid for diagnostic or therapeutic purposes. Indications: septic arthritis (urgent, crystals), inflammatory arthritis (gout, pseudogout), hemorrhagic effusion (trauma, coagulopathy), and therapeutic drainage for symptomatic relief.

Harvard.text: Joining together two bones to reduce pain and provide stability to a damaged, arthritic, or painful joint.

LLM.text: Surgical fusion of a joint by removing or preparing articular surfaces and stabilizing the bones until osseous union occurs. It relieves pain and provides stability at the cost of joint motion.

Harvard.text: Joint disease or disorder.

LLM.text: Any disease or disorder affecting a joint.

Harvard.text: Surgically rebuilding or replacing a joint, usually to relieve arthritis or fix an abnormality.

LLM.text: Surgical reconstruction or replacement of a joint to relieve pain, restore alignment, or improve function. It may be partial or total and is commonly performed for advanced degenerative joint disease, fracture, inflammatory arthritis, or other destructive joint conditions.

Harvard.text: A procedure where a surgeon makes a small cut in the skin and inserts tiny lenses, lighting, and other instruments to diagnose or repair joint problems.

LLM.text: Minimally invasive joint visualization and intervention via a rigid arthroscope inserted through small portals, used for meniscal and ligamentous repair, chondroplasty, loose body removal, and synovectomy.

Harvard.text: Smooth white tissue that covers the ends of bones where they come together to form joints.

LLM.text: Smooth cartilage covering the ends of bones within a joint, allowing low-friction movement and distributing load.

Harvard.text: Bony projections on vertebra.

LLM.text: Projections from the vertebral arch that form facet joints with adjacent vertebrae and help guide and limit spinal movement.

Harvard.text: A life-threatening lack of oxygen due to drowning, choking, or an obstruction of the airways.

LLM.text: A life-threatening lack of oxygen due to drowning, choking, or an obstruction of the airways. Management: remove obstruction, rescue breathing, CPR if needed. Foreign body airway obstruction: Heimlich maneuver (abdominal thrusts) for conscious adults; back blows and chest thrusts for infants.

Harvard.text: Breathing in a foreign object. Also, the process of suctioning fluid, tissue, or other substances from the body.

LLM.text: The inhalation of foreign material (oropharyngeal secretions, gastric contents, food, liquid, or blood) into the larynx and lower respiratory tract. Aspiration pneumonitis (Mendelson syndrome) is a chemical lung injury caused by acidic gastric fluid.

Harvard.text: A drug that relieves pain, fever, and swelling, and inhibits the formation of blood clots.

LLM.text: Acetylsalicylic acid, a salicylate that relieves pain and fever, reduces inflammation, and irreversibly inhibits platelet aggregation; it can cause gastrointestinal bleeding and is generally avoided in children with viral illness.

Harvard.text: Live-in facilities for adults who need help with certain things, but do not need round-the-clock care. They provide residents with supervision and certain services, such as meals, transportation, or help with dressing, grooming, and other daily activities.

LLM.text: Residential setting with assistance for ADLs. Less intensive than nursing home.

Harvard.text: The part of the cerebral cortex involved in processing information, rather than movement or sensory experiences.

LLM.text: Cerebral cortex involved in integrating information and supporting memory, language, judgment, and complex behavior.

Harvard.text: A disease that inflames and narrows airways, causing wheezing, shortness of breath, coughing, and tightness in the chest.

LLM.text: A chronic inflammatory disorder of the airways characterized by recurrent episodes of wheezing, breathlessness, chest tightness, and cough. Airflow limitation is often reversible. It involves eosinophilic inflammation, mucus hypersecretion, and smooth muscle hypertrophy.

Harvard.text: Blurry vision caused by an irregular curve in the cornea of the eye.

LLM.text: A refractive error caused by an irregular curvature of the cornea or lens, resulting in light rays being focused at multiple points rather than a single point on the retina, leading to blurred or distorted vision at all distances.

Harvard.text: A substance that contracts skin tissues and shrinks pores.

LLM.text: A substance that contracts tissue and reduces secretions or minor bleeding.

Harvard.text: Showing no signs or symptoms of disease, whether or not disease is present.

LLM.text: Having a disease or abnormality without noticeable symptoms.

Harvard.text: The absence of electrical activity in the heart.

LLM.text: Complete cessation of cardiac electrical activity, presenting as a flat line on the ECG with no QRS complexes, P waves, or other organized electrical activity.

Harvard.text: Being unable to control movement; symptoms include shaking and an unsteady walk.

LLM.text: Lack of voluntary coordination of muscle movements, resulting from dysfunction of the cerebellum, posterior columns, or peripheral nerves. Types: cerebellar (gait and limb ataxia, dysarthria, nystagmus), sensory (impaired proprioception causing sensory ataxia, positive Romberg sign), and vestibular (vertigo, nystagmus, nausea).

Harvard.text: An abnormal build-up of fatty plaque inside an artery.

LLM.text: A localized accumulation of lipid, inflammatory cells, and fibrous tissue within an arterial wall, forming part of an atherosclerotic plaque.

Harvard.text: The buildup of fatty deposits (plaque) in the walls of arteries, causing narrowing and reduced blood flow; the disease responsible for most heart attacks and many strokes.

LLM.text: Chronic inflammatory disease of medium and large arteries characterized by accumulation of lipids, inflammatory cells, and fibrous tissue within the arterial wall, forming atherosclerotic plaques. Initiating event is endothelial dysfunction from risk factors (hypertension, smoking, diabetes, dyslipidemia).

Harvard.text: A mixture of fats, cholesterol, and other tissue that builds up on artery walls.

LLM.text: An atherosclerotic plaque is a lesion within the arterial intima composed of a necrotic lipid core covered by a fibrous cap, representing the pathological substrate of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease.

Harvard.text: A type of stroke that occurs when a large artery to the brain is completely blocked by the formation of a clot.

LLM.text: An ischemic stroke caused by thrombosis or artery-to-artery embolism arising from atherosclerotic disease in a large artery supplying the brain.

Harvard.text: A foot infection caused by fungus; symptoms include cracking and peeling skin and itchiness. Also known as tinea pedis.

LLM.text: A superficial fungal infection of the skin of the feet, usually caused by dermatophytes, producing scaling, fissures, itching, or maceration between the toes.

Harvard.text: Another name for the topmost vertebra of the neck, which lies just beneath the skull. Also called C-1.

LLM.text: First cervical vertebra articulating with occipital condyles at the atlanto-occipital joint for nodding movement. Lacks a body and spinous process; has anterior/posterior arches and lateral masses. Transverse foramina transmit vertebral arteries. The anterior arch has a facet for the axis dens.

common_names: topmost vertebra of the neck, which lies just beneath the skull

Harvard.text: Having an inherited predisposition to allergies.

LLM.text: Relating to an inherited or acquired tendency to develop allergic reactions such as eczema, allergic rhinitis, or asthma.

Harvard.text: A long-term skin condition, most common in babies and children, in which areas of the skin are dry, itchy, red, and may crack. Also known as eczema.

LLM.text: A chronic, relapsing inflammatory skin disease characterized by pruritus, xerosis, and eczematous lesions. It reflects epidermal-barrier dysfunction and immune dysregulation, with flares triggered by irritants, allergens, infection, stress, or climate.

Harvard.text: A seasonal or year-round allergy marked by sneezing, runny nose, and congestion.

LLM.text: Allergic inflammation of the nasal lining causing sneezing, itching, congestion, or discharge.

Harvard.text: The inherited tendency to develop allergies.

LLM.text: The genetic predisposition to develop immediate (IgE-mediated, type I) hypersensitivity reactions to common environmental allergens (pollen, dust mites, foods, pet dander).

Harvard.text: Abbreviation for adenosine triphosphate, an energy-storing molecule that is found in all human cells.

LLM.text: Adenosine triphosphate, the principal energy-transfer molecule in cells; hydrolysis of its phosphate bonds powers many cellular processes.

Harvard.text: The upper chambers of the heart. There are two of these—the right atrium and the left atrium.

LLM.text: The two upper chambers of the heart, which receive blood from the systemic and pulmonary veins and pass it to the ventricles.

Harvard.text: A disorder in which the two upper chambers of the heart beat fast and erratically. Because blood isn’t pumped out of these chambers fully, it may pool and form clots that could lead to a stroke.

LLM.text: The most common sustained cardiac arrhythmia, characterized by rapid, irregular atrial activity (350-600 bpm) with irregular ventricular response. ECG shows absent P waves, irregularly irregular RR intervals, and narrow QRS complexes (unless aberrant conduction).

Harvard.text: Also known as the AV node. A major part of the electrical system in the heart that acts as a gateway between the atria and the ventricles. An electrical signal generated by the sinoatrial node (the heart's natural pacemaker) moves through the heart until it reaches the atrioventricular node, a cluster of cells at the bottom of the right atrium. The AV node delays the signal before it is passed to the ventricles. This lets the atria fully contract before the ventricles contract.

LLM.text: Located in the posterior-inferior region of the interatrial septum near the coronary sinus. It receives impulses from the SA node via internodal pathways and delays them by approximately 120-200 milliseconds before transmitting them to the ventricles. This delay allows atrial contraction to complete before ventricular contraction.

Harvard.text: One of the heart's two upper chambers (the plural form is atria). The right atrium receives deoxygenated blood from the body; the left atrium receives oxygenated blood from the lungs.

LLM.text: One of the two upper chambers of the heart that receive blood returning to the heart. The right atrium receives deoxygenated blood from the superior and inferior venae cavae and the coronary sinus; the left atrium receives oxygenated blood from the four pulmonary veins.

Harvard.text: Wasting away of an organ or tissue due to undernourishment, disease, or aging.

LLM.text: Wasting or decrease in the size and function of a tissue, organ, or muscle.

Harvard.text: An overgrowth of abnormally shaped cells in areas of the breast that produce milk (lobules). atypical lobular hyperplasia is not cancerous but may become cancer.

LLM.text: A noninvasive breast lesion in which abnormal cells partially fill and expand lobules; it is benign but associated with an increased future risk of breast cancer.

Harvard.text: A chart that shows a person’s ability to hear at different pitches or frequencies.

LLM.text: A chart that shows a person’s ability to hear at different pitches or frequencies.

Harvard.text: A health professional who assesses hearing and fits hearing aids.

LLM.text: A health professional who assesses hearing and fits hearing aids.

Harvard.text: A complete hearing test that involves listening to sounds of different frequencies and volume.

LLM.text: Measurement of hearing sensitivity at different sound frequencies and intensities, usually using headphones or insert earphones.

Harvard.text: A nerve in the inner ear that transmits information about sound to the brain.

LLM.text: The portion of the vestibulocochlear nerve that carries hearing signals from the inner ear to the brain.

Harvard.text: Sensations such as chills, flashes of light, or a blind spot that come just before the occurrence of medical problems such as migraines or seizures.

LLM.text: A temporary sensory, visual, or other neurological symptom that may precede a migraine or seizure.

Harvard.text: Proteins created by the immune system that mistakenly target healthy cells, tissues, or organs.

LLM.text: Antibodies that mistakenly react with the body's own cells or tissues.

Harvard.text: A disease in which the immune system mistakenly identifies healthy tissues and organs as threats and responds by attacking and destroying them.

LLM.text: Autoimmune diseases result from loss of immunological self-tolerance, leading to immune-mediated attack on the body's own tissues.

Harvard.text: When the body’s immune system mistakenly views the body’s own tissues and organs as foreign invaders and attacks them.

LLM.text: An immune response directed against the body’s own cells, tissues, or molecules, which can cause autoimmune disease when persistent or damaging.

Harvard.text: Removal of fat from one part of the body to use as filler in another part, for example, to fill wrinkles and lines in the face and lips.

LLM.text: A procedure that removes a person's own fat from one body area and transfers it to another area for soft-tissue volume restoration or contouring.

Harvard.text: The part of the nervous system that controls involuntary actions, such as blood pressure or breathing. It also plays an important role in the fight or flight response to danger.

LLM.text: The part of the peripheral nervous system that regulates involuntary functions, including heart rate, vascular tone, digestion, sweating, pupil size, and bladder activity.

Harvard.text: Damage to the nerves that control involuntary body functions, such as digestion, heart rate, and bladder and bowel function.

LLM.text: Damage to nerves that control involuntary functions such as heart rate, blood pressure, digestion, sweating, bladder function, and sexual function. Diabetes is a common cause, but other diseases, toxins, and medicines may contribute. Symptoms depend on the affected organs and require evaluation of the underlying cause.

Harvard.text: Surgically opening and examining a body after death to see if any diseases are present and to determine the cause of death.

LLM.text: A postmortem examination of a body to determine cause and manner of death, performed by a forensic pathologist (medical examiner/coroner) or, for hospital autopsies, a pathologist.

Harvard.text: Abbreviation for atrioventricular node, a major part of the electrical system in the heart that acts as a gateway between the atria and the ventricles. An electrical signal generated by the sinoatrial node (the heart's natural pacemaker) moves through the heart until it reaches the atrioventricular node, a cluster of cells at the bottom of the right atrium. The AV node delays the signal before it is passed to the ventricles. This lets the atria fully contract before the ventricles contract.

LLM.text: A specialized group of cardiac cells that delays and then conducts electrical impulses from the atria to the ventricles.

Harvard.text: The tearing away of one part of the body from another—for example, a tendon tearing away from a bone.

LLM.text: An injury in which tissue is forcibly torn from the body by shearing or pulling. Common forms include dental, fingertip, nail, and degloving avulsions. Management focuses on hemorrhage control, debridement, tissue preservation, and urgent consultation.

Harvard.text: The armpit.

LLM.text: Relating to the armpit or to structures located in the axilla, including axillary lymph nodes and vessels.

Harvard.text: The second vertebra of the neck (from the skull); also called the C-2 vertebra.

LLM.text: Second cervical vertebra with the dens (odontoid process) projecting superiorly, serving as a pivot for atlas rotation, allowing approximately 50 percent of cervical rotation. Has a large spinous process and flat superior articular facets.

Harvard.text: The long, slender extension of a nerve cell that conducts electrical impulses away from the nerve's cell body and on to nearby nerves.

LLM.text: The single long process of a neuron that conducts action potentials away from the cell body toward the axon terminal for synaptic transmission.

Harvard.text: The end of an axon.

LLM.text: The end of a nerve-cell axon that releases chemical messengers to communicate with another cell.

Harvard.text: White blood cells that come from bone marrow, and produce antibodies to fight off disease.

LLM.text: A lymphocyte that develops in the bone marrow and can differentiate into antibody-producing plasma cells or memory B cells after activation.

Harvard.text: Tiny single-celled organisms. Some bacteria cause disease, although most are harmless.

LLM.text: Single-celled microscopic organisms lacking a nucleus, which can exist independently or in colonies; some are beneficial to health (microbiome) while others cause infectious disease.

Harvard.text: Ability to maintain equilibrium while stationary or moving.

LLM.text: The ability to maintain the body's center of mass over its base of support, relying on input from the vestibular system, vision, and proprioception. It is essential for walking, standing, and performing daily activities without falling. Age-related decline, medications, and neurological disorders can impair balance, increasing fall risk.

Harvard.text: A procedure to open clogged heart arteries. A surgeon inserts and inflates a tiny balloon. It widens the blocked artery then expands a small wire mesh tube to keep the artery open.

LLM.text: A procedure that uses an inflatable balloon catheter to widen a narrowed artery, often followed by stent placement.

Harvard.text: A surgical procedure to open a narrowed vessel or tube, such as the urethra, esophagus, or artery. A small, deflated balloon is inserted into the area and inflated to widen it.

LLM.text: A procedure that widens a narrowed body passage or vessel by inflating a balloon at the affected site.

Harvard.text: One of several types of weight loss surgery performed on people who are dangerously overweight, to restrict or reduce food intake and/or absorption.

LLM.text: Weight loss procedures and surgery, collectively known as bariatric surgery, are invasive interventions for severe obesity that produce substantial and sustained weight loss by altering gastrointestinal anatomy and physiology.

Harvard.text: An imaging test that allows doctors to see the inside of the esophagus and upper stomach. It involves swallowing a barium solution, which coats the esophagus and makes it possible for x-rays to see the inside of the intestine.

LLM.text: X-ray imaging using barium sulfate contrast. Barium swallow, barium enema, upper GI series. Evaluates GI tract morphology and function.

Harvard.text: The abnormal growth of stomach or small intestine cells in the esophagus, resulting from damage caused by the reflux of stomach acid; occasionally may transform into cancer.

LLM.text: A change in the lower esophageal lining caused by chronic reflux and associated with an increased risk of esophageal adenocarcinoma.

Harvard.text: The most common skin cancer. Basal cell carcinoma doesn’t spread to internal organs.

LLM.text: The most common malignant skin tumor, arising from basal keratinocyte-lineage cells and associated with cumulative ultraviolet exposure and Hedgehog-pathway abnormalities. It commonly presents as a pearly papule or nodule with telangiectasia, ulceration, or a rolled border.

Harvard.text: Clusters of nerve cells deep in the brain that play an important role in movement.

LLM.text: Deep gray matter nuclei in the cerebral hemispheres for motor control, cognition, and emotion. Key structures: caudate nucleus, putamen, globus pallidus (internal/external segments), subthalamic nucleus, substantia nigra. Direct pathway facilitates movement; indirect inhibits it.

Harvard.text: An electrocardiogram (EKG) tracing taken in a healthy individual for later comparison to subsequent EKGs.

LLM.text: An electrocardiogram obtained for comparison with later tracings or before a treatment, procedure, or change in clinical status.

Harvard.text: The artery that supplies blood to the cerebellum, the brainstem, and the back of the brain.

LLM.text: The artery formed by the union of the vertebral arteries that supplies the brainstem, cerebellum, and posterior brain.

Harvard.text: Harmless; often used to refer to a tumor that is not cancerous and does not usually spread.

LLM.text: Not malignant and not expected to invade nearby tissue or spread to distant sites, although a benign lesion can still cause problems because of its size or location.

Harvard.text: A severe headache that occurs when orgasm is reached.

LLM.text: A sudden severe headache occurring during sexual activity or at orgasm after dangerous secondary causes have been excluded.

Harvard.text: A noncancerous enlargement of the prostate gland that obstructs the flow of urine. Often called BPH.

LLM.text: Noncancerous enlargement of the prostate that may obstruct urine flow and cause hesitancy, weak stream, urgency, frequency, nocturia, or incomplete emptying. Assessment uses the symptoms, examination, and selected tests.

Harvard.text: Anti-anxiety medications that work by helping to maintain levels of the neurotransmitter gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) in the brain.

LLM.text: A class of drugs that enhance the effect of the inhibitory neurotransmitter gamma-aminobutyric acid at the GABA-A receptor, increasing the frequency of chloride channel opening and producing anxiolytic, sedative, anticonvulsant, and muscle relaxant effects.

Harvard.text: The period of grief and mourning after a death.

LLM.text: Natural grief response to the death of a loved one, marked by sadness, yearning, and preoccupation with the deceased, experienced in waves that diminish over weeks to months with preserved self-esteem. Distinct from major depression by its wave-like quality and preserved self-worth.

Harvard.text: A nervous system or heart disorder caused by lack of the vitamin thiamine (B1).

LLM.text: A nutritional deficiency disease caused by inadequate thiamine (vitamin B1), occurring in two forms. Wet beriberi presents with high-output heart failure, peripheral vasodilation, edema, and tachycardia due to impaired cardiac energy metabolism.

Harvard.text: A test to try to reproduce heartburn symptoms; used by doctors to diagnose GERD (gastroesophageal reflux disease).

LLM.text: A historical provocative test in which acid is introduced into the esophagus to reproduce heartburn symptoms; it has largely been replaced by more direct evaluation of reflux.

Harvard.text: A class of drugs that slow the heartbeat, lessen the force of each contraction, and reduce the contraction of blood vessels in the heart, brain, and throughout the body by blocking the action of beta-adrenergic substances such as adrenaline (epinephrine) at the beta receptor. Beta blockers, also known as beta adrenergic blocking agents, are used to treat many cardiovascular conditions, including abnormal heart rhythms, angina, and high blood pressure. They also improve survival after a heart attack.

LLM.text: A class of medications that block the effects of adrenaline on the body's beta receptors. They slow down the heart rate and reduce blood pressure, making them widely used for treating heart conditions, high blood pressure, and anxiety.

common_names: beta adrenergic blocking agents, are used to treat many cardiovascular conditions, including abnormal heart rhythms, angina, and high blood pressure

Harvard.text: A richly colored compound (red, yellow, or orange) found in many plants, fruits, and vegetables that the body can convert into vitamin A.

LLM.text: A carotenoid pigment found in plants that can be converted by the body into vitamin A.

Harvard.text: Cells that make and secrete insulin; located in the islets of Langerhans of the pancreas.

LLM.text: Pancreatic cells that produce and release insulin.

Harvard.text: A medication that opens airways by relaxing the muscles around the airway; used to treat asthma or COPD (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease).

LLM.text: Drugs that activate beta-adrenergic receptors, producing effects such as relaxation of airway smooth muscle or increased cardiac stimulation depending on receptor selectivity.

Harvard.text: An abnormal protein deposited in the brain in Alzheimer’s disease.

LLM.text: Peptides generated from amyloid precursor protein that can accumulate as plaques in the brain in Alzheimer disease.

Harvard.text: Medications that stop the liver from making excess glucose (sugar) and improve sensitivity to insulin.

LLM.text: A class of glucose-lowering medicines that reduce hepatic glucose production and improve insulin sensitivity; metformin is the principal example.

Harvard.text: A thick, yellow-green fluid produced by the liver that aids in digestion.

LLM.text: A fluid produced by the liver that helps digest and absorb dietary fats.

Harvard.text: Fatty substances made by the gallbladder that aid in digestion.

LLM.text: Substances produced by the liver that aid digestion and absorption of fats and fat-soluble vitamins. They are also measured when a hepatobiliary disorder, including intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy, is suspected.

Harvard.text: A machine that helps people get more air into their lungs when sleeping by increasing the pressure or force of air when breathing in; often used to treat sleep apnea.

LLM.text: Noninvasive ventilation that provides different pressures during inhalation and exhalation to support breathing.

Harvard.text: Heavy bouts of drinking interspersed with periods of abstinence; often refers to the consumption of five or more alcoholic beverages within one day.

LLM.text: A pattern of consuming enough alcohol over a short period to produce a high blood alcohol concentration and increased risk of injury or acute toxicity.

Harvard.text: The ability of both eyes to focus on an object and form a single visual image.

LLM.text: Vision that uses both eyes together to produce a single image and support depth perception.

Harvard.text: A type of dementia caused when blood flow is interrupted to the white matter of the brain, which lies beneath the cerebral cortex.

LLM.text: A form of vascular cognitive impairment caused by diffuse small-vessel disease affecting the brain's deep white matter.

Harvard.text: How quickly and completely the body can absorb and use a nutrient.

LLM.text: The fraction of an administered drug that reaches the systemic circulation in its unchanged active form. It is expressed as a percentage and is determined by the route of administration and the extent of first-pass metabolism. For intravenous administration, bioavailability is 100 percent by definition.

Harvard.text: A natural compound found in soybeans that may help prevent cancer from spreading. It is a type of flavonoid.

LLM.text: A naturally occurring isoflavone found mainly in legumes and other plants. It is studied for biologic effects but is not established as a treatment for disease.
