Harvard.text: Usually used regarding prostate cancer. It refers to a post-treatment increase in the level of prostate-specific antigen in the bloodstream, indicating that prostate cancer has recurred or spread following the original treatment. Also called biochemical failure.

LLM.text: A rise in a disease-specific laboratory marker after treatment, suggesting recurrent or persistent disease before clinical or imaging findings become apparent.

Harvard.text: An treatment that helps people learn to gain control over normally unconscious body functions, such as breathing and heart rates.

LLM.text: A technique that provides information about a physiological process, such as muscle activity, heart rate, or breathing, to help a person learn voluntary control of it.

Harvard.text: Normal fluctuations over time in the levels of a substance being measured (such as cholesterol).

LLM.text: Natural variation in a measured biologic quantity within the same person over time or between people, independent of measurement error.

Harvard.text: A distinctive biological indicator of an event, process, or condition.

LLM.text: Measurable indicator of disease. Cancer biomarkers: diagnostic, prognostic, predictive.

Harvard.text: The removal of a small piece of tissue from the body for examination under a microscope.

LLM.text: Removal of tissue for histological examination to diagnose disease. Types: needle biopsy (fine needle aspiration, core needle), excisional, incisional, punch, endoscopic. Sites: breast, lung, liver, lymph node, bone marrow. Complications: bleeding, infection, seeding (rare).

Harvard.text: Medications, including alendronate and etidronate, used to prevent and treat osteoporosis by slowing the breakdown of bone.

LLM.text: A medicine that reduces bone breakdown and is used to prevent or treat osteoporosis and some other bone disorders.

Harvard.text: An episode of temporary memory loss resulting from the ingestion of alcohol or other drugs.

LLM.text: A period of partial or complete memory loss, commonly associated with alcohol or other causes of impaired consciousness.

Harvard.text: Where the bladder and urethra meet.

LLM.text: The narrow lower part of the urinary bladder where it connects to the urethra and contributes to urinary continence.

Harvard.text: Cosmetic surgery to improve the appearance of droopy eyelids by removing excess skin and fat.

LLM.text: Surgical reconstruction or reshaping of the eyelids, often involving removal or repositioning of excess skin, muscle, or orbital fat. It may be functional, cosmetic, or reconstructive.

Harvard.text: A small pocket of fluid that develops between the upper layers of skin; often caused by friction or burns.

LLM.text: A fluid-filled elevation between or within layers of skin or mucosa, caused by friction, burns, infection, allergy, or an autoimmune blistering disorder.

Harvard.text: Substance that prevents a biological activity or process.

LLM.text: A substance that prevents or reduces a biologic process by blocking a receptor, channel, enzyme, or other target.

Harvard.text: A measure of the amount of alcohol in the blood.

LLM.text: The concentration of ethanol in blood, commonly expressed as mass per volume or as a percentage. Interpretation depends on sampling, timing, metabolism, tolerance, co-ingestants, and local standards; clinical impairment cannot be inferred from a single value without context.

Harvard.text: A coagulated mass that occurs when blood cells stick together and form a solid.

LLM.text: A mass of coagulated blood within a blood vessel or body cavity. A clot may be protective when it stops bleeding, but an abnormal thrombus can obstruct blood flow or embolize to the lungs, brain, heart, or other organs.

Harvard.text: The force blood exerts against the walls of the arteries. Optimal blood pressure is less than 120/80 mm Hg.

LLM.text: The force exerted by blood against arterial walls, measured in millimeters of mercury (mmHg). Systolic pressure (peak during ventricular ejection, normally approximately 120 mmHg) and diastolic pressure (minimum during ventricular relaxation, normally approximately 80 mmHg).

Harvard.text: A test that measures levels of urea in the blood to assess how well the kidneys are functioning.

LLM.text: A blood test that measures urea nitrogen and helps assess kidney function and hydration.

Harvard.text: Hollow tubes that transport blood throughout the body; includes arteries, veins, and capillaries.

LLM.text: Tubular structures that transport blood through the body, including arteries, arterioles, capillaries, venules, and veins.

Harvard.text: Abbreviation for bone mineral density, the amount of mineralized bone tissue in a given area.

LLM.text: A measurement of bone mineral content adjusted for area, used to assess bone strength and help diagnose osteoporosis.

Harvard.text: Abbreviation for body-mass index, a measure of body fat estimated from a person’s height and weight. A healthy BMI is defined as 18.5 to 24.9. BMI = weight (in kilograms) divided by height (in meters) squared. Using English units, multiply weight in pounds by 703, then divide the result by height in inches, and divide that result by height in inches.

LLM.text: A weight-to-height index calculated as weight in kilograms divided by height in meters squared. It is used as a population-level measure related to body size, not as a complete individual health assessment.

Harvard.text: A measure of body fat estimated from a person’s height and weight. A healthy BMI is defined as 18.5 to 24.9. BMI = weight (in kilograms) divided by height (in meters) squared. Using English units, multiply weight in pounds by 703, then divide the result by height in inches, and divide that result by height in inches.

LLM.text: A weight-to-height index calculated as weight in kilograms divided by height in meters squared. It is used to classify weight categories in populations and clinical screening.

Harvard.text: A soft mass of chewed food. Alternatively, a single large dose of a medication given intravenously.

LLM.text: A discrete amount of medication or fluid given over a short period, usually by injection or infusion. In digestion, a bolus is chewed food ready to be swallowed.

Harvard.text: The total amount of bone tissue in the body.

LLM.text: The amount of mineralized bone tissue in the skeleton or in a specified region.

Harvard.text: The amount of mineralized bone tissue in a given area.

LLM.text: The concentration of mineral in bone, usually measured by dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry to assess fracture risk and osteoporosis.

Harvard.text: A test in which radioactive material is injected into a person's bloodstream to help produce images of bones; often used to detect cancer or bone diseases.

LLM.text: Skeletal imaging using Tc-99m MDP. Detects osteoblastic activity. Sensitivity: high; specificity: low. Used for metastasis detection, fracture, infection, metabolic bone disease. "Hot spots" indicate increased uptake; "cold spots" indicate decreased uptake.

Harvard.text: Stomach growling; the rumbling noises caused by gas moving through the intestine.

LLM.text: Rumbling or gurgling sounds produced by the movement of gas and fluid through the intestines. They may be normal or altered in gastrointestinal obstruction and other disorders.

Harvard.text: Brand name for a drug made of botulinum toxin type A that is injected into muscles and weakens them to ease the appearance of wrinkles.

LLM.text: A purified preparation of botulinum neurotoxin used by injection to temporarily block acetylcholine release and reduce muscle contraction or glandular secretion; it has medical and cosmetic uses.

Harvard.text: Hard, bony growths that form on the middle joints of fingers in people with osteoarthritis.

LLM.text: Firm bony enlargements of the proximal interphalangeal finger joints, usually caused by osteoarthritis.

Harvard.text: The small or large intestine.

LLM.text: The small and large intestines, which receive digested food, absorb nutrients and water, and form and transport stool.

Harvard.text: Abbreviation for benign prostatic hyperplasia, a noncancerous enlargement of the prostate gland that obstructs the flow of urine.

LLM.text: Abbreviation for benign prostatic hyperplasia, a noncancerous enlargement of the prostate that may obstruct urine flow.

Harvard.text: A network of nerves that are rooted at the cervical spine and provide sensation and movement to the shoulder and arm.

LLM.text: Nerve network (C5-T1) formed by roots, trunks, divisions, and cords, giving rise to upper limb nerves. Roots unite into superior/middle/inferior trunks, dividing into anterior/posterior divisions, recombining into lateral/posterior/medial cords. Major branches: musculocutaneous, axillary, radial, median, ulnar.

Harvard.text: Treatment in which a surgeon implants seeds or pellets of radioactive material in the body to destroy cancer cells.

LLM.text: Radiation treatment in which a radioactive source is placed inside or near a tumor to deliver a concentrated dose.

Harvard.text: A slow heart rate, usually below 60 beats per minute.

LLM.text: A heart rate <60 beats per minute. May be physiologic (athletes) or pathologic due to sinus node dysfunction, AV block, or medication effects. Symptomatic bradycardia causes fatigue, dizziness, syncope, or heart failure. Evaluation includes ECG, Holter monitoring, and assessment of reversible causes.

Harvard.text: Technologies that allow doctors to view the structure of the brain or see how different parts of the brain function; examples include computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), functional MRI (fMRI), and positron emission tomography (PET).

LLM.text: Medical imaging used to examine brain structure or function, including CT, MRI, vascular imaging, and selected nuclear medicine techniques.

Harvard.text: The part of the brain that connects the brain with the spinal cord and controls movement, sensation, and reflexes.

LLM.text: The lower part of the brain connecting the cerebrum with the spinal cord and controlling essential functions such as breathing and consciousness.

Harvard.text: Electrical impulses generated by the firing of nerve cells in the brain (neurons).

LLM.text: Electrical activity generated by the coordinated firing of neurons and recorded by electroencephalography.

Harvard.text: Cosmetic surgery to increase the size of the breasts.

LLM.text: Surgery or another procedure intended to increase breast volume or alter breast shape, commonly using an implant or transferred tissue.

Harvard.text: A form of meditation aimed at bringing on a state of relaxation.

LLM.text: A mindfulness or relaxation practice that uses attention to breathing to stabilize awareness and reduce physiological or emotional arousal.

Harvard.text: The part of the brain (in the frontal lobe of the left hemisphere) responsible for language comprehension and speech.

LLM.text: A language-related region of the dominant inferior frontal gyrus involved in speech production, language formulation, and aspects of syntax. Lesions may cause expressive aphasia.

Harvard.text: The airways that connect the lungs to the trachea (windpipe) and allow air to pass into and out of the lungs.

LLM.text: The right and left main bronchi and their branches that conduct air from the trachea into the lungs.

Harvard.text: A small airway in the respiratory system that connects to the alveoli (air sacs); a branch of the bronchial tubes.

LLM.text: Small airways (less than 2 mm diameter) without cartilage, branching from segmental bronchi to terminal bronchioles (conducting zone) to respiratory bronchioles (transitional, alveoli bud from walls) to alveolar ducts to alveolar sacs to alveoli.

Harvard.text: Medication that eases breathing by relaxing the muscles surrounding the bronchial tubes.

LLM.text: A medicine that relaxes airway muscle and widens the airways to improve breathing.

Harvard.text: Unusual sound, heard through a stethoscope, that blood makes when it rushes past an obstruction, like a blockage in an artery.

LLM.text: An abnormal sound heard over a blood vessel, usually with a stethoscope, caused by turbulent blood flow.

Harvard.text: A bump of bone or tissue that forms at the big toe joint, causing inflammation and considerable pain.

LLM.text: A bony prominence (exostosis) at the medial aspect of the first metatarsal head, causing lateral deviation of the great toe (hallux valgus). The deformity is characterized by a structural abnormality at the first metatarsophalangeal joint, with the first metatarsal deviating medially and the proximal phalanx deviating laterally.

Harvard.text: A small, painful bony bump that forms on the outside of the foot, at the base of the small toe.

LLM.text: A painful prominence at the outer side of the fifth metatarsophalangeal joint, often associated with footwear pressure or altered foot mechanics.

Harvard.text: A protective, fluid-filled sac located in or near the joints that cushions the movement of bone against tendons, skin, and muscle.

LLM.text: A small fluid-filled sac that reduces friction between moving tissues near a joint.

Harvard.text: Pain and swelling of the bursa, the small fluid filled pads that act as cushions in or near the joints.

LLM.text: Inflammation of a bursa, a fluid-filled sac that reduces friction between tendons, muscles, bones, and skin. Bursae are lined by synovial cells and normally contain a thin layer of lubricating synovial fluid.

Harvard.text: A procedure used to divert the flow of blood or other fluids. When referring to the heart, shorthand for coronary artery bypass surgery, used to divert blood flow around a blocked coronary artery.

LLM.text: Surgical creation of alternative route around blocked vessel. Uses vein or prosthetic graft.

Harvard.text: Abbreviation for coronary artery bypass graft. Surgery to improve blood flow to the heart by diverting blood around a blocked artery.

LLM.text: Coronary artery bypass grafting, a surgical procedure that creates a route around a narrowed or blocked coronary artery to improve blood flow to heart muscle.

Harvard.text: The buildup of calcium deposits in soft tissue, causing it to harden. Often seen in breast tissue by mammography or in coronary arteries by x-ray or cardiac CT scans.

LLM.text: Calcification is abnormal deposition of calcium salts in tissue; its significance depends on the site, pattern, underlying injury, and associated disease. calcium or phosphate metabolism is abnormal.

Harvard.text: A hormone that can stimulate bone growth and is sometimes used to treat osteoporosis.

LLM.text: A 32-amino-acid peptide hormone secreted by the parafollicular C-cells of the thyroid gland in response to elevated serum calcium. It lowers blood calcium by inhibiting osteoclast-mediated bone resorption and increasing renal calcium excretion.

Harvard.text: A mineral that the body needs for many vital functions, including bone formation, regulation of heart rate and blood pressure, and muscle contraction.

LLM.text: A mineral and intracellular second messenger required for bone mineralization, muscle contraction, neurotransmitter release, blood coagulation, and enzyme regulation. Plasma calcium is present as ionized, protein-bound, and complexed fractions.

Harvard.text: A class of drugs that lowers blood pressure, slows the heart rate, and decreases the heart's need for oxygen by blocking the movement of calcium into the heart and the muscle cells surrounding blood vessels.

LLM.text: Agents that block L-type calcium channels, reducing calcium influx into cardiac and smooth muscle cells. Dihydropyridines (amlodipine, nifedipine) cause vasodilation and are used for hypertension and angina.

Harvard.text: Hardened, thick skin that forms after repeated friction; often found on hands and the bottom of feet.

LLM.text: A localized area of thickened, hardened skin caused by repeated pressure or friction.

Harvard.text: The unit for measuring the amount of energy in food.

LLM.text: A unit of energy measurement used in nutrition to quantify the energy content of foods and energy expenditure of the body. One kilocalorie (kcal, commonly called a Calorie with capital C) equals the energy required to raise 1 kilogram of water by 1 degree Celsius.

Harvard.text: One of two types of tissue that form bone; this type is commonly found at the center of long bones and makes up a large part of the hip and spine. Also known as trabecular bone.

LLM.text: Porous, trabecular bone found inside many bones, especially near joints and in the vertebrae.

Harvard.text: A group of diseases in which abnormal cells grow in an uncontrolled way, sometimes forming tumors.

LLM.text: Cancer is uncontrolled growth of abnormal cells that can invade nearby tissue and spread to distant organs; behavior and treatment depend on its tissue of origin and molecular features. or spread to distant sites. Cancer may arise in any tissue and is classified by its site and cell type. Early detection and treatment improve outcomes.

Harvard.text: The body’s smallest blood vessels; they deliver oxygen and nutrients to tissues.

LLM.text: The smallest blood vessels, where oxygen, nutrients, and waste products move between blood and tissues.

Harvard.text: An chemical found in hot chili peppers that is used in some pain relief creams.

LLM.text: A compound from chili peppers used in some topical medicines to reduce certain types of pain.

Harvard.text: The sugars and starches in food that provide the body with most of its fuel. Carbohydrates are one of three primary nutrients along with fats and proteins.

LLM.text: A class of organic compounds composed of carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen (general formula Cm(H2O)n), serving as the primary energy source for the body.

Harvard.text: Keeping track of the grams of carbohydrates eaten in order to control weight.

LLM.text: Method for diabetes management. Matching insulin to carbohydrate intake. Education essential.

Harvard.text: An odorless, colorless gas that is toxic to humans and animals at high levels; it is produced by cars, furnaces, fireplaces, and other equipment powered by combustion.

LLM.text: A colorless, odorless gas that can prevent blood from carrying oxygen and cause life-threatening poisoning.

Harvard.text: Any substance that can cause cancer.

LLM.text: Substance causing cancer. Types: chemical (benzene, asbestos, aflatoxin), physical (radiation), biological (HPV, HBV, HCV). Mechanisms: DNA damage, mutations, epigenetic changes. IARC classifications: Group 1 (carcinogenic), Group 2A (probably carcinogenic), Group 2B (possibly carcinogenic), Group 3 (not classifiable).

Harvard.text: The process by which a normal cell becomes cancerous.

LLM.text: The process by which normal cells acquire changes that lead to cancer.

Harvard.text: A cancerous tumor that develops in the tissue that lines the organs of the body (the epithelium).

LLM.text: Malignant tumor of epithelial origin. Types: squamous cell carcinoma, adenocarcinoma, basal cell carcinoma, transitional cell carcinoma. Most common cancer type ( 80-90\% of malignancies). Examples: lung carcinoma, breast carcinoma, colon carcinoma.

Harvard.text: Pertaining to the heart.

LLM.text: Relating to the heart.

Harvard.text: The sudden cessation of contractions capable of circulating blood to the body and brain. Also called sudden cardiac arrest. Cardiac arrest usually occurs as a result of a rapid ventricular rhythm (ventricular tachycardia) or a chaotic one (ventricular fibrillation). Death occurs within minutes unless cardiopulmonary resuscitation and defibrillation are available.

LLM.text: Sudden loss of effective heart pumping, causing unresponsiveness, absent normal breathing, and no detectable pulse. Initial rhythms may be shockable or nonshockable; treatment requires immediate cardiopulmonary resuscitation, defibrillation when indicated, and advanced resuscitation care.

Harvard.text: A procedure to diagnose or treat heart problems; a long, thin, flexible tube is inserted into a blood vessel in the arm, neck, or upper thigh and maneuvered into the heart to evaluate various heart functions.

LLM.text: Invasive procedure involving insertion of catheters into the heart via peripheral arteries or veins. Diagnostic catheterization measures intracardiac pressures, saturations, and performs coronary angiography. Indications include evaluation of CAD, valvular disease, cardiomyopathy, and congenital heart disease.

Harvard.text: Heart-muscle cells.

LLM.text: Muscle cells of the heart that generate force for cardiac contraction.

Harvard.text: The amount of blood the heart is able to pump into circulation; specifically measured as the amount of blood the left side of the heart can pump in one minute.

LLM.text: The volume of blood pumped by the heart per minute, calculated as the heart rate multiplied by the stroke volume.

Harvard.text: A pacemaker-based therapy for heart failure that improves the heart's pumping efficiency by coordinating (resynchronizing) the beat of the ventricles.

LLM.text: Biventricular pacing that synchronizes contraction of the left and right ventricles in patients with heart failure, reduced EF, and prolonged QRS duration (especially LBBB). CRT improves symptoms, exercise capacity, and quality of life, and reduces heart failure hospitalizations and mortality.

Harvard.text: When fluid or blood pools within the sac surrounding the heart, squeezing the heart and interfering with its ability to pump.

LLM.text: Cardiac tamponade occurs when fluid or blood under pressure around the heart restricts filling, reducing cardiac output and potentially causing obstructive shock. and causing reduced circulation. It is a medical emergency.

Harvard.text: Temporarily stopping the heart during heart surgery.

LLM.text: Deliberate temporary arrest and protection of the heart during cardiac surgery, usually achieved with a cold or blood-based solution that alters myocardial electrical and metabolic activity.

Harvard.text: Pertaining to the heart and lungs.

LLM.text: Relating to the heart and lungs or to their combined function.

Harvard.text: The use of a machine (heart/lung machine) to circulate and oxygenate the blood while surgery is performed on the heart.

LLM.text: A technique that temporarily circulates and oxygenates blood during some heart operations.

Harvard.text: A pump used to oxygenate and circulate blood through the body while the heart is stopped during open-heart surgery.

LLM.text: A machine that temporarily circulates and oxygenates blood during selected heart or major-vessel operations while the heart and lungs are not performing their usual functions.

Harvard.text: A combination of chest compressions and mouth-to-mouth breathing that keep oxygenated blood circulating to the brain and tissues. Commonly known as CPR.

LLM.text: A sequence of chest compressions, ventilation, defibrillation when indicated, and advanced life-support interventions for cardiac arrest. Its purpose is to maintain circulation and oxygen delivery until spontaneous circulation is restored or definitive treatment is provided.

Harvard.text: A component of physical fitness that relates to the ability of the circulatory and respiratory systems to supply oxygen during sustained physical activity. Also known as cardiorespiratory fitness.

LLM.text: The ability of the heart, lungs, and circulation to deliver oxygen during sustained physical activity.

Harvard.text: Pertaining to the heart and blood vessels.

LLM.text: Relating to the heart and blood vessels, including circulation, blood pressure, and diseases of the cardiac or vascular system.

Harvard.text: The use of an electrical shock to stop an abnormal heart rhythm (an arrhythmia) and restore a normal one (sinus rhythm). Cardioversion can be external, using pads applied to the chest, or internal, from a pacemaker-like device called an implantable cardioverter defibrillator (ICD).

LLM.text: Existing or occurring at the same time as another condition, treatment, or event.

Harvard.text: An herb said to expel gas from the digestive system, easing stomach discomfort.

LLM.text: A substance traditionally used to reduce intestinal gas or discomfort by promoting passage of gas through the digestive tract.

Harvard.text: Compounds such as lycopene and beta carotene that give red, yellow, and orange color to certain plants.

LLM.text: Plant pigments, including beta-carotene, that contribute yellow, orange, or red color and may have antioxidant or provitamin-A activity.

Harvard.text: One of two major blood vessels found on either side of the neck. The carotid arteries supply blood to the brain.

LLM.text: The paired arterial system supplying the head and neck. Each common carotid artery divides into internal and external carotid arteries; the internal carotid supplies the brain and orbit, while the external carotid supplies most external head and neck structures.

Harvard.text: Narrowing of the carotid artery by the buildup of plaque. Sometimes called carotid artery stenosis. It is a major risk factor for ischemic stroke.

LLM.text: Narrowing or blockage of the carotid arteries, most often caused by atherosclerotic plaque. It can reduce cerebral blood flow or release emboli and is an important cause of transient ischemic attack and ischemic stroke.

Harvard.text: An abnormal sound heard with a stethoscope in the carotid artery; people who have carotid bruits have a greater risk of having a stroke.

LLM.text: An audible sound over a carotid artery caused by turbulent blood flow. It may occur with carotid atherosclerosis but does not reliably indicate the severity of stenosis; suspected disease is assessed with appropriate vascular imaging and risk evaluation.

Harvard.text: An ultrasound image of the carotid arteries.

LLM.text: An ultrasound examination that assesses the structure and blood flow of the carotid arteries.

Harvard.text: Surgery to remove fatty plaque buildup from the carotid artery and restore blood flow to the brain.

LLM.text: Surgical removal of atherosclerotic plaque from a carotid artery to reduce stroke risk in selected patients. Suitability depends on symptoms, degree of narrowing, operative risk, life expectancy, and current clinical guidance.

Harvard.text: A condition that occurs when the median nerve, which runs from the forearm through the hand, is compressed; symptoms include pain, tingling, and numbness, as well as hand weakness.

LLM.text: The most common entrapment neuropathy, caused by compression of the median nerve as it passes through the carpal tunnel, a narrow fibro-osseous canal bounded by the carpal bones and the flexor retinaculum (transverse carpal ligament) at the wrist.

Harvard.text: Stiff connective tissue that provides support to other tissues and cushions joints.

LLM.text: A tough, flexible avascular connective tissue found in joints, the ear, nose, rib cage, and intervertebral discs. Composed of chondrocytes embedded in an extracellular matrix of collagen fibers, proteoglycans, and water, providing resilience and compressive strength.

Harvard.text: A joint in which the bones are firmly connected by cartilage, so that only slight movement is possible.

LLM.text: A joint in which bones are connected by cartilage and allow limited movement.

Harvard.text: A research study that compares one group of people with a particular disease to a very similar group that does not have the same disease.

LLM.text: Observational study comparing cases with disease to controls without. Looks back at exposures.

Harvard.text: The transition phase of the hair-growth cycle.

LLM.text: The transitional phase of the hair-growth cycle between active growth and resting.

Harvard.text: Sudden paralysis of some or all muscles brought on by laughter, anger, fright, or strong emotions; a hallmark of narcolepsy.

LLM.text: Sudden temporary loss of muscle tone triggered by strong emotion, commonly associated with narcolepsy.

Harvard.text: A clouding or fogging of the lens of the eye that may blur or tint vision.

LLM.text: A cataract is an opacity or clouding of the crystalline lens that impairs the transmission of light to the retina, resulting in blurred vision, glare, decreased contrast sensitivity, and progressive vision loss, and it is the leading cause of preventable blindness worldwide.

Harvard.text: A strong emotional reaction to a minor event.

LLM.text: A disproportionately intense emotional or behavioral response to a situation that may appear minor to others, often occurring with cognitive impairment or neurologic disease.

Harvard.text: An agent with a strong laxative effect.

LLM.text: An agent that promotes bowel evacuation, usually by increasing stool water, intestinal motility, or both.

Harvard.text: A thin tube that is inserted into the body to provide or drain fluids, or to carry tiny surgical instruments and cameras in minimally invasive surgeries.

LLM.text: Flexible tube for drainage or infusion. Types: urinary (Foley), intravenous, central venous, arterial. Materials: silicone, latex, PVC.

Harvard.text: A positively charged ion; cations in the body include sodium, potassium, and magnesium.

LLM.text: An ion with a positive electrical charge, such as sodium, potassium, calcium, or hydrogen.

Harvard.text: A bundles of nerve roots that look like a horse’s tail, located at the end of the spinal cord.

LLM.text: The bundle of lumbar, sacral, and coccygeal nerve roots below the end of the spinal cord.

Harvard.text: Intense, long-lasting burning pain usually caused by damage to a peripheral nerve.

LLM.text: Severe persistent burning pain and sensory disturbance caused by injury to a peripheral nerve, now commonly classified within complex regional pain syndrome type II.

Harvard.text: A hole in the tooth caused by advanced decay.

LLM.text: A localized hole or structural defect in a tooth caused by dental caries.

Harvard.text: Abbreviation for complete blood count—tests run on a blood sample to provide information on red cells, white cells, and platelets.

LLM.text: A blood test that measures red cells, white cells, hemoglobin, hematocrit, and platelets.

Harvard.text: Abbreviation for coronary care unit, a ward in a hospital that provides specialized care and extensive monitoring for patients with heart problems.

LLM.text: A hospital unit providing continuous monitoring and specialized treatment for people with serious acute cardiac disease.

Harvard.text: A disease characterized by damage to the small intestine caused by an oversensitivity to gluten, a protein found in wheat, rye, and barley. Celiac disease can interfere with the proper absorption of nutrients from food.

LLM.text: An immune-mediated enteropathy triggered by gluten ingestion in genetically predisposed individuals (HLA-DQ2/DQ8). Gliadin peptides from wheat, barley, and rye activate an autoimmune response against tissue transglutaminase (tTG), causing villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, and intraepithelial lymphocytosis in the small intestine.

Harvard.text: A network of nerves in the upper abdomen; medication is sometimes injected here as part of a therapy to ease pain called a nerve block.

LLM.text: A network of nerves in the upper abdomen that supplies abdominal organs and may be targeted for pain treatment.

Harvard.text: The basic building block of all living organisms.

LLM.text: The fundamental structural and functional unit of all living organisms. Human cells are eukaryotic, characterized by a nucleus containing DNA and membrane-bound organelles.

Harvard.text: The end stage in the life of a cell when the cell can no longer divide.

LLM.text: A state in which a cell remains metabolically active but permanently stops dividing, often in response to aging, stress, or cellular damage.

Harvard.text: A type of immune response mounted against viruses, certain types of parasites, and perhaps cancer cells.

LLM.text: An immune response mediated mainly by T lymphocytes and other cells rather than by antibodies. It is important in defense against intracellular pathogens and in immune surveillance.

Harvard.text: The layer of tooth material that covers the root.

LLM.text: A mineralized connective tissue covering the tooth root. It provides attachment for periodontal-ligament fibers and is thinner near the cemento-enamel junction and thicker toward the root apex.

Harvard.text: A lack of concentration or alertness as well as a sense of lethargy and loss of motivation; involves the central nervous system.

LLM.text: A sense of reduced mental energy, concentration, alertness, or motivation arising primarily from central nervous-system processes.

Harvard.text: The brain, brainstem, and spinal cord.

LLM.text: The part of the nervous system comprising the brain and spinal cord, enclosed within the skull and vertebral column.

Harvard.text: A disorder in which breathing repeatedly stops during sleep, because the brain doesn’t properly signal the muscles that control breathing.

LLM.text: Apneas from variability in respiratory effort without airway obstruction. Associated with heart failure (Cheyne-Stokes respiration), high altitude, and opioid use.

Harvard.text: The part of the brain that controls coordinated movement.

LLM.text: Largest brain portion (approximately 10 percent of volume but over 50 percent of neurons) in the posterior cranial fossa behind the brainstem. Two hemispheres and a vermis, divided into vestibulocerebellum (balance, eye movements), spinocerebellum (posture, gait, coordination), and cerebrocerebellum (motor planning, cognition).

Harvard.text: A weakening and ballooning of the wall of an artery in the brain.

LLM.text: An abnormal focal enlargement of an artery in or around the brain. It may remain asymptomatic or rupture and cause subarachnoid hemorrhage. Risk factors include hypertension, smoking, certain inherited disorders, and family history.

Harvard.text: An invasive imaging procedure used to make detailed x-ray pictures of the blood vessels in the brain; dye is injected into the carotid arteries to highlight the blood vessels on x-rays.

LLM.text: Contrast imaging of cerebral vessels. Evaluates aneurysms, AVMs, stenosis. Invasive procedure.

Harvard.text: The part of the brain involved in all forms of conscious experience, including thought, language, and memory.

LLM.text: The outermost layer of the cerebrum, composed of gray matter (neuronal cell bodies) folded into gyri (ridges) and sulci (grooves), greatly increasing surface area.

Harvard.text: Bleeding in the brain caused by the rupture of a blood vessel; another term for hemorrhagic stroke.

LLM.text: Bleeding within the brain parenchyma, a type of hemorrhagic stroke causing mass effect, edema, and neurological deficits. Causes: hypertension (most common—basal ganglia, thalamus), cerebral amyloid angiopathy (lobar, elderly), arteriovenous malformation, aneurysm, anticoagulants, trauma, tumors.

Harvard.text: A type of stroke caused when a blood vessel that supplies blood to the brain is blocked by a blood clot.

LLM.text: Cerebral infarction, or ischemic stroke, results from occlusion of a cerebral artery causing irreversible neuronal damage. The most common cause is thromboembolism from atherosclerotic carotid or intracranial arteries, or cardioembolism from atrial fibrillation or cardiac thrombus.

Harvard.text: Pertaining to the blood vessels in the brain.

LLM.text: Relating to the blood vessels and circulation of the brain.

Harvard.text: The medical term for a stroke.

LLM.text: An acute neurological deficit caused by interruption of blood flow to the brain or bleeding within the brain. See Stroke.

Harvard.text: A substance that helps keep dirt out of the ear and lubricates the skin in the ear. More commonly known as earwax.

LLM.text: A substance that helps keep dirt out of the ear and lubricates the skin in the ear. More commonly known as earwax.

Harvard.text: A pinched nerve, causing sharp pain, tingling, and numbness in the areas served by the nerve.

LLM.text: A condition caused by compression, irritation, or inflammation of a spinal nerve root in the cervical spine, resulting in pain, numbness, tingling, and weakness in the distribution of the affected nerve root.

Harvard.text: The part of the spine located in the neck and consisting of the top seven vertebrae.

LLM.text: The upper segment of the vertebral column consisting of seven cervical vertebrae, C1 through C7, supporting the head and protecting the cervical spinal cord. It permits substantial flexion, extension, rotation, and lateral flexion while transmitting the vertebral arteries through the transverse foramina of C1-C6.

Harvard.text: Inflammatory arthritis involving the neck portion of the spine.

LLM.text: A degenerative condition of the cervical spine involving disc degeneration, osteophyte formation, and facet joint arthropathy that may compress nerve roots or the spinal cord. It can cause neck pain, radiculopathy, or myelopathy, and is a common cause of cervical spinal stenosis in older adults.

Harvard.text: Headache related to neck problems. Also called cervical headache.

LLM.text: A headache caused by a disorder of the cervical spine or its soft tissues, with pain referred from the neck to the head.

Harvard.text: Abbreviation for chronic fatigue syndrome, a disorder of ongoing, severe tiredness that interferes with a person’s ability to function well, isn’t improved with rest, and isn’t caused by another illness.

LLM.text: Chronic fatigue syndrome, a condition involving substantial persistent fatigue with post-exertional worsening and associated symptoms that are not explained by another disorder.

Harvard.text: A way of testing for food allergy, usually in double-blind experiments in which neither patient nor doctor knows which food is taken in pill form.

LLM.text: A controlled exposure to a suspected trigger, such as a food or medication, to assess whether it produces a reproducible reaction.

Harvard.text: A chemical solution applied to the skin to cause it to blister and peel, revealing a new layer of skin; treatment is used to improve the appearance of the skin, reducing lines, wrinkles, age spots, and other problems.

LLM.text: Application of a chemical solution to the skin to produce controlled exfoliation and regeneration of superficial or deeper skin layers.

Harvard.text: A treatment for low back pain that involves injecting the enzyme chymopapain into a herniated disk.

LLM.text: An intradiscal treatment intended to dissolve part of a herniated intervertebral disk, historically using an enzyme preparation.

Harvard.text: Using drugs or chemicals to prevent cancer.

LLM.text: The use of drugs or natural agents to prevent, delay, or reverse cancer development, e.g., tamoxifen or raloxifene in high-risk breast cancer, HPV and hepatitis B vaccination, and aspirin in colorectal cancer.

Harvard.text: The use of chemicals to treat disease; often used to destroy cancer cells.

LLM.text: Treatment using medicines that kill cancer cells, inhibit their growth, or prevent replication. It may be given alone or with surgery, radiation, immunotherapy, or targeted therapy; the drugs, schedule, benefits, and adverse effects depend on the cancer and treatment goal.

Harvard.text: Abnormal breathing where cycles of deep, labored breathing where cycles of deep, labored breathing are followed by cycles of weak breathing that can result in a total, temporary lack of airflow.

LLM.text: Crescendo-decrescendo breathing pattern with periods of apnea, seen in heart failure and stroke. It is a form of central sleep apnea.

Harvard.text: Someone who treats disease by manipulation and adjustment of body structures, often the spine.

LLM.text: A healthcare practitioner who provides manual or manipulative treatment, especially for musculoskeletal conditions, according to the practitioner's training and local regulation.

Harvard.text: A chemical found in green, leafy vegetables thought to help prevent cancer.

LLM.text: A water-soluble, copper-containing derivative of chlorophyll used in some products and studied for effects such as odor control; clinical uses depend on evidence and context.

Harvard.text: Severe iron-deficiency characterized by a yellow-green tinge to the skin.

LLM.text: An outdated term for a greenish or pale complexion historically associated with severe iron-deficiency anemia, especially in young women.

Harvard.text: A substance that causes the gallbladder to squeeze, increasing the discharge of bile.

LLM.text: A substance that promotes emptying of the gallbladder into the intestine.

Harvard.text: A hormone that signals the gallbladder to contract, releasing bile, and causes the pancreas to release enzymes used in digestion.

LLM.text: CCK is a peptide hormone produced by I-cells in the duodenal and jejinal mucosa in response to fatty acids (long-chain fatty acids are the most potent stimuli) and amino acids in the chyme.

Harvard.text: An agent that promotes bile production.

LLM.text: A substance that promotes production or secretion of bile by the liver.

Harvard.text: A waxy, fat-like substance produced by the liver and found in all food from animal sources; an essential component of body cells and a precursor of bile acids and some hormones.

LLM.text: A lipid required for cell membranes and synthesis of steroid hormones and bile acids. Excess atherogenic cholesterol can contribute to arterial plaque.

Harvard.text: A nerve cell that produces acetylcholine.

LLM.text: A nerve cell that releases acetylcholine as its principal neurotransmitter.

Harvard.text: Arthritis caused by calcium crystals.

LLM.text: Calcification of cartilage visible on X-ray. Associated with CPPD disease. Found in knees, wrists, pubic symphysis. May be incidental or symptomatic.

Harvard.text: A cartilage cell.

LLM.text: A mature cartilage cell that produces and maintains the cartilage extracellular matrix.

Harvard.text: A painful condition caused by irritation to or wearing away of the cartilage on the underside of the knee cap; known as runner’s knee.

LLM.text: Softening and degeneration of cartilage, especially articular cartilage. The term is often used for changes affecting the patella and causing anterior knee pain.

Harvard.text: A thin layer of blood vessels and connective tissue between the white of the eye (sclera) and the retina.

LLM.text: A medical term describing the named biologic or clinical concept; its defining feature is the process, structure, exposure, or finding specified by the term, interpreted in context.

Harvard.text: A threadlike structure, found in the nucleus of each cell, that carries almost all of a cell’s genes.

LLM.text: A chromosome is a DNA-protein structure carrying genetic information; humans normally have 46 chromosomes in most body cells.

Harvard.text: Any condition that lasts a long time or recurs over time.

LLM.text: Persisting or recurring over a long period, in contrast to acute; the appropriate duration depends on the disease or clinical context.

Harvard.text: A disorder of ongoing, severe tiredness that interferes with a person’s ability to function well, isn’t improved with rest, and isn’t caused by another illness.

LLM.text: A complex, debilitating disorder characterized by profound fatigue lasting >6 months that is not relieved by rest and is worsened by physical or mental exertion (post-exertional malaise). Associated symptoms: unrefreshing sleep, cognitive impairment (brain fog), orthostatic intolerance, joint pain, headaches, and sore throat.

Harvard.text: Any type of kidney disease that lasts longer than three months and impairs kidney function.

LLM.text: Chronic kidney disease is the progressive loss of kidney function over months to years, typically from diabetes, hypertension, or glomerular diseases. It is staged by estimated glomerular filtration rate and albuminuria, with end-stage renal disease requiring dialysis or transplantation.

Harvard.text: Pain that persists after an injury has healed or a disease is over.

LLM.text: Pain persisting longer than three months or beyond normal tissue healing time, often lacking an ongoing identifiable cause. It involves complex interactions between biological, psychological, and social factors that can amplify pain signaling in the nervous system.

Harvard.text: Long-term, severe pain that doesn’t spring from an injury or illness, that interferes with daily life, and is often accompanied by other problems, such as depression, irritability, and anxiety.

LLM.text: Persistent pain accompanied by significant physical, emotional, or social effects that interfere with daily life.

Harvard.text: Severe, frequent, short-lasting migraine-like headache attacks.

LLM.text: A primary headache disorder causing frequent, short-lasting, severe one-sided headaches with autonomic symptoms and a characteristic response to indomethacin.

Harvard.text: A fat globule that ferries triglyceride from the intestine to the liver and fat tissue.

LLM.text: Transports dietary lipids. Largest, least dense lipoprotein.

Harvard.text: A nearly liquid mass of partly digested food and digestive juices; found in the stomach and intestine.

LLM.text: A semifluid mixture of partially digested food and gastric or intestinal secretions that passes from the stomach into the small intestine.

Harvard.text: A group of inflammatory hair disorders that can cause irreversible damage to the follicle that results in permanent hair loss and scarring. Also known as scarring alopecia.

LLM.text: Hair loss caused by destruction and scarring of hair follicles, usually leading to permanent loss in affected areas.

Harvard.text: Small, hairlike structures on the surface of some cells.

LLM.text: Small hair-like structures on cells that move fluid, particles, or mucus across a tissue surface.

Harvard.text: Part of the eye that produces the aqueous humor (fluid that nourishes the eye) and contains the ciliary muscle, which controls focusing of the lens.

LLM.text: Circumferential structure between iris and choroid, with ciliary muscle (accommodation control via zonular fibers) and ciliary processes (aqueous humor production). Part of the uveal tract (iris, ciliary body, choroid).

Harvard.text: The body’s biological clock that regulates the sleep/wake cycle and other physiological processes.

LLM.text: The approximately 24-hour endogenous biological cycle regulating sleep-wake behavior, hormone secretion, body temperature, metabolism, and other physiological processes. Generated by the suprachiasmatic nucleus of the hypothalamus, which is entrained to the environment primarily by light via the retinohypothalamic tract.

Harvard.text: A circle of arteries at the base of the brain, connecting major brain arteries and supplying blood to all parts of the brain.

LLM.text: A ring-like arterial anastomosis at the base of the brain that provides collateral blood flow between the anterior (internal carotid) and posterior (vertebrobasilar) circulations. It is formed by the anterior cerebral, anterior communicating, internal carotid, posterior cerebral, and posterior communicating arteries.

Harvard.text: A chronic disease of the liver that progressively destroys the liver’s ability to aid in digestion and detoxification.

LLM.text: Cirrhosis is advanced liver scarring with regenerative nodules that distorts blood flow and liver function, potentially causing portal hypertension, jaundice, ascites, and liver failure. distortion of the hepatic architecture and formation of regenerative nodules. The most common causes include chronic hepatitis C infection, alcoholic liver disease, non-alcoholic steatohepatitis, chronic hepatitis B infection, and autoimmune hepatitis.

Harvard.text: Abbreviation for creatine kinase, an enzyme found in the heart, brain, and skeletal muscle. Levels of creatine kinase are tested to diagnose certain illnesses.

LLM.text: Creatine kinase, an enzyme found in skeletal muscle, heart muscle, and brain whose blood level may rise after tissue injury.

Harvard.text: A migraine headache preceded by visual disturbances; also known as a migraine with aura.

LLM.text: A migraine associated with an aura, such as temporary visual or sensory symptoms.

Harvard.text: A muscle cramp, usually felt in the calf, caused by poor blood flow to the legs.

LLM.text: Muscle pain or cramping brought on by exertion and relieved by rest, usually because of reduced arterial blood flow to a limb.

Harvard.text: A study that tests a therapy in humans, rather than in laboratories or on animals.

LLM.text: A planned study in which people receive or are observed for an intervention to evaluate its safety, effects, or outcomes. Trials may be conducted in phases and for many types of health interventions.

Harvard.text: An explosive increase in the number of fighter cells released by the immune system to fight a threat in the body.

LLM.text: Rapid multiplication of genetically or immunologically related cells derived from a single precursor after activation.

Harvard.text: Medications that dissolve blood clots and restore blood flow through a blocked artery.

LLM.text: A medicine that dissolves a blood clot; the medical term is thrombolytic.

Harvard.text: A short-lived, extremely painful headache that occurs repeatedly over a period of a few weeks or months and then disappears for months or years.

LLM.text: A primary headache disorder causing severe one-sided orbital or periorbital pain in attacks lasting about 15--180 minutes, often with tearing, conjunctival redness, nasal symptoms, eyelid swelling, or facial sweating on the same side.

Harvard.text: The process where a liquid, such as blood, comes together to form a soft, semi-solid mass, like a clot.

LLM.text: To change from a liquid to a semisolid or solid state, especially the formation of a blood clot through coagulation.

Harvard.text: A narrowed area in the aorta (the main artery that leaves the heart) present from birth.

LLM.text: A localized narrowing of a tubular anatomical structure, especially coarctation of the aorta, which obstructs blood flow and produces characteristic pressure differences.

Harvard.text: Part of the ear that converts sound into electrical signals that the brain interprets as a particular sound.

LLM.text: Snail-shaped hearing organ in the inner ear, coiled approximately 2.5 turns around the modiolus. Three fluid-filled chambers: scala vestibuli (perilymph), scala media (endolymph, organ of Corti), scala tympani (perilymph).

Harvard.text: A small electronic device that is implanted in the inner ear to restore some hearing to a deaf person.

LLM.text: A cochlear implant is an electronic medical device that bypasses damaged or absent inner ear hair cells to provide direct electrical stimulation of the auditory nerve, restoring a perception of sound in individuals with severe to profound sensorineural hearing loss who derive limited benefit from hearing aids.

Harvard.text: A small organic molecule, often made from B vitamins, that helps enzymes function in the body.

LLM.text: A non-protein organic molecule that binds to an enzyme (apoenzyme) and is required for its catalytic activity. Coenzymes often act as transient carriers of specific chemical groups or electrons.

Harvard.text: A form of therapy that aimed at recognizing and changing negative thoughts and behaviors.

LLM.text: A structured, time-limited psychotherapy that identifies and modifies maladaptive thought patterns (cognitive distortions) and behaviors. It is based on the cognitive model that thoughts, feelings, and behaviors are interconnected. CBT uses techniques including cognitive restructuring, behavioral activation, exposure, and skills training.

Harvard.text: All of the brain mechanisms involved with thinking, reasoning, learning, and remembering.

LLM.text: The mental processes involved in attention, memory, language, reasoning, learning, judgment, and problem solving.

Harvard.text: Problems with memory, language, thinking, or other brain functions, varying from mild to serious difficulty.

LLM.text: Decline in one or more cognitive domains: memory, attention, language, visuospatial, executive function. Types: subjective cognitive decline, mild cognitive impairment (MCI), dementia. MCI: functional independence preserved, impairment on testing. Dementia: functional impairment.

Harvard.text: The capacity of the brain to use alternative neural pathways or thinking strategies in response to neurological injury from conditions such as Alzheimer’s disease.

LLM.text: The brain's ability to use alternative strategies or networks to maintain function despite injury or disease.

Harvard.text: Severe abdominal pain caused by spasms in the intestines or in a portion of the kidneys.

LLM.text: Sudden, severe, often cramping pain caused by contraction or obstruction of a hollow organ. The term is also used for recurrent unexplained crying in an otherwise healthy infant.

Harvard.text: A fibrous protein that is the main component of connective tissue in the body.

LLM.text: The major structural protein of connective tissue, composed of three polypeptide chains arranged in a triple helix. Different collagen types provide tensile strength to skin, bone, cartilage, tendons, blood vessels, and basement membranes.

Harvard.text: An enzyme that breaks down collagen.

LLM.text: An enzyme that breaks down collagen in connective tissue.

Harvard.text: A system of minor arteries, known as collaterals, that can serve as an alternate blood supply to the heart when a major coronary artery is blocked.

LLM.text: Alternative vascular pathways that develop when coronary arteries become chronically narrowed. Collaterals connect different coronary artery territories and can partially compensate for stenosis. They develop gradually in response to ischemia and are more prominent in patients with chronic coronary artery disease.

Harvard.text: A break at the end of the main bone of the forearm, the radius.

LLM.text: A fracture of the distal radius with dorsal displacement and angulation of the distal fragment, usually caused by falling on an outstretched hand.

Harvard.text: The large intestine; a muscular tube that is 5 to 6 feet long. It compacts and moves solid waste.

LLM.text: The largest part of the large intestine, extending from the cecum to the rectum. Anatomically divided into ascending colon (right side), transverse colon (across the abdomen), descending colon (left side), and sigmoid colon (S-shaped, leading to the rectum).

Harvard.text: A procedure to see inside the colon, using a long, lighted flexible tube mounted with a tiny camera.

LLM.text: Colonoscopy uses a flexible camera to examine the rectum and entire colon, allowing biopsy and removal of polyps or other lesions.

Harvard.text: A growth on the colon or rectal wall that may develop into cancer.

LLM.text: A gland-forming growth in the colon or rectum that may develop into colorectal cancer.

Harvard.text: Surgery that brings one end of the large intestine out through an opening in the abdomen for elimination of stool.

LLM.text: A surgically created opening that brings part of the colon through the abdominal wall to divert stool into an external appliance.

Harvard.text: An antibody-rich form of breast milk, produced at the end of pregnancy and for a short time after birth, which strengthens a newborn’s immune system.

LLM.text: The thick, yellowish fluid produced by the mammary glands in late pregnancy and the first few days postpartum. Rich in immunoglobulins (especially IgA), proteins, leukocytes, and growth factors.

Harvard.text: Deep unconsciousness where the person is alive but unable to move or respond.

LLM.text: A state of profound unresponsiveness in which a person cannot be awakened and does not show purposeful responses. It is a medical emergency with many possible causes.

Harvard.text: Estrogen combined with progestogen, prescribed to augment a woman’s depleted hormones during menopause.

LLM.text: Hormone therapy containing both estrogen and a progestogen, generally used when endometrial protection is needed in a person with a uterus.

Harvard.text: A condition, usually inherited, in which LDL cholesterol and triglyceride levels are very high.

LLM.text: A lipid disorder characterized by elevated cholesterol and triglycerides, often with increased atherogenic lipoproteins.

Harvard.text: A migraine headache without any visual symptoms, such as not a blind spot, beforehand. Also called a migraine without aura.

LLM.text: A migraine without a preceding aura.

Harvard.text: Any disease caused by bacteria, viruses, or other pathogens that is spread from person to person.

LLM.text: Any disease caused by bacteria, viruses, or other pathogens that is spread from person to person.

Harvard.text: Hard, tightly-packed tissue that forms the outer shell of bones. Also called cortical bone or lamellar bone.

LLM.text: Dense outer bone tissue organized into osteons that provides strength and structural support.

Harvard.text: Proteins that kill viruses, bacteria, and other microbes directly or flag them for destruction by white blood cells.

LLM.text: A group of blood proteins that supports immune defense by destroying microbes and promoting inflammation and phagocytosis.

Harvard.text: Often referred to as CBC. A broad panel of screening tests that examine different parts of the blood and can be used to diagnose anemia, infection, and many other diseases.

LLM.text: A panel measuring red blood cells, white blood cells, platelets, hemoglobin, hematocrit, red-cell indices, and often a white-cell differential. Results are interpreted using age-, sex-, and laboratory-specific reference ranges.

Harvard.text: A prolonged, intense reaction to bereavement that affects one in 10 people who lose a loved one. Key signs are inability to accept the death; frequent nightmares and intrusive, upsetting memories; detachment from others; constant yearning for the deceased; and excessive loneliness. Sometimes called traumatic or chronic grief.

LLM.text: Persistent, intense grief that substantially interferes with daily functioning and lasts longer than expected for the person's cultural and social context.

Harvard.text: A migraine where one or more of the symptoms, such as visual problems, linger for at least a day after the headache is gone.

LLM.text: An older, nonspecific term for migraine accompanied by prolonged or prominent neurologic symptoms; the specific syndrome should be identified when possible.

Harvard.text: A pharmacy that mixes custom medications for patients and doctors.

LLM.text: A pharmacy that prepares customized formulations for an individual patient when a suitable commercially manufactured product is unavailable or unsuitable.

Harvard.text: The collapse of a bone, most often a bone in the spine (vertebra).

LLM.text: Collapse of a vertebra or other bone because of compression, often related to osteoporosis or trauma.

Harvard.text: An imaging technique that uses a computer and x-rays passed through the body at different angles to create a detailed, nearly three-dimensional picture of the body.

LLM.text: Cross-sectional imaging using rotating X-ray tube and detectors. Produces axial images, reconstructable into sagittal, coronal, 3D. CT number measured in Hounsfield units (HU): water = 0, air = -1000, bone = +1000. Contrast: iodine-based, enhances vascular structures and perfused organs. Speed: seconds.

Harvard.text: The start of pregnancy, when an egg is fertilized by a sperm.

LLM.text: The beginning of pregnancy, usually referring to fertilization and the subsequent establishment of pregnancy.

Harvard.text: Hearing loss caused by a blockage in the middle ear that prevents sound waves from reaching the inner ear.

LLM.text: Hearing loss caused by impaired transmission of sound through the outer or middle ear. Audiometry commonly shows an air-bone gap, and causes include earwax, middle-ear fluid, perforation, otosclerosis, and ossicular disease.

Harvard.text: A rounded knob at the end of a bone.

LLM.text: A rounded projection at the end of a bone that contributes to a joint.

Harvard.text: Cells in the retina that are sensitive to color and light.

LLM.text: Retinal photoreceptor cells responsible for color vision and detailed vision in relatively bright light.

Harvard.text: An accumulation of mucus or of blood in an organ.

LLM.text: A passive vascular phenomenon of engorgement of a tissue or organ with blood from impaired venous or lymphatic drainage. Chronic venous congestion produces stasis, hypoxia, dilated vessels, edema, hemorrhage, and hemosiderin-laden macrophages, exemplified by the lungs (heart failure cells) and liver (nutmeg liver).

Harvard.text: An older term for heart failure, a disorder caused by a decrease in the heart’s ability to pump blood. Congestive heart failure referred specifically to the type of heart failure associated with the accumulation of excess fluid in the lungs or extremities.

LLM.text: A historical term for heart failure with clinical fluid congestion. Current terminology is heart failure, which may occur with or without congestion and is classified by left-ventricular ejection fraction, symptoms, and disease stage.

Harvard.text: A type of vaccine made by attaching an antigen (a substance that the body deems harmful) to a protein. It is often used to immunize babies and young children.

LLM.text: A vaccine in which a poorly immunogenic polysaccharide antigen is linked to a carrier protein to improve the immune response, especially in infants and young children.

Harvard.text: Estrogen medications produced from the urine of pregnant horses.

LLM.text: A mixture of estrogenic compounds historically derived from the urine of pregnant mares and used in some hormone-therapy formulations.

Harvard.text: The clear, thin membrane that covers the inside of the eyelid and the white part of the eyeball.

LLM.text: A thin mucous membrane that lines the inner eyelids (palpebral conjunctiva) and covers the front surface of the sclera (bulbar conjunctiva). It protects and lubricates the eye and permits smooth movement of the eyelids.

Harvard.text: Swelling or infection of the thin lining on the inside of the eyelid and the white part of the eyeball.

LLM.text: Inflammation of the conjunctiva, the thin, transparent mucous membrane lining the inner surface of the eyelids and the anterior surface of the sclera. Conjunctivitis is the most common cause of red eye and is classified by etiology.

Harvard.text: A group of tissues in the body that provide internal support and bind other tissues in the body, including bone, cartilage, tendons, and ligaments.

LLM.text: A diverse type of tissue that supports, binds, protects, and insulates organs and structures throughout the body.

Harvard.text: The process by which the brain transforms newly acquired information into long-term memories.

LLM.text: An area of lung in which air spaces are filled with fluid, cells, or other material, increasing its density on imaging. Causes include pneumonia, edema, hemorrhage, and tumor.

Harvard.text: A rash or skin irritation that results when skin contacts an allergen or irritating substance.

LLM.text: An inflammatory skin reaction caused by contact with an external substance. It may be allergic, involving delayed immune sensitization, or irritant, caused by direct chemical or physical injury.

Harvard.text: Estrogen and progestogen taken daily by women whose estrogen levels are low, usually due to menopause or a hysterectomy.

LLM.text: A hormone regimen in which estrogen and progestogen are taken continuously rather than sequentially.

Harvard.text: A therapy for obstructive sleep apnea in which a machine delivers a continuous stream of air which prevents the collapse of the airway during sleep.

LLM.text: Noninvasive respiratory support that delivers a constant positive pressure throughout the breathing cycle to keep the upper airway or alveoli open.

Harvard.text: Proteins that help shorten the length of muscle cells, enabling them to contract.

LLM.text: Proteins, especially actin and myosin, that interact to generate force and shorten muscle cells.

Harvard.text: Shortening of a muscle, usually because of disease or lack of use, that limits joint movement.

LLM.text: Permanent or semi-permanent limitation of passive joint range of motion caused by shortening or structural change in muscle, tendon, capsule, fascia, skin, or other periarticular tissue. Prevention and treatment depend on cause and stage.

Harvard.text: A fluid injected into the bloodstream or swallowed so that organs will show up on x-rays.

LLM.text: A substance administered or placed in the body to make tissues, organs, or body spaces more visible during imaging.

Harvard.text: A group of people in a medical study who receive either no treatment or the standard treatment, which is compared against a group who receive the treatment being studied.

LLM.text: The comparison group in a study, which may receive usual care, a placebo, or no intervention according to the study design.

Harvard.text: Asthma medications taken daily to prevent or control symptoms.

LLM.text: Long-term asthma medicines taken regularly to reduce airway inflammation and prevent symptoms or exacerbations.

Harvard.text: A bruise. An injury that causes swelling, pain, and discoloration but doesn’t break the skin.

LLM.text: A closed soft-tissue injury caused by blunt force, producing bleeding into tissues without an open wound. It commonly causes pain, swelling, and ecchymosis; severe contusions may involve muscle necrosis, compartment syndrome, internal bleeding, or associated bone and organ injury.

Harvard.text: Rapid uncontrollable shaking of the body caused by muscles contracting and relaxing repeatedly.

LLM.text: A sudden episode of involuntary, often rhythmic muscle contractions that may occur with a seizure or other disturbance of brain function.

Harvard.text: An area of hardened, thickened skin usually caused by friction.

LLM.text: A localized thickening of skin caused by repeated pressure or friction, often occurring on the toes or feet.

Harvard.text: The clear dome that covers the front of the eye.

LLM.text: Transparent, avascular, dome-shaped anterior eye surface providing approximately two-thirds of total refractive power. Five layers: epithelium (stratified squamous, rapidly regenerating), Bowman's membrane, stroma (thickest, regular collagen), Descemet's membrane, endothelium (single cell layer maintaining transparency).

Harvard.text: Pertaining to the arteries that supply blood to the heart.

LLM.text: Relating to the arteries or circulation that supply the heart muscle.

Harvard.text: A test that shows how blood moves through the blood vessels supplying the heart to identify narrowed arteries. It uses x-rays and the injection of a fluid called a contrast agent that can be seen on the x-rays.

LLM.text: Invasive imaging of the coronary arteries using catheter-delivered contrast and X-ray fluoroscopy. It shows coronary anatomy and stenosis and can support treatment planning; noninvasive tests may be appropriate in other clinical settings.

Harvard.text: Blood vessel that carries oxygen-rich blood to the heart muscle.

LLM.text: One of the blood vessels branching from the aorta that supplies oxygen-rich blood directly to the heart muscle.

Harvard.text: Surgery to improve blood flow to the heart by diverting blood around a blocked coronary artery.

LLM.text: Surgery that uses a graft to route blood around a narrowed or blocked coronary artery.

Harvard.text: A condition in which one or more of the arteries feeding the heart become so narrow in spots that blood flow is impaired or stopped entirely, causing chest pain or a heart attack. Often called heart disease or coronary heart disease.

LLM.text: Narrowing or occlusion of coronary arteries, usually due to atherosclerosis, reducing blood flow to the myocardium. Risk factors include hypertension, diabetes, hyperlipidemia, smoking, family history, and obesity. CAD can present as stable angina, acute coronary syndromes (unstable angina, NSTEMI, STEMI), or sudden cardiac death.

common_names: heart disease or coronary heart disease

Harvard.text: Surgery to remove fatty plaque that has built up on the walls of a coronary artery.

LLM.text: Surgical removal of atherosclerotic plaque from the inner lining of a coronary artery.

Harvard.text: A commonly used term for coronary artery disease, a condition in which one or more of the arteries feeding the heart become so narrow in spots that blood flow is impaired or stopped entirely, causing chest pain or a heart attack.

LLM.text: Disease caused by reduced blood flow through the coronary arteries, usually due to atherosclerotic plaque. It may cause angina, myocardial infarction, heart failure, or sudden cardiac death. Also called coronary artery disease.

Harvard.text: Temporary constriction of an artery that supplies blood to the heart, slowing or stopping blood flow.

LLM.text: Temporary contraction of a coronary artery that reduces blood flow to the heart muscle and may cause angina or infarction.

Harvard.text: A ward in a hospital that provides specialized care and monitoring for patients with heart problems.

LLM.text: A hospital unit providing continuous monitoring and specialized care for acute cardiac illness.

Harvard.text: The large bundle of nerve fibers linking the left and right sides of the brain.

LLM.text: Brain's largest white matter tract with approximately 200 million axons connecting left and right hemispheres. Four parts: rostrum, genu, body, splenium. Facilitates interhemispheric communication for sensory, motor, and cognitive integration.

Harvard.text: Sponge-like tissue in the penis that fills with blood during sexual arousal, causing an erection.

LLM.text: One of two columns of erectile tissue in the penis that fill with blood during erection.

Harvard.text: The egg follicle remnant left behind after an egg has been released during ovulation. The corpus luteum secretes the hormone progesterone to stimulate the growth of the endometrium.

LLM.text: The temporary endocrine structure formed from an ovarian follicle after ovulation; it produces progesterone during the luteal phase and early pregnancy.

Harvard.text: A cylinder of soft tissue surrounding a man’s urethra and running the length of the penis.

LLM.text: A column of erectile tissue surrounding the penile urethra and expanding distally to form the glans.

Harvard.text: One of the muscles that forms frown lines on the forehead.

LLM.text: A small facial muscle that draws the eyebrows downward and inward, contributing to frowning.

Harvard.text: The middle layer and main structure of the hair shaft, consisting mainly of compact bundles of the protein keratin.

LLM.text: The outer layer of an organ or structure, such as the cerebral cortex, adrenal cortex, or outer layer of a hair shaft.

Harvard.text: Hard, tightly-packed tissue that forms the outer shell of bones. Also called compact bone.

LLM.text: Dense bone forming the outer shell of most bones and providing much of the skeleton's mechanical strength.

Harvard.text: Steroid medications made to mimic hormones produced naturally by the adrenal glands. They are used to treat a wide range of health problems.

LLM.text: Synthetic glucocorticoids with potent anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive effects. Examples include prednisone, prednisolone, methylprednisolone, dexamethasone, and hydrocortisone. They suppress inflammatory gene expression and inhibit immune cell function.

Harvard.text: A hormone made in the brain that triggers the body’s fight-or-flight reaction to external threats.

LLM.text: A hypothalamic hormone that stimulates the pituitary gland to release adrenocorticotropic hormone and helps coordinate the stress response.

Harvard.text: One of a class of stress hormones released during the fight-or-flight stress response.

LLM.text: The primary glucocorticoid produced by the adrenal cortex (zona fasciculata) under ACTH control; essential for stress response, metabolism, and homeostasis. Functions: gluconeogenesis, glycogenolysis, protein catabolism, lipolysis, anti-inflammatory/immunosuppressive effects, and maintenance of vascular tone.

Harvard.text: Abbreviation for cyclooxygenase-2 inhibitors, medications that reduce pain and swelling by targeting a particular enzyme known as cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2).

LLM.text: Medicines that inhibit cyclooxygenase-2, an enzyme involved in prostaglandin production and inflammation.

Harvard.text: Abbreviation for continuous positive airway pressure, a therapy for obstructive sleep apnea in which a machine delivers a continuous stream of air which prevents the collapse of the airway during sleep.

LLM.text: Continuous positive airway pressure delivered through a mask to splint open the upper airway during sleep. It is commonly used for obstructive sleep apnea and can reduce apneas and related symptoms when used consistently.

Harvard.text: Abbreviation for cardiopulmonary resuscitation, a combination of chest compressions and mouth-to-mouth breathing that keep oxygenated blood circulating to the brain and tissues.

LLM.text: Cardiopulmonary resuscitation is an emergency procedure using chest compressions and, when appropriate, rescue breaths or an automated external defibrillator to support circulation and breathing during cardiac arrest.

Harvard.text: Inflammation and damage to blood vessels supplying blood to the head and neck. Also called giant cell arteritis.

LLM.text: Giant-cell arteritis, an inflammatory disease of medium and large arteries, especially branches of the external carotid artery, that can cause headache, visual loss, and systemic symptoms.

Harvard.text: Intense, often irrepressible urge for something; often a symptom of dependence on drugs, alcohol or addiction.

LLM.text: A strong, often difficult-to-control desire for a substance, behavior, or experience, commonly seen in substance-use disorders.

Harvard.text: A protein made by the liver. High amounts of C-reactive protein may indicate that arteries are clogged (atherosclerosis).

LLM.text: An acute-phase reactant produced by the liver in response to inflammation (IL-6). CRP rises within 4-6 hours of inflammatory stimulus and peaks at 36-50 hours. Uses: monitoring inflammatory disease activity (RA, vasculitis), detecting infection postoperatively, and cardiovascular risk stratification (hs-CRP: high-sensitivity).

Harvard.text: An enzyme that leaks into the bloodstream in high amounts if a muscle is damaged. Can be used to detect heart attack or muscle damage from other diseases.

LLM.text: An enzyme found in muscle, brain, and heart. CK-MB: cardiac isoenzyme (used historically for MI diagnosis, largely replaced by troponin). CK-MM: skeletal muscle (elevated in rhabdomyolysis, trauma, statins, myopathy). Total CK: elevated in muscle injury, myocardial infarction, seizures, hypothyroidism, and statin myopathy.

Harvard.text: A waste product created by muscle metabolism. Doctors sometimes test creatinine levels to examine kidney function.

LLM.text: A breakdown product of muscle creatine phosphate produced at a constant rate, filtered by the glomerulus and minimally reabsorbed; serum creatinine is the most used marker of kidney function.

Harvard.text: A blood or urine test that helps doctors determine if the kidneys are working properly.

LLM.text: A blood or urine test measuring creatinine to help assess kidney filtration and muscle-related creatinine production.

Harvard.text: Grating, grinding, or popping sound or feeling made when a joint is moved.

LLM.text: A crackling, grating, or popping sensation or sound caused by movement of tissue, bone, joint surfaces, or air in soft tissue.

Harvard.text: A rare, untreatable, rapid form of dementia that is fatal.

LLM.text: A rapidly progressive fatal neurodegenerative disease caused by abnormal prion protein, characterized by dementia, myoclonus, ataxia, and other neurologic signs.

Harvard.text: A chronic disease that causes swelling of the digestive tract, pain, and diarrhea.

LLM.text: A chronic inflammatory bowel disease that can affect any part of the gastrointestinal tract and commonly causes abdominal pain, diarrhea, weight loss, or systemic inflammation.

Harvard.text: The part of the tooth that is visible above the gum line. Also a restoration that covers the crown of the tooth.

LLM.text: The visible part of a tooth above the gum line, or a dental restoration that covers and protects a damaged tooth.

Harvard.text: Use of extreme cold to freeze and destroy diseased tissue.

LLM.text: The therapeutic application of extreme cold (typically using liquid nitrogen at $-196^C$) to destroy abnormal or diseased tissue.

Harvard.text: Abbreviation for C-reactive protein, a protein made by the liver. High amounts of C-reactive protein may indicate that arteries are clogged (atherosclerosis).

LLM.text: C-reactive protein. Acute phase reactant. Marker of inflammation.

Harvard.text: Part of the eye that changes shape so that the eye can focus on objects at different distances.

LLM.text: The transparent flexible structure inside the eye that focuses light onto the retina.

Harvard.text: Computerized x-rays that provide detailed views of the body and brain. Also known as a computed tomography (CT) scan.

LLM.text: Computed tomography, an imaging method that uses multiple X-ray measurements and computer reconstruction to produce cross-sectional images.

Harvard.text: Use of a CT scan and an injectable dye to show arteries and blood vessels in detail.

LLM.text: CT imaging with IV contrast timed to visualize arteries. Coronary CTA: assesses coronary artery stenosis and plaque, calcium scoring (Agatston). CTA chest: pulmonary embolism (PE protocol), aortic dissection. CTA head/neck: stroke evaluation, aneurysm, dissection, and vasculitis.

Harvard.text: The pinching of a nerve at the elbow, causing numbness in the pinkie and ring fingers and part of the hand.

LLM.text: Cubital tunnel syndrome: ulnar nerve compression at elbow (cubital tunnel: Osborne's ligament, FCU aponeurosis, medial epicondyle, olecranon). Clinical: paresthesias ulnar 1.5 digits, nocturnal, Tinel at elbow, Froment sign (IP flexion of thumb with key pinch), Wartenberg sign (abduction of small finger), thenar/hypothenar wasting late.

Harvard.text: An indentation in the optic disc that grows abnormally large with glaucoma.

LLM.text: An abnormal enlargement or depression of the optic-disc cup, often assessed in evaluating glaucoma.

Harvard.text: Using a spoon-shaped instrument to remove diseased tissue or sample tissue.

LLM.text: Removal of tissue from a body cavity or surface with a curette, used for diagnosis, treatment, or removal of abnormal tissue.

Harvard.text: A disorder caused by high levels of the stress-hormone cortisol resulting in damage to the body, including abdominal obesity, rounded red face, and other symptoms.

LLM.text: An endocrine disorder caused by prolonged exposure to too much cortisol or glucocorticoid medicine. It may result from steroid treatment or from a pituitary, adrenal, or other tumor. Common features include weight gain mainly around the trunk, a round face, fat at the back of the neck, thin easily bruised skin with purple stretch marks, muscle weakness, high blood pressure, and high blood glucose. Untreated disease can cause infections, blood clots, bone loss, and cardiovascular complications.

Harvard.text: The outermost, single-cell layer of the hair shaft.
