LLM.text: The thin outermost layer of a hair shaft formed by overlapping cells that protect the inner cortex.

Harvard.text: A condition in which skin turns blue due to a lack of oxygen in the blood, often because of heart failure or lung disease.

LLM.text: A bluish discoloration of the skin and mucous membranes resulting from excessive amounts of deoxygenated hemoglobin in the capillary blood. It becomes clinically apparent when the concentration of deoxygenated hemoglobin exceeds 5 grams per deciliter, which corresponds to an oxygen saturation of approximately 85 percent.

Harvard.text: A chemical in the body that widens blood vessels in the penis. This increases blood flow to the penis, causing an erection.

LLM.text: A cellular signaling molecule involved in smooth-muscle relaxation, phototransduction, and other physiologic processes.

Harvard.text: Use of estrogen and progestogen for 10–14 days of the month to relieve symptoms of menopause.

LLM.text: Hormone therapy in which estrogen is given continuously or for part of a cycle and progestogen is added for a defined number of days.

Harvard.text: An enzyme that helps blood cells known as platelets stick to each other, a key step in the formation of a blood clot.

LLM.text: An enzyme family that helps convert arachidonic acid into prostaglandins and related mediators involved in pain, inflammation, and platelet function.

Harvard.text: An abnormal growth in the body that is noncancerous.

LLM.text: A cyst is a closed sac containing fluid, air, cells, or semisolid material and may occur in skin, organs, glands, or other tissues.

Harvard.text: An eye condition in which the retina (the macula) becomes swollen with fluid.

LLM.text: Swelling of the macula caused by fluid collecting in small cyst-like spaces within the retina.

Harvard.text: Proteins in the body that act as messengers between immune system cells.

LLM.text: Small signaling proteins released by immune and other cells that regulate inflammation, immunity, blood-cell production, and tissue responses.

Harvard.text: Drug-induced hair loss that occurs some weeks after the start of chemotherapy; hair grows back after cessation of treatment.

LLM.text: Hair loss caused by exposure to a cytotoxic treatment or other toxic injury to actively growing hair follicles.

Harvard.text: A type of dopamine receptor (see neurotransmitter receptors) that seems to be particularly important in addiction.

LLM.text: A dopamine receptor involved in movement, motivation, reward, and some psychiatric disorders.

Harvard.text: A substance found in soybeans.

LLM.text: A naturally occurring isoflavone found in soy and other legumes that can be converted by intestinal bacteria into related compounds.

Harvard.text: A guide to the amount of nutrients in a given food; Daily values are given in percentages based on a 2,000-calorie-per-day diet.

LLM.text: A reference amount used on U.S. Nutrition Facts labels to show how much a nutrient in one serving contributes to a typical daily diet.

Harvard.text: A mild and common condition that is characterized by an itchy, flaky scalp and that may extend to the ears, face, and chest. Also known as seborrheic dermatitis.

LLM.text: A common scalp condition causing small white or yellow flakes and sometimes itching. It is often related to oily skin, seborrheic dermatitis, or the scalp's reaction to the normal yeast Malassezia; it is not usually contagious. Persistent severe flaking, redness, sores, or hair loss may indicate another scalp disorder.

Harvard.text: Painful swelling of the tendons at the wrist that move the thumb.

LLM.text: Painful inflammation or thickening of the tendons on the thumb side of the wrist, causing pain with thumb movement and gripping.

Harvard.text: Weakness or a loss of physical strength.

LLM.text: A state of weakness or loss of strength, often associated with illness, aging, or prolonged inactivity.

Harvard.text: A unit of measurement for the loudness of a sound. The highest decibels indicate the loudest sounds.

LLM.text: A logarithmic unit (dB) used to measure the intensity of sound. The decibel scale compares a given sound pressure level to a reference level (0 dB = 20 micropascals, the threshold of normal hearing at 1 kHz). The scale is logarithmic: an increase of 10 dB represents a tenfold increase in sound intensity. Normal conversation: 60 dB.

Harvard.text: Memory for facts or events (episodic memory); also called explicit memory.

LLM.text: Memory for facts and events that can be consciously recalled.

Harvard.text: An herbal product or tea made by boiling a plant in water.

LLM.text: A preparation made by simmering plant material in water to extract soluble substances.

Harvard.text: Type of medication used to relieve nasal congestion.

LLM.text: A medicine that reduces swelling of the nasal lining and relieves nasal congestion.

Harvard.text: Stage of sleep where the brain is less responsive to outside stimuli.

LLM.text: The deepest stage of non-rapid-eye-movement sleep, during which arousal is difficult and physical restoration occurs.

Harvard.text: A dangerous condition in which blood clots form in veins deep in the body, usually the legs. They may break off and block blood flow in the lungs, seriously damaging organs or causing death.

LLM.text: Formation of a blood clot in a deep vein, most often in the leg.

Harvard.text: Coping strategies a person adopts to make it easier to operate in the world.

LLM.text: The body’s protective mechanisms against infection, injury, and other threats, including physical barriers and immune responses.

Harvard.text: The delivery of an electric shock to the heart to stop an abnormal rhythm and restore a normal heartbeat.

LLM.text: Delivery of an unsynchronized electrical shock to terminate ventricular fibrillation or pulseless ventricular tachycardia by depolarizing a critical mass of myocardium. It is distinct from synchronized cardioversion, which times the shock to the QRS complex.

Harvard.text: A device that delivers an electric shock to the heart to restore normal rhythm. Used to treat cardiac arrest and other dangerous heart rhythm problems.

LLM.text: Device delivering electric shock to heart. Types: external (AED, manual), internal (implantable). Used for ventricular fibrillation, pulseless ventricular tachycardia. Energy: biphasic 120-200 J.

Harvard.text: Any disease in which the organs or tissues in the body are damaged progressively over time.

LLM.text: A disorder caused by progressive structural or functional deterioration of tissues or organs, often related to aging, wear, genetic factors, or chronic injury.

Harvard.text: Normal, and sometimes painful, deteriorations in the disks of the spine that occur with age.

LLM.text: Age-related or injury-related deterioration of an intervertebral disk that may cause back or neck pain.

Harvard.text: Arthritis that occurs when the cartilage in joints breaks down over time; also called osteoarthritis.

LLM.text: Progressive loss of cartilage and changes in a joint, commonly referring to osteoarthritis.

Harvard.text: Arthritis of the spine that worsens over time; often caused by aging.

LLM.text: Forward displacement of one vertebra over another caused by degenerative changes in the spine.

Harvard.text: A pattern of falling asleep and waking up later than wanted that tends to worsen progressively over time.

LLM.text: A circadian-rhythm disorder in which sleep and waking occur substantially later than desired.

Harvard.text: Sudden, severe confusion that occurs because of a mental or physical illness.

LLM.text: Delirium is an acute fluctuating disturbance of attention and awareness caused by an underlying medical, medication-related, toxic, or environmental factor.

Harvard.text: Slow brain activity that occurs when a person is in deep sleep.

LLM.text: Large, slow brain waves associated with deep non-REM sleep.

Harvard.text: A false or irrational belief held by a person despite evidence to the contrary.

LLM.text: A fixed belief that is not consistent with available evidence or the person’s sociocultural context and is not readily changed by reasoned discussion. Delusions may be persecutory, grandiose, referential, somatic, nihilistic, or erotomanic.

Harvard.text: A loss of brain function that worsens over time and affects memory, thinking, behavior, and language.

LLM.text: Dementia is acquired decline in one or more cognitive domains that interferes with independent function; causes include neurodegenerative, vascular, metabolic, infectious, and other disorders. Alzheimer disease, vascular disease, Lewy body disease, frontotemporal disorders, and other conditions. Evaluation is important because some causes of cognitive decline may be treatable.

Harvard.text: Loss of brain function, common among former boxers, caused by repeated blows to the head.

LLM.text: A progressive brain disorder associated with repeated head trauma, historically described in some professional boxers.

Harvard.text: The process by which bacteria destroy tooth enamel.

LLM.text: Loss of mineral from a tissue, such as tooth enamel or bone, which may weaken the tissue.

Harvard.text: A substance that soothes irritated tissues and mucous membranes.

LLM.text: A substance that soothes irritated or inflamed mucous membranes by forming a protective coating.

Harvard.text: The parts of a nerve cell that receive signals from other nerve cells.

LLM.text: Branching extensions of nerve cells that receive signals from other neurons or sensory receptors.

Harvard.text: Spidery-looking immune system cells that help protect the body from harmful substances.

LLM.text: Immune cells that capture foreign material and present antigens to T cells, helping initiate an adaptive immune response.

Harvard.text: A defense mechanism characterized by the inability to recognize or admit that addiction is the cause of problems, rather than a solution or mere byproduct. Denial can also refer to the refusal to accept an upsetting reality, such as a serious illness or death or the feelings that follow either.

LLM.text: A defense mechanism in which a person refuses to accept an unpleasant reality. It is a common initial response to traumatic events and terminal illness diagnoses. While adaptive in the short term, chronic denial can prevent appropriate medical treatment and psychological processing.

Harvard.text: A metal post inserted into the alveolar bone to support an artificial tooth or other prosthesis.

LLM.text: A biocompatible fixture placed in the jawbone to support a replacement tooth. The fixture may become integrated with surrounding bone and is restored with a crown, bridge, or denture.

Harvard.text: The layer of hardened tooth tissue under the enamel and around the pulp.

LLM.text: Calcified tissue beneath enamel forming bulk of tooth. Contains dentinal tubules with fluid and processes. Sensitive to stimuli when exposed. Reparative dentin formed in response to irritation.

Harvard.text: The substance found in the nucleus of cells that contains the genetic instructions for that living organism.

LLM.text: The molecule that stores hereditary genetic information in cells.

Harvard.text: A structure situated at the base of the hair follicle that contains nerves and blood vessels that fuel the cellular processes of the developing hair shaft.

LLM.text: A structure at the base of a hair follicle that supplies signals and nutrients important for hair growth.

Harvard.text: A rare disease in which the muscles become weak and stiff and a skin rash appears.

LLM.text: Dermatomyositis is an autoimmune inflammatory myopathy characterized by proximal muscle weakness and distinctive skin findings, with possible lung, swallowing, or cancer associations. knuckles), heliotrope rash (purple periorbital), shawl/V sign erythema, and proximal muscle weakness; associated with interstitial lung disease, and in adults an increased risk of malignancy (ovary, lung, GI).

Harvard.text: The middle layer of skin that contains most of the skin’s structures, like collagen, nerves, glands, and hair follicles.

LLM.text: Thick connective tissue layer beneath the epidermis providing structural support, elasticity, and nourishment. Two layers: papillary (superficial, loose connective tissue with dermal papillae interdigitating with epidermal ridges) and reticular (deep, dense irregular connective tissue).

Harvard.text: An extract made of dried animal thyroid glands.

LLM.text: A thyroid-hormone preparation made from dried animal thyroid tissue and containing thyroid hormones.

Harvard.text: The process of removing harmful, or toxic, substances from a person’s body.

LLM.text: Removal of toxic substance from body. Methods: activated charcoal, gastric lavage (rarely used), whole bowel irrigation, hemodialysis, hemoperfusion, chelation, supportive care.

Harvard.text: The sudden, strong need to urinate due to spasms in bladder muscles. Also called urge incontinence.

LLM.text: Involuntary bladder-muscle contractions that can cause urgency and urge incontinence.

Harvard.text: The layer of muscle in the bladder wall that squeezes urine out of the bladder.

LLM.text: The smooth muscle in the bladder wall that contracts to expel urine.

Harvard.text: The softening of an erection.

LLM.text: The return of an erectile tissue to its non-erect state.

Harvard.text: A disease in which the body does not properly produce or use insulin, resulting in abnormally high levels of sugar (glucose) in the blood.

LLM.text: Diabetes is chronic hyperglycemia caused by inadequate insulin secretion, insulin resistance, or both, with long-term risks to the eyes, kidneys, nerves, heart, and blood vessels. inadequate insulin secretion, impaired insulin action, or both. Chronic hyperglycemia can damage the eyes, kidneys, nerves, heart, and blood vessels. Major forms include type 1, type 2, and gestational diabetes.

Harvard.text: A complication of diabetes in which substances called ketones build up in the blood to dangerously high levels.

LLM.text: An acute, life-threatening complication of diabetes characterized by excessive ketone production and metabolic acidosis, usually with elevated blood glucose but sometimes with only modest glucose elevation. Triggers include infection, insufficient insulin, myocardial infarction, pancreatitis, certain medicines, fasting, or other physiologic stress.

Harvard.text: A complication of diabetes that occurs when the small blood vessels in the retina are damaged. It can impair vision or even lead to blindness.

LLM.text: A microvascular complication of diabetes mellitus and a leading cause of blindness in working-age adults. Non-proliferative DR (NPDR): microaneurysms, dot-blot hemorrhages, exudates (hard and cotton-wool spots), and venous beading. Proliferative DR (PDR): retinal neovascularization, vitreous hemorrhage, and tractional retinal detachment.

Harvard.text: The dome-shaped sheet of muscle at the base of the lungs that helps move air in and out of the lungs.

LLM.text: Dome-shaped musculotendinous partition separating thoracic/abdominal cavities, primary inspiration muscle. Central tendon with muscular periphery from xiphoid, lower six costal cartilages, and lumbar vertebrae via crura and arcuate ligaments. Innervated by phrenic nerves (C3-C5). Contraction flattens the dome increasing thoracic volume.

Harvard.text: The relaxation phase of the normal heart cycle.

LLM.text: The phase of the cardiac cycle when the heart muscle relaxes, allowing the chambers to fill with blood.

Harvard.text: The bottom number of a blood pressure reading, such as 134/78. It represents the pressure in the arteries when the heart relaxes between beats.

LLM.text: The pressure in the arteries while the heart relaxes between contractions.

Harvard.text: The inability of the heart to relax properly between beats (diastole), making it difficult for the ventricles to fill completely with blood from the atria. This can occur when the heart muscle bulks up due to overwork or other causes or when the heart muscle stiffens and loses it flexibility.

LLM.text: Heart failure in which impaired ventricular relaxation or increased stiffness limits filling of the heart.

Harvard.text: Use of high-frequency electric currents to heat deep muscle and joint tissue as a form of physical therapy.

LLM.text: The use of high-frequency electrical current to generate heat for surgical purposes, including cutting tissue, coagulating blood vessels to stop bleeding (hemostasis), and destroying abnormal tissue (electrocautery, electrocoagulation).

Harvard.text: The part of plant foods the body can’t digest or absorb. Also called roughage.

LLM.text: Plant material that is not fully digested and supports bowel function and other aspects of health.

Harvard.text: The recommended amount of vitamins and minerals individuals should consume per day.

LLM.text: Reference values for nutrient intake: RDA (Recommended Dietary Allowance), AI (Adequate Intake), UL (Tolerable Upper Intake Level), EAR (Estimated Average Requirement).

Harvard.text: Vitamins, minerals, herbs, and other substances taken in hopes of improving health.

LLM.text: Products such as vitamins, minerals, herbs, or other substances taken to supplement the diet.

Harvard.text: The series of hollow organs, including the mouth, esophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine (colon), rectum, and anus, which break down and digest food and expel waste.

LLM.text: The continuous hollow passage from the mouth through the throat, esophagus, stomach, intestines, and anus.

Harvard.text: A finger or toe.

LLM.text: A finger or toe.

Harvard.text: An exam in which a doctor inserts a lubricated, gloved finger into the rectum to check for abnormalities.

LLM.text: Examination of the rectum and nearby structures using a lubricated, gloved finger.

Harvard.text: A drug that increases the strength of heart muscle contractions.

LLM.text: A group of cardiac glycosides, including digoxin, that can increase cardiac contraction and affect heart rhythm.

Harvard.text: A form of the hormone testosterone that spurs the prostate gland to enlarge (benign prostatic hyperplasia).

LLM.text: A potent androgen formed from testosterone that contributes to prostate growth and male sexual development.

Harvard.text: To widen or enlarge.

LLM.text: To become wider or cause a passage, vessel, or opening to become wider.

Harvard.text: The immediate transfer of an infectious agent from a reservoir to a susceptible host by direct contact or droplet spread.

LLM.text: Spread of an infectious organism through immediate contact or short-range respiratory droplets from an infected source.

Harvard.text: A rare form of lupus that causes a rash or scarring of skin.

LLM.text: A chronic form of cutaneous lupus that causes persistent, inflamed skin plaques that may scar.

Harvard.text: One of the small, shock-absorbing cushions found between the bones that make up the spinal column (vertebrae).

LLM.text: A flat, round structure; in the spine, an intervertebral disk separates adjacent vertebrae and cushions movement.

Harvard.text: The surgical removal of part of a disk (a small, shock absorbing cushion located between the bones of the spinal column).

LLM.text: A surgical procedure that removes part or all of a spinal disc to relieve pressure on a spinal nerve or the spinal cord. roots or the spinal cord, causing radiculopathy or myelopathy. Indicated in severe disk herniation causing unremitting pain, progressive motor weakness, or cauda equina syndrome.

Harvard.text: Swelling of one or more of the pillow-like disks located between the bones of the spinal column.

LLM.text: Inflammation or infection of an intervertebral disc and adjacent vertebral endplates, often causing severe localized back pain and sometimes fever. usually caused by bacterial infection. It causes localized back pain, stiffness, fever, and reluctance to move, particularly in children.

Harvard.text: The movement of a bone from its normal position.

LLM.text: Complete loss of normal contact between the surfaces of a joint, usually caused by trauma or structural disease and potentially accompanied by fracture, nerve, or blood-vessel injury.

Harvard.text: A substance found in cruciferous vegetables, like cabbage, Brussels sprouts, and broccoli, which may play a role in cancer prevention.

LLM.text: A sulfur-containing compound studied for its ability to activate cellular protective and detoxification pathways.

Harvard.text: A drug that eases the heart's workload and decreases the buildup of fluid in the lungs and other parts of the body by promoting the excretion of water and salts. Diuretics (also called water pills) are used to treat high blood pressure, heart failure, and some congenital heart defects.

LLM.text: A drug that increases urine production, used for edema (heart failure, cirrhosis, renal disease), hypertension, and electrolyte disorders.

common_names: water pills) are used to treat high blood pressure, heart failure, and some congenital heart defects

Harvard.text: The bulging out of small pouches or sacs of tissue from the colon wall.

LLM.text: Diverticulitis is inflammation or infection of a diverticulum, usually in the colon, causing localized abdominal pain, fever, altered bowel habits, or complications such as abscess. diverticulosis affecting 10-25 percent of individuals with diverticula. The pathophysiology involves microperforation of a diverticulum with fecal contents entering the pericolic tissues, inciting inflammation and potential abscess formation.

Harvard.text: A small pouch or sac of tissue that bulges out of the colon wall. The plural form is diverticula.

LLM.text: A pouch-like projection from the wall of a hollow organ, especially the intestine.

Harvard.text: A substance found in citrus fruits.

LLM.text: A citrus-derived compound found in the oils of orange, lemon, and other citrus fruits.

Harvard.text: An abbreviation for deoxyribonucleic acid, the substance in cells that contains the genetic instructions that direct their function.

LLM.text: Deoxyribonucleic acid, the hereditary material in humans and most organisms. Double helix of two antiparallel strands (sugar-phosphate backbone, nitrogenous bases: A-T, G-C). Human genome: 3 billion base pairs, 20,000 protein-coding genes.

Harvard.text: Commonly used abbreviation for do-not-resuscitate order, a legal document that tells health professionals not to revive a person if his or her heart or breathing stops.

LLM.text: An abbreviation for do-not-resuscitate, indicating that cardiopulmonary resuscitation should not be attempted if breathing or heartbeat stops.

Harvard.text: When the genetic trait carried by one allele of a gene pair eclipses the trait carried by another; for example, when a gene carries alleles for two different eye colors, the dominant eye color gene determines the person’s eye color. do-not-resuscitate order: A legal document that tells health professionals not to revive a person if his or her heart or breathing stops. Commonly referred to as a DNR.

LLM.text: Allele whose phenotype is expressed in heterozygotes. Autosomal dominant disorders: Huntington disease, marfan syndrome, achondroplasia. Requires only one copy for expression.

Harvard.text: A chemical messenger (neurotransmitter) that affects movement and thought processes.

LLM.text: A neurotransmitter involved in movement, motivation, reward, attention, and regulation of several hormonal functions.

Harvard.text: A test that uses sound waves to measure how fast blood is flowing through blood vessels.

LLM.text: Ultrasound technique using the Doppler effect to evaluate blood flow. Color Doppler: direction and velocity of flow (red = toward transducer, blue = away). Spectral Doppler: waveform analysis (arterial: pulsatile; venous: continuous). Pulsed-wave: measures flow at a specific depth.

Harvard.text: Near the back of the body or an organ.

LLM.text: Relating to the back side of the body; synonym for posterior in human anatomy.

Harvard.text: A rounded or curved back caused by spinal fractures from osteoporosis. Commonly called dowager’s hump.

LLM.text: Excessive forward curvature of the upper spine, often associated with vertebral fractures or degenerative change.

Harvard.text: A medical study in which the researchers and participants don’t know which group is receiving the medication or treatment being studied and which is getting a placebo (fake, inactive version of the medication).

LLM.text: A study design in which neither participants nor the researchers assessing outcomes know who receives each intervention during the blinded phase.

Harvard.text: An x-ray test done to check for colon cancer or other bowel diseases.

LLM.text: An imaging examination of the colon using barium and air to outline the bowel wall on X-rays.

Harvard.text: A rounded or curved back (resembling a hump) caused by spinal fractures from osteoporosis.

LLM.text: An exaggerated forward curvature of the upper spine, usually thoracic kyphosis, which may result from vertebral compression fractures, osteoporosis, or degenerative changes.

Harvard.text: Medication used to treat high blood pressure or an enlarged prostate gland.

LLM.text: An alpha-1 blocker used to relax smooth muscle and treat high blood pressure or urinary symptoms from an enlarged prostate.

Harvard.text: Inflammation of the sac surrounding the heart (pericardium).

LLM.text: An inflammatory pericarditis occurring weeks after myocardial injury, such as myocardial infarction or cardiac surgery, and possibly causing fever, chest pain, or pericardial effusion.

Harvard.text: Abbreviation for dietary reference intake, the recommended amount of vitamins and minerals individuals should consume per day.

LLM.text: A set of nutrient reference values used to plan and assess dietary intake for healthy people.

Harvard.text: Tiny yellow deposits in the retina of the eye.

LLM.text: Yellowish-white deposits of extracellular material that accumulate beneath the retinal pigment epithelium between the retinal pigment epithelium basement membrane and Bruch membrane, and they are the hallmark clinical finding in dry age-related macular degeneration.

Harvard.text: Stinging, burning, or irritation that occurs when the eye doesn’t produce enough moisture.

LLM.text: A condition in which the eyes do not produce enough tears or tears evaporate too quickly, causing irritation and visual discomfort.

Harvard.text: A small device that helps a person breathe in dry medication so it reaches the lungs.

LLM.text: A device that delivers powdered medicine to the lungs when the user inhales through it.

Harvard.text: An x-ray test used to measure bone density and check for osteoporosis.

LLM.text: A low-dose imaging test that measures bone mineral density and can help assess fracture risk.

Harvard.text: A test to measure bone density, usually in the spine or the hip.

LLM.text: An older bone-density measurement technique that uses two photon energies to estimate bone mineral content.

Harvard.text: A tube or vessel in the body which carries the secretion of a gland; Secretion examples are tears, breast milk, etc.

LLM.text: A tube or channel that carries a fluid, such as bile, pancreatic juice, or secretions from a gland.

Harvard.text: Inflammation of the duodenum, which is the upper part of the small intestine.

LLM.text: Inflammation of the duodenal mucosa, caused by Helicobacter pylori infection, acid-related disease, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, infection, coeliac disease, or inflammatory bowel disease. Symptoms may include epigastric pain, nausea, vomiting, and gastrointestinal bleeding.

Harvard.text: The upper part of the small intestine.

LLM.text: Duodenum concerns duodenum, a body structure, substance, or clinical concept whose meaning depends on location, function, and patient context. Four parts. Descending part has the major duodenal papilla for bile/pancreatic duct entry via the hepatopancreatic ampulla. Brunner's glands produce alkaline mucus. Most common peptic ulcer site.

Harvard.text: A tool that uses sound waves to reveal blood flow problems.

LLM.text: An ultrasound test that combines structural imaging with Doppler measurement of blood flow through vessels.

Harvard.text: A condition that deforms the hand, causing fingers to curl toward the palm.

LLM.text: A progressive thickening and shortening of tissue in the palm that can pull one or more fingers into flexion and limit hand opening.

Harvard.text: A thin protective membrane covering the brain and spinal cord.

LLM.text: The outermost, thickest meningeal layer, a tough fibrous membrane. In the cranium it is two layers: periosteal (outer, adherent to skull) and meningeal (inner), which separate to form dural venous sinuses (e.g., superior sagittal, cavernous). Dural folds: falx cerebri, tentorium cerebelli, falx cerebelli.

Harvard.text: A legal document in which an individual appoints another person to make medical, financial, or other decisions when the individual becomes unable to make those decisions.

LLM.text: A legal authorization allowing a designated person to act or make decisions for another person when specified conditions are met. In healthcare, it may appoint a healthcare proxy.

Harvard.text: A speech disability caused by an injury to the brain centers controlling the face, mouth, neck, or throat. People with dysarthria may be able to understand speech and form the right words in their mind but cannot articulate them.

LLM.text: Impaired clarity, strength, or coordination of speech caused by dysfunction of the muscles or nervous pathways used for speaking. components of speech production, including the lips, tongue, palate, vocal cords, and respiratory muscles.

Harvard.text: Painful sexual intercourse.

LLM.text: Painful sexual intercourse.

Harvard.text: Pain or discomfort in the upper abdomen; upset stomach or indigestion.

LLM.text: Chronic or recurrent pain or discomfort centered in the upper abdomen. Organic causes: peptic ulcer disease, GERD, gastritis, gastric cancer. Functional dyspepsia is diagnosed after exclusion of organic pathology with normal upper endoscopy. Rome IV criteria define subtypes: epigastric pain syndrome and postprandial distress syndrome.

Harvard.text: Difficulty chewing and swallowing food. Dysphagia is extremely common after a stroke.

LLM.text: Difficulty swallowing, classified as oropharyngeal (difficulty initiating a swallow, choking, coughing, nasal regurgitation) or esophageal (sensation of food sticking retrosternally).

Harvard.text: Abnormal changes in cells of a tissue. The cells aren’t cancerous, but they can sometimes progress to cancer.

LLM.text: Disordered cellular growth and maturation characterized by structural abnormalities within a tissue, representing a pre-neoplastic condition that may progress to invasive carcinoma.

Harvard.text: Difficulty breathing or shortness of breath.

LLM.text: The subjective sensation of difficult or uncomfortable breathing. See Shortness of Breath. It may result from cardiopulmonary, metabolic, neuromuscular, or psychological causes.

Harvard.text: A disorder in which muscles twitch, causing uncontrollable twisting movements.

LLM.text: A movement disorder characterized by sustained or intermittent muscle contractions causing abnormal, often repetitive, movements and postures.

Harvard.text: A tube leading from the eardrum to the outer ear.

LLM.text: A tube leading from the eardrum to the outer ear.

Harvard.text: A thin membrane separating the ear canal and middle ear.

LLM.text: A thin membrane separating the ear canal and middle ear.

Harvard.text: A substance that lubricates the inner ear and helps protect it from dirt, damage, and infections.

LLM.text: Cerumen, a waxy secretion produced by the ceruminous glands in the outer third of the external auditory canal. Earwax lubricates and protects the skin of the ear canal, trapping dust, debris, and microorganisms to prevent them from reaching the tympanic membrane.

Harvard.text: Abbreviation for electron-beam computed tomography, a high-speed imaging technology use to evaluate the heart and measure calcium deposits in arteries.

LLM.text: Electron-beam computed tomography, a rapid imaging method used especially to assess the heart and calcium in coronary arteries.

Harvard.text: When muscles move joints by lengthening. Also known as cerumen.

LLM.text: Muscle action in which a muscle produces force while lengthening.

Harvard.text: An abbreviation for electrocardiogram, a test that measures the electrical activity of the heart and detects heart problems.

LLM.text: A recording of the heart’s electrical activity used to evaluate rhythm and other cardiac problems.

Harvard.text: A diagnostic tool that uses high-frequency sound waves (ultrasound) to make images of the heart's size, structure and motion.

LLM.text: Ultrasound imaging of the heart, the primary modality for assessing cardiac structure and function. Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) is the most common approach; transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) provides better views of posterior structures (left atrium, mitral valve, aorta).

Harvard.text: A serious condition related to high blood pressure that can threaten the life of a pregnant woman and her fetus.

LLM.text: Eclampsia is a new-onset seizure during pregnancy or the postpartum period associated with preeclampsia or pregnancy-related hypertension. It is an emergency requiring airway and blood-pressure management, magnesium sulfate for seizure prevention or treatment, and urgent obstetric planning.

Harvard.text: Pregnancy in which a fertilized egg implants in an abnormal location outside the uterus, usually in the fallopian tubes. Ending the pregnancy is necessary.

LLM.text: Implantation of a fertilized ovum outside the uterine cavity, most commonly in the fallopian tube (95\%). Risk factors: prior ectopic, PID, tubal surgery, IUD, smoking, and assisted reproductive technology. Presents with lower abdominal pain, amenorrhea, and vaginal bleeding. Rupture causes hemodynamic instability.

Harvard.text: When an eyelid, usually the lower one, flips outward so that the inner surface is exposed.

LLM.text: Ectropion is outward turning of an eyelid, usually the lower lid, causing tearing, irritation, dryness, and incomplete eyelid closure. It may be involutional, paralytic, cicatricial, or mechanical; persistent corneal exposure can damage vision.

Harvard.text: A condition in which areas of the skin are dry, itchy, red, and cracked. Also known as atopic dermatitis.

LLM.text: A group of inflammatory skin conditions characterized by pruritic, erythematous, scaly patches. Atopic dermatitis is the most common form. Nummular eczema presents as coin-shaped lesions. Dyshidrotic eczema affects palms and soles with vesicles. Eczema herpeticum is a disseminated HSV infection in eczema patients, a medical emergency.

Harvard.text: Commonly used abbreviation for erectile dysfunction, the inability to get or maintain an erection sufficient for intercourse.

LLM.text: Erectile dysfunction: inability to obtain or maintain an erection adequate for sexual activity.

Harvard.text: Swelling caused by abnormal accumulation of fluid in tissues.

LLM.text: Swelling caused by excess fluid trapped in body tissues. Types: pitting (press leaves indentation), non-pitting (myxedema, lymphedema). Causes: heart failure, kidney disease, liver cirrhosis, venous insufficiency, lymphatic obstruction, medications (calcium channel blockers, NSAIDs).

Harvard.text: Abbreviation for electroencephalogram, a test that measures the electrical activity of the brain and detects problems.

LLM.text: An EEG records electrical activity generated by the brain through scalp electrodes and helps evaluate seizures, encephalopathy, and selected sleep or neurologic disorders.

Harvard.text: An abnormal buildup of fluid in a joint or tissue.

LLM.text: Abnormal accumulation of fluid in a body space, such as a joint, pleural cavity, or pericardial sac.

Harvard.text: A nerve responsible transmitting sound and information about balance to the brain. Also called the auditory nerve.

LLM.text: The vestibulocochlear nerve, which carries hearing and balance signals from the inner ear to the brain.

Harvard.text: A sudden discharge of a fluid from a duct; often used to describe the expulsion of seminal fluid from the urethra of the penis during orgasm.

LLM.text: The expulsion of seminal fluid from the male urethra during sexual climax, a reflex coordinated by the sympathetic nervous system (T10-L2) and involving contraction of the epididymis, vas deferens, seminal vesicles, prostate, and bulbospongiosus muscle.

Harvard.text: The percent of blood pumped out of the left ventricle with each heartbeat. A normal ejection fraction is in the range of 55% to 70%.

LLM.text: The percentage of blood in a ventricle ejected during contraction, calculated as stroke volume divided by end-diastolic volume. It helps describe ventricular systolic function and classify some forms of heart failure, but it does not measure filling pressures, congestion, symptoms, or overall heart-failure severity by itself. Interpretation depends on the ventricle studied, imaging method, clinical findings, and applicable definitions.

Harvard.text: An abbreviation for electrocardiogram, a test that measures the electrical activity of the heart and detects heart problems.

LLM.text: A recording of the heart’s electrical activity.

Harvard.text: A flexible, stretchy protein found in skin and connective tissue.

LLM.text: A flexible connective-tissue protein that allows skin, blood vessels, and other tissues to stretch and recoil.

Harvard.text: A test that measures the electrical activity of the heart and detects heart problems.

LLM.text: An electrocardiogram records the heart’s electrical signals and helps identify rhythm disturbances, conduction disease, ischemia, infarction, and chamber strain.

Harvard.text: A test that measures the electrical activity of the brain and detects problems.

LLM.text: EEG: a recording of electrical activity of the brain via scalp electrodes, reflecting cortical neuronal activity. Uses: diagnosis and classification of seizures/epilepsy (interictal epileptiform discharges, spikes/waves), status epilepticus monitoring, assessment of encephalopathy, sleep disorders, and determination of brain death.

Harvard.text: A permanent hair removal technique that destroys follicles one at a time with a hair-thin needle inserted into the base of the follicle.

LLM.text: Permanent hair removal using electrical energy delivered through a fine probe into a hair follicle.

Harvard.text: Minerals in the body that are electrically charged and play an important role in body processes, such as regulating fluid levels in the body. Examples include calcium and sodium.

LLM.text: A mineral that carries an electrical charge in body fluids, such as sodium, potassium, or calcium.

Harvard.text: A test that checks the health of muscles and the nerves that control them.

LLM.text: A test that records the electrical activity of skeletal muscles, often together with nerve-conduction studies, to evaluate peripheral nerve, nerve-root, neuromuscular-junction, and muscle disorders.

Harvard.text: A high-speed imaging technology use to evaluate the heart and measure calcium deposits in arteries. Sometimes referred to as EBCT.

LLM.text: A rapid computed-tomography technique used to image the heart and detect calcium deposits in arteries.

Harvard.text: A procedure used to provoke known or suspected arrhythmias.

LLM.text: A procedure that records or provokes electrical activity in the heart to investigate suspected arrhythmias.

Harvard.text: A way of diagnosing food allergies in which suspected foods are removed from the diet one at a time until the food causing a problem is found.

LLM.text: Diets in which suspected foods are removed and later reintroduced to help identify food-related symptoms.

Harvard.text: A chemical found in certain plants, such as raspberries and strawberries, that might help protect against cancer.

LLM.text: A plant-derived polyphenol found in foods such as berries and nuts.

Harvard.text: A type of stroke that occurs when a blood clot that has formed elsewhere in the body breaks off and travels through the bloodstream until it blocks an artery that normally supplies blood to the brain.

LLM.text: An ischemic stroke caused by a clot or other material that travels from elsewhere and blocks a brain artery.

Harvard.text: Blockage of a blood vessel by a clot (an embolus) that has traveled from another part of the body.

LLM.text: An embolism is the occlusion of a blood vessel by a detached mass that has traveled through the bloodstream from its site of origin. The most common form is thromboembolism, where a fragment of a thrombus dislodges and travels to a distant site through the venous or arterial circulation.

Harvard.text: A blood clot or particle that forms in one part of the body then moves through the bloodstream and lodges in a blood vessel elsewhere, blocking blood flow.

LLM.text: A detached intravascular mass, such as a blood clot, fat droplet, air bubble, or other material, that travels through the circulation and may obstruct a vessel.

Harvard.text: Any drug or other substance used to cause vomiting.

LLM.text: A substance that induces vomiting.

Harvard.text: Abbreviation for electromyography—a test that checks the health of muscles and the nerves that control them.

LLM.text: A test that evaluates muscle activity and the nerves controlling muscles.

Harvard.text: The discharge or release of a substance, usually a fluid.

LLM.text: The discharge or release of a substance, usually a fluid. In male reproduction, emission refers to the movement of semen into the posterior urethra in preparation for ejaculation.

Harvard.text: Herbs that stimulate menstrual blood flow.

LLM.text: A substance traditionally used to stimulate menstrual flow.

Harvard.text: The hard outside layer of tooth material.

LLM.text: Hard, highly mineralized outer layer of tooth crown. Avascular, aneural, cannot regenerate. Enamel hypoplasia causes defects. Dental caries begins in enamel. Fluoride strengthens enamel.

Harvard.text: A severe and sometimes deadly inflammation of the brain that can be caused by a number of different viruses.

LLM.text: Encephalitis is inflammation of brain tissue, often infectious or autoimmune, causing altered mental status, seizures, fever, focal deficits, or movement abnormalities. fever, headache, altered mental status, seizures, or focal neurologic deficits and requires urgent medical evaluation.

Harvard.text: A multistage process by which sensation, perception, or thought is transformed into neural representations that can be stored in memory.

LLM.text: The process by which sensory or cognitive information is converted into a form that can be stored in memory.

Harvard.text: Surgical removal of plaque or blood clots in an artery.

LLM.text: Surgical removal of atherosclerotic plaque and diseased inner lining from an artery to improve blood flow, commonly performed in the carotid arteries.

Harvard.text: Continually present among people in a geographic region.

LLM.text: Regular presence of a disease or infectious agent in a particular population or geographic area at an expected baseline level.

Harvard.text: An inflammation of the heart lining or valves, usually caused by bacterial infection.

LLM.text: Endocarditis is infection or inflammation of the endocardium, usually involving heart valves, and may cause fever, emboli, valve destruction, and heart failure. Acute bacterial endocarditis: Staph aureus (most common in IV drug users and prosthetic valves), rapid destruction. Subacute: viridans group streptococci (pre-existing valve disease).

Harvard.text: The inner layer of the wall of the heart.

LLM.text: The innermost layer of the heart wall, a thin membrane of endothelial cells and underlying connective tissue that lines the cardiac chambers and covers the heart valves. The endocardium is continuous with the endothelium of blood vessels and provides a smooth, non-thrombogenic surface.

Harvard.text: Painkilling substances made by the body.

LLM.text: Pain-relieving opioid peptides produced naturally by the body.

Harvard.text: The lining of the uterus.

LLM.text: The lining of the uterus.

Harvard.text: Substances in the body that reduce pain and create a feeling of well-being.

LLM.text: Natural opioid peptides that reduce pain and can contribute to feelings of well-being.

Harvard.text: A thin, flexible tube equipped with a light and camera that is used to see inside an organ or body cavity.

LLM.text: A flexible or rigid instrument with a light and camera used to inspect an internal body passage or cavity and sometimes perform procedures. bronchoscope, colonoscope, gastroscope, arthroscope, cystoscope. Essential for diagnosis and intervention.

Harvard.text: Inserting a flexible tube equipped with a light and camera into the body to see inside a body cavity or organ.

LLM.text: Examination of an internal body passage or cavity with an endoscope; tissue sampling and treatment may be performed during the procedure. endoscopes. Upper endoscopy examines the esophagus, stomach, and duodenum. Colonoscopy examines the colon and terminal ileum. Both allow direct visualization, biopsy, and therapeutic interventions including polypectomy, hemostasis, and dilation.

Harvard.text: Proteins that cause blood vessels to narrow and blood pressure to rise.

LLM.text: Peptides made by vascular endothelium that constrict blood vessels and can raise blood pressure.

Harvard.text: Chemicals in the body that cause blood vessels to expand or relax, lowering blood pressure. Often referred to as EDRF.

LLM.text: A substance released by the endothelium that relaxes blood vessels; it is largely identified with nitric oxide.

Harvard.text: Complete, or nearly complete, kidney failure. Dialysis or a transplant is needed for survival.

LLM.text: The final stage of chronic kidney disease (CKD stage 5), defined by GFR <15 mL/min/1.73 $m^2$ or the need for renal replacement therapy. Uremia develops with accumulation of toxins causing nausea, anorexia, pruritus, pericarditis, encephalopathy, and bleeding diathesis.

Harvard.text: A chemical produced in the brain that reduces pain.

LLM.text: An endogenous opioid peptide involved in reducing pain.

Harvard.text: Part of the nervous system that controls the gastrointestinal system.

LLM.text: The network of nerve cells in the gastrointestinal tract that regulates movement, secretion, and local blood flow.

Harvard.text: Disease affecting the intestinal tract.

LLM.text: Relating to disease of the intestine.

Harvard.text: A place where a ligament, tendon, or muscle attaches to bone.

LLM.text: The site at which a tendon, ligament, or joint capsule attaches to bone.

Harvard.text: An eyelid, usually the lower lid, which folds inward so that the eyelashes rub against and irritate the surface of the eye.

LLM.text: Inward turning of an eyelid margin, causing eyelashes to rub the eye and produce irritation, tearing, corneal injury, or infection.

Harvard.text: A substance that speeds up another chemical reaction. For example, digestive enzymes help speed up the digestion of food.

LLM.text: Enzyme concerns enzyme, a body structure, substance, or clinical concept whose meaning depends on location, function, and patient context. activation energy. Specificity: lock-and-key or induced fit models. Kinetics: Michaelis-Menten equation (Vmax, Km). Regulation: allosteric control, covalent modification (phosphorylation), proteolytic activation, feedback inhibition.

Harvard.text: White blood cells that play an important role in allergic reactions.

LLM.text: White blood cells involved in allergic inflammation and defense against some parasites.

Harvard.text: The outer layer of the wall of the heart.

LLM.text: The outermost layer of the heart wall, which is the visceral layer of the serous pericardium. It consists of a single layer of mesothelial cells and underlying connective tissue containing blood vessels, nerves, and adipose tissue. The epicardium produces pericardial fluid that lubricates the heart surface.

Harvard.text: Pain and swelling in the tendons in the elbow, usually because of overuse.

LLM.text: Painful inflammation or degeneration of a tendon attachment near a joint epicondyle, commonly at the elbow.

Harvard.text: The occurrence of more cases of disease than expected within a population in a geographic area over a set period of time.

LLM.text: Sudden increase in disease cases above expected level. Examples: cholera outbreak, measles outbreak.

Harvard.text: An investigation of the links between certain behaviors or risk factors and the occurrence of disease or good health in a population.

LLM.text: A population-based investigation of disease occurrence, causes, risks, or health outcomes.

Harvard.text: The outermost layer of skin.

LLM.text: Outermost skin layer, stratified squamous keratinized epithelium approximately 0.1 mm thick, with five layers (superficial to deep): stratum corneum (dead keratinized cells), lucidum (clear layer, thick skin only), granulosum (keratinization begins), spinosum (spiny layer, Langerhans cells), basale (stem cells, melanocytes, Merkel cells).

Harvard.text: The space between the spinal cord and the bones of the spinal column where painkillers are injected.

LLM.text: The space outside the dura mater around the spinal cord, where local anesthetic may be injected.

Harvard.text: A chemical that narrows blood vessels, increases heart rate, and helps trigger the fight-or-flight response to danger. Also called adrenaline.

LLM.text: A hormone and neurotransmitter that increases heart activity and narrows many blood vessels during stress.

Harvard.text: A device used to inject a dose of medication (epinephrine) when a severe allergic reaction occurs.

LLM.text: A brand of epinephrine auto-injector used for emergency treatment of anaphylaxis and other severe allergic reactions; emergency medical care is still required after use.

Harvard.text: Cells which line organs and structures in the body, protecting or enclosing them.

LLM.text: Cells that cover body surfaces and line organs, cavities, and glands.

Harvard.text: A layer of cells which lines organs and structures in the body, protecting or enclosing them.

LLM.text: Epithelium concerns epithelium, a body structure, substance, or clinical concept whose meaning depends on location, function, and patient context. body (skin, mucous membranes, serous membranes) and form glands.

Harvard.text: The inability to get or maintain an erection sufficient for intercourse. Sometimes referred to as ED.

LLM.text: Erectile dysfunction is recurrent or persistent difficulty achieving or maintaining a penile erection firm enough for satisfactory sexual activity. It may result from vascular, neurological, hormonal, structural, medication-related, psychological, or mixed causes. Associated conditions include cardiovascular disease, diabetes, hypogonadism, neurological disorders, Peyronie disease, anxiety, depression, and relationship or other psychosocial factors.

Harvard.text: A group of muscles and tendons in the back.

LLM.text: A group of muscles running along the back that extend and stabilize the spine.

Harvard.text: Designing and arranging work objects so that the user is comfortable, efficient, and less likely to be injured.

LLM.text: The design of tasks, tools, and environments to fit human capabilities and reduce discomfort, error, and injury.

Harvard.text: Substances derived from or made from a fungus; often used to treat headache.

LLM.text: Compounds derived from a fungus and used in some treatments, including certain headache disorders.

Harvard.text: The act of bringing up air from the stomach through the mouth with a characteristic sound. Commonly known as belching.

LLM.text: The release of swallowed or stomach gas through the mouth.

Harvard.text: Redness of the skin because of widening of capillaries just below the surface of the skin.

LLM.text: Redness of the skin or mucous membranes caused by increased blood flow to dilated superficial capillaries, often associated with inflammation, infection, or another underlying condition. It commonly blanches with pressure, unlike purpura.

Harvard.text: Painful, red lumps beneath the skin; associated with Crohn's disease.

LLM.text: The most common form of panniculitis, characterized by painful, erythematous, tender nodules and plaques on the bilateral shins, representing an inflammatory reaction of the subcutaneous fat.

Harvard.text: A test involving red blood cells; used to check for different infections, inflammations, and cancers.

LLM.text: A non-specific inflammatory marker measuring the rate at which erythrocytes settle in 1 hour. Normals: males age/2, females (age+10)/2. Markedly elevated >100 mm/hr: suggests infection (endocarditis), autoimmune (giant cell arteritis, polymyalgia rheumatica, SLE, RA), malignancy (multiple myeloma), and chronic kidney disease.

Harvard.text: A hormone that controls red blood cell production.

LLM.text: A glycoprotein hormone (EPO) that regulates erythropoiesis--the production of red blood cells in the bone marrow. Produced primarily by interstitial peritubular cells in the kidney ( 90\%) and hepatocytes ( 10\%) in response to tissue hypoxia.

Harvard.text: A test to measure the pressure inside the lower part of the esophagus.

LLM.text: Diagnostic test measuring esophageal motor function by recording intraluminal pressures during swallowing. A catheter with pressure sensors is passed through the nose into the stomach and withdrawn to record pressures at multiple levels. High-resolution manometry using closely spaced sensors provides a spatiotemporal color plot.

Harvard.text: Irritation and swelling of the esophagus.

LLM.text: Esophagitis is inflammation or injury of the esophageal lining caused by reflux, infection, medication, allergy, radiation, or other mechanisms.

Harvard.text: The tube that carries food and liquids from the mouth to the stomach.

LLM.text: A muscular tube that transports food and liquids from the pharynx (throat) to the stomach.

Harvard.text: Two fatty acids, omega-3 and omega-6, that the body needs for good health but can’t make so they must come from foods and supplements.

LLM.text: Fatty acids that the body cannot make in sufficient amounts and must obtain from food.

Harvard.text: High blood pressure with no known cause; also called primary hypertension.

LLM.text: Persistent elevation of systemic arterial blood pressure without an identifiable single secondary cause. It results from interacting genetic, vascular, renal, metabolic, and environmental factors and increases the risk of stroke, coronary disease, heart failure, kidney disease, and retinopathy.

Harvard.text: Artificially made hormones used to manage menopausal symptoms.

LLM.text: Estrogen compounds used in some hormone treatments.

Harvard.text: A person who specializes in non-medical skin care and beauty treatments.

LLM.text: A person trained in nonmedical skin-care and cosmetic treatments.

Harvard.text: The primary form of the sex hormone estrogen produced by women.

LLM.text: The principal biologically active estrogen hormone during the reproductive years.

Harvard.text: The main sex hormone in women.

LLM.text: A group of steroid hormones involved in reproductive development, menstrual regulation, bone health, and other physiologic functions.

Harvard.text: A site on the surface of some cells to which estrogen molecules attach.

LLM.text: A cellular protein that binds estrogen and mediates its effects on target tissues.

Harvard.text: Use of medications containing the sex hormone estrogen by women to replace naturally-occurring estrogen lost during menopause.

LLM.text: Treatment using estrogen to replace hormone lost during menopause or because of ovarian failure.

Harvard.text: A medication used to treat bone loss due to Paget's disease.

LLM.text: A bisphosphonate used in selected conditions involving abnormal bone remodeling.

Harvard.text: A tube connecting the middle ear and the back of the nose that lets air into the middle ear.

LLM.text: Auditory/pharyngotympanic tube connecting the middle ear to the nasopharynx, approximately 36 mm long in adults. Cartilaginous medial two-thirds and bony lateral third. Functions: equalizing middle ear/atmospheric pressure, draining middle ear secretions, and protecting from nasopharyngeal pathogens.

Harvard.text: Having a thyroid gland that works properly.

LLM.text: Having normal thyroid function.

Harvard.text: A chemical that forwards a message from one neuron to another.

LLM.text: A chemical messenger that increases the likelihood that a receiving neuron will generate a signal.

Harvard.text: A brain chemical that damages neurons.

LLM.text: A substance that overstimulates neurons and can injure or kill them.

Harvard.text: The component of thinking that organizes, plans, decides, and inhibits inappropriate impulses.

LLM.text: Mental abilities used to plan, organize, make decisions, control impulses, and adapt behavior.

Harvard.text: A structured program of physical activity that helps an individual become physically fit.

LLM.text: Planned physical activity performed to improve or maintain fitness and health.

Harvard.text: The use of a treadmill, stationary bicycle, or other exercise machine while hooked up to heart-monitoring equipment. The test is used to determine if the heart's blood supply is sufficient and if the rhythm remains normal when the heart is stressed.

LLM.text: A noninvasive cardiac diagnostic test that evaluates the cardiovascular response to graded physical exertion, primarily used to diagnose coronary artery disease, assess functional capacity, and guide prognosis.

Harvard.text: A protrusion or bulging of the eye that occurs with Graves’ eye disease. Tissues behind the eye swell, forcing the eyeball forward. Also called proptosis.

LLM.text: Abnormal protrusion of the eyeball (globe) from the orbit, most commonly caused by thyroid eye disease (Graves ophthalmopathy--an autoimmune condition associated with hyperthyroidism). The proptosis results from inflammation, edema, and fibrosis of the extraocular muscles and proliferation of orbital fat within the fixed bony orbit.

Harvard.text: Abnormal bony growths in the ear caused by swimming regularly in cold water. Sometimes called surfer's ear.

LLM.text: A benign bony growth; in the ear canal, repeated cold-water exposure can cause surfer’s ear.

Harvard.text: A research technique for learning about people’s activity patterns and psychological processes that involves paging them at random times to obtain brief reports.

LLM.text: A research method that collects brief reports about a person’s activities or feelings at randomly selected times.

Harvard.text: A common phenomenon whereby people jump to a different expression of addiction. For example, people with heroin addiction might transition to alcohol addiction. Hopping is especially common during the recovery process.

LLM.text: A shift from one manifestation of an addiction to another, such as from substance use to compulsive gambling.

Harvard.text: The specific way in which a person manifests addiction, for example, through the use of cocaine, or compulsive gambling.

LLM.text: The particular behavior or substance through which an addiction is manifested.

Harvard.text: To straighten out a joint (for example, extending the arms overhead).

LLM.text: To straighten a joint or increase the angle between bones.

Harvard.text: An infection or irritation of the outer ear, ear canal, or both. Also called swimmer’s ear.

LLM.text: Inflammation or infection of the outer ear canal, commonly called swimmer's ear.

Harvard.text: A surgical technique to remove a cataract from the eye.

LLM.text: Cataract surgery that removes the cloudy lens while leaving the lens capsule largely in place.

Harvard.text: A product made from substances that are drawn out of a plant or herb.

LLM.text: A concentrated preparation made by drawing active substances from a plant, herb, or other source.

Harvard.text: Six paired muscles that direct the eyes’ circular, side-to-side, and up-and-down movements.

LLM.text: Six muscles controlling eye movement: four rectus (superior, inferior, medial, lateral) and two oblique (superior, inferior).

Harvard.text: An outside factor that has an effect on a person’s environment or well-being.

LLM.text: An outside influence that affects a person, tissue, or biological process.

Harvard.text: Paired joints that link a vertebra to its neighboring vertebrae. They allow the spine to move as a unit.

LLM.text: Zygapophysial joints connecting adjacent vertebral articular processes. Orientation varies: cervical (45 degrees, allowing rotation), thoracic (coronal, allowing rotation but limiting flexion/extension), lumbar (sagittal, allowing flexion/extension but limiting rotation). Innervated by medial branches of dorsal rami.

Harvard.text: Surgical destruction of certain nerves and nerve roots to relieve pain.

LLM.text: A procedure that interrupts selected sensory nerves supplying spinal facet joints to reduce chronic pain.

Harvard.text: Test results that show that a disease or substance isn’t present, even though it is.

LLM.text: A test result that indicates a condition is absent when it is actually present.

Harvard.text: An inherited disorder in which the liver overproduces very low-density lipoprotein, causing high levels of cholesterol or triglycerides, or both.

LLM.text: An inherited disorder causing elevated cholesterol, triglycerides, or both.

Harvard.text: An inherited disorder in which the liver cannot properly remove low-density lipoprotein particles from the blood, causing a very high cholesterol level.

LLM.text: An inherited disorder causing persistently high low-density lipoprotein cholesterol, usually because of impaired LDL-receptor pathway function. It increases the risk of premature atherosclerotic disease; diagnosis uses lipid levels, family history, physical findings, and genetic testing when available.

Harvard.text: A laboratory test to determine the relative levels of high-density lipoprotein, low-density lipoprotein, and total cholesterol in the blood. Also referred to as a lipoprotein analysis, full lipid profile, or cholesterol profile.

LLM.text: A blood test measuring cholesterol and triglyceride levels, usually after fasting.

Harvard.text: A blood test that determines the amount of sugar (glucose) in the blood after an overnight fast of at least eight hours.

LLM.text: A blood test that measures glucose after fasting and helps diagnose diabetes or impaired glucose regulation.

Harvard.text: One of two main types of skeletal muscle fibers. Fast-twitch fibers are recruited most heavily when bursts of power are needed, as in sprinting. See also slow-twitch fiber.

LLM.text: A skeletal-muscle fiber specialized for rapid, powerful contractions.

Harvard.text: One of the three major nutrients, along with carbohydrates and proteins.

LLM.text: A nutrient and energy source composed mainly of lipids.

Harvard.text: A lack of energy. A decrease over time in the ability to perform a physical or mental task.

LLM.text: Fatigue is a persistent sense of low energy or reduced capacity that may result from sleep problems, anemia, infection, endocrine disease, medication, mood disorder, or systemic illness. relieved by rest. It may result from sleep disturbance, anemia, infection, endocrine disease, chronic organ disease, medication exposure, or psychological and neurological conditions.

Harvard.text: Components of fats that can be used for energy by cells.

LLM.text: Organic components of fats used for energy and for building cell membranes and signaling molecules.

Harvard.text: The first stage of atherosclerosis, a build-up of fatty materials in the wall of a blood vessel.

LLM.text: An early atherosclerotic lesion formed by lipid accumulation in an artery wall.

Harvard.text: Feverish; having a high body temperature.

LLM.text: Feverish; having a high body temperature.

Harvard.text: A mass of dry, hard stool that gets lodged in the rectum.

LLM.text: A large, firm mass of stool retained in the rectum or colon that cannot be evacuated normally. It may cause abdominal or rectal pain, distention, overflow diarrhoea, urinary symptoms, nausea, or bowel obstruction and is associated with constipation, immobility, dehydration, neurological disease, and medications.

Harvard.text: A test that checks for colorectal cancer by detecting blood in the stool.

LLM.text: A stool test that detects small amounts of blood that are not visible to the naked eye. Methods include chemical guaiac testing and immunochemical testing such as FIT. It may be used for colorectal-cancer screening or evaluation of suspected gastrointestinal blood loss, but it is not diagnostic by itself; a positive result requires clinical follow-up and often colon evaluation.

Harvard.text: Thigh bone.

LLM.text: Longest, heaviest, strongest body bone. Proximal: head, neck, trochanters. Shaft: linea aspera. Distal: condyles, epicondyles. The neck connects head to shaft at approximately 125 degrees.

Harvard.text: A protein that captures and stores iron.

LLM.text: Intracellular iron storage protein reflecting total body iron stores. Low ferritin: iron deficiency anemia (<30 ng/mL, absolute; <100 can be consistent with iron deficiency in inflammation).

Harvard.text: A collection of birth defects resulting from exposure of the fetus to alcohol during pregnancy.

LLM.text: A collection of birth defects resulting from exposure of the fetus to alcohol during pregnancy, representing the most severe form of fetal alcohol spectrum disorder (FASD).

Harvard.text: A substance found in plant foods that the body can’t digest.

LLM.text: Fiber concerns fiber, a body structure, substance, or clinical concept whose meaning depends on location, function, and patient context. cholesterol, blood glucose. Insoluble (whole grains, vegetables) adds bulk, prevents constipation. Recommended: 25-30 g/day.

Harvard.text: Rapid and uncoordinated contractions of heart muscle fibers. When this occurs, the heart can't properly contract or pump blood.

LLM.text: Rapid, irregular, and uncoordinated contraction of muscle fibers. Atrial fibrillation causes an irregular atrial rhythm; ventricular fibrillation is a cardiac arrest rhythm requiring immediate resuscitation.

Harvard.text: A stringy protein that is the primary component of a blood clot.

LLM.text: A threadlike protein that forms the structural mesh of a blood clot.

Harvard.text: A protein that helps stop bleeding by aiding in forming blood clots.

LLM.text: A soluble plasma protein, also called coagulation factor I, that is converted to fibrin during blood clot formation. Its concentration may increase with inflammation and decrease with severe liver disease or consumption coagulopathy.

Harvard.text: A tumor that is not cancer; usually found in the breast.

LLM.text: The most common benign tumor of the female breast, a proliferation of stromal and epithelial elements presenting as a firm, rubbery, smooth, mobile, painless mass, most often in women aged fifteen to thirty. The mass slips easily under the fingers (breast mouse), and ultrasonography shows a well-defined oval hypoechoic lesion.

Harvard.text: A cell that helps form the collagen and elastic fibers of connective tissue.

LLM.text: A connective-tissue cell that produces collagen and other extracellular-matrix components.

Harvard.text: A tumor that is not cancer, which is found in the uterus.

LLM.text: A benign smooth-muscle tumor, most often arising in the uterus.

Harvard.text: A condition causing pain and tender spots throughout the body.

LLM.text: Fibromyalgia is a chronic pain-amplification disorder with widespread pain, fatigue, unrefreshing sleep, and cognitive symptoms without a single defining tissue lesion. months), fatigue, sleep disturbance, cognitive dysfunction (fibro fog), and somatic symptoms, affecting 2-4\% of population (female:male 9:1).

Harvard.text: A buildup of fat on the inside of a blood vessel that interferes with blood flow.

LLM.text: A raised arterial lesion containing fibrous tissue and lipid that can narrow the vessel.

Harvard.text: The calf bone.

LLM.text: Slender lateral leg bone, not weight-bearing, serving for muscle attachment and forming the lateral malleolus. Head provides biceps femoris and lateral collateral ligament attachment; the common peroneal nerve wraps around its neck, vulnerable to injury. Lateral malleolus extends more distally and posteriorly than the medial malleolus.

Harvard.text: A procedure to treat glaucoma in which a surgeon creates a drainage hole in the eye to relieve pressure.

LLM.text: An operation that creates an alternate drainage pathway to lower pressure inside the eye, usually in glaucoma.

Harvard.text: A medication for treating benign prostatic hyperplasia (enlargement of the prostate gland).

LLM.text: A 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor used for benign prostatic enlargement and some types of hair loss.

Harvard.text: An area where two bones meet that is fixed, or doesn’t move.

LLM.text: A joint with little or no movement, often because bones are joined by dense tissue.

Harvard.text: Soft, not erect.

LLM.text: Relaxed, soft, or lacking normal muscle tone or erection.

Harvard.text: Reappearance or worsening of symptoms.

LLM.text: A temporary worsening or recurrence of symptoms.

Harvard.text: A condition in which the arch is flat all the time or flattens when bearing weight.

LLM.text: Reduction or absence of the medial longitudinal arch, causing the sole to approach or contact the ground during standing. Flexible flat feet are common and often asymptomatic; rigid or painful flat feet may result from structural deformity, tendon dysfunction, or arthritis.

Harvard.text: Excess gas in the stomach or intestines that is expelled from the anus.

LLM.text: Passage of intestinal gas through the anus. It reflects swallowed air and bacterial fermentation of undigested carbohydrates and may be increased by dietary factors, constipation, malabsorption, altered gut motility, or functional gastrointestinal disorders; persistent symptoms require assessment for associated disease.

Harvard.text: Gas expelled through the anus.

LLM.text: Gas passed through the anus.

Harvard.text: Chemicals found in fruits, vegetables, wine, and tea that may protect cells from damage and have health benefits.

LLM.text: Plant polyphenols found in many fruits, vegetables, teas, and other foods.

Harvard.text: Bend a joint (for example, flexing the knees).

LLM.text: To bend a joint and decrease the angle between its bones.

Harvard.text: A component of physical fitness that refers to the range of motion available at a joint.

LLM.text: The range through which a joint or group of joints can move, influenced by muscles, tendons, ligaments, joint structure, and pain.

Harvard.text: Changes that occur in the body, such as rapid breathing and heartbeat, when a person is confronted with a perceived physical or emotional threat. Also called the stress response.

LLM.text: The coordinated stress response that prepares the body to confront or escape a perceived threat.

Harvard.text: Tiny spots or lines that appear in a person’s field of vision when the jelly-like fluid of the eye breaks down with age. They are usually harmless, but can signal serious eye problems.

LLM.text: Mobile spots, threads, cobwebs, or rings in the visual field caused by vitreous opacities casting shadows on the retina. Most arise from posterior vitreous detachment, an age-related separation of the vitreous gel from the retina; hemorrhage, vitritis, and asteroid hyalosis are other causes.

Harvard.text: A term coined by positive psychology pioneer Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi to describe an effortless, active state of being during which one loses awareness of time, self, and distractions. Flow hinges on balancing the size of a challenge and the level of skill a person brings to it.

LLM.text: A state of highly focused, effortless involvement in an activity, often with reduced awareness of time.

Harvard.text: A test that uses special dye and a camera to examine blood flow in the retina.

LLM.text: An eye test in which fluorescein dye is injected into a vein and sequential photographs are taken of the retinal circulation. It helps identify leakage, blocked vessels, abnormal new vessels, and other retinal or choroidal abnormalities.

Harvard.text: A mineral that protects teeth from decay and cavities.

LLM.text: Mineral that strengthens tooth enamel and inhibits bacterial acid production. Sources: water fluoridation (0.7 ppm optimal), toothpaste, professional applications. Mechanism: incorporates into hydroxyapatite forming fluorapatite (more acid-resistant), promotes remineralization, inhibits bacterial enzymes.

Harvard.text: A test that gives moving images of the inside of the body; could be likened to an x-ray movie.

LLM.text: Real-time X-ray imaging used to visualize dynamic processes.

Harvard.text: Lipid-laden cells, named for their foamy appearance under the microscope. As foam cells build up on the inside of blood vessel walls, they form a plaque that can block blood flow.

LLM.text: Lipid-filled cells, usually macrophages, that contribute to atherosclerotic plaque.

Harvard.text: Damage to a specific nerve, causing pain or numbness.

LLM.text: Damage to a single peripheral nerve or a small group of nerves.

Harvard.text: Peaceful, relaxing words or phrases used during stress relief exercises.

LLM.text: Calming words or phrases used to anchor attention during relaxation or stress-management exercises.

Harvard.text: A group of cells that form a small sac.

LLM.text: A small sac or tissue structure, such as a hair follicle or ovarian follicle.

Harvard.text: A hormone released by the pituitary gland that stimulates the production of eggs in women and sperm in men.

LLM.text: A pituitary hormone that supports ovarian follicle development and sperm production.

Harvard.text: A small bundle that includes one to four follicles, oil glands, a tiny muscle, and other tissue.

LLM.text: A natural hair-growth unit containing one or more follicles and associated structures.

Harvard.text: Transplantation of follicular units, which mimic natural hair growth.

LLM.text: Hair-restoration surgery that transplants individual follicular units to thinning areas.

Harvard.text: An inflammation of the hair follicle.

LLM.text: Inflammation of a hair follicle, often caused by bacteria, yeast, friction, occlusion, or ingrown hairs, producing small itchy or tender bumps.

Harvard.text: Sensitivities to certain foods that can cause symptoms ranging from the mild (like hives) to the life threatening (such as anaphylaxis).

LLM.text: Immune reactions to particular food proteins that can cause symptoms ranging from hives to anaphylaxis.

Harvard.text: Cosmetic surgery to minimize creases on the forehead and between the eyebrows, and to lift sagging eyebrows.

LLM.text: Cosmetic surgery that reduces forehead lines and raises drooping eyebrows.

Harvard.text: A small dimple in the middle of the retina that provides sharp central vision.

LLM.text: A tiny depression in the center of the retina that provides the sharpest and most detailed visual acuity.

Harvard.text: A break in a bone.

LLM.text: A break in the continuity of bone, classified by location, pattern (transverse, oblique, spiral, comminuted), displacement, and whether the fracture communicates with the external environment (open vs. closed). Fracture healing occurs through inflammatory, reparative, and remodeling phases.

Harvard.text: An algorithm for estimating the probability of breaking a bone because of low bone mass over a period of 10 years.

LLM.text: A calculator that estimates a person’s ten-year probability of major osteoporotic or hip fracture.

Harvard.text: Part of a disk in the back that has broken off from the main portion of the disk.

LLM.text: A piece of an intervertebral disk that has separated from the main disk.

Harvard.text: An unstable molecule in the body that plays a role in aging and can damage tissue; antioxidants help prevent free radical damage.

LLM.text: A molecule or atom containing an unpaired electron, making it chemically reactive. Excessive free-radical activity can contribute to oxidative injury.

Harvard.text: The pitch of a sound; measured by the speed at which sound waves vibrate.

LLM.text: Increased daytime micturition, typically more than seven episodes per day, distinguished from polyuria (high urine volume) and nocturia (nighttime voiding). Common causes include urinary tract infection, benign prostatic hyperplasia, overactive bladder, and diabetes mellitus.

Harvard.text: How much amplification a hearing aid produces in both high and low frequencies.

LLM.text: The span from the lowest to highest sound frequencies amplified by a hearing aid.

Harvard.text: The amplification that a hearing aid produces across different sound frequencies.

LLM.text: The amount of amplification a hearing aid provides across different sound frequencies.

Harvard.text: Part of the brain that plays a role in determining consequences and choosing behaviors.

LLM.text: The largest lobe of the cerebral cortex, lying anterior to the central sulcus, comprising the primary motor cortex (precentral gyrus, Brodmann 4), premotor and supplementary motor areas, prefrontal cortex, and Broca's area (dominant hemisphere, expressive language).

Harvard.text: A brain disorder that can cause dementia, aphasia, neurotic behavior, and gradual changes in personality and emotional control.

LLM.text: A group of progressive disorders affecting the frontal and temporal brain lobes, causing changes in behavior, language, or executive function.

Harvard.text: Inflammation of various tissues of the shoulder, along with growth of abnormal bands of tissue that cause the shoulder to become so stiff that movement is severely limited.

LLM.text: Adhesive capsulitis: progressive shoulder pain and stiffness. Stages: freezing (pain), frozen (stiffness), thawing (recovery). Associated with diabetes, thyroid disease, immobilization. Treatment: physical therapy, corticosteroid injection, manipulation under anesthesia, arthroscopic capsular release.

Harvard.text: A simple sugar found in corn syrup, honey, and many sweet fruits.

LLM.text: A simple sugar found naturally in fruit, honey, and some syrups.

Harvard.text: Abbreviation for follicle-stimulating hormone, a hormone released by the pituitary gland that stimulates the production of eggs in women and sperm in men.

LLM.text: Follicle-stimulating hormone, a pituitary hormone involved in ovarian follicle development and sperm production.

Harvard.text: Gut problems that aren’t caused by an infection or structural problem with the gastrointestinal system.

LLM.text: Digestive symptoms caused by altered gut function without an evident structural disease or infection.

Harvard.text: Recognition of the need to urinate but being unable to get to the bathroom in time due to mental or physical problems, such as limited mobility.

LLM.text: Involuntary urine leakage because a person cannot reach or use the toilet in time despite recognizing the need to void.

Harvard.text: Surgery that restructures the stomach to prevent acid reflux.
