LLM.text: Surgery that wraps the upper stomach around the lower esophagus to reduce gastroesophageal reflux.

Harvard.text: Imaging test that provides multi-dimensional pictures of the back of the eyeball.

LLM.text: The documentation of the appearance of the retina, optic nerve, and retinal vasculature using a specialized camera that illuminates and photographs the posterior segment of the eye, providing a permanent, objective record of retinal findings that can be used for comparison over time, patient education, and telemedicine consultations.

Harvard.text: Organisms and microorganisms, such as yeasts and molds, that can live as a parasite on plants and animals.

LLM.text: A eukaryotic microorganism with a chitin cell wall and ergosterol-containing membrane, classified as yeasts, moulds, or dimorphic fungi. Reproducing by spores, fungi cause superficial, mucosal, subcutaneous, and systemic infections, especially in immunocompromised hosts.

Harvard.text: A hearing aid’s power, measured in the number of decibels that it can add to sound.

LLM.text: The amount by which a hearing aid increases sound intensity, measured in decibels.

Harvard.text: The cycle that the feet and legs make when walking, beginning when one heel hits the ground and ending when the same heel hits the ground again.

LLM.text: The sequence of leg and foot movements from one heel strike to the next heel strike of the same foot.

Harvard.text: A substance that promotes breast milk production.

LLM.text: A substance that promotes breast milk production.

Harvard.text: A chemical messenger in the brain that may help decrease anxiety and promote slow-wave sleep. Often referred to as GABA.

LLM.text: The principal inhibitory neurotransmitter in the brain.

Harvard.text: An abnormal but harmless mass of tissue, usually nerve cells.

LLM.text: A collection of neuronal cell bodies located outside the central nervous system (CNS).

Harvard.text: A harmless sac of fluid on top of a joint or tendon, usually on the wrist or back of the hand.

LLM.text: A benign, fluid-filled cyst arising near a joint or tendon sheath, most often at the wrist or hand. It may be painless or cause pressure, discomfort, or limitation of movement.

Harvard.text: Death of tissue in part of the body because blood has stopped flowing there.

LLM.text: Gangrene is tissue death caused by loss of blood supply, infection, or both; it can progress to systemic toxicity and requires urgent assessment of circulation and infection. bowel, and represents a form of coagulative necrosis. Dry gangrene occurs in tissues with gradual arterial occlusion, where the dead tissue becomes dry, shrunken, and dark brown or black.

Harvard.text: Inflammation of the lining of the stomach.

LLM.text: Gastritis is inflammation or injury of the stomach lining caused by infection, medications, alcohol, autoimmune disease, stress-related illness, or other factors.

Harvard.text: A condition in which food and acid flow back into the esophagus from the stomach, causing heartburn.

LLM.text: A condition in which repeated reflux of stomach contents causes troublesome symptoms or complications. See Acid Reflux.

Harvard.text: Relating to all or some of the organs of the digestive tract, from the mouth to the anus.

LLM.text: Relating to the digestive system.

Harvard.text: The digestive tract.

LLM.text: The continuous digestive passage from the mouth through the esophagus, stomach, intestines, rectum, and anus.

Harvard.text: Structures on chromosomes that are passed from parent to child. The basic unit of material that passes traits from parent to child.

LLM.text: Basic unit of heredity, segment of DNA encoding a functional product (protein or RNA). Structure: promoter, coding sequence (exons), introns, terminator. Genes are located at specific positions (loci) on chromosomes.

Harvard.text: Correction of a genetic defect by replacing an abnormal gene with a normal gene.

LLM.text: Treatment by introducing, removing, or changing genetic material. Approaches: gene addition (functional copy), gene silencing (siRNA, antisense), gene editing (CRISPR-Cas9). Examples: Luxturna (RPE65 mutation), Zolgensma (SMN1 in spinal muscular atrophy).

Harvard.text: A copy of a brand-name drug whose patent has expired. These drugs are less expensive than brand-name drugs.

LLM.text: A medicine equivalent to a brand-name medicine in active ingredient, strength, dosage form, and intended use, usually sold under a nonproprietary name.

Harvard.text: Referring to inherited characteristics or genes.

LLM.text: Relating to genes, heredity, or inherited characteristics.

Harvard.text: An antioxidant chemical found in certain plants, like soybeans.

LLM.text: A soy-derived isoflavone with estrogen-like and antioxidant activity.

Harvard.text: Abbreviation for gastroesophageal reflux disease, a condition in which food and acid flow back into the esophagus from the stomach, causing heartburn.

LLM.text: Gastroesophageal reflux disease, in which stomach contents repeatedly flow back into the esophagus.

Harvard.text: A trained medical professional who helps families who are caring for older adults.

LLM.text: A professional who helps coordinate health and support services for an older adult.

Harvard.text: A physician who specializes in the care of older patients.

LLM.text: A physician specializing in the health care of older adults, including complex illness, multiple conditions, medications, function, and goals of care.

Harvard.text: A form of diabetes that appears during pregnancy.

LLM.text: Glucose intolerance first recognized during pregnancy affecting approximately six to nine percent of pregnancies. Results from insulin resistance induced by placental hormones including human placental lactogen, cortisol, and progesterone combined with insufficient beta cell compensation.

Harvard.text: Abbreviation for glomerular filtration rate, the rate at which the kidneys filter excess water and other wastes. A test by the same name is used to determine how well the kidneys are functioning.

LLM.text: Glomerular filtration rate, an estimate of how efficiently the kidneys filter blood.

Harvard.text: Inflammation and damage to blood vessels that supply the head and neck.

LLM.text: A large-vessel vasculitis of adults >50 (peak 70-80) affecting cranial branches of carotid arteries, with risk of permanent vision loss from anterior ischemic optic neuropathy. Clinical: new-onset headache (temporal), scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, visual disturbances (amaurosis fugax, diplopia), polymyalgia rheumatica symptoms.

Harvard.text: Another term for gums: a form of oral tissue that covers the roots of teeth and surrounding bone.

LLM.text: The oral tissue surrounding and protecting the roots of the teeth.

synonyms: gums: a form of oral tissue that covers the roots of teeth and surrounding bone

Harvard.text: Inflammation of the gums.

LLM.text: Inflammation of the gingiva (gums) characterized by redness, swelling, bleeding on probing. Reversible with improved oral hygiene and professional cleaning. If untreated, progresses to periodontitis.

Harvard.text: Any organ or tissue that secretes fluids, such as hormones, for use elsewhere in the body or as waste.

LLM.text: An organized group of epithelial cells specialized for secretion.

Harvard.text: The head of the penis.

LLM.text: The expanded, sensitive distal end of the penis containing the external urethral opening and covered by the foreskin when present.

Harvard.text: A condition in which the pressure inside the eye is too high, causing eye damage.

LLM.text: Glaucoma is progressive optic-nerve damage often associated with elevated or dysregulated intraocular pressure, leading to irreversible visual-field loss if untreated. ganglion cells and their axons, resulting in characteristic optic nerve head changes and visual field loss, with elevated intraocular pressure being the most important modifiable risk factor.

Harvard.text: In men with prostate cancer, the Gleason score provides a rough estimate of how fast the cancer is growing.

LLM.text: A grading system that estimates the aggressiveness of prostate cancer from its microscopic appearance.

Harvard.text: A shoulder joint that connects the ball of the humerus to the glenoid.

LLM.text: Ball-and-socket synovial joint between humeral head and glenoid cavity. Most mobile body joint allowing flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, medial/lateral rotation, circumduction. Mobility trades for stability, making it the most commonly dislocated joint. Stabilized by glenoid labrum, glenohemoral ligaments, and rotator cuff.

Harvard.text: The socket of the scapula that connects to the humerus at the shoulder.

LLM.text: The shallow socket of the scapula that forms the shoulder joint with the humeral head.

Harvard.text: The rate at which the kidneys filter excess water and other wastes. A test by the same name is used to determine how well the kidneys are functioning.

LLM.text: Volume of plasma filtered by the glomeruli per unit time normally ninety to one hundred twenty milliliters per minute per one point seven three square meters body surface area. Estimated by the CKD-EPI equation using serum creatinine, age, sex, and race.

Harvard.text: Tiny clusters of capillaries in the kidneys that filter waste products from the blood.

LLM.text: Microscopic capillary networks in the kidneys where blood filtration begins.

Harvard.text: A hormone produced in the pancreas that raises blood sugar levels.

LLM.text: A peptide hormone produced by the alpha cells of the pancreatic islets (Langerhans).

Harvard.text: Steroid hormones released by the adrenal gland when there seems to be a threat, and the stress response is triggered.

LLM.text: A class of steroid hormones produced by the zona fasciculata of the adrenal cortex, regulated by the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis.

Harvard.text: A simple sugar that is the body’s main source of energy.

LLM.text: A monosaccharide (C6H12O6) that is the primary energy source for cells. Types: D-glucose (dextrose, naturally occurring enantiomer) and L-glucose (synthetic). Routes of entry: dietary carbohydrates (digested to glucose), gluconeogenesis (synthesis from non-carbohydrate precursors), glycogenolysis (breakdown of stored glycogen).

Harvard.text: Blood sugar levels that are higher than normal, but not yet high enough for a diagnosis of diabetes.

LLM.text: Impaired handling of glucose resulting in blood-glucose concentrations above normal but below the diagnostic threshold for diabetes in a defined testing context. It often reflects insulin resistance or inadequate insulin secretion and is associated with increased risk of type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease.

Harvard.text: A chemical messenger in the brain that may play a role in mood disorders and schizophrenia.

LLM.text: The principal excitatory neurotransmitter in the central nervous system. Synthesized from glutamine or alpha-ketoglutarate and acting on ionotropic receptors (AMPA, kainate, NMDA) for fast synaptic transmission and metabotropic receptors (mGluR1-8) for modulation.

Harvard.text: A protein found in beta cells, the cells that create insulin.

LLM.text: An enzyme that converts glutamate to GABA; antibodies to it can occur in type 1 diabetes.

Harvard.text: A ranking of foods according to how quickly and how much they raise blood sugar.

LLM.text: Ranking of carbohydrates by effect on blood glucose. High GI foods spike glucose. Low GI foods provide sustained energy. Useful for diabetes management.

Harvard.text: A ranking of how much a typical serving of a particular food will raise blood sugar.

LLM.text: A measure that combines a food’s glycemic index with the amount of available carbohydrate in a serving to estimate its effect on blood glucose.

Harvard.text: The body’s fuel reserves. This substance, stored primarily in the liver and muscles, is later converted into glucose to provide cells with energy.

LLM.text: A branched polysaccharide composed of glucose units linked by alpha-1,4 glycosidic bonds (linear) and alpha-1,6 bonds (branching points, every 8-10 residues). Glycogen serves as the main storage form of glucose in animals.

Harvard.text: The product formed by the attachment of glucose (blood sugar) to hemoglobin (the oxygen-carrying protein in red blood cells). Usually referred to as hemoglobin A1c, or HbA1c.

LLM.text: Hemoglobin with glucose attached, reflecting average blood glucose over roughly two to three months.

Harvard.text: Abbreviation for gonadotropin-releasing hormone, a hormone responsible for the release of follicle-stimulating hormone and luteinizing hormone from the pituitary gland.

LLM.text: Gonadotropin-releasing hormone, which stimulates pituitary release of LH and FSH.

Harvard.text: Drugs used to treat prostate cancer by blocking the release of luteinizing hormone that do not cause a temporary surge in testosterone.

LLM.text: Medicines that block GnRH signaling and reduce pituitary release of reproductive hormones.

Harvard.text: Cells that produce mucus that line the gastrointestinal tract and lungs.

LLM.text: Specialized epithelial cells that secrete mucus, especially in the intestine and airways.

Harvard.text: An enlarged thyroid gland that creates a lump in the neck.

LLM.text: Enlargement of the thyroid gland, which can be diffuse or nodular. Causes: iodine deficiency (most common worldwide), Hashimoto thyroiditis, Graves disease, multinodular goiter, and thyroid cancer. May be associated with normal, hyperthyroid, or hypothyroid function.

Harvard.text: A hormone responsible for the release of follicle-stimulating hormone and luteinizing hormone from the pituitary gland.

LLM.text: A hypothalamic hormone that controls pituitary secretion of FSH and LH.

Harvard.text: A test used to detect glaucoma that examines the area where fluid drains out of the eye.

LLM.text: An ophthalmological examination technique that allows direct visualization of the anterior chamber angle, the anatomical region where the cornea and iris meet and where the trabecular meshwork is located, and it is essential for distinguishing between open-angle and angle-closure forms of glaucoma.

Harvard.text: A form of arthritis that occurs when uric acid builds up in the joints; The big toe, knee, and ankle joints are most often affected.

LLM.text: Gout is inflammatory arthritis caused by monosodium urate crystal deposition, classically causing abrupt severe pain and swelling in a joint and potentially forming tophi or kidney stones. episodes of acute inflammatory arthritis and may cause chronic tophi or kidney stones.

Harvard.text: Transplanting tissue from one part of the body to another.

LLM.text: Tissue or a synthetic material transferred to another site to replace, repair, reinforce, or bypass a damaged body structure.

Harvard.text: A metric unit of weight equivalent to one-thousandth of a kilogram.

LLM.text: A metric unit of mass equal to one-thousandth of a kilogram.

Harvard.text: An autoimmune disease that causes the thyroid gland to produce too much thyroid hormone. It is usually accompanied by an enlarged thyroid gland and swollen, bulging, red eyes that appear to stare, as well as occasional double vision and vision loss.

LLM.text: An autoimmune disorder in which antibodies stimulate the thyroid-stimulating hormone receptor, causing hyperthyroidism and sometimes eye or skin manifestations.

Harvard.text: A fracture in a young, soft bone in which the bone bends and breaks only on the outer edge of the bend.

LLM.text: An incomplete fracture in which a young bone bends and cracks rather than breaking all the way through.

Harvard.text: A broad range of reactions to bereavement, including sadness, tears, shock, confusion, and anger, among others.

LLM.text: The natural emotional response to loss, particularly the death of a loved one, but also following other significant losses such as divorce, job loss, or declining health. It encompasses a range of feelings including sadness, anger, guilt, and numbness, often occurring in waves rather than linear stages.

Harvard.text: A substance produced by the body to stimulate tissue growth.

LLM.text: Proteins that stimulate cell growth, proliferation, differentiation, and survival. Major families: EGF (epidermal growth factor), FGF (fibroblast growth factor), PDGF (platelet-derived), VEGF (vascular endothelial), TGF-beta (transforming), NGF (nerve), IGF (insulin-like), HGF (hepatocyte).

Harvard.text: The area of sexually sensitive tissue located on the roof of the vagina just inside the opening. Also known as the Grafenberg spot.

LLM.text: A proposed area of sexually sensitive tissue on the front wall of the vagina.

Harvard.text: A legal process of appointing a person to make decisions about important matters (such as health and finances) for someone who is unfit to make those decisions on his or her own.

LLM.text: A legal arrangement in which an appointed person makes decisions for someone unable to make them independently.

Harvard.text: The esophagus.

LLM.text: The esophagus, the tube carrying food from the throat to the stomach.

Harvard.text: Diseases including gingivitis and periodontitis that attack the gum tissue and the structures supporting the teeth. Also called periodontal disease.

LLM.text: Inflammation or infection affecting the gums and supporting tissues of the teeth.

Harvard.text: A form of oral tissue that covers the roots of teeth and surrounding bone. Also called the gingiva.

LLM.text: The soft oral tissue surrounding and supporting the teeth.

Harvard.text: The root of the hair shaft.

LLM.text: The enlarged base of a hair follicle where the hair shaft is produced.

Harvard.text: Cells in the ear that transmit sound messages to the brain and play a vital role in hearing.

LLM.text: The sensory receptor cells of the inner ear that convert mechanical sound vibrations into electrical neural signals, and they are named for the bundle of stereocilia projecting from their apical surface.

Harvard.text: The portion of hair that extends beyond the surface of the skin. It contains three layers: the cuticle, cortex, and medulla (not always present).

LLM.text: The portion of a hair that projects above the skin surface.

Harvard.text: A perception of something that is not really there.

LLM.text: A perception in the absence of an external stimulus, experienced as real and occurring in objective space.

Harvard.text: A sometimes painful condition in which the toe curls up and under (resembling a hammer).

LLM.text: A deformity in which a toe bends downward at a middle joint.

Harvard.text: A treatment strategy aimed at minimizing the harm associated with an object of addiction. This strategic approach helps people learn how to limit the degree to which they use their object of addiction, or limit the risks associated with their use, but they do not necessarily stop altogether.

LLM.text: Treatment that aims to reduce health and social harms from addictive behavior, even when abstinence is not immediate.

Harvard.text: A disease in which the body’s immune system prevents the thyroid gland from producing enough thyroid hormone.

LLM.text: A chronic autoimmune inflammation of the thyroid that commonly causes progressive hypothyroidism and may produce a firm, enlarged thyroid gland.

Harvard.text: A commonly used term for allergic rhinitis—seasonal or year-round allergic condition marked by sneezing, runny nose, and congestion. The most common type of allergy, it is caused by an IgE-mediated immune response to inhaled airborne allergens.

LLM.text: Seasonal or persistent allergic rhinitis caused by inhaled allergens.

Harvard.text: Abbreviation for hemoglobin A1c, the product formed by the attachment of glucose (blood sugar) to hemoglobin (a protein in red blood cells). A test for HbA1c is a useful measure of blood sugar control.

LLM.text: Hemoglobin with glucose attached; its measurement estimates average blood glucose over the previous two to three months.

Harvard.text: Abbreviation for high-density lipoprotein, the so-called good cholesterol. This lipoprotein (a substance made up of fats and protein) is believed to remove cholesterol from the arteries.

LLM.text: High-density lipoprotein, a class of particles that transports cholesterol and other lipids in the blood. HDL concentration is one component of cardiovascular risk assessment; it should not be interpreted as a protective or harmful measure by itself.

Harvard.text: A legal form allowing a person to appoint someone else to make their medical decisions. Also known as a durable power of attorney for health care.

LLM.text: A legal appointment authorizing another person to make healthcare decisions when a patient cannot make them.

common_names: durable power of attorney for health care

Harvard.text: An electronic device worn in or behind the ear by people with hearing problems that makes sounds louder.

LLM.text: Amplification device for hearing loss. Types: behind-the-ear (BTE), in-the-ear (ITE), receiver-in-canal (RIC). Components: microphone, amplifier, speaker, battery. Fitting: audiogram-based. Adjustments: volume, programs.

Harvard.text: The common term for a myocardial infarction. It refers to the damage that occurs when blood flow to part of the heart is blocked or drastically restricted. The blockage usually stems from the rupture of an atherosclerotic plaque.

LLM.text: Acute myocardial injury caused most often by blockage of a coronary artery, usually from rupture of an atherosclerotic plaque and thrombosis. It may cause chest pressure, shortness of breath, sweating, nausea, or atypical symptoms and requires emergency treatment.

Harvard.text: The difficulty or inability of the electrical signal that triggers a heart contraction to pass through the atrioventricular node.

LLM.text: A delay or interruption in the conduction of cardiac impulses from the atria to the ventricles through the atrioventricular (AV) node and His-Purkinje system. Classification: first-degree AV block: PR interval >200 ms, each atrial impulse conducts to the ventricles, typically asymptomatic.

Harvard.text: The inability of the heart to pump enough blood to meet the needs of the body's organs.

LLM.text: A clinical syndrome in which impaired cardiac structure or function causes inadequate cardiac output, elevated filling pressures, or both. Symptoms and signs may include breathlessness, fatigue, reduced exercise tolerance, pulmonary or systemic congestion, and fluid retention. Heart failure may be classified by left-ventricular ejection fraction and by symptom severity, such as NYHA class I--IV; ejection fraction alone does not establish or fully characterize the syndrome.

Harvard.text: An extra or unusual sound heard during the heartbeat. A murmur may or may not be a sign of a problem in the heart.

LLM.text: An audible extra sound produced by turbulent blood flow within the heart or great vessels, heard on auscultation.

Harvard.text: The number of times the heart contracts in a minute, normally 60–100 times.

LLM.text: The number of cardiac contractions (heartbeats) per minute. Normal resting heart rate (sinus rhythm): 60-100 bpm in adults; higher in children (70-120 at age 1-2 years, 80-130 in neonates).

Harvard.text: A burning pain in the chest or throat, caused when stomach acid backs up into the esophagus.

LLM.text: Heartburn is a burning retrosternal sensation caused by reflux of gastric contents; frequent or complicated symptoms may indicate gastroesophageal reflux disease. the throat and is often associated with regurgitation of sour or bitter-tasting fluid into the mouth. Despite its name, heartburn is a symptom of gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GORD), not a cardiac symptom.

Harvard.text: Bony bumps found on the finger joints in some people with osteoarthritis.

LLM.text: Firm bony enlargements of the distal interphalangeal finger joints, usually caused by osteoarthritis.

Harvard.text: An abnormal growth of bone or calcium on the heel bone.

LLM.text: A bony growth arising from the heel bone, often associated with plantar-fascia strain. The spur itself may cause no symptoms; heel pain is more often related to surrounding soft-tissue inflammation.

Harvard.text: Bacteria that damages the lining the stomach. It is to blame for most ulcers and stomach inflammation. Often called H. pylori.

LLM.text: A gram-negative, spiral-shaped bacterium adapted to colonize the stomach. It can cause chronic gastritis, peptic ulcer disease, and increase the risk of gastric cancer and gastric MALT lymphoma.

Harvard.text: Cells that help fight disease by activating and directing other immune system cells.

LLM.text: CD4-positive immune cells that coordinate responses by activating other immune cells.

Harvard.text: The vomiting of bright red blood, indicating bleeding in the upper digestive tract.

LLM.text: Vomiting of blood, indicating upper gastrointestinal bleeding proximal to the ligament of Treitz. Blood may be bright red (acute, brisk bleeding) or resemble coffee grounds (altered blood that has been in contact with gastric acid).

Harvard.text: Blood that leaks out of blood vessels and collects in the body.

LLM.text: A localized collection of blood outside blood vessels, usually caused by injury or a bleeding disorder.

Harvard.text: Blood in the urine.

LLM.text: Presence of red blood cells in the urine, categorized as microscopic (>3 RBCs per high-power field on urine microscopy) or gross (macroscopic, visible color change from pink to dark red). Microscopic hematuria is often asymptomatic and detected on routine urinalysis.

Harvard.text: Poor vision or blindness in half of the visual field, affecting one or both eyes.

LLM.text: Loss of vision in half the visual field of one or both eyes. Homonymous hemianopia affects the same side in both eyes and localizes to a contralateral lesion posterior to the optic chiasm, most often stroke or tumor.

Harvard.text: Muscle weakness on one side of the body.

LLM.text: Weakness affecting one side of the body, less severe than hemiplegia (paralysis). It results from a lesion of the corticospinal tract anywhere from the motor cortex to the spinal cord, most commonly from stroke, but also from tumors, trauma, or demyelination. The pattern of weakness helps localize the lesion.

Harvard.text: Paralysis on one side of the body.

LLM.text: Paralysis of one side of the body (the face, arm, and leg on the same side), caused by damage to the corticospinal tract (pyramidal tract) at any level from the cerebral cortex to the spinal cord.

Harvard.text: A genetic condition in which the body absorbs and stores too much iron.

LLM.text: Hemochromatosis is excessive iron accumulation that can injure the liver, pancreas, heart, joints, skin, and endocrine organs; inherited and acquired forms exist. progressive iron deposition in parenchymal organs. Hereditary hemochromatosis is most commonly caused by homozygous C282Y mutations in the HFE gene affecting approximately one in two hundred individuals of Northern European descent.

Harvard.text: The use of a machine to remove wastes and impurities from the blood when the kidneys are not working properly.

LLM.text: Extracorporeal blood purification in which blood passes through a dialyzer containing a semipermeable membrane to remove selected solutes and excess fluid. Conventional outpatient treatment is often scheduled about three times weekly for several hours, but frequency and duration vary with the clinical situation and modality. Vascular access is required; an arteriovenous fistula is generally preferred when feasible. Adequacy is assessed with measures such as Kt/V or urea reduction ratio, together with clinical status. Complications can include hypotension, access infection, thrombosis, and dialyzer reactions.

Harvard.text: The oxygen-carrying substance that gives red blood cells their color.

LLM.text: Hemoglobin is the iron-containing protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen and carbon dioxide; its concentration and structure help evaluate anemia and hemoglobin disorders. heme groups that bind oxygen. Each heme contains iron (Fe2+) that reversibly binds O2. Cooperative binding produces sigmoidal oxygen dissociation curve. P50 (pO2 at 50\% saturation) 27 mmHg.

Harvard.text: Coughing up or spitting up blood from the lungs.

LLM.text: Expectoration of blood from the lower respiratory tract. Must be differentiated from hematemesis and epistaxis. Causes: bronchitis, pneumonia, TB, bronchiectasis, lung cancer, PE.

Harvard.text: Bleeding from a damaged blood vessel.

LLM.text: Extravasation of blood from the cardiovascular system (heart, arteries, veins, capillaries).

Harvard.text: A type of stroke that occurs when a blood vessel leaks or bursts inside the brain, cutting off the supply of oxygen and nutrition to that part of the brain.

LLM.text: A neurological deficit caused by rupture of a cerebral blood vessel, accounting for 13\% of all strokes but 40\% of stroke mortality. Intracerebral hemorrhage: hypertensive (basal ganglia, thalamus, pons, cerebellum), amyloid angiopathy (lobar, elderly), vascular malformations, anticoagulation. Subarachnoid hemorrhage: aneurysm rupture.

Harvard.text: Abbreviation for high-efficiency particulate air, a type of highly efficient air filter.

LLM.text: A high-efficiency particulate air filter that removes a large proportion of airborne particles.

Harvard.text: A drug that prevents blood from clotting.

LLM.text: An anticoagulant that reduces formation and extension of blood clots.

Harvard.text: Protection occurring when so many people in a region are immune to an infectious disease that it can’t spread to others.

LLM.text: Resistance of population to invasion by infectious agent when sufficient proportion immune. Threshold varies by disease (measles 95\%, polio 80\%).

Harvard.text: When part of a spinal disk bulges out of a tear or weak spot in the disk’s tough outer shell. Also known as prolapsed disk.

LLM.text: A herniated disk occurs when spinal disk material extends through a fissure and may compress a nerve root, producing back pain, radiating pain, numbness, or weakness. intervertebral disc, most commonly occurring in the lumbar spine (L4-L5 and L5-S1 account for 95 percent of lumbar herniations) and cervical spine (C5-C6 and C6-C7), potentially compressing spinal nerves.

Harvard.text: A painful blistering skin rash caused by the chicken pox virus; also known as shingles.

LLM.text: A painful, usually one-sided blistering rash caused by reactivation of latent varicella-zoster virus in a sensory nerve ganglion. It typically follows a band-like distribution and may cause persistent nerve pain after the rash resolves.

Harvard.text: The measurement of a sound’s frequency.

LLM.text: The SI unit of frequency, equal to one cycle per second.

Harvard.text: When part of the stomach pushes upward into the chest through an abnormal opening in the diaphragm.

LLM.text: Protrusion of part of the stomach through the esophageal opening in the diaphragm into the chest. It may be sliding or paraesophageal and can be associated with reflux or other symptoms.

Harvard.text: When blood flowing through arteries pushes on artery walls with abnormally high force over a sustained period of time. Also called hypertension.

LLM.text: Persistently elevated pressure of blood against artery walls.

Harvard.text: So-called good cholesterol. This lipoprotein (a substance made of fat and protein) removes cholesterol from arteries.

LLM.text: A lipoprotein that transports cholesterol in the blood and is commonly called HDL.

Harvard.text: A treatment that destroys tumors with heat generated by ultrasound energy.

LLM.text: A treatment that concentrates ultrasound energy to heat and destroy a targeted area of tissue. Its uses depend on the device, disease, and clinical setting.

Harvard.text: Part of the brain that plays an important role in processing long-term memories.

LLM.text: Curved medial temporal lobe structure, part of the limbic system, critical for new declarative memory formation (episodic and spatial) and short-to-long-term memory conversion. Has dentate gyrus, hippocampus proper (CA1-CA4), subiculum, and entorhinal cortex. One of few adult neurogenesis sites (dentate gyrus).

Harvard.text: Excessive facial or body hair in women.

LLM.text: Excess terminal hair growth in women in a male-pattern distribution (face--upper lip, chin, sideburns; chest, back, lower abdomen, inner thighs). Hirsutism affects 5-10\% of women of reproductive age. Pathophysiology: increased androgen production or increased end-organ sensitivity.

Harvard.text: A substance released by the immune system when it is exposed to an allergen. Histamines cause many allergy symptoms.

LLM.text: A biogenic amine (imidazolylethylamine) synthesised from L-histidine by histidine decarboxylase, stored in basophils, mast cells, and platelets, and released during allergic and inflammatory responses.

Harvard.text: Abbreviation for human immunodeficiency virus, the virus that leads to acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS). HIV damages immune cells so that they are no longer able to fight off other infections.

LLM.text: Human immunodeficiency virus: a retrovirus (HIV-1, HIV-2) causing progressive CD4+ T-cell depletion and AIDS if untreated. Transmitted via sexual contact, blood/blood products, mother-to-child.

Harvard.text: An itchy rash of usually short duration. Also known as urticaria.

LLM.text: Hives, or urticaria, are transient raised itchy wheals caused by dermal edema, commonly from allergy, infection, medications, physical triggers, or spontaneous mast-cell activation. or chronic and can result from infection, foods, medications, physical triggers, or autoimmune mechanisms; swelling of the airway is an emergency.

Harvard.text: Abbreviation for human leukocyte antigen, a protein found on the surface of white blood cells that helps the body recognize and fight foreign substances.

LLM.text: Human leukocyte antigen, a cell-surface protein system involved in immune recognition and tissue compatibility.

Harvard.text: A small machine worn for a day or more to continuously record the heart’s electrical activity. Holter monitors are used to help diagnose heart rhythm problems.

LLM.text: Continuous ECG recording for 24-48 hours to detect arrhythmias, quantify burden (atrial fibrillation, PVCs, PACs), and correlate symptoms with rhythm. Patient diary logs symptoms. Indications: palpitations, syncope, presyncope, and assessment of arrhythmia control. Reveals paroxysmal arrhythmias not captured on standard 12-lead ECG.

Harvard.text: The body’s ability to keep blood pressure, temperature, water levels, oxygen levels, and more set at the right levels for cells to survive.

LLM.text: The maintenance of stable internal conditions despite external changes. Key regulated variables: temperature, pH, glucose, electrolytes, blood pressure, fluid balance. Mechanisms: negative feedback loops (most common), positive feedback (rare, e.g., labor, blood clotting).

Harvard.text: An amino acid formed as part of the normal breakdown of protein.

LLM.text: An amino acid formed during methionine metabolism. Persistently elevated blood levels may occur with genetic, nutritional, renal, or other disorders.

Harvard.text: A rare genetic disease that causes blood levels of homocysteine to rise too high.

LLM.text: An autosomal recessive metabolic disorder caused by deficiency of cystathionine beta-synthase (CBS), leading to accumulation of homocysteine and methionine.

Harvard.text: Use of medications to boost levels of hormones that decrease with age.

LLM.text: Treatment blocking hormone effects in hormone-sensitive cancers. Examples: tamoxifen (breast cancer), leuprolide (prostate cancer), aromatase inhibitors.

Harvard.text: Powerful chemicals that affect many processes in the body, including sexual function, mood, and growth.

LLM.text: Chemical messengers released by glands or tissues that regulate processes throughout the body.

Harvard.text: A person or other living organism that can be infected by a virus or other pathogen under natural conditions.

LLM.text: A person or other living organism that can be infected by a virus or other pathogen under natural conditions. The host may be a human, animal, or plant. In medical contexts, the host is the patient in whom an infection or disease develops.

Harvard.text: A sudden, intense, hot feeling in the face or upper part of the body, along with rapid heartbeat, sweating, and flushing. A symptom of menopause.

LLM.text: A sudden episode of heat, flushing, sweating, and sometimes palpitations, commonly occurring during menopause.

Harvard.text: Abbreviation for hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, a system that controls many hormonal activities in the body, including the stress response.

LLM.text: The hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, a hormone system central to the stress response.

Harvard.text: Usually abbreviated as HIV, the virus that leads to acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS). HIV damages immune cells so that they are no longer able to fight off other infections.

LLM.text: A retrovirus belonging to the Lentivirus genus that causes acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS). HIV has two species: HIV-1 and HIV-2. The virus targets CD4+ T cells, macrophages, and dendritic cells. HIV has a complex genome encoding structural proteins, enzymes (reverse transcriptase, integrase, protease), and regulatory proteins.

Harvard.text: A protein found on the surface of white blood cells that helps the body recognize and fight foreign substances.

LLM.text: A protein on cell surfaces that helps the immune system distinguish self from foreign material.

Harvard.text: An agent used in moisturizers; binds water to the skin to promote hydration.

LLM.text: A substance that attracts and retains water, commonly used to hydrate skin.

Harvard.text: Immunity from infection and disease that comes from the release of antibodies in the blood.

LLM.text: The component of adaptive immunity mediated by antibodies produced by B lymphocytes (plasma cells) that neutralize extracellular pathogens and toxins. Humoral responses defend against bacteria, viruses outside cells, and parasites.

Harvard.text: An inherited disorder characterized by involuntary jerky movements and dementia.

LLM.text: An autosomal dominant neurodegenerative disorder caused by a CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion in the huntingtin gene on chromosome 4p16.3. The disease is characterized by the triad of progressive chorea, cognitive decline, and psychiatric manifestations.

Harvard.text: A hydrating sugar secreted by cells.

LLM.text: A naturally occurring carbohydrate polymer that binds water in connective tissue, skin, joints, and the eye.

Harvard.text: A test used to diagnose gastrointestinal problems; it measures the amount of hydrogen in the breath, which rise when food isn’t being absorbed properly.

LLM.text: Non-invasive test for carbohydrate malabsorption (lactose, fructose) and small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO). Patient ingests a substrate (lactose, glucose, or lactulose). Breath hydrogen is measured at baseline and q15-30 minutes for 2-3 hours. Rise in H2 >20 ppm from baseline: positive (bacterial fermentation).

Harvard.text: The addition of hydrogen to a compound. Hydrogenation is used to solidify liquid vegetable oils. The process creates trans fats, which are harmful to the heart and blood vessels.

LLM.text: A chemical process that adds hydrogen to a compound; in foods it can convert liquid oils into more solid fats.

Harvard.text: A hard substance that is a major component of bones and teeth.

LLM.text: A calcium-phosphate mineral forming much of the hardness of bones and teeth.

Harvard.text: The theory that modern cleanliness means children are not exposed to as many germs at an early age, which results in a more allergies.

LLM.text: The theory that limited early-life microbial exposure may increase susceptibility to allergies and immune disorders.

Harvard.text: Overproduction of the hormone aldosterone, which causes the kidneys to retain sodium and water, often leading to high blood pressure.

LLM.text: Hyperaldosteronism, also known as Conn syndrome when caused by an adrenal adenoma, is characterized by excessive aldosterone production causing hypertension, hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis.

Harvard.text: An increased sensitivity to pain.

LLM.text: An abnormally increased response to a painful stimulus.

Harvard.text: High levels of cholesterol in the blood.

LLM.text: Elevated serum total cholesterol and LDL cholesterol levels, a major modifiable risk factor for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. It may be primary, due to familial hypercholesterolemia from LDL receptor mutations, or secondary to diet, obesity, hypothyroidism, or nephrotic syndrome.

Harvard.text: An abnormally high amount of sugar in the blood.

LLM.text: Blood glucose above the expected range for the testing conditions. Acute hyperglycemia can cause osmotic diuresis, dehydration, and electrolyte disturbances. Chronic hyperglycemia leads to microvascular (retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy) and macrovascular complications.

Harvard.text: High levels of insulin in the bloodstream.

LLM.text: An abnormally high concentration of insulin in the blood.

Harvard.text: High levels of blood lipids (fats and waxes such as cholesterol).

LLM.text: Elevated levels of lipids in the blood—total cholesterol, LDL, triglycerides, and/or reduced HDL—a major modifiable risk factor for atherosclerosis and cardiovascular disease. Primary (genetic: familial hypercholesterolemia) or secondary (hypothyroidism, diabetes, nephrotic syndrome, obesity, alcohol).

Harvard.text: Difficulty seeing objects that are nearby; farsightedness.

LLM.text: A refractive error in which light focuses behind the retina when the eye is relaxed. See Farsightedness.

Harvard.text: Overproduction by the thyroid glands of parathyroid hormone.

LLM.text: Excessive secretion of parathyroid hormone (PTH) leading to hypercalcemia. Classified as primary (parathyroid adenoma or hyperplasia), secondary (chronic kidney disease, vitamin D deficiency), or tertiary (autonomous PTH secretion after prolonged secondary hyperparathyroidism).

Harvard.text: Increased production of cells in a normal tissue or organ; may be harmless or a sign of precancerous changes.

LLM.text: An increase in the number of normal cells in a tissue or organ, resulting in its enlargement. It may be physiological (e.g., endometrial proliferation) or pathological (e.g., benign prostatic hyperplasia), and is distinct from hypertrophy, which is an increase in cell size.

Harvard.text: Noncancerous growths commonly found in the colon and rectum.

LLM.text: A usually benign overgrowth of mucosal cells, often found in the colon or rectum.

Harvard.text: The medical term for high blood pressure. Hypertension is a major risk factor for stroke, especially hemorrhagic and lacunar strokes, because it puts excess stress on the walls of blood vessels and damages their delicate inner lining.

LLM.text: Persistently elevated arterial blood pressure. The diagnostic threshold depends on the guideline and the measurement method; diagnosis generally requires properly obtained readings on more than one occasion or other appropriate confirmation. It increases the risk of cardiovascular, cerebrovascular, and kidney disease.

Harvard.text: A stroke in which there is bleeding in the cerebellum because high blood pressure has weakened arteries in the brain.

LLM.text: Bleeding into the cerebellum caused by rupture of a vessel damaged by high blood pressure.

Harvard.text: A stroke in which high blood pressure causes a blood vessel deep in the brain to rupture.

LLM.text: Bleeding into brain tissue caused by rupture of a blood vessel associated with hypertension.

Harvard.text: A condition in which the thyroid gland makes too much thyroid hormone.

LLM.text: Excessive thyroid hormone production causing thyrotoxicosis (elevated serum T4 and T3 concentrations). Causes include Graves disease (most common), toxic multinodular goiter, and toxic adenoma. Symptoms include weight loss, tremor, heat intolerance, palpitations, and anxiety.

Harvard.text: High levels of triglycerides in the blood. A normal triglyceride level is less than 150 mg/dL.

LLM.text: Elevated serum triglyceride levels, classified as mild at 150 to 499 mg per dL, moderate at 500 to 999, and severe above 1000. Severe hypertriglyceridemia increases the risk of acute pancreatitis. Causes include obesity, diabetes, alcohol use, and genetic disorders of lipoprotein metabolism.

Harvard.text: Abnormally high levels of uric acid in the blood.

LLM.text: An abnormally high concentration of uric acid in the blood, which may be asymptomatic or contribute to gout and uric-acid kidney stones.

Harvard.text: Vivid dream-like sounds or images that occur while on the verge of falling asleep.

LLM.text: Vivid sensory experiences occurring while a person is falling asleep.

Harvard.text: A diagram that summarizes the stages of sleep recorded in a sleep laboratory.

LLM.text: A chart showing the timing and stages of sleep during a recording.

Harvard.text: An agent that promotes and aids sleep.

LLM.text: A medication that induces, maintains, or improves sleep, used for insomnia.

Harvard.text: A condition in which blood sugar drops to an abnormally low level.

LLM.text: An abnormally low blood-glucose concentration that may cause sweating, tremor, palpitations, hunger, confusion, seizures, or loss of consciousness. Causes include glucose-lowering medicines, missed meals, alcohol, and critical illness. Treatment depends on the person’s ability to swallow and the cause; severe or recurrent episodes require urgent assessment.

Harvard.text: Extremely low levels of testosterone in circulation.

LLM.text: Reduced or absent function of the gonads, leading to inadequate production of sex hormones (testosterone in males, estrogen in females) and impaired gamete production. Male hypogonadism: low testosterone causing decreased libido, erectile dysfunction, infertility, reduced muscle mass, and osteoporosis. Female: estrogen deficiency causing amenorrhea, hot flashes, and osteoporosis.

Harvard.text: A mild form of mania, in which a person has lots of energy, talks faster than normal, has racing thoughts, and elevated mood.

LLM.text: Distinct period of abnormally elevated, expansive, or irritable mood with increased energy lasting at least four consecutive days, observable by others but without marked functional impairment, hospitalisation, or psychotic features.

Harvard.text: Breathing that is more shallow and slow than normal.

LLM.text: Abnormally shallow or reduced breathing, especially when it occurs repeatedly during sleep.

Harvard.text: The medical term for low blood pressure.

LLM.text: Abnormally low blood pressure, generally systolic <90 mmHg or mean arterial pressure <65 mmHg. Causes include hypovolemia, cardiac failure, sepsis, anaphylaxis, and medications. Orthostatic hypotension is a drop upon standing. Severe hypotension (shock) requires urgent fluid resuscitation and vasopressors.

Harvard.text: A system that controls many hormonal activities in the body, including the stress response. Often called the HPA axis.

LLM.text: A network linking the hypothalamus, pituitary gland, and adrenal glands to regulate stress hormones and other functions.

Harvard.text: A small area in the brain that produces hormones that control body temperature, hunger, moods, the stress response, and other key functions.

LLM.text: A small region of the brain at the base of the third ventricle, bounded by the optic chiasm, mammillary bodies, and infundibulum. It weighs approximately 4 grams and is the master homeostasis regulator. Controls autonomic and endocrine systems (via the pituitary through the hypophyseal portal system), temperature, hunger, thirst, sleep-wake cycles, and emotion.

Harvard.text: A disease in which the thyroid gland does not make enough thyroid hormone.

LLM.text: Insufficient thyroid hormone production causing decreased metabolic rate. Most common endocrine disorder, affecting up to 5 percent in the general population and up to 20 percent in women over 60 years.

Harvard.text: When all or part of the body doesn’t get enough oxygen.

LLM.text: Inadequate oxygen availability at the tissue level. It may result from low arterial oxygen, anemia, reduced blood flow, or impaired cellular oxygen use.

Harvard.text: An operation to remove a woman’s uterus.

LLM.text: Surgical removal of the uterus. The cervix, fallopian tubes, and ovaries may or may not also be removed, depending on the procedure and clinical indication. Hysterectomy permanently ends menstruation and the ability to carry a pregnancy, but it does not cause immediate menopause when functioning ovaries remain. Indications include cancer, fibroids, severe bleeding, adenomyosis, endometriosis, chronic pelvic pain, and uterine prolapse.

Harvard.text: Complications or poor effects caused by medical treatment.

LLM.text: An illness or condition caused by medical examination or treatment. Examples: hospital-acquired infections, drug side effects, surgical complications, radiation-induced damage. Prevention: proper technique, informed consent, monitoring, reporting systems.

Harvard.text: Abbreviation for inflammatory bowel disease, a general term for two disorders—ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease—that cause the intestines to become swollen and inflamed.

LLM.text: Inflammatory bowel disease, including Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis, causing chronic intestinal inflammation.

Harvard.text: Abbreviation for implantable cardioverter defibrillator, a device implanted in the chest and connected to the heart that delivers a shock to stop a potentially deadly rhythm and restore a normal (sinus) rhythm.

LLM.text: Implantable cardioverter-defibrillator, a device that detects dangerous heart rhythms and delivers a corrective shock.

Harvard.text: Stabbing, very intense headaches that come on suddenly and are very brief.

LLM.text: A sudden, severe, stabbing headache that usually lasts only seconds.

Harvard.text: A condition or disease of unknown origin.

LLM.text: Of unknown cause. Examples: idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, idiopathic thrombocytopenia.

Harvard.text: Abbreviation for immunoglobulin E, the substance responsible for most allergic reactions.

LLM.text: Immunoglobulin E, the antibody class mediating immediate (type I) hypersensitivity and defense against parasites. Binds high-affinity Fc-epsilon-RI receptors on mast cells and basophils; allergen cross-linking triggers degranulation and release of histamine and leukotrienes, causing allergic rhinitis, asthma, urticaria, and anaphylaxis.

Harvard.text: The final section of the small intestine.

LLM.text: Longest distal segment (3.5 m) with thinner walls, shorter villi, and Peyer's patches on the antimesenteric border. Absorbs vitamin B12, bile salts, remaining nutrients. Ileocecal valve prevents colonic backflow. Crohn's disease most commonly affects the terminal ileum; resection may cause B12 deficiency and bile salt malabsorption.

Harvard.text: Two muscles, running from the end of the spine to the thighbone, that are responsible for lifting the knee.

LLM.text: The psoas major and iliacus muscles, which work together to flex the hip.

Harvard.text: A category of allergic reaction, triggered by specific allergens and involving IgE. The majority of allergic reactions to pollens, pets, dust, mold, food, and insect venom are of this type.

LLM.text: A rapid, typically immunoglobulin-E-mediated hypersensitivity reaction in which allergen cross-linking of mast-cell or basophil receptors releases inflammatory mediators. It can cause urticaria, bronchospasm, gastrointestinal symptoms, or anaphylaxis.

Harvard.text: To restrict the movement of a limb or other part of the body to help in healing.

LLM.text: To restrict movement of a body part, often with a splint or cast, to support healing.

Harvard.text: The body’s ability to resist infection and disease.

LLM.text: The ability of the body to recognize and resist infectious agents or other foreign substances through innate or adaptive defenses.

Harvard.text: Injection of harmless bacteria or viruses to spur the body to produce antibodies so it can resist a particular disease.

LLM.text: The process of inducing protection against an infection, usually through vaccination. Recommended vaccines and schedules depend on age, previous doses, pregnancy, immune status, medical conditions, travel, exposure risk, and current public-health guidance.

Harvard.text: Substances made by the immune system that attack foreign substances. Also known as antibodies.

LLM.text: An antibody protein produced by immune cells to recognize and help neutralize foreign substances.

Harvard.text: The substance responsible for most allergic reactions.

LLM.text: An antibody class that plays a central role in many immediate allergic reactions.

Harvard.text: A part of the body—such as the eye or ovaries—where the immune system isn’t able to function because it may damage the tissue there.

LLM.text: A body site where immune responses are limited to reduce risk of tissue damage.

Harvard.text: Medication that stifles the body's immune response; often given after an organ transplant to prevent rejection of the new organ.

LLM.text: A medicine that reduces immune-system activity, often to prevent transplant rejection or treat autoimmune disease.

Harvard.text: Treating disease by enhancing or suppressing the body’s immune system.

LLM.text: Treatment using immune system to fight cancer. Types: checkpoint inhibitors (PD-1, PD-L1, CTLA-4), CAR T-cell therapy, cytokines, cancer vaccines. Examples: pembrolizumab, nivolumab, ipilimumab, axicabtagene ciloleucel.

Harvard.text: Something firmly fixed into place, such as a wisdom tooth.

LLM.text: Firmly wedged or unable to move from its normal position, as with an impacted tooth.

Harvard.text: A mass of hardened feces blocking the rectum or colon.

LLM.text: Obstruction caused by material that is firmly lodged, such as hardened stool in the bowel.

Harvard.text: Blood sugar levels that are higher than normal but not yet diabetic. This term is used when the high blood sugar levels are found with a fasting plasma glucose test.

LLM.text: Blood glucose above the normal range after fasting but below the diagnostic threshold for diabetes.

Harvard.text: Blood sugar levels that are higher than normal but not yet diabetic. This term is used when the high blood sugar levels are found with an oral glucose tolerance test.

LLM.text: Blood glucose above the normal range after a glucose challenge but below the diagnostic threshold for diabetes.

Harvard.text: A test that sends sound waves to the eardrum to determine if a problem in the middle ear is causing hearing loss.

LLM.text: A group of tests, including tympanometry, that measure the movement of the eardrum and middle-ear function.

Harvard.text: A device implanted in the chest and connected to the heart that delivers a shock to stop a potentially deadly rhythm and restore a normal (sinus) rhythm.

LLM.text: An implanted device that detects dangerous ventricular rhythms and treats them with antitachycardia pacing or an electrical shock.

Harvard.text: The inability of the penis to become firm or to stay firm enough to have sexual intercourse.

LLM.text: An older term for erectile dysfunction.

Harvard.text: Latin for in place.

LLM.text: In its original place or position.

Harvard.text: Vaccines containing microbes that have been killed, and, therefore, are unable to cause disease.

LLM.text: Vaccines made from microorganisms that have been killed and cannot reproduce.

Harvard.text: A cut made into the skin or an organ during surgery.

LLM.text: A deliberate surgical cut made into the skin or other tissue.

Harvard.text: Involuntary passing of urine or feces.

LLM.text: The involuntary loss of control over urination (urinary incontinence) or defecation (fecal incontinence).

Harvard.text: The time between when a person is exposed to an infection and when symptoms appear.

LLM.text: The time between when a person is exposed to an infection and when symptoms appear.

Harvard.text: An area of dead tissue caused by insufficient blood supply.

LLM.text: An area of dead tissue caused by inadequate blood supply.

Harvard.text: The death of tissue due to a lack of blood.

LLM.text: Tissue death from prolonged ischemia. Examples: myocardial infarction, cerebral infarction.

Harvard.text: The growth of harmful organisms that can cause disease, such as bacteria, in the body.

LLM.text: Measures to prevent healthcare-associated infections: hand hygiene, personal protective equipment (PPE), isolation precautions (contact, droplet, airborne), sterilization, disinfection. See infection control.

Harvard.text: Arthritis caused by harmful organisms such as bacteria.

LLM.text: Inflammation of a joint caused by infection, usually bacterial and sometimes viral or fungal. Acute pain, swelling, warmth, fever, and restricted movement require urgent evaluation because joint damage can develop quickly.

Harvard.text: Heart attack involving the back part of the heart-muscle wall.

LLM.text: A heart attack affecting the lower or inferior portion of the heart muscle.

Harvard.text: The large vein that carries blood from the lower half of the body to the heart.

LLM.text: Body's largest vein, formed by common iliac vein union at L5, returning lower body deoxygenated blood to the right atrium. Ascends right of the aorta, pierces the diaphragm at T8, enters the pericardium. Receives hepatic, renal, gonadal, and lumbar veins. IVC thrombosis/compression causes bilateral lower extremity edema and DVT.

Harvard.text: A cancer that has spread from where it first developed into surrounding tissue.

LLM.text: Cancer that has grown beyond its site of origin into surrounding tissue.

Harvard.text: The body’s reaction to injury or infection. It is characterized by swelling, heat, redness, and pain.

LLM.text: The body's protective response to injury or infection. Cardinal signs: redness (rubor), heat (calor), swelling (tumor), pain (dolor), loss of function (functio laesa). Mediators: histamine, prostaglandins, cytokines, complement. Acute: neutrophil-predominant. Chronic: lymphocyte/macrophage-predominant.

Harvard.text: A general term for two disorders, ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease, that cause the intestines to become swollen and inflamed. Often referred to as IBD.

LLM.text: Chronic relapsing inflammatory conditions of the gastrointestinal tract encompassing Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis, resulting from a dysregulated immune response in genetically susceptible individuals triggered by environmental factors and alterations in the gut microbiome.

Harvard.text: The slow injection of a fluid into a vein or tissues.

LLM.text: Slow administration of a fluid or medicine into a vein or tissue.

Harvard.text: A condition in which the side of a toenail pierces the skin, causing pain, swelling, and sometimes infection.

LLM.text: Ingrown toenail (onychocryptosis) occurs when the nail edge grows into the surrounding skin, causing pain, redness, and swelling. It is common in adolescents and adults, exacerbated by improper nail trimming, tight shoes, and trauma. Treatment includes partial nail avulsion with matrixectomy (phenol application) for recurrent cases.

Harvard.text: A chemical that stops the transmission of a message from one nerve cell to another.

LLM.text: A chemical messenger that reduces signaling between nerve cells.

Harvard.text: Substances injected into the skin to fill in wrinkles or add plumpness to the lips.

LLM.text: Materials injected beneath or into skin to restore volume or soften wrinkles.

Harvard.text: Inserting fluids, such as medications, into the body by means of a hollow needle and syringe.

LLM.text: Introduction of a medication, fluid, or other substance into the body with a needle or other injection device.

Harvard.text: The body’s basic defenses against disease or infection that are present from birth.

LLM.text: First line of defense against pathogens, present from birth. Rapid (minutes to hours), germline-encoded, lacks immunological memory.

Harvard.text: The deepest part of the ear, consisting of the cochlea and the labyrinth.

LLM.text: The deepest part of the ear, consisting of the cochlea and the labyrinth.

Harvard.text: A condition that cannot be treated by surgery.

LLM.text: Not suitable for surgical treatment, often because surgery cannot safely remove or correct the condition.

Harvard.text: The inability to fall asleep or remain asleep long enough to feel rested.

LLM.text: Insomnia is persistent difficulty initiating or maintaining sleep, or early awakening, with daytime impairment despite adequate opportunity and circumstances for sleep. too early despite adequate opportunity for sleep, with resulting daytime impairment. It may be acute or chronic and is often triggered by stress, anxiety, depression, or poor sleep habits.

Harvard.text: A hormone made by the pancreas that controls the amount of glucose (sugar) in the blood.

LLM.text: A pancreatic hormone that helps cells take up glucose and lowers blood glucose.

Harvard.text: A condition in which the body produces insulin but can’t use it properly. This leads to diabetes.

LLM.text: Diminished biological response to physiological insulin concentrations resulting in impaired glucose disposal in peripheral tissues and failure to suppress hepatic glucose production. Pathophysiological hallmark of type two diabetes and metabolic syndrome.

Harvard.text: Now called type 1 diabetes. It occurs when the body doesn’t produce enough insulin to control blood sugar levels properly.

LLM.text: Type 1 diabetes, in which the pancreas produces little or no insulin and replacement insulin is required.

Harvard.text: A device that emits broadband light to improve the look of the skin or remove unwanted hair.

LLM.text: Broadband light treatment used for selected cosmetic skin conditions and hair reduction.

Harvard.text: In exercise, a measure of how hard the body is working. Cues like breathing, talking, and sweating help measure intensity through perceived exertion.

LLM.text: The degree of effort or physiological demand during physical activity.

Harvard.text: Proteins made by the body to protect against viruses, bacteria, and other harmful agents.

LLM.text: Signaling proteins that help coordinate immune responses, especially against viral infections.

Harvard.text: A group of substances that act as messengers in the immune system.

LLM.text: Cytokines that carry signals between immune cells and regulate inflammation.

Harvard.text: A type of lipoprotein. It consists of remnants of very-low-density lipoprotein (VLDL) that eventually turn into low-density lipoprotein (LDL).

LLM.text: A lipoprotein remnant formed as very-low-density lipoprotein is metabolized toward LDL.

Harvard.text: Pain and cramping in the legs during exercise that is caused by narrowed or blocked arteries. Also known as peripheral artery disease of the legs.

LLM.text: Reproducible muscle discomfort, usually in the calf, thigh, or buttock, induced by walking and relieved by rest, caused by exertional arterial insufficiency. It is distinguished from rest pain and nonvascular musculoskeletal pain by history and vascular testing.

common_names: peripheral artery disease of the legs

Harvard.text: An internationally accepted amount of a substance based on its biological activity or effect; used as a measurement for fat-soluble vitamins.

LLM.text: international unit is a biological, genetic, biochemical, or chemical term used in medicine; its significance depends on its structure, function, concentration, pathway, or clinical context.

Harvard.text: Short-term talk therapy focused on identifying and addressing problems in current relationships and building social skills.

LLM.text: A structured, time-limited psychotherapy focused on improving relationships, communication, and coping with interpersonal losses or role transitions; it is used especially for depression.

Harvard.text: A planned, often group, meeting with a person with addiction, with the aim of overcoming denial and inducing the individual to seek treatment.

LLM.text: An action intended to prevent, diagnose, treat, or change a health condition or outcome, such as a medicine, procedure, counseling, or public-health measure.

Harvard.text: A study that compares one group that receives a medication or other therapy (an intervention) and another group does not (controls).

LLM.text: A study in which researchers assign or provide an intervention and compare its outcomes with a control.

Harvard.text: One of the small, shock-absorbing cushions located between the vertebrae of the spine.

LLM.text: A fibrocartilaginous cushion between spinal vertebrae that absorbs shock and permits movement.

Harvard.text: The opening between vertebrae through which a spinal nerve exits the spinal column (plural: foramina).

LLM.text: An opening between adjacent vertebrae through which a spinal nerve exits.

Harvard.text: An adverse reaction that may have similar symptoms to an allergic reaction but does not engage the immune system, and thus is not an allergy.

LLM.text: An adverse response to a substance that does not involve the immune mechanism of an allergy.

Harvard.text: A hemorrhagic stroke caused by the rupture of a blood vessel and subsequent bleeding into the brain tissue.

LLM.text: Bleeding directly into the brain parenchyma, accounting for approximately ten to fifteen percent of all strokes and carrying a high mortality rate of approximately forty percent at thirty days.

Harvard.text: A small artificial lens permanently fixed inside the eye to replace the natural lens during cataract surgery.

LLM.text: Artificial lens replacing natural lens after cataract extraction. Types: monofocal (distance vision), multifocal/bifocal (near and distance), toric (astigmatism), extended depth of focus. Implantation via small incision, folds for insertion. Complications: posterior capsule opacification, dysphotopsia, infection, retinal detachment.

Harvard.text: Inability of the urinary sphincter to close completely.

LLM.text: Weakness of the urinary sphincter that causes stress urinary incontinence.

Harvard.text: Salt compounds containing iodine that are used to control severe hyperthyroidism in special circumstances. They work by decreasing the thyroid gland’s production and secretion of thyroid hormone.

LLM.text: Salts containing iodine, sometimes used in carefully selected thyroid disorders.

Harvard.text: The colored ring in front of the lens that controls the size of the pupil and how much light enters the eye.

LLM.text: Iris concerns iris, a body structure, substance, or clinical concept whose meaning depends on location, function, and patient context. light entry. Two muscles: sphincter pupillae (parasympathetic CN III, constricts in bright light) and dilator pupillae (sympathetic, dilates in darkness). Iris root attaches to the ciliary body.

Harvard.text: Substances such as tobacco, wood smoke, perfumes, and others that cause allergy-like symptoms, although the response is not an allergic reaction.

LLM.text: Substances that provoke inflammation or allergy-like symptoms without necessarily causing an immune allergy.

Harvard.text: Inadequate blood supply to an organ or part of the body.

LLM.text: Reduced blood flow causing oxygen deprivation. Can lead to tissue damage or death.

Harvard.text: The most common form of heart disease, in which narrowed or blocked coronary arteries have difficulty supplying sections of the heart muscle with the blood they need (ischemia).

LLM.text: Heart disease caused by inadequate blood flow through narrowed or blocked coronary arteries.

Harvard.text: A stroke caused by an interruption in the flow of blood to the brain; almost always caused by a blood clot blocking a blood vessel.

LLM.text: A neurologic deficit caused by inadequate blood flow to part of the brain, usually from thrombotic or embolic arterial occlusion. Causes include atherosclerotic disease, cardiac embolism, and small-vessel disease.

Harvard.text: Clusters of hormone-producing cells, including alpha and beta cells, that appear throughout the pancreas.

LLM.text: Clusters of endocrine cells in the pancreas that produce hormones including insulin and glucagon.

Harvard.text: A form of high blood pressure (hypertension) characterized by elevated systolic blood pressure and normal diastolic pressure.

LLM.text: Elevated systolic blood pressure with normal diastolic pressure, commonly related to arterial stiffness in older adults and associated with increased cardiovascular risk.

Harvard.text: An action in which a muscle generates force but does not contract or extend enough to move a joint, such as when pushing against an immovable object.

LLM.text: Describing muscle contraction that produces force without a meaningful change in muscle length or joint movement.

Harvard.text: An actions in which a muscle generates force by contracting or lengthening to move an attached joint through its range of motion, such as lifting a dumbbell from knee-height to shoulder-height.

LLM.text: Describing muscle contraction in which muscle length changes to move a joint under a relatively constant external load.

Harvard.text: The section of the small intestine between the duodenum and the ileum.

LLM.text: Middle segment (2.5 m) with prominent circular folds and tall villi for a velvety appearance. Richer blood supply and thicker walls than the ileum. Primary nutrient absorption site for carbohydrates, amino acids, fatty acids, vitamins, minerals. Fewer Peyer's patches. More commonly affected by Crohn's disease.

Harvard.text: A feeling of fatigue that occurs as the biological clock resets itself after traveling across time zones, usually by airplane.

LLM.text: Temporary circadian rhythm disruption after rapid travel across time zones, causing sleep disturbance, fatigue, impaired concentration, and sometimes gastrointestinal symptoms.

Harvard.text: A junction in the body where bones are linked together.

LLM.text: Articulation between two or more bones permitting movement. Structural classification: fibrous (sutures, syndesmoses, gomphoses -- immovable/slightly movable), cartilaginous (synchondroses, symphyses -- slightly movable), synovial (freely movable -- plane, hinge, pivot, condyloid, saddle, ball-and-socket).

Harvard.text: An exercise that helps prevent and treat incontinence by strengthening pelvic floor muscles.

LLM.text: A pelvic-floor muscle contraction exercise used to improve pelvic-floor strength and control of selected types of urinary or fecal incontinence.

Harvard.text: An unusually hard or thick scar that forms after surgery or an injury.

LLM.text: An overgrowth of scar tissue extending beyond the original wound margins, caused by excessive collagen deposition during wound healing. Keloids are more common in darker skin types (Fitzpatrick IV to VI) and occur at sites of trauma, surgery, piercings, and burns. They are pruritic and painful.

Harvard.text: A procedure in which a laser is used to correct vision problems by reshaping the cornea.

LLM.text: Surgical removal or reshaping of part of the cornea, often to correct vision.

Harvard.text: A protein and the major component of the cuticle and cortex layers of hair; the same protein is found in nails, feathers, claws, and hooves.

LLM.text: A tough structural protein found in skin, hair, nails, and other epithelial tissues.

Harvard.text: Cells of the epidermis that produce a tough protein called keratin and form a soft, protective sheet for the body.

LLM.text: The predominant cells of the epidermis that produce keratin and form the skin’s protective barrier.

Harvard.text: Persistent dryness of the eye.

LLM.text: Chronic dryness and inflammation of the cornea and conjunctiva, commonly called dry-eye syndrome. Symptoms include burning, grittiness, redness, fluctuating vision, and light sensitivity; causes include reduced tear production, excessive evaporation, medicines, and autoimmune disease.

Harvard.text: A skin rash that sometimes occurs along with an autoimmune condition called Reiter's syndrome.

LLM.text: Thickened, scaly skin lesions associated with reactive arthritis.

Harvard.text: Heart disease caused by a lack of selenium, an element that the body needs to function properly.

LLM.text: Heart disease caused by a lack of selenium, an element that the body needs to function properly.

Harvard.text: Substances produced when the body burns fat for energy or when the body doesn’t have enough insulin.

LLM.text: Acidic byproducts produced when the body breaks down fat for energy instead of glucose (ketogenesis). Ketones can be detected in blood and urine.

Harvard.text: The final stage of chronic kidney disease. At this point, the kidneys can no longer eliminate waste products from the body.

LLM.text: The inability of the kidneys to maintain fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base homeostasis and to excrete metabolic wastes. Acute kidney injury (AKI): sudden decline in GFR over hours-days—prerenal (hypoperfusion), intrinsic (acute tubular necrosis, glomerulonephritis, interstitial nephritis), postrenal (obstruction).

Harvard.text: A surgical procedure that eases or eliminates the pain of spinal fractures. It also restores vertebrae that have collapsed due to fractures to their normal size.

LLM.text: A minimally invasive procedure that uses a balloon to create space in a collapsed vertebral body and then injects bone cement to stabilize a painful compression fracture.

Harvard.text: Blood pressure that frequently fluctuates between normal and abnormal during the course of a day, often within only a few minutes.

LLM.text: Blood pressure that fluctuates substantially over short periods.

Harvard.text: The inner ear. It contains the cochlea, which is responsible for hearing, as well as structures that are needed for balance.

LLM.text: The inner ear. It contains the cochlea, which is responsible for hearing, as well as structures that are needed for balance.

Harvard.text: A tear in the skin.

LLM.text: A wound caused by tearing of body tissue, typically caused by trauma from a sharp object (knife, glass, metal) or blunt force that splits the skin. Lacerations involve the skin and may extend into subcutaneous tissue, muscle, tendon, nerve, or blood vessels.

Harvard.text: The gland that produces tears.

LLM.text: The paired almond-shaped exocrine glands that secrete the aqueous layer of the tear film, located in the lacrimal fossa of the superior lateral orbit (orbital part) and the upper eyelid (palpebral part).

Harvard.text: An enzyme that breaks down milk sugar (lactose) in the body.

LLM.text: An enzyme that breaks down the milk sugar lactose in the small intestine.

Harvard.text: A rare but potentially lethal condition in which blood lactic acid levels increase.

LLM.text: Metabolic acidosis associated with increased lactate production or reduced lactate clearance. Causes include impaired tissue oxygen delivery, medicines, liver disease, seizures, and other disorders.

Harvard.text: A sugar found in milk and dairy products.

LLM.text: The principal sugar in milk, composed of glucose and galactose. Lactase in the small intestine digests it.

Harvard.text: The inability of the body to easily digest lactose, a sugar found in milk and dairy products.

LLM.text: Lactose intolerance results from insufficient lactase activity, causing bloating, abdominal pain, gas, or diarrhea after consuming lactose. lactose, the primary disaccharide in milk and dairy products. The lactase enzyme is produced by enterocytes of the small intestinal brush border and hydrolyzes lactose into glucose and galactose for absorption.

Harvard.text: A small ischemic stroke caused by the blockage of one of the smaller blood vessels in the brain; the most common effect is weakness or disability on one side of the body.

LLM.text: An ischemic stroke caused by blockage of a small artery deep within the brain.

Harvard.text: Hard, dense tissue that forms the outer shell of bones. Also called compact bone.

LLM.text: Mature, organized bone tissue arranged in layers.

Harvard.text: One of the two thin, plate-like parts of each vertebra.

LLM.text: A thin plate of bone forming part of a vertebral arch.

Harvard.text: An operation in which all or part of one or both laminae is removed.

LLM.text: Laminectomy removes part of a vertebral lamina to decompress the spinal canal or nerve roots, often for stenosis, tumor, or selected disk disease. canal. Indications: spinal stenosis (lumbar and cervical), herniated disc (with central stenosis), and spinal tumor. Decompression of the entire spinal canal. Often combined with discectomy (lumbar) or foraminotomy (nerve root decompression).

Harvard.text: Cells of the immune system that work in the skin to fight infection.

LLM.text: Immune cells in the epidermis that capture antigens and help initiate immune responses.

Harvard.text: Fine, soft hair that grows all over the body of a fetus and is typically shed before birth.

LLM.text: Fine, soft hair that grows all over the body of a fetus and is typically shed before birth.

Harvard.text: A surgical procedure carried out with tiny instruments inserted through small openings in the skin.

LLM.text: A minimally invasive surgical technique using a laparoscope (a thin, lighted telescope) inserted through a small incision (typically at the umbilicus) to visualize the abdominal and pelvic organs. Carbon dioxide gas is insufflated to create a working space. Additional small incisions (ports) allow insertion of instruments.

Harvard.text: A concentrated beam of light; lasers are used in certain surgeries and other medical procedures.

LLM.text: A device that produces a concentrated beam of light used for diagnosis, treatment, or surgery.

Harvard.text: A surgical procedure to ease snoring by removing or reshaping some of the tissues in the mouth (usually the uvula and soft palate) that vibrate and cause the noise of snoring.

LLM.text: A procedure that reshapes or removes selected soft-palate and uvula tissue to reduce snoring.

Harvard.text: Permanent hair removal technique that uses a laser to target and heat melanin in the hair shaft, which damages the hair follicle.

LLM.text: Hair reduction using laser energy absorbed by pigment in the hair follicle.

Harvard.text: Surgery that uses a laser to seal off blood vessels in the eye; used to treat a number of eye diseases.

LLM.text: A laser treatment that seals or destroys abnormal blood vessels, especially in the retina.

Harvard.text: A surgical technique for treating an enlarged prostate (benign prostatic hyperplasia). It uses a high-energy laser to remove large amounts of prostate tissue with little bleeding.

LLM.text: A procedure that uses laser energy to remove or vaporize enlarged prostate tissue.

Harvard.text: An allergic reaction to the proteins found in natural rubber.

LLM.text: An immune-mediated hypersensitivity reaction to natural rubber latex. Contact may cause dermatitis, urticaria, rhinitis, asthma, or anaphylaxis, especially in healthcare and occupational settings.

Harvard.text: A drug or substance that induces bowel movements or makes the stool softer and looser.
