LLM.text: A drug that promotes bowel evacuation, used for constipation and bowel preparation. Classes: bulk-forming (psyllium, methylcellulose), osmotic (polyethylene glycol, lactulose, magnesium salts), stimulant (senna, bisacodyl), stool softener (docusate), and lubricant (mineral oil). Choice depends on constipation type and patient factors.

Harvard.text: Abbreviation for low-density lipoprotein. This so-called bad cholesterol can build up on artery walls, narrowing the artery and making a heart attack or stroke more likely.

LLM.text: Low-density lipoprotein; the 'bad' cholesterol that transports cholesterol to peripheral tissues and is the principal driver of atherosclerosis. Elevated LDL is a major modifiable cardiovascular risk factor; guidelines target LDL levels based on global risk (statin intensity).

Harvard.text: When fear of not sleeping develops after a short period of not sleeping well, and this anxiety causes ongoing trouble falling or staying asleep.

LLM.text: Persistent difficulty sleeping that is maintained by anxiety and conditioned behaviors associated with sleep.

Harvard.text: Use of a panel of light-emitting diodes (LEDs) to stimulate skin cells and improve the look of the skin.

LLM.text: Use of low-energy light-emitting diodes to influence skin cells and improve selected skin concerns.

Harvard.text: One of the main arteries that supplies blood to the heart; it runs down the front surface of the heart.

LLM.text: A major coronary artery supplying the front wall and septum of the left ventricle.

Harvard.text: The left upper chamber of the heart.

LLM.text: Receives oxygenated blood from 4 pulmonary veins. Most posterior chamber forming the cardiac base on chest radiography. Smooth walls from absorbed pulmonary veins; small auricle with pectinate muscles. Mitral valve separates it from the left ventricle.

Harvard.text: One of the main arteries that supplies blood to the heart; it curves around the back of the heart.

LLM.text: A coronary artery that curves around the left side and back of the heart.

Harvard.text: The left lower chamber of the heart. It pumps blood out of the heart to other organs in the body.

LLM.text: Thickest cardiac chamber (13-15 mm), pumping oxygenated blood into the aorta for systemic distribution. Generates approximately 120 mmHg systolic pressure. Receives blood through the mitral valve; ejects through the aortic valve.

Harvard.text: A thickening of the wall of the lower left chamber of the heart, which is responsible for pumping blood to organs throughout the body.

LLM.text: Thickening of the muscular wall of the heart's left ventricle.

Harvard.text: A surgically implanted pump that augments the pumping action of the left ventricle.

LLM.text: An implanted mechanical pump that helps the left ventricle circulate blood.

Harvard.text: A device used to check the prescription of eyeglasses.

LLM.text: An instrument used to measure the prescription and optical properties of eyeglass lenses.

Harvard.text: A hormone produced by fat cells that acts on the brain to suppress appetite and burn stored fat.

LLM.text: A hormone produced mainly by adipose tissue that signals stored-energy status to the brain and influences appetite and energy balance.

Harvard.text: An infected, diseased, or wounded area of tissue.

LLM.text: A general term for any abnormal change in tissue structure due to disease or injury.

Harvard.text: Asthma medications that work by blocking leukotrienes, chemicals made in the body as part of an allergic reaction.

LLM.text: Medicines that reduce leukotriene effects and help prevent asthma or allergy symptoms.

Harvard.text: Asthma medications that work by blocking the production or action of leukotrienes, chemicals made in the body as part of an allergic reaction.

LLM.text: Medicines that reduce asthma or allergy symptoms by blocking leukotriene production or action.

Harvard.text: Chemicals that cause airways to swell when an allergic reaction occurs or in diseases like asthma.

LLM.text: Inflammatory signaling molecules that can narrow and swell airways during allergic reactions.

Harvard.text: A man-made version of the thyroid hormone thyroxine.

LLM.text: The sodium salt of synthetic thyroxine used to replace deficient thyroid hormone.

Harvard.text: Abbreviation for luteinizing hormone, a hormone that controls ovulation in women. In men, luteinizing hormone triggers production of testosterone.

LLM.text: Luteinizing hormone, a pituitary hormone involved in ovulation and testosterone production.

Harvard.text: Sexual desire.

LLM.text: Sexual desire or drive, influenced by biological, psychological, and social factors.

Harvard.text: A blood-sucking parasite known as Pediculus humanus capitis that can cause an itchy scalp; infestations are highly contagious and especially common in school-age children.

LLM.text: Pediculosis: infestation by blood-sucking lice—head lice (Pediculus humanus capitis, common in children, scalp), body lice (Pediculus humanus corporis, clothing/seams, associated with poor hygiene and epidemic typhus transmission), and pubic/crab lice (Pthirus pubis, sexually transmitted).

Harvard.text: A band of tissue that connects bones.

LLM.text: A dense, fibrous connective tissue band that connects bone to bone, providing passive joint stability and guiding joint motion. Ligaments are composed predominantly of type I collagen fibers (parallel orientation, crimped pattern) and elastin fibers (10-20\% in some ligaments), arranged in bundles.

Harvard.text: Any material that is tied around a blood vessel to stop it from bleeding.

LLM.text: Any cord, wire, rope, fabric, or flexible object used to constrict the neck, bind limbs, suspend the body, or inflict injury. The resulting pale groove-shaped abrasion may be horizontal with petechiae in homicidal strangulation, or oblique and upward in hanging.

Harvard.text: Antioxidant chemicals found in seeds like flax and sesame, as well as some fruits, vegetables, and grains.

LLM.text: Plant compounds found in seeds, grains, fruits, and vegetables that have antioxidant activity.

Harvard.text: A group of structures in the brain that help control memory, emotions, sexual arousal, and motivation.

LLM.text: A set of interconnected brain structures located in the medial temporal lobe and around the corpus callosum, involved in emotion, memory, motivation, behaviour, and autonomic regulation. The term was coined by Paul Broca (1878, le grand lobe limbique) and expanded by Papez (1937, Papez circuit) and MacLean (1952, 'visceral brain').

Harvard.text: The border between the cornea and the white of the eye.

LLM.text: The border where the cornea meets the white outer coat of the eye.

Harvard.text: A man-made version of the thyroid hormone triiodothyronine.

LLM.text: A synthetic form of the thyroid hormone triiodothyronine used in selected thyroid disorders.

Harvard.text: An enzyme secreted by the pancreas that helps the body break down fats.

LLM.text: An enzyme that breaks down fats into smaller molecules. Blood lipase testing is commonly used when pancreatitis is suspected, although an abnormal result is not specific in every case.

Harvard.text: Fats, oils, and waxes that serve as building blocks for cells or as energy sources. Lipids are also capable of accumulating in the artery walls to form plaque.

LLM.text: Fats, oils, and related substances used for energy, cell structure, and signaling.

Harvard.text: Dents or depressions in the skin that are caused by a loss of fatty tissue.

LLM.text: Loss of subcutaneous adipose tissue at specific sites, most commonly caused by repeated subcutaneous injections of insulin or other medications, or associated with autoimmune conditions and HIV lipodystrophy.

Harvard.text: A buildup of fatty tissue.

LLM.text: Localized thickening or accumulation of fatty tissue, commonly at repeated insulin-injection sites.

Harvard.text: A noncancerous tumor or growth composed of fat cells.

LLM.text: The most common benign soft tissue tumor, composed of mature adipocytes. It presents as a soft, mobile, painless subcutaneous nodule, commonly on the trunk, neck, and proximal extremities. Lipomas grow slowly and may be multiple (familial multiple lipomatosis). Diagnosis is clinical; ultrasound or MRI for deep or atypical lesions.

Harvard.text: A combination of fat (lipid) and protein molecules bound together as packages. The combination allows fats and cholesterol to move easily through the blood.

LLM.text: Complex of lipids and proteins transporting hydrophobic lipids in aqueous blood. Classes: chylomicrons (dietary lipids), VLDL (endogenous triglycerides), LDL (cholesterol delivery), HDL (reverse cholesterol transport). ApoB-100 in LDL; apoA-1 in HDL. Elevated LDL cholesterol is a major risk factor for atherosclerosis.

Harvard.text: A test that measures the amount of triglycerides, total cholesterol, HDL (good cholesterol), and LDL (bad cholesterol) in a person’s blood.

LLM.text: A blood test measuring cholesterol, triglycerides, and lipoprotein fractions such as LDL and HDL.

Harvard.text: A molecule made up of fat and protein that is very similar to harmful LDL.

LLM.text: An LDL-like lipoprotein whose elevated level is an inherited cardiovascular risk factor.

Harvard.text: A cosmetic procedure that removes fat from an area of the body.

LLM.text: A surgical procedure that removes localized deposits of subcutaneous fat through a cannula connected to suction. It contours selected areas but is not a treatment for obesity and carries risks such as bleeding, infection, contour irregularity, and fluid shifts.

Harvard.text: Vaccines made from a weakened virus or microbe. These weakened viruses and microbes don't cause disease; instead they teach the body to recognize the substance as harmful and destroy it if there is contact with it in the future.

LLM.text: Vaccines containing weakened organisms that stimulate immunity without usually causing disease.

Harvard.text: A vital organ that removes waste products from the body and helps with digestion.

LLM.text: The largest internal organ, located in the right upper quadrant of the abdomen beneath the diaphragm.

Harvard.text: A legal document that states what a person would and wouldn’t want if he or she is no longer able to make health care decisions.

LLM.text: A type of advance directive that records a person's preferences for future medical treatment if the person cannot communicate or decide.

Harvard.text: Bleeding that occurs in the white matter of the brain beneath the cerebral cortex.

LLM.text: Bleeding into a lobe of the brain, beneath the cerebral cortex.

Harvard.text: A surgical procedure to severe one or more branches of nerves into the frontal lobe of the brain.

LLM.text: A historical brain operation that severed connections involving the frontal lobes.

Harvard.text: Milk-producing glands of the breast.

LLM.text: Small subdivisions of an organ; in the breast, milk-producing glandular units.

Harvard.text: In reference to cancer, generally means cancer that is limited to a specific gland or other tissue, without any distant spread; an organ-confined cancer.

LLM.text: Limited to a particular area or organ, without evidence of distant spread.

Harvard.text: An area of the brain stem that helps control the brain’s alertness, responses to certain stimuli, and stress and anxiety levels.

LLM.text: A brainstem nucleus involved in alertness, attention, stress responses, and norepinephrine release.

Harvard.text: A memory that lasts from a few minutes to decades.

LLM.text: Memory that can persist from minutes to many years.

Harvard.text: A weight-loss plan that limits calories to 800–1,500 a day.

LLM.text: A diet that restricts energy intake to support weight loss or another therapeutic goal.

Harvard.text: So-called bad cholesterol. If there is too much LDL in the blood, it can collect on artery walls, narrowing them and making heart attacks and strokes more likely.

LLM.text: A lipoprotein that transports cholesterol and can contribute to artery-wall plaque when elevated.

Harvard.text: A ring of muscle where the esophagus and stomach meet. It relaxes to let food into the stomach and closes to prevent stomach acids from backing up and irritating the esophagus.

LLM.text: A ring of muscle between the esophagus and stomach that helps prevent acid reflux.

Harvard.text: A procedure in which a hollow needle is inserted into the lower part of the spinal canal to withdraw fluid for testing. Also called a spinal tap.

LLM.text: Insertion of a needle into the lower spinal canal to obtain cerebrospinal fluid or administer selected medicines.

Harvard.text: The lower portion of the spine. It includes the five lowermost bones (vertebrae) of the spine and is the start of the lower back.

LLM.text: The five vertebrae forming the lower back.

Harvard.text: Narrowing of the spinal canal in the lower portion of the spine (known as the lumbar spine).

LLM.text: Narrowing of the spinal canal or nerve openings in the lower back.

Harvard.text: The hollow part of a tube, like a blood vessel, or the cavity in a hollow organ.

LLM.text: The inner space of a hollow organ, vessel, or tube.

Harvard.text: A natural substance found in green leafy vegetables.

LLM.text: A carotenoid pigment found in leafy greens and concentrated in the retina.

Harvard.text: A hormone that controls ovulation in women. In men, luteinizing hormone triggers production of testosterone.

LLM.text: LH: a gonadotropin secreted by the anterior pituitary, regulating gonadal steroidogenesis. In females: stimulates theca cells to produce androgens (aromatized to estradiol); mid-cycle LH surge triggers ovulation (used in ovulation prediction and timing of intercourse/IVF). In males: stimulates Leydig cells to produce testosterone.

Harvard.text: A drug that slows the production of hormones by the testicles in men or the ovaries in women.

LLM.text: A medicine that initially stimulates and then suppresses reproductive-hormone production with continued use.

Harvard.text: Abbreviation for left-ventricular assist device, a surgically implanted pump that augments the pumping action of the left ventricle.

LLM.text: Left-ventricular assist device, an implanted pump that helps the left ventricle circulate blood.

Harvard.text: An infectious disease transmitted by a tick bite.

LLM.text: A tick-borne infection caused by Borrelia burgdorferi (Ixodes scapularis, deer tick), endemic to the northeastern and upper midwestern US. Early localized: erythema migrans (bullseye rash, >5cm) at tick bite site, fatigue, fever, myalgia.

Harvard.text: Small, bean-shaped organs that filter germs and foreign matter out of the body. Also called lymph glands.

LLM.text: Small immune organs that filter lymph and help detect infection or abnormal cells.

Harvard.text: A system of channels that drains excess clear fluid, called lymph, from tissues and returns it into the bloodstream.

LLM.text: A network of lymphatic vessels, lymph nodes, and lymphoid organs (tonsils, thymus, spleen, Peyer patches) that returns interstitial fluid (lymph) to the bloodstream, transports dietary fat (chyle), and serves as the conduit for immune surveillance.

Harvard.text: Blockage in or damage to the lymphatic systems, causing lymphatic fluid to build up in tissues, making them swell.

LLM.text: Persistent swelling caused by accumulation of lymphatic fluid in tissues, usually in an arm or leg.

Harvard.text: A type of white blood cell that can recognize foreign substances in the body.

LLM.text: A type of white blood cell (leukocyte) that is the primary cellular component of the adaptive immune system. Lymphocytes account for 20-40\% of circulating white blood cells (1.0--4.8$10^9/L$). Three main types: (1) T lymphocytes (T cells): develop in the thymus, responsible for cell-mediated immunity.

Harvard.text: A type of cancer that affects cells in the lymphatic system.

LLM.text: A malignancy of lymphocytes, divided into Hodgkin lymphoma (HL—Reed-Sternberg cells, cervical/supraclavicular nodes, B symptoms, younger adults) and non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL—heterogeneous, more common, aggressive or indolent).

Harvard.text: The presence of larger-than-normal red blood cells in circulation—even though there are too few of them—caused by lack of folate and vitamin B12.

LLM.text: Anemia in which red blood cells are larger than normal, commonly because of vitamin B12 or folate deficiency.

Harvard.text: Substances that provide energy and that the body needs for growth. The main categories are: fat, carbohydrate, and protein.

LLM.text: Nutrients needed in large amounts: carbohydrates, protein, fat. Provide energy and structural components.

Harvard.text: A type of white blood cell that destroys cell debris, bacteria, and foreign agents.

LLM.text: Macrophage concerns macrophage, a body structure, substance, or clinical concept whose meaning depends on location, function, and patient context.

Harvard.text: The area in the center of the retina that produces sharp, clear central vision and allows one to see fine detail.

LLM.text: The macula is a specialized region of the central retina approximately five and a half millimeters in diameter that is responsible for high-acuity central vision, color perception, and fine detail discrimination, and it contains the highest density of cone photoreceptors in the eye.

Harvard.text: An eye disease that slowly destroys sharp, clear central vision.

LLM.text: A progressive degenerative disease of the central retina (macula) and the leading cause of irreversible vision loss in individuals over age 50 in developed countries, affecting approximately 10 percent of those over 65 and 30 percent over 80.

Harvard.text: The build-up of fluid in the macula caused by fluid leaking from blood vessels in the eye. It can blur and damage vision.

LLM.text: Swelling of the macula caused by fluid leaking from retinal blood vessels.

Harvard.text: Swallowing too much air during a meal, causing excessive gas and discomfort. Also known as stomach bubble syndrome.

LLM.text: Stomach discomfort and bloating caused by swallowing excessive air while eating.

Harvard.text: A scan that creates detailed pictures of internal organs; commonly referred to as MRI. Magnetic resonance imaging uses radio waves, a strong magnetic field, and a computer to produce images of organs and internal tissues.

LLM.text: Uses strong magnetic field and radiofrequency pulses to generate images from hydrogen protons. Excellent soft tissue contrast. No ionizing radiation. Sequences: T1-weighted (fat bright, fluid dark), T2-weighted (fluid bright), FLAIR (suppresses CSF), DWI (diffusion restriction). Contrast: gadolinium-based.

Harvard.text: A test to measure sleepiness during the day. A tester measures how long it takes a person who is sitting up in a chair or bed to fall asleep after he or she has been asked to stay awake.

LLM.text: A sleep test that measures how long a person can remain awake in a quiet setting during the day.

Harvard.text: Depression that interferes with daily life for an extended period. Episodes of major depression during bereavement can be distinguished from normal sadness by such symptoms as persistent feelings of worthlessness, thoughts about death, feelings of guilt, persistent trouble functioning, and marked mental and physical sluggishness.

LLM.text: A depressive disorder causing persistent low mood or loss of interest with significant functional impairment.

Harvard.text: Molecules that help protect the body from foreign substances. These molecules display proteins on the surface of cells so that protective immune system cells can kill the protein if it is harmful to the body.

LLM.text: A cell-surface molecule that presents protein fragments to immune cells.

Harvard.text: An unhealthy physiological response to stressors, in which the stress response often does not turn off even when the stressor disappears.

LLM.text: A persistent or disproportionate stress reaction that harms health or functioning.

Harvard.text: A general feeling of illness that can be a sign of disease.

LLM.text: Malaise is a disease, symptom, syndrome, or clinical finding; its causes, diagnostic features, severity, complications, and treatment depend on clinical assessment.

Harvard.text: Cancerous.

LLM.text: Cancerous and capable of invading nearby tissue or spreading to distant sites.

Harvard.text: A dangerous type of high blood pressure marked by an unusually sudden rise in blood pressure to very high levels, often accompanied by headache, blurred vision, and seizures.

LLM.text: Severely elevated BP greater than 180/120 with end-organ damage. Renal findings include hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis with onion-skinning and fibrinoid necrosis. Treat with IV antihypertensives. Poor prognosis if untreated. May cause AKI, encephalopathy, and retinopathy.

Harvard.text: Failure to eat or to properly absorb the nutrients needed for good health.

LLM.text: Malnutrition includes inadequate, excessive, or imbalanced nutrient intake and can impair growth, immunity, wound healing, muscle function, and organ reserve. form, and function. Undernutrition: protein-energy malnutrition, micronutrient deficiencies. Overnutrition: overweight, obesity, related comorbidities. Screen with MNA (Mini Nutritional Assessment), MUST (Malnutrition Universal Screening Tool).

Harvard.text: Abbreviation for monoamine oxidase inhibitors, medications used to treat depression. They work by making the chemical messengers serotonin and norepinephrine more available.

LLM.text: Monoamine oxidase inhibitors are a class of antidepressant drugs that inhibit the enzyme monoamine oxidase, which breaks down serotonin, norepinephrine, and dopamine in the brain. By inhibiting this enzyme, MAOIs increase the levels of these neurotransmitters in the synaptic cleft.

Harvard.text: A cell involved in allergic reactions. When stimulated, it releases chemicals like histamine that signal infection and cause inflammation.

LLM.text: A tissue-resident immune cell with large granules containing histamine, heparin, tryptase, and cytokines; bears high-affinity IgE receptors (Fc-epsilon-RI).

Harvard.text: The bone in the skull behind the ear.

LLM.text: The portion of the temporal bone located behind the ear.

Harvard.text: A cosmetic surgery to reshape and lift drooping breasts. Commonly known as a breast lift.

LLM.text: Surgery that lifts and reshapes sagging breasts.

Harvard.text: Sexual self-stimulation.

LLM.text: Self-stimulation of the genitals for sexual pleasure. It is a common human behavior; it is generally not harmful unless it causes injury, distress, or interferes with daily life.

Harvard.text: Refers to the middle of something.

LLM.text: The inner region of an organ; in the kidney it contains the renal pyramids, and in the brainstem it regulates vital functions.

Harvard.text: Fewer than normal healthy red blood cells in circulation, caused by a lack of folate or vitamin B12. Red cells become large and deformed, and are unable to carry oxygen efficiently.

LLM.text: Anemia caused by impaired DNA synthesis, usually related to vitamin B12 or folate deficiency, with abnormally large red blood cells.

Harvard.text: A type of medication taken to treat type 2 diabetes.

LLM.text: Short-acting medicines that stimulate pancreatic insulin release to lower blood glucose.

Harvard.text: A substance that gives the skin, hair, and eyes their natural color.

LLM.text: Melanin concerns melanin, a body structure, substance, or clinical concept whose meaning depends on location, function, and patient context.

Harvard.text: Cells located deep in the epidermis that produce melanin, the pigment that colors skin.

LLM.text: Dendritic pigment-producing neural crest-derived cells in the epidermal basal layer and hair follicles, comprising approximately 5-10 percent of basal keratinocytes. Produce melanin (eumelanin, brown-black; pheomelanin, yellow-red) in melanosomes, transferred to keratinocytes via dendritic processes for UV protection.

Harvard.text: The most dangerous type of skin cancer.

LLM.text: Melanoma is a disease, symptom, syndrome, or clinical finding; its causes, diagnostic features, severity, complications, and treatment depend on clinical assessment.

Harvard.text: A hormone that regulates the body’s sleep-wake cycle.

LLM.text: A hormone produced mainly by the pineal gland that helps regulate sleep-wake timing.

Harvard.text: A thin layer of tissue that surrounds or lines organs or cavities.

LLM.text: A thin tissue layer that surrounds a cell, organ, or body cavity.

terms.term: Memory T Cells And B Cells

Harvard.text: Immune cells that remember harmful agents that have entered the body in the past. When they spot the substance again, they spur the immune system to eliminate the invader.

LLM.text: Long-lived immune cells that respond rapidly when they encounter a previously recognized antigen.

terms.normalized_term: memory t cells and b cells

Harvard.text: An illness caused by a fluid imbalance in the inner ear.

LLM.text: A disorder of the inner ear characterized by recurrent episodes of vertigo, fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, and aural fullness, usually associated with abnormal endolymphatic fluid regulation.

Harvard.text: The three membranes that cover and protect the brain and spinal cord.

LLM.text: The three membranes enveloping the brain and spinal cord: dura mater (outermost, tough), arachnoid mater (middle, avascular), and pia mater (innermost, adherent to the CNS surface). The subarachnoid space (between arachnoid and pia) contains cerebrospinal fluid. The epidural and subdural spaces are sites of hemorrhage.

Harvard.text: Swelling of the membranes that cover and protect the brain and spinal cord.

LLM.text: Meningitis is inflammation of the membranes around the brain and spinal cord, caused by infection or noninfectious inflammation and presenting with headache, fever, neck stiffness, or altered mental status. infection but also by bacteria, fungi, parasites, medicines, or autoimmune disease. Symptoms may include fever, headache, neck stiffness, light sensitivity, or altered mental status and require urgent assessment.

Harvard.text: The point marking the end of menstruation, officially designated as one year after a woman’s final period.

LLM.text: Menopause is the permanent end of menstrual periods after loss of ovarian follicular activity, accompanied by hormonal changes and possible vasomotor, genitourinary, sleep, and bone effects. woman’s final period.

Harvard.text: Units used to estimate the oxygen consumption, or metabolic cost, of physical activity, and, hence, its intensity. One metabolic equivalent (MET) is the estimated energy cost of the body at rest.

LLM.text: Units estimating the energy cost of physical activity relative to resting metabolism.

Harvard.text: A cluster of risk factors that accelerate the progression of heart disease.

LLM.text: Cluster of conditions: abdominal obesity, hypertension, hyperglycemia, high triglycerides, low HDL. Increases cardiovascular disease and diabetes risk.

Harvard.text: The chemical reactions that occur in all living organisms to maintain life. An example is converting food into energy that the body needs to function.

LLM.text: Metabolism concerns metabolism, a body structure, substance, or clinical concept whose meaning depends on location, function, and patient context. anabolism (synthesis, consumes energy). Central pathways: glycolysis, TCA cycle, oxidative phosphorylation, pentose phosphate pathway. Metabolic regulation ensures energy homeostasis.

Harvard.text: The spread of cancer cells from the primary site to another part of the body.

LLM.text: Metastasis is spread of malignant cells from a primary tumor to noncontiguous tissues through lymphatic, blood, or body-cavity routes, forming secondary tumors. hematogenous, direct extension, transcoelomic. Common sites: lungs, liver, bone, brain. Distant metastasis indicates Stage IV disease.

Harvard.text: A device that delivers a specific dose of an inhaled asthma medication.

LLM.text: A pressurized inhaler delivering a metered dose of medication. Requires proper technique for effective delivery. Spacer devices improve drug delivery and reduce oropharyngeal deposition. Most common delivery device for asthma and COPD maintenance.

Harvard.text: Bacteria in the gut that help with the digestion of complex sugars.

LLM.text: A methane-producing microorganism commonly found in the human intestine.

Harvard.text: Abbreviation for metabolic equivalents, units used to estimate the oxygen consumption, or metabolic cost, of physical activity, and, hence, its intensity. One MET is the estimated energy cost of the body at rest.

LLM.text: Metabolic equivalents, units used to express the intensity or energy cost of physical activity.

Harvard.text: Abbreviation for major histocompatibility complex molecule, molecules that help protect the body from foreign substances. These molecules display proteins on the surface of cells so that protective immune system cells can kill the protein if it is harmful to the body.

LLM.text: A major histocompatibility complex molecule that displays antigens to T cells.

Harvard.text: Leakage of small amounts of a protein called albumin into the urine caused by kidney disease or damage.

LLM.text: Excretion of 30 to 300 mg of albumin daily undetectable by standard dipstick. Earliest marker of diabetic nephropathy and cardiovascular risk predictor. Detected by urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio on spot specimen. Normal less than 30 mg/g creatinine. Signals early glomerular damage in diabetes warranting RAAS blockade initiation.

Harvard.text: A tiny bulge that develops in the wall of a blood vessel.

LLM.text: A small bulge in the wall of a blood vessel.

Harvard.text: A microorganism.

LLM.text: A microorganism, such as a bacterium, fungus, protozoan, or virus.

Harvard.text: A cosmetic procedure in which tiny crystals under high pressure are sprayed on the face. This buffs away the outer layer of skin, eliminates fine lines, and improves the look of the skin.

LLM.text: A cosmetic procedure that mechanically removes a superficial layer of skin.

Harvard.text: A unit of mass, equal to one-thousandth of a milligram. Abbreviated as mcg.

LLM.text: A unit of mass equal to one-millionth of a gram, commonly used to express doses or concentrations of medicines and biological substances.

Harvard.text: Reducing a substance to very small particles.

LLM.text: Processed into very small particles to improve dispersion or absorption.

Harvard.text: Vitamins and minerals needed to maintain normal body functions and prevent certain illnesses.

LLM.text: Vitamins and minerals required in small amounts for enzymatic, hormonal, structural, hematologic, neurologic, and immune functions. They include fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, and K), water-soluble vitamins, and essential minerals.

Harvard.text: A condition in which the smallest blood vessels in the walls of the heart are narrowed or inelastic.

LLM.text: Disease affecting small blood vessels, which may reduce blood flow to organs or tissues.

Harvard.text: The body's small blood vessels.

LLM.text: The network of the body’s smallest blood vessels, including arterioles, capillaries, and venules.

Harvard.text: Emptying the bladder. Also called urination or voiding.

LLM.text: The process of urination, coordinated by the pontine micturition center, parasympathetic (pelvic nerve, S2-S4) contraction of the detrusor muscle, and relaxation of the internal (involuntary) and external (voluntary, pudendal nerve) urethral sphincters.

Harvard.text: The air-filled cavity behind the eardrum that contains the three small bones that transmit sound vibrations to the inner ear.

LLM.text: An air-filled space between the eardrum and inner ear that contains the malleus, incus, and stapes. These ossicles transmit sound vibrations to the inner ear, and the auditory tube helps equalize middle-ear pressure.

Harvard.text: A severe headache with pain that usually begins on one side of the head. Symptoms may include visual disturbances (called aura), nausea, vomiting, and sensitivity to light or noise.

LLM.text: A recurrent headache disorder often causing moderate-to-severe pain, nausea, and sensitivity to light or sound.

Harvard.text: A severe headache preceded by visual disturbances such as flashing lights, seeing lines, or a blind spot.

LLM.text: A primary headache disorder characterized by recurrent attacks of fully reversible visual, sensory, or speech symptoms that develop gradually over at least five minutes and last no more than sixty minutes, followed by headache with the characteristics of migraine.

Harvard.text: A severe headache that is not preceded by visual disturbances such as flashing lights. Also known as common migraine.

LLM.text: A primary headache disorder characterized by recurrent attacks of moderate to severe, pulsating, unilateral headache lasting four to seventy-two hours, associated with nausea, vomiting, photophobia, and phonophobia.

Harvard.text: The loss of some brain functions, such as memory, thinking, or language, that is noticeable, but doesn’t interfere with ability to carry out daily tasks.

LLM.text: A transitional cognitive state between normal aging and dementia, characterized by subjective cognitive complaints confirmed by objective cognitive impairment that is not severe enough to significantly interfere with daily activities.

Harvard.text: A metric unit of weight equivalent to one-thousandth of a gram. Abbreviated as mg.

LLM.text: A metric unit of mass equal to one-thousandth of a gram; its abbreviation is mg.

Harvard.text: A practice with its roots in Buddhism that encourages people to be more fully aware of the present moment. Often achieved through meditation.

LLM.text: A practice of deliberately attending to present-moment experiences with an open, nonjudgmental attitude; it may be used as a behavioral or psychological intervention.

Harvard.text: A form of meditation with roots in ancient Buddhist practice through which a person has a calm awareness of his or her body and feelings and is fully engaged in the present; also called insight meditation.

LLM.text: A meditation practice that trains sustained, nonjudgmental awareness of present-moment sensations, thoughts, and emotions.

Harvard.text: A well-established acceptance-based therapy, used principally in treatment of depression and anxiety.

LLM.text: A psychotherapy approach combining cognitive behavioral techniques with mindfulness practices to change unhelpful thoughts and improve awareness and emotional regulation.

Harvard.text: An eye drop that constricts the pupil; used to treat glaucoma.

LLM.text: A substance or medicine that constricts the pupil.

Harvard.text: Small structures within cells that create break down nutrients and create energy for cells. Known as the power producers or energy factories of cells.

LLM.text: Double-membrane organelles known as the "powerhouse of the cell," generating ATP through oxidative phosphorylation. Outer membrane is permeable; inner membrane is highly folded (cristae) and contains the electron transport chain and ATP synthase.

Harvard.text: The valve that controls the one-way flow of blood from the left atrium to the left ventricle.

LLM.text: Left atrioventricular (bicuspid) valve with anterior and posterior cusps supported by chordae tendineae and papillary muscles. Anterior cusp is larger and proximate to the aortic valve. Mitral valve prolapse is the most common valvular abnormality. Mitral stenosis (most commonly rheumatic) and regurgitation are significant.

Harvard.text: A valve problem in which one or both of the mitral valve flaps collapse backward into the left atrium. This may allow a small amount of blood to leak backward (regurgitate) through the valve.

LLM.text: A valvular heart disease where the mitral valve leaflets prolapse into the left atrium during systole. Most patients are asymptomatic; some develop palpitations, atypical chest pain, or dyspnea. Diagnosis by echocardiography. Complications include mitral regurgitation, infective endocarditis, and arrhythmias.

Harvard.text: A narrowing of the mitral valve opening that limits blood flow from the left atrium to the left ventricle.

LLM.text: Narrowing of the mitral valve that restricts blood flow from the left atrium to the left ventricle.

Harvard.text: Medications used to treat depression. They work by making the chemical messengers serotonin and norepinephrine more available.

LLM.text: Antidepressants that inhibit monoamine oxidase, the enzyme responsible for breaking down serotonin, norepinephrine, and dopamine. MAOIs include phenelzine, tranylcypromine, isocarboxazid, and selegiline (transdermal). They are effective for atypical depression and treatment-resistant depression.

Harvard.text: An antibody is a protein molecule that can bind to a virus and mark it for destruction by the immune system. A monoclonal antibody is a man-made substance used to treat some viral and other diseases.

LLM.text: An antibody produced by a single cloned B-cell line, specific for one epitope, generated by hybridoma technology or recombinant methods (name suffix -mab).

Harvard.text: White blood cells that protect the body from disease by attacking and consuming foreign particles.

LLM.text: Large circulating white blood cells that can enter tissues and become macrophages or dendritic cells.

Harvard.text: A type of fat abundant in vegetable oils such as olive, peanut, sesame, and canola oils. Monounsaturated fats don’t raise levels of unhealthy LDL cholesterol, and may even lower it.

LLM.text: A fat whose fatty acids contain one carbon-carbon double bond. It occurs in foods such as olive oil, avocados, nuts, and some seeds.

Harvard.text: A thickening of nerve tissue between the toes that causes irritation, tingling, or a burning pain in the ball of the foot.

LLM.text: A painful thickening of tissue around a digital nerve, usually between the third and fourth toes, causing forefoot pain, burning, or tingling.

Harvard.text: A hormone that helps the small intestine contract and move food through the digestive tract.

LLM.text: A hormone that helps regulate contractions and movement in the upper gastrointestinal tract.

Harvard.text: The ability of the digestive tract to move its contents.

LLM.text: The ability of an organ, especially the intestine, to move its contents.

Harvard.text: A nerve cell that directs activity in a specific group of muscle fibers.

LLM.text: A nerve cell that controls skeletal or smooth muscle activity.

Harvard.text: The pairing of a nerve cell and the group of muscle fibers it commands.

LLM.text: A single alpha motor neuron and all the skeletal muscle fibers it innervates. The number of muscle fibers per motor unit determines precision of control: small motor units (few fibers, e.g., extraocular and hand muscles) provide fine movement; large motor units (hundreds to thousands of fibers, e.g., gastrocnemius) provide gross power.

Harvard.text: Abbreviation for magnetic resonance imaging--a scan that creates detailed pictures of internal organs. MRIs use radio waves, a strong magnetic field, and a computer to produce images of organs and internal tissues.

LLM.text: Magnetic resonance imaging uses a strong magnetic field, radiofrequency energy, and computer processing to produce detailed images of body tissues without ionizing radiation. Contrast material may be used when clinically appropriate.

synonyms: magnetic resonance imaging--a scan that creates detailed pictures of internal organs

Harvard.text: Tissue that lines the tube-like structures of the body such as the respiratory and gastrointestinal tracts.

LLM.text: Mucosa is the moist epithelial lining of body passages such as the mouth, nose, airways, gastrointestinal tract, and reproductive or urinary tracts.

Harvard.text: Small cysts that form between the nail bed and the top joint of the finger.

LLM.text: Small fluid-filled cysts near the end joint of a finger, often associated with osteoarthritis.

Harvard.text: A thin layer that lines many cavities and structures in the body that are exposed to air in the environment, such as the nose, mouth, and lungs.

LLM.text: A moist tissue lining body cavities that open to the outside, including the nose, mouth, and lungs.

Harvard.text: Memory loss and impaired thinking caused by tiny strokes that are often too small to notice until a sizable area of the brain is affected.

LLM.text: Cognitive decline caused by the cumulative effects of multiple small strokes.

Harvard.text: An enlargement of the thyroid gland with more than one lump or nodule appearing on the neck.

LLM.text: An enlarged thyroid containing multiple nodules.

Harvard.text: An autoimmune disease in which the body’s immune system mistakenly attacks myelin, the substance that covers nerve fibers.

LLM.text: A chronic autoimmune demyelinating disease of the central nervous system, most commonly presenting in young adults. Characterized by relapsing-remitting episodes of neurological dysfunction (optic neuritis, transverse myelitis, brainstem syndromes). Diagnosis: McDonald criteria with MRI dissemination in space and time.

Harvard.text: A sleep test to measure daytime sleepiness. It times how quickly a person falls asleep when asked to rest in a quiet, darkened room during the day.

LLM.text: A daytime sleep study that measures how quickly a person falls asleep during scheduled naps.

Harvard.text: An sound heard during an examination of the heart caused by abnormal flow of blood through heart chambers or valves. Many heart murmurs do not indicate heart problems; others do.

LLM.text: An extra or unusual heart sound caused by turbulent blood flow. Murmurs are described by timing, location, intensity, quality, radiation, and response to position; their significance ranges from innocent flow sounds to valve or structural disease.

Harvard.text: Weakness felt in muscles when they have been tired out.

LLM.text: Reduced ability of a muscle to generate force after sustained or repeated activity.

Harvard.text: Cells bundled together to make up muscle tissue. Also known as muscle cells.

LLM.text: Individual contractile cells that combine to form skeletal muscle.

Harvard.text: A headache characterized by constant pressure, mild to moderate pain, and the feeling that a tight band is squeezing the head. Also known as a tension headache.

LLM.text: A pressure-like headache related to sustained contraction of scalp, neck, or jaw muscles.

Harvard.text: The ability of muscle to continue to perform without stopping because of fatigue.

LLM.text: The ability of a muscle or muscle group to sustain repeated or prolonged effort.

Harvard.text: The thin layer of smooth muscle lining of the colon or rectum.

LLM.text: A smooth-muscle layer in the wall of a hollow organ, especially the intestine.

Harvard.text: Related to the muscles and the skeleton.

LLM.text: Relating to muscles, bones, joints, tendons, ligaments, and related tissues.

Harvard.text: Abbreviation for medicated urethral system for erection. In this therapy, a small drug pellet is inserted into the tip of the penis to produce an erection.

LLM.text: A medicated urethral system that delivers a pellet into the urethra to treat erectile dysfunction.

Harvard.text: The process by which a change occurs in genetic material and is inherited by the next generation.

LLM.text: A heritable or acquired alteration in the DNA sequence. Variants may be single-nucleotide substitutions, insertions, deletions, copy-number changes, or larger rearrangements and may be benign, pathogenic, or of uncertain significance.

Harvard.text: Pain or tenderness in a muscle.

LLM.text: Muscle pain or tenderness.

Harvard.text: An abnormal weakness in a muscle or group of muscles.

LLM.text: Abnormal muscle weakness that worsens with use.

Harvard.text: A type of drug that widens the pupil.

LLM.text: A substance or medicine that dilates the pupil.

Harvard.text: A fatty material that surrounds and protects some nerve fibers.

LLM.text: Myelin is an insulating sheath around nerve fibers that speeds electrical conduction; it is produced by oligodendrocytes in the CNS and Schwann cells in the PNS.

Harvard.text: A test that uses a special dye and X-rays to detect spinal cord problems. The dye is injected into the space surrounding the spinal cord, making the spinal cord, spinal canal, and nerve roots appear in detail on the X-ray.

LLM.text: Contrast injected into subarachnoid space for spinal imaging. Used when MRI contraindicated. CT myelography more common now.

Harvard.text: A disorder in which the spinal cord is compressed, diseased, or damaged.

LLM.text: A general term for any neurological deficit resulting from spinal cord pathology, encompassing a wide range of causes and clinical presentations.

Harvard.text: Medical term for heart attack, the sudden death of part of the heart muscle from lack of oxygen.

LLM.text: Irreversible death of heart-muscle tissue caused by prolonged inadequate blood flow. See Heart Attack.

Harvard.text: Tearing of one of the walls of the heart. It usually occurs immediately after a heart attack.

LLM.text: A tear in the heart wall or other heart structure, usually a severe complication of myocardial infarction.

Harvard.text: Inflammation of the heart muscle (myocardium).

LLM.text: Myocarditis is inflammation of heart muscle, often infectious or immune-mediated, that can cause chest pain, arrhythmias, heart failure, or sudden cardiac dysfunction. (coxsackievirus, adenovirus, SARS-CoV-2). Presents with chest pain, dyspnea, arrhythmias, and elevated troponin. Diagnosis: ECG, echocardiography, cardiac MRI with Lake Louise criteria, and endomyocardial biopsy.

Harvard.text: The middle layer of heart tissue. The muscular myocardium is sandwiched between the outer layer (epicardium) and the inner layer (endocardium).

LLM.text: The thick muscular middle layer of the heart wall composed of cardiac muscle cells (cardiomyocytes). The myocardium is responsible for the contractile function of the heart. It contains intercalated discs with gap junctions that allow electrical coupling between cells.

Harvard.text: A muscle cell.

LLM.text: A muscle cell.

Harvard.text: Long interlocking strands that make up muscle fibers.

LLM.text: Contractile structures inside muscle fibers made of repeating sarcomeres.

Harvard.text: The fundamental muscle proteins that form myofibrils. Myofilaments slide over one another, bunching up and generating force, when a muscle contracts.

LLM.text: Actin and myosin protein filaments that slide past each other to produce muscle contraction.

Harvard.text: Nearsightedness. An optical error in which light rays meet and focus before reaching the retina, making objects that are far away appear blurry.

LLM.text: A refractive error in which light focuses in front of the retina, causing blurred distance vision. See Nearsightedness.

Harvard.text: A protein that helps muscle contract and relax.

LLM.text: A motor protein that interacts with actin to generate muscle force.

Harvard.text: A small quantity of a substance; equivalent to one-billionth of a gram (454 grams make 1 pound) in one-thousandth of a liter (1 liter is approximately 1 quart). Abbreviated as ng/ml.

LLM.text: A concentration unit equal to one billionth of a gram per milliliter, commonly used for reporting concentrations of hormones, drugs, proteins, and other analytes.

Harvard.text: A sleep disorder that causes extreme sleepiness and uncontrollable sleep attacks, making a person fall asleep at inappropriate times during the day.

LLM.text: Narcolepsy is a chronic sleep-wake disorder with excessive daytime sleepiness and, in some people, cataplexy, sleep paralysis, and hypnagogic hallucinations. sleep attacks, with or without cataplexy (sudden bilateral loss of muscle tone triggered by strong emotions). Narcolepsy type 1: with cataplexy, caused by loss of hypocretin/orexin neurons in the hypothalamus.

Harvard.text: Lines in the skin leading from the nose to the outer corners of the mouth. Also known as smile or laugh lines.

LLM.text: Skin creases running from the sides of the nose toward the corners of the mouth.

Harvard.text: A type of white blood cell of the immune system. These cells destroy other cells that fail to display the right chemical flags signaling that they are normal cells.

LLM.text: Immune cells that destroy infected or abnormal cells without prior exposure to a specific antigen.

Harvard.text: A device that converts a liquid medicine into a mist that can be breathed in.

LLM.text: A device that converts a liquid medicine into an inhalable aerosol, using a jet compressor, ultrasonic mechanism, or vibrating mesh. Medication is delivered through a mouthpiece or face mask and may include a bronchodilator, corticosteroid, antibiotic, or saline solution when prescribed for the relevant condition. Nebulizers can be useful when a person cannot coordinate an inhaler, is very young, or is severely breathless, but a properly used inhaler with a spacer may be equally effective for many medicines. Treatment choice depends on the medication, device, patient, and clinical situation. Follow the prescribed dose and treatment time, and clean and dry the device according to the manufacturer's and medication instructions to reduce contamination.

Harvard.text: The premature death of living cells or tissues.

LLM.text: Necrosis is death of cells or tissue within a living body caused by ischemia, infection, toxins, trauma, inflammation, or other injury.

Harvard.text: Use of a hollow needle to remove a small sample of tissue for examination.

LLM.text: Removal of a small tissue sample through a hollow needle for microscopic examination.

Harvard.text: A helper treatment given before a primary treatment is started, such as when chemotherapy is done before surgery in order to shrink a tumor.

LLM.text: Treatment before primary treatment to shrink tumor. Examples: chemotherapy before surgery.

Harvard.text: Relating to an infant younger than 4 weeks of age.

LLM.text: Relating to a newborn, especially during the first 28 days after birth.

Harvard.text: An abnormal growth of tissue, either cancerous or benign.

LLM.text: Abnormal growth of tissue, may be benign or malignant. Benign neoplasms: localized, slow-growing, do not metastasize. Malignant neoplasms (cancer): invasive, metastasize, can be fatal. Classification: carcinoma (epithelial origin), sarcoma (mesenchymal origin), leukemia (hematopoietic), lymphoma (lymphoid).

Harvard.text: Inflammation of the kidneys.

LLM.text: Inflammation of kidney tissue.

Harvard.text: Kidney disease.

LLM.text: Disease or damage of the kidneys, which may impair filtration, fluid balance, or other kidney functions.

Harvard.text: Injection of a medication into one or more nerves to relieve pain.

LLM.text: Injection of medicine near a nerve or nerve group to reduce pain or interrupt nerve signals.

Harvard.text: A molecule in the body that promotes the growth and repair of nerve cells.

LLM.text: A protein that supports the development, survival, and maintenance of certain sensory and sympathetic nerve cells.

Harvard.text: When referring to prostatectomy, the surgical procedure that preserves the nerves needed to allow the penis to become erect.

LLM.text: Surgical preservation of nerves needed for erectile function, especially during prostate surgery.

Harvard.text: A burning or stabbing pain that follows the path of a nerve.

LLM.text: Neuralgia is sharp, burning, or electric pain along the distribution of a nerve, caused by irritation, compression, infection, injury, or other disease.

Harvard.text: Clumps of sticky proteins found in the brains of people with Alzheimer's disease.

LLM.text: Abnormal deposits of beta-amyloid surrounded by damaged nerve processes in Alzheimer disease.

Harvard.text: Twisted strands of proteins that are found inside the dead or dying nerve cells of people with Alzheimer's disease.

LLM.text: Twisted tau-protein fibers inside damaged neurons, characteristic of Alzheimer disease.

Harvard.text: Powerful tranquilizing drugs used to treat schizophrenia.

LLM.text: Antipsychotic medicines used to treat disorders such as schizophrenia.

Harvard.text: A physician trained to diagnose and treat disorders of the nervous system, including the brain and spinal cord.

LLM.text: A physician specializing in disorders of the brain, spinal cord, nerves, and muscles.

Harvard.text: The tiny space between the end of a nerve and the surface of a muscle.

LLM.text: The neuromuscular junction is the synapse between motor neuron and skeletal muscle fiber, where acetylcholine released from presynaptic terminals binds to nicotinic acetylcholine receptors on the postsynaptic motor end plate, causing depolarization and muscle contraction.

Harvard.text: A nerve cell.

LLM.text: The fundamental excitable cell of the nervous system specialized for receiving, integrating, and transmitting electrical and chemical signals. Structural components: cell body (soma), dendrites (receptive), axon (conducting), and synaptic terminals (releasing neurotransmitters).

Harvard.text: Nerve damage and resulting loss of sensation, movement, or other function.

LLM.text: Disease or dysfunction of peripheral nerves causing pain, numbness, tingling, weakness, or altered reflexes. Common causes include diabetes, alcohol, nutritional deficiency, toxins, compression, autoimmune disease, and inherited disorders.

Harvard.text: Small proteins that aid in transmitting signals between nerve cells.

LLM.text: Short chains of amino acids that act as signaling molecules in the nervous system.

Harvard.text: A rare infection of the brain or spinal cord that occurs when syphilis goes untreated for many years.

LLM.text: Neurosyphilis is infection of the nervous system by Treponema pallidum and can cause meningitis, stroke, sensory loss, cognitive change, or tabes dorsalis.

Harvard.text: A chemical messenger released by nerve cells that transmits messages to nearby other nerve cells.

LLM.text: Neurotransmitters are endogenous chemical messengers that transmit signals across synapses from one neuron to another or to target cells such as muscle or gland cells.

Harvard.text: Cell structures (usually proteins) that recognize specific neurotransmitters and bind to them. Once bound, a receptor often changes shape, causing a cascade of chemical events within the cell. These events can alter which genes are turned on or off and can make the cell more or less likely to release its neurotransmitters.

LLM.text: Cell proteins that recognize neurotransmitters and alter cell activity when bound.

Harvard.text: Keeping the body in a straight line from head to toe except for the slight natural curves of the spine.

LLM.text: A posture in which the body is arranged in a straight, balanced line while preserving normal spinal curves.

Harvard.text: A standing or seated position in which the chin is parallel to the floor; the shoulders, hips, and knees are at even heights; and the knees and feet point straight ahead.

LLM.text: A body position that keeps joints and the spine near their natural alignment with minimal muscle strain and no excessive flexion, extension, or rotation.

Harvard.text: A position in which the back is straight except for the slight natural curves of the spine.

LLM.text: A spinal alignment in which the normal cervical and lumbar curves are maintained without excessive flexion, extension, or rotation.

Harvard.text: An abnormally low number of white blood cells.

LLM.text: A reduced neutrophil count ($<1.510^9/L$; severe $<0.5$), increasing risk of bacterial and fungal infection, especially febrile neutropenia.

Harvard.text: White blood cells that seek out and engulf foreign cells.

LLM.text: The most abundant type of white blood cell. Neutrophils rapidly migrate to sites of infection or injury and ingest microorganisms and cellular debris.

Harvard.text: Medications that widen blood vessels; usually used to treat chest pain from angina and other heart problems.

LLM.text: Vasodilator drugs that release nitric oxide, causing relaxation of vascular smooth muscle through activation of guanylyl cyclase and increased cyclic GMP. They primarily cause venodilation at low doses, reducing preload and myocardial oxygen demand, and arterial dilation at higher doses, reducing afterload.

Harvard.text: A compound produced by the endothelium (the lining of the interior walls of arteries) that helps widen blood vessels and counteract high blood pressure. Also called endothelium-derived relaxing factor.

LLM.text: A signaling molecule that relaxes blood-vessel muscle and promotes vasodilation.

Harvard.text: A drug that relaxes blood vessels and increases the supply of blood and oxygen to the heart while reducing its workload. It is commonly used to treat angina.

LLM.text: A nitrate medicine that relaxes vascular smooth muscle and is used mainly to relieve or prevent angina; it can lower blood pressure and should not be combined with phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors.

Harvard.text: Abbreviation for the N-methyl-D-aspartame receptor, a molecule on the surface of a brain cell that admits calcium when activated by the chemical messenger glutamate.

LLM.text: A glutamate-gated ion channel involved in excitatory neurotransmission, synaptic plasticity, learning, memory, and central sensitization.

Harvard.text: Nerve endings that detect pain and transmit pain information to the brain and spinal cord.

LLM.text: Sensory nerve endings that detect potentially tissue-damaging stimuli and transmit pain signals.

Harvard.text: Waking up more than once during the night to urinate.

LLM.text: Complaint of waking one or more times during the night to void, with each void preceded and followed by sleep. Highly prevalent in older adults and significantly impairs sleep quality and quality of life.

Harvard.text: A small rounded bump or knot of tissue.

LLM.text: Small, palpable mass <2 cm. Can be solid or cystic. Examples: thyroid nodule, rheumatoid nodule, pulmonary nodule. Evaluation depends on location.

Harvard.text: A chart or graph of mathematical calculations of risk; used in making treatment recommendations and predicting outcomes.

LLM.text: A graphical tool that estimates a quantity or risk from related measurements. The Rumack–Matthew nomogram is used in selected cases of acute acetaminophen ingestion.

Harvard.text: The sum of all cholesterol types other than high-density lipoprotein (HDL). These include very-low-density lipoprotein, low-density lipoprotein, and intermediate-density lipoprotein.

LLM.text: Total cholesterol minus HDL cholesterol; it represents cholesterol carried by atherogenic lipoproteins and is used to assess cardiovascular risk.

Harvard.text: Now called type 2 diabetes. A disease in which levels of blood sugar (glucose) are too high initially because cells can’t properly use insulin (a hormone that helps cells absorb glucose from the bloodstream). Over time the production of insulin may decline.

LLM.text: An older term for type 2 diabetes mellitus, a metabolic disorder characterized by insulin resistance and progressive impairment of insulin secretion.

Harvard.text: A test that does not require any medical instruments to break the skin or enter the body.

LLM.text: A diagnostic test that evaluates anatomy, physiology, or disease without entering the body or breaching a body cavity, such as external imaging or blood-pressure measurement.

Harvard.text: A rare and very serious condition associated with type 2 diabetes. Symptoms include extremely high (more than 800 mg/dl) blood sugar levels, severe dehydration, and changes in mental status, ultimately resulting in coma.

LLM.text: A severe complication of diabetes marked by very high blood glucose, dehydration, and increased blood osmolality, usually without substantial ketoacidosis.

Harvard.text: A condition in which the walls of the small blood vessels in the retina leak serum and tiny pockets of swelling form in the walls of blood vessels. Also called background retinopathy.

LLM.text: Retinal disease in which small vessels leak or become damaged without abnormal new-vessel growth.

Harvard.text: The sleep phase that includes deep sleep, the type considered most important for preventing daytime sleepiness.

LLM.text: Sleep stages that do not include rapid eye movements, including deep slow-wave sleep.

Harvard.text: A drug that reduces swelling and pain.

LLM.text: A medicine that inhibits cyclooxygenase enzymes and reduces prostaglandin production, producing analgesic, anti-inflammatory, and fever-reducing effects. NSAIDs can cause gastrointestinal, kidney, cardiovascular, or other adverse effects.

Harvard.text: A hormone produced by adrenal glands that puts the body on heightened alert when a threat is perceived (the fight-or-flight response). Also known as norepinephrine.

LLM.text: A hormone and neurotransmitter involved in alertness, stress responses, and blood-vessel constriction.

Harvard.text: A hormone produced by adrenal glands that puts the body on heightened alert when a threat is perceived (the fight-or-flight response). Also known as noradrenaline.

LLM.text: A hormone and neurotransmitter that supports alertness, heart function, and the stress response.

Harvard.text: A buildup of fluid in the brain that causes the brain to swell, and leads to slowing of mental function, trouble walking, and a loss of bladder control.

LLM.text: A disorder in which cerebrospinal fluid accumulates and causes gait difficulty, cognitive decline, and urinary problems despite near-normal measured pressure.

Harvard.text: Abbreviation for nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug, a drug that reduce swelling and pain.

LLM.text: A nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug used to reduce pain, fever, and inflammation.

Harvard.text: Tests that use tiny amounts of short-lived radioactive substances that can target particular organs or cell receptors to diagnose disease.

LLM.text: Diagnostic tests using small amounts of radioactive material to assess organs or identify disease.

Harvard.text: Part of the brain’s reward pathway that is most tightly and consistently responsive to pleasure. Also known as the pleasure center.

LLM.text: A brain region involved in reward, motivation, and reinforcement.

Harvard.text: The gel-like shock-absorbing central portion of each spinal disc.

LLM.text: The soft, gel-like central portion of an intervertebral disk, surrounded by the annulus fibrosus.

Harvard.text: Dietary supplement containing concentrated forms of a presumed bioactive substance originally derived from food and used to enhance health in dosages exceeding those normally obtainable from food.

LLM.text: A food-derived product marketed as providing health or medicinal benefits beyond basic nutrition; evidence, composition, and regulatory oversight vary by product.

Harvard.text: Substances in foods that the body needs to survive.

LLM.text: Substances obtained from food that are required for energy, growth, tissue maintenance, and normal physiological function, including macronutrients, vitamins, minerals, and water.

Harvard.text: A body weight that is much higher than is healthy. Defined as having a body mass index of 30 or more. Obesity puts a person at greater risk of developing numerous chronic diseases.

LLM.text: Obesity is excess adipose tissue that impairs health, influenced by genetic, metabolic, environmental, behavioral, and social factors and associated with cardiometabolic, respiratory, musculoskeletal, and other disease. $30\,kg/m^2$ (class I: 30-34.9, class II: 35-39.9, class III: $40$). Major risk factor for type 2 diabetes, hypertension, cardiovascular disease, sleep apnea, osteoarthritis, certain cancers, and reduced life expectancy.

Harvard.text: The psychoactive drug or rewarding behavior with which a person with addiction has a pathological relationship.

LLM.text: A substance or rewarding behavior to which a person develops a harmful compulsive relationship.

Harvard.text: A disorder marked by heavy snoring and interrupted breathing during sleep. It increases the risk of developing high blood pressure and having a stroke and is more common in people who are obese.

LLM.text: Recurrent partial or complete upper-airway collapse during sleep, causing disrupted breathing and often daytime symptoms. Evaluation may include sleep testing; treatment is individualized and can include positive-airway-pressure therapy, weight management, oral appliances, positional therapy, or surgery.

Harvard.text: The region in the back of the brain responsible for visual processing.

LLM.text: The most posterior of the four cerebral lobes, located behind the parieto-occipital sulcus and above the tentorium cerebelli. The occipital lobe is the primary visual processing center of the brain.

Harvard.text: The closing or blocking of a hollow organ or body part.

LLM.text: Complete blockage of vessel. May be natural (thrombosis) or iatrogenic (embolization).

Harvard.text: Something not visible to the naked eye but seen under a microscope or through lab tests.

LLM.text: Hidden or not visible without microscopy or laboratory testing.

Harvard.text: Beneficial fats, also known as n-3 fatty acids. These are polyunsaturated fat found in fatty fish, such as salmon.

LLM.text: Polyunsaturated fats found especially in fatty fish and some plant foods.

Harvard.text: Fatty acids found in certain foods that the body needs for good health but can’t make on its own. Also known as n-6 fatty acids.

LLM.text: Essential polyunsaturated fats found in many plant oils and foods.

Harvard.text: A gene that, under certain conditions, can cause cancer.

LLM.text: A gene that, when activated, overexpressed, or altered, can promote uncontrolled cell proliferation or survival. Oncogenes commonly arise from normal proto-oncogenes through mutation, amplification, translocation, or abnormal regulation.

Harvard.text: A physician who deals with the diagnosis and treatment of cancer. There are three types—medical oncologists, radiation oncologists, and surgical oncologists.

LLM.text: A physician who specializes in the diagnosis and treatment of cancer. Includes medical oncologists (systemic therapy), radiation oncologists (radiotherapy), and surgical oncologists (operative management).

Harvard.text: A rare and potentially fatal disorder in which a person may stop breathing, especially at night. Also called congenital central hypoventilation syndrome.

LLM.text: A rare disorder in which automatic breathing is impaired, especially during sleep; also called congenital central hypoventilation syndrome.

Harvard.text: Toenail fungus.

LLM.text: Fungal nail infection, most commonly caused by dermatophytes (Trichophyton rubrum), affecting toenails more than fingernails. It presents as nail thickening, discoloration (yellow-brown), subungual debris, and nail separation. Diagnosis is confirmed by KOH preparation or fungal culture.

Harvard.text: A surgical procedure in which an enlarged prostate is removed through an incision in the abdomen.

LLM.text: Surgical removal of enlarged prostate tissue through an abdominal incision.

Harvard.text: A physician who specializes in treating the eye and eye disease.

LLM.text: A medical doctor specializing in diseases and surgery of the eyes.

Harvard.text: An instrument with a light and mirrors for examining the deep interior of the eye.

LLM.text: Instrument for examining retina and optic nerve. Direct: larger, brighter image. Indirect: wider field. Essential for fundoscopic examination.

Harvard.text: Any painkilling drug such as morphine or codeine derived from the opium poppy.

LLM.text: A natural alkaloid derived from the opium poppy (Papaver somniferum) or a semi-synthetic derivative that binds to opioid receptors.

Harvard.text: Any narcotic, natural or synthetic, that behaves in the body like an opium-derived drug.

LLM.text: A natural or synthetic substance that acts on opioid receptors to relieve pain and may cause sedation or dependence.

Harvard.text: The front surface of the optic nerve, where all the retinal nerve fibers come together to carry an image to the brain.

LLM.text: The point where the optic nerve leaves the retina; it has no photoreceptors and forms the blind spot.

Harvard.text: A cable of specialized nerve fibers that transmit visual impulses from the eye to the brain.

LLM.text: CN II exiting through the optic disc (blind spot), passing through the optic canal, and partially decussating at the optic chiasm. Technically a CNS tract with oligodendrocyte myelination and meningeal coverings, making it susceptible to demyelinating disease (optic neuritis in MS).

Harvard.text: A technician who helps select and fit eyeglasses or contact lenses for people with vision problems.

LLM.text: A technician who fits and dispenses eyeglasses or contact lenses.

Harvard.text: A health care professional licensed to examine the eye, and diagnose and treat some eye diseases.

LLM.text: An optometrist examines vision and eye health, prescribes corrective lenses, and in some jurisdictions diagnoses and treats selected eye diseases.

Harvard.text: A test to check for diabetes. It involves fasting overnight and having blood sugar levels checked before and after drinking a sugary solution.

LLM.text: A diagnostic test measuring plasma glucose response after a standardized oral glucose load. It is used in selected evaluations of diabetes, impaired glucose tolerance, and gestational diabetes when fasting glucose or HbA1c is insufficient.

Harvard.text: The layer of soft pinkish tissue that lines the interior of the mouth.

LLM.text: The moist stratified squamous epithelial lining of the oral cavity. It includes masticatory, lining, and specialized mucosa and provides barrier protection, sensation, lubrication, and sites for minor salivary glands.

Harvard.text: The bony socket that holds the eyeball.

LLM.text: The bony cavity of the skull that contains the eye, extraocular muscles, nerves, vessels, and associated tissues.

Harvard.text: X-ray treatment to the eye; sometimes used in more serious cases of Graves’ eye disease.

LLM.text: Radiation treatment directed at tissues within the eye socket, sometimes used for severe thyroid eye disease.

Harvard.text: Surgery to remove the testicles. Usually done to remove a cancerous testicle or to lower testosterone levels and slow or halt the growth of prostate cancer.

LLM.text: Surgical removal of one or both testicles. Radical inguinal orchiectomy is diagnostic and therapeutic for testicular cancer; bilateral orchiectomy is a hormonal therapy for prostate cancer.

Harvard.text: The protein framework of bone tissue.

LLM.text: The nonmineral component of a tissue, especially the protein-rich framework produced by bone-forming cells before mineral deposition.

Harvard.text: The series of pleasurable, rhythmic muscle contractions that mark the peak of sexual arousal and the release of muscle tension.

LLM.text: Orgasm is a subjective peak of sexual pleasure accompanied by characteristic autonomic, muscular, and genital responses that vary among individuals.

Harvard.text: A medical doctor who specializes in correcting disorders of the bones, joints, muscles, and tendons.

LLM.text: A physician specializing in disorders and injuries of bones, joints, muscles, and related tissues.

Harvard.text: A custom shoe insert that helps cushion or realign the foot.

LLM.text: An externally applied device that supports, aligns, prevents deformity, protects, or assists movement of a body segment. It differs from a prosthesis, which replaces a missing body part.

Harvard.text: A sudden drop in blood pressure upon standing or getting out of bed, causing dizziness.

LLM.text: Decrease in SBP >=20 mmHg or DBP >=10 mmHg within 3 minutes of standing. Causes: dehydration, medications (antihypertensives, diuretics, alpha-blockers, antidepressants), autonomic dysfunction (diabetes, Parkinson disease), and prolonged bed rest. Symptoms: dizziness, lightheadedness, syncope, falls.

Harvard.text: A process in which bone heals around an implant to create a stable anchor.

LLM.text: Direct structural and functional connection between living bone and the surface of a load-bearing implant under appropriate conditions. It depends on implant stability, surface characteristics, bone quality, healing, and control of infection and occlusal forces.

Harvard.text: Three bones in the middle ear that move in response to sound vibrations.

LLM.text: Three smallest body bones forming the ossicular chain in the middle ear: malleus (hammer, attached to tympanic membrane), incus (anvil), stapes (stirrup, footplate in oval window).

Harvard.text: The process by which bone is formed.

LLM.text: The process of forming bone tissue.

Harvard.text: A joint disease in which the cartilage that lines the joints slowly deteriorates. Also called degenerative joint disease.

LLM.text: Osteoarthritis is a degenerative joint disorder involving cartilage loss, subchondral bone change, pain, stiffness, and functional limitation, influenced by age, injury, and joint loading. bone sclerosis, osteophyte formation, and synovial inflammation, affecting knees, hips, hands (DIP/PIP Heberden/Bouchard nodes), spine. Risk factors: age, obesity, joint injury, malalignment, genetics, female sex.

Harvard.text: Cells that build bone tissue.

LLM.text: Cells that form new bone.

Harvard.text: Cells that remove bone tissue.

LLM.text: Cells that break down and resorb bone tissue.

Harvard.text: A cell that is embedded in fully formed bone.

LLM.text: Mature bone cells embedded within bone tissue that help maintain it.

Harvard.text: A condition in which bones are soft and weak, usually due to a lack of vitamin D or an inability of the body to use vitamin D properly.

LLM.text: Osteomalacia is inadequate mineralization of adult bone, commonly from vitamin-D deficiency or phosphate disorders, causing bone pain, weakness, and fractures.

Harvard.text: A bone infection caused by bacteria or fungi.

LLM.text: Osteomyelitis is infection and inflammation of bone caused by bacteria, fungi, or other organisms, producing pain, fever, swelling, and possible bone destruction or chronic drainage. Staphylococcus aureus responsible for the majority of cases.

Harvard.text: The building blocks of compact bone, the hard, tightly-packed tissue that forms the outer shell of bones.

LLM.text: Cylindrical structural units of compact bone arranged around central canals.

Harvard.text: A doctor licensed to practice medicine, perform surgery, and prescribe drugs. The training is similar to that of a regular M.D., but more emphasis is placed on the importance of the musculoskeletal system and the body’s ability to heal itself.

LLM.text: A physician trained in medicine and surgery who earns a Doctor of Osteopathic Medicine degree.

Harvard.text: Mild thinning and weakening of the bones; bone density is lower than normal but not low enough to be classified as osteoporosis.

LLM.text: Bone mineral density (BMD) that is lower than normal but not low enough to be classified as osteoporosis. T-score between -1.0 and -2.5 on DXA scan. A risk factor for osteoporosis and fractures.

Harvard.text: An outgrowth of bone on a joint or spinal disk; commonly called a bone spur.

LLM.text: A bony outgrowth, commonly called a bone spur, that develops near a joint or along the spine and may cause pain, stiffness, or nerve compression.

Harvard.text: Significant thinning and weakening of bones over time, making them vulnerable to breaks.

LLM.text: Osteoporosis is a systemic skeletal disorder characterized by reduced bone strength and increased susceptibility to fragility fractures, which may occur after minimal trauma or ordinary activity. It commonly affects the spine, hip, wrist, and other bones and may remain asymptomatic until a fracture occurs.

Harvard.text: An operation in which bone is cut to change its alignment or shorten or lengthen it.

LLM.text: A surgical procedure involving cutting and repositioning of bone to correct deformity, realign joint surfaces, alter weight-bearing forces, or change limb length.

Harvard.text: The bony shell that surrounds the inner ear.

LLM.text: The otic capsule is the dense bony shell (otic capsule bone) that surrounds and protects the inner ear structures, including the cochlea, vestibule, and semicircular canals, forming the hardest bone in the human body.

Harvard.text: An infection of the skin lining the ear canal of the outer ear. Also called swimmer’s ear.

LLM.text: Inflammation or infection of the external ear canal, commonly causing ear pain, itching, tenderness, or discharge.

Harvard.text: An infection of the middle ear.

LLM.text: A group of inflammatory conditions of the middle ear, most commonly caused by viral or bacterial infection, with Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, and Moraxella catarrhalis being the most frequent bacterial pathogens.

Harvard.text: An abnormal bony growth in the middle ear that causes hearing loss.

LLM.text: Otosclerosis is abnormal remodeling of middle-ear bone that restricts the stapes and causes progressive conductive hearing loss, sometimes with an inner-ear component.

Harvard.text: Synonymous with epidemic. Sometimes used to refer to a local epidemic as compared to a larger, general epidemic.

LLM.text: A greater-than-expected occurrence of a disease or health event in a defined population, location, or time period.

Harvard.text: The external part of the ear, as well as the external ear canal and the eardrum.

LLM.text: The visible auricle and the external auditory canal, which collect and conduct sound toward the eardrum.

Harvard.text: A person who receives treatment at a hospital or other medical facility but does not stay overnight.

LLM.text: A person who receives medical evaluation or treatment without being admitted overnight to a hospital or other inpatient facility.

Harvard.text: The loudest sound that a hearing aid can produce.

LLM.text: The amount of a substance produced or eliminated by the body or by an organ over a specified time, such as urine output or cardiac output.

Harvard.text: Surgical removal of one or both ovaries.

LLM.text: Surgical removal of one or both ovaries.

Harvard.text: Frequent urination and urges to urinate.

LLM.text: A clinical syndrome of urinary urgency, usually with frequency and nocturia, with or without urge incontinence, due to detrusor overactivity during filling. Causes: idiopathic (most), neurogenic (stroke, spinal injury, MS, Parkinson), bladder outlet obstruction, and aging; worsened by caffeine and diuretics.

Harvard.text: A condition of declining kidney function. It is part of the progression of kidney disease, developing after microalbuminuria (when a damaged kidney begins to leak small amounts of a protein called albumin into urine) and before chronic kidney disease.

LLM.text: Abnormally high protein loss in the urine that is detectable by routine testing and may indicate kidney disease.

Harvard.text: A body weight above the healthy range but not obese. Usually defined as a body mass index of 25 to 29.9.

LLM.text: Overweight in adults commonly refers to BMI 25.0–29.9, though health risk assessment should include body composition, distribution, and other factors.

Harvard.text: The release of a mature egg from the ovary, at which time it is available to be fertilized by sperm.
