LLM.text: The release of a mature egg from the ovary, at which time it is available to be fertilized by sperm.

Harvard.text: An unstable molecule in the body that plays a role in aging and can damage tissue. Also known as a free radical.

LLM.text: A reactive molecule that can damage cells and tissues by promoting oxidation.

Harvard.text: A process in which oxygen combines with a substance, altering its structure and changing or destroying its normal function.

LLM.text: A chemical process that changes a substance through loss of electrons or reaction with oxygen.

Harvard.text: Blood that has moved through the lungs where it has absorbed oxygen; oxygenated blood moves from the lungs into the heart, from which it is then pumped throughout the body.

LLM.text: Blood that has acquired oxygen in the lungs and carries it to body tissues.

Harvard.text: Medicines used to relieve pain. They include nonopioid analgesics, opioid analgesics, and adjuvant medicines used for selected pain conditions.

LLM.text: Medicines used to relieve pain. They include nonopioid analgesics, opioid analgesics, and adjuvant medicines used for selected pain conditions.

Harvard.text: The tissues that make up the roof of the mouth.

LLM.text: The roof of the mouth, consisting of a bony hard palate in front and a muscular soft palate behind.

Harvard.text: Treatment that relieves the symptoms of a serious illness, but does not cure the disease itself.

LLM.text: Specialized medical care for serious illness focusing on symptom relief and quality of life. Not limited to end-of-life. Can be provided alongside curative treatment. Components: pain management, symptom control, psychosocial support, spiritual care, advance care planning. Referral early in disease course.

Harvard.text: To examine a part of the body by touching it carefully.

LLM.text: To examine body tissues by carefully feeling them with the hands.

Harvard.text: Sensation that the heart is beating rapidly or irregularly.

LLM.text: The subjective sensation of a rapid, forceful, or irregular heartbeat. Palpitations are a common symptom with a broad differential.

Harvard.text: Paralysis in part of the body, often with loss of sensation and uncontrolled body movements.

LLM.text: Weakness or paralysis of a body part caused by dysfunction of its motor nerves, muscles, spinal pathways, or brain; the distribution and onset help identify the cause.

Harvard.text: A gland in the abdomen that produces digestive enzymes and hormones.

LLM.text: Retroperitoneal gland (15-20 cm) behind the stomach, spanning from duodenum to spleen. Exocrine function: acinar cells secrete digestive enzymes (amylase, lipase, proteases) and bicarbonate into pancreatic duct to duodenum.

Harvard.text: A disease outbreak affecting large populations or a whole region, country, or continent.

LLM.text: Epidemic spread across multiple countries/continents. Examples: COVID-19, Spanish flu, HIV/AIDS.

Harvard.text: An abnormal layer of tissue that forms over joints or the cornea of the eye.

LLM.text: An abnormal layer of vascularized tissue that grows over a joint or the cornea.

Harvard.text: Threads of muscle that pull the heart valves between the upper and lower chambers of the heart closed during heart contractions.

LLM.text: Cone-shaped muscles inside the ventricles that attach to the atrioventricular valve cusps through chordae tendineae and help prevent valve prolapse during ventricular contraction.

Harvard.text: Paralysis of the legs and lower part of the body.

LLM.text: Paralysis of both legs and usually part of the lower trunk.

Harvard.text: Sleep disorders, such as night terrors or sleep walking, that periodically interfere with sleep.

LLM.text: Unwanted movements, behaviors, emotions, or experiences that occur during sleep or at the transition between sleep and wakefulness.

Harvard.text: Part of the nervous system that calms body systems excited by the stress hormones.

LLM.text: The craniosacral division of the autonomic nervous system mediating 'rest-and-digest' functions. Preganglionic fibers from cranial nerves III, VII, IX, X, and sacral nerves S2-S4 synapse on ganglia near or within target organs (short postganglionic fibers).

Harvard.text: Glands responsible for releasing a hormone that controls calcium levels and influences bone loss and growth.

LLM.text: Usually four small endocrine glands behind the thyroid that secrete parathyroid hormone to regulate blood calcium and phosphate levels.

Harvard.text: A hormone that controls levels of calcium and phosphorous in the blood and influences bone loss and growth.

LLM.text: A hormone that regulates calcium and phosphate levels in the blood and supports bone remodeling.

Harvard.text: Part of the brain. It plays a role in sensory processes, like pain and touch, and language.

LLM.text: The cerebral lobe posterior to the central sulcus and above the lateral sulcus, containing the primary somatosensory cortex (postcentral gyrus, Brodmann 3,1,2) processing touch, pain, temperature, and proprioception, plus the somatosensory association cortex.

Harvard.text: A brain disorder that causes movement problems, including shaking, difficulty walking, and rigidity in muscles.

LLM.text: A progressive neurodegenerative disorder caused by selective loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta, leading to dopamine depletion in the striatum. The pathological hallmark is the presence of Lewy bodies, intracellular inclusions composed of aggregated alpha-synuclein protein, within surviving neurons.

Harvard.text: A sudden, violent attack or convulsion; or the worsening of symptoms or recurrence of disease.

LLM.text: A sudden attack or episodic surge of a symptom, sign, or physiologic activity, such as pain, coughing, arrhythmia, seizure, or autonomic symptoms.

Harvard.text: A rare form of headache. Sufferers experience a severe throbbing, drilling pain on one side of the face or behind the eye.

LLM.text: A rare headache disorder causing brief, repeated attacks of severe one-sided head or facial pain.

Harvard.text: Immunity that is conferred by another, such as a mother’s antibodies protecting her baby during gestation and shortly after birth.

LLM.text: Protection against infection provided by antibodies received from another source rather than produced by the person's own immune system.

Harvard.text: A test used to diagnose whether a rash was caused by a reaction to certain allergens, such as poison ivy or a cosmetic ingredient, or an irritant such as soap.

LLM.text: A skin test used to identify delayed allergic contact reactions to substances applied under adhesive patches.

Harvard.text: The thick bone that protects the knee joint; also known as the kneecap.

LLM.text: The largest sesamoid bone, embedded in the quadriceps tendon. It articulates with the femoral trochlea to form the patellofemoral joint and improves the mechanical efficiency of knee extension. It is triangular and covered by thick articular cartilage.

Harvard.text: A tiny organism such as a virus, bacterium, or parasite that can invade the body and produce disease.

LLM.text: A tiny organism such as a virus, bacterium, or parasite that can invade the body and produce disease.

Harvard.text: The underlying abnormalities that contribute to or are characteristic of a disease.

LLM.text: Study of disease. Includes general pathology (cell injury, inflammation, neoplasia) and systemic pathology (organ-specific diseases).

Harvard.text: A method that allows a person to control, within limits, the amount and timing of pain medication he or she receives. It is usually done by pressing a button to release the medication from a computerized pump into an IV.

LLM.text: A method in which a patient self-administers prescribed doses of analgesic medication using a programmable pump with preset safety limits. The medication, dose, and lockout interval are individualized according to the patient's condition and monitoring needs.

Harvard.text: Proteins that recognize classes of pathogens and stimulate the innate immune system to signal the adaptive immune system.

LLM.text: Immune receptors that detect common molecular features of pathogens or damaged cells.

Harvard.text: Abbreviation for polycystic ovary syndrome, an inherited disorder characterized by the formation of abnormal cysts in enlarged ovaries; a leading cause of female infertility and a common cause of excess facial or body hair (hirsutism).

LLM.text: Common endocrine disorder affecting six to twelve percent of reproductive-aged women characterized by hyperandrogenism, ovulatory dysfunction, and polycystic ovarian morphology on ultrasound. See Polycystic Ovary Syndrome.

Harvard.text: Abbreviation for phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors, drugs that can help a man achieve and maintain an erection.

LLM.text: Medicines that increase penile blood flow by inhibiting phosphodiesterase type 5; they are used mainly to treat erectile dysfunction.

Harvard.text: The greatest amount of bone tissue that a person has during his or her life.

LLM.text: The greatest amount and strength of bone reached during early adulthood; it is influenced by genetics, nutrition, physical activity, hormones, and health conditions.

Harvard.text: A measure of how fast a person can blow air out of the lungs.

LLM.text: The maximum speed of air expelled during a forceful expiration, measured with a peak-flow meter to help monitor variable airflow obstruction such as asthma.

Harvard.text: A device to assess lung function, often used to diagnose and monitor asthma.

LLM.text: A handheld device that measures the maximum speed of forced expiration, often used to monitor asthma.

Harvard.text: A blood-sucking parasite commonly known as the louse (plural, lice) that can cause an itchy scalp; infestations are highly contagious and especially common in school-age children.

LLM.text: A blood-sucking parasite commonly known as the louse (plural, lice) that can cause an itchy scalp; infestations are highly contagious and especially common in school-age children.

Harvard.text: A rare disease brought on by severe niacin deficiency that causes diarrhea, dermatitis, and dementia.

LLM.text: Pellagra is niacin deficiency classically causing dermatitis, diarrhea, and neuropsychiatric changes; malnutrition, malabsorption, alcoholism, or certain medicines may contribute.

Harvard.text: The sling of muscles that support the intestines and bladder, as well as the uterus in women. Weak or damaged pelvic floor muscles can cause incontinence or diminished sexual pleasure, among other problems.

LLM.text: A group of muscles and connective tissues supporting the pelvic organs and controlling urinary and fecal continence.

Harvard.text: An inflatable or bendable device that is implanted in the penis to allow a man with erectile dysfunction to have erections when he wishes.

LLM.text: Inflatable or malleative device for erectile dysfunction. Types: two-piece, three-piece (reservoir, pump, cylinders). Surgical implantation. Complications: infection, erosion, mechanical failure, dissatisfaction.

Harvard.text: Enzymes secreted by the stomach to break down protein.

LLM.text: A stomach enzyme that begins digestion of proteins.

Harvard.text: A raw, crater-like sore in the lining of the stomach or duodenum that causes burning stomach pain.

LLM.text: An open sore in the stomach or duodenal lining caused most often by Helicobacter pylori infection or nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug use. It may cause burning upper-abdominal pain, bleeding, perforation, or obstruction. Also called peptic ulcer disease.

Harvard.text: Surgical removal of part of a spinal disk that is bulging out abnormally and pressing on a nerve root or the spinal column.

LLM.text: Removal of part of a herniated spinal disk through a small skin incision.

Harvard.text: A pain relief therapy that uses needles to deliver low-voltage electrical current under the skin to stop pain signals from reaching the brain.

LLM.text: Electrical stimulation delivered through the skin to reduce pain signals.

Harvard.text: A procedure used to open blocked coronary arteries. A small, thin tube with a tiny balloon at its tip is inserted into a narrowed coronary artery. The balloon is then inflated to widen the narrowed area. A stent may be put in place to hold the artery open. Percutaneous transluminal coronary angioplasty is also known as balloon angioplasty.

LLM.text: Balloon-based treatment that widens a narrowed coronary artery, often followed by stent placement.

Harvard.text: A hole, such as an ulcer, in an organ or tissue.

LLM.text: An abnormal hole through the wall of an organ or tissue.

Harvard.text: Concern about sexual performance that is so severe that it leads to sexual dysfunction.

LLM.text: Anxiety about sexual performance that can interfere with sexual function.

Harvard.text: Passage of a fluid through a specific organ or an area of the body.

LLM.text: Blood flow through tissue. Adequate perfusion essential for organ function.

Harvard.text: A test result that indicates abnormal blood flow or areas of damaged or dead heart muscle.

LLM.text: An area receiving abnormally low blood flow, identified by an imaging or functional test.

Harvard.text: Inflammation of the pericardium, the heart's sac-like covering.

LLM.text: Pericarditis is inflammation of the sac around the heart, causing sharp positional chest pain and sometimes pericardial effusion, tamponade, or constrictive disease. pericarditis presents with sharp, pleuritic chest pain that improves with leaning forward, pericardial friction rub, and diffuse ST elevation on ECG.

Harvard.text: The fibrous sac that surrounds the heart and the roots of the major blood vessels.

LLM.text: The fibroserous sac surrounding the heart and proximal great vessels. Outer fibrous pericardium (anchors to diaphragm, sternum) and inner serous pericardium (parietal layer lining the sac; visceral layer/epicardium on the heart) with the pericardial cavity (15-50 mL serous fluid) between them.

Harvard.text: The transition time in a woman’s life that begins when ovaries produce less estrogen and menstruation becomes less frequent, and ends when the ovaries no longer produce eggs and menstruation stops.

LLM.text: The transition time in a woman’s life that begins when ovaries produce less estrogen and menstruation becomes less frequent, and ends when the ovaries no longer produce eggs and menstruation stops.

Harvard.text: The area of skin between the vagina and anus in women, and between the scrotum and anus in men.

LLM.text: The region between the external genitalia and anus, bounded by the pubic symphysis, coccyx, and ischial tuberosities. It contains structures of the urogenital and anal regions and stretches during childbirth.

Harvard.text: A sleep disorder in which the legs jerk or cramp repeatedly during the sleep.

LLM.text: Repeated involuntary limb movements during sleep that may disrupt rest.

Harvard.text: An exercise strategy that varies reps, sets, and resistance to alternate heavier and lighter workouts over a period of time.

LLM.text: Planned variation of exercise volume and intensity over time.

Harvard.text: Diseases, including gingivitis and periodontitis, that attack the gum tissue and the structures supporting the teeth. Also called gum disease.

LLM.text: Inflammation and destruction of the tissues supporting the teeth, usually caused by dental plaque. It can lead to gum bleeding, bone loss, loose teeth, and tooth loss.

Harvard.text: An advanced stage of gum disease that attacks the teeth’s supporting structures.

LLM.text: Periodontitis is inflammatory destruction of the tissues and bone supporting teeth, usually related to dental plaque, causing bleeding gums, pockets, loosening, and tooth loss.

Harvard.text: A condition caused by atherosclerosis in the arteries in the legs or leading to them.

LLM.text: Narrowing of arteries supplying the limbs, usually caused by atherosclerosis. It may cause exertional leg pain relieved by rest, reduced pulses, nonhealing wounds, or critical limb ischemia. Also called peripheral arterial disease.

Harvard.text: The parts of the nervous system outside of the brain, brain stem, and spinal cord.

LLM.text: The portion of the nervous system consisting of nerves and ganglia outside the brain and spinal cord. The PNS connects the central nervous system (CNS) to peripheral tissues and organs. Components: (1) Cranial nerves (12 pairs)—emerging from the brain/brainstem, innervating head, neck, and viscera.

Harvard.text: Damage to the long nerves radiating from the spine to the arms and legs.

LLM.text: A disorder of peripheral nerves causing sensory, motor, and/or autonomic symptoms in a distal, symmetric 'stocking-glove' pattern.

Harvard.text: Narrowing of blood vessels that supply blood to the legs, arms, stomach, or kidneys.

LLM.text: Disease involving narrowed or blocked blood vessels outside the heart and brain.

Harvard.text: Side vision, or what the eye perceives outside the direct line of vision.

LLM.text: The portion of the visual field outside the direct line of sight.

Harvard.text: Wavelike movement of intestinal muscles that propels food through the digestive tract.

LLM.text: Peristalsis is coordinated, wave-like contraction of smooth muscle that propels food, fluid, or other contents through the gastrointestinal tract and some ducts.

Harvard.text: Treatment for kidney failure that uses a machine to remove toxins from the bloodstream.

LLM.text: Dialysis using the peritoneal membrane as the exchange surface. Continuous ambulatory peritoneal dialysis (CAPD) uses manual exchanges, whereas automated peritoneal dialysis (APD) uses a cycler, often overnight. It can provide home-based therapy and may offer hemodynamic stability. Complications include peritonitis, catheter infection, inadequate ultrafiltration, and fluid imbalance. A Tenckhoff catheter is commonly used.

Harvard.text: Inflammation of the membrane that line the abdominal cavity and surrounds most abdominal organs.

LLM.text: Peritonitis is inflammation or infection of the peritoneum, often from perforation, surgery, ascites infection, or abdominal disease, and may cause severe pain, ileus, sepsis, and shock. organ, appendicitis, abdominal trauma, or infection of ascitic fluid. Severe abdominal pain, guarding, fever, vomiting, or shock requires urgent medical evaluation.

Harvard.text: A form of anemia in which red blood cells enlarge and decrease in size due to an inability to properly absorb vitamin B12.

LLM.text: A type of vitamin B12 deficiency anemia caused by autoimmune destruction of gastric parietal cells, leading to lack of intrinsic factor and impaired B12 absorption in the terminal ileum.

Harvard.text: A device worn around the neck or wrist that allows a person to call for help by pressing a button.

LLM.text: A wearable or nearby device that lets a person summon help during an emergency.

Harvard.text: A device placed in the vagina to support or correct the position of the uterus, rectum, or bladder.

LLM.text: A removable device placed in the vagina to provide structural support for pelvic organ prolapse (uterine prolapse, cystocele, rectocele) or stress urinary incontinence.

Harvard.text: A characteristic frame of mind that leads a person to expect negative outcomes and to view the world as a negative or fearful place.

LLM.text: A tendency to expect negative outcomes or interpret situations unfavorably.

Harvard.text: Pinpoint-sized red or purple spots that appear in clusters on the skin, caused by bleeding under the skin.

LLM.text: Small, pinpoint, non-blanching red or purple spots on the skin or mucous membranes caused by extravasation of red blood cells from capillaries into the surrounding tissue. They are typically less than 2 millimeters in diameter and result from decreased platelet count, platelet dysfunction, or increased vascular fragility.

Harvard.text: Abbreviation for positron emission tomography, a medical imaging test that uses a radioactive substance to assess organ and tissue function in the body and to look for disease.

LLM.text: An imaging study that detects the distribution of a radioactive tracer to assess tissue metabolism or function.

Harvard.text: Scarring of some of the tissue inside the penis, causing the penis to bend at an angle during an erection.

LLM.text: A disorder in which scar tissue forms in the erectile tissue of the penis, causing curvature, pain, or difficulty with sexual intercourse.

Harvard.text: A test to determine whether stomach acid is backing up into the esophagus. For this test, a sensing probe is inserted through the nose and positioned above the lower esophageal sphincter.

LLM.text: Measurement of esophageal pH. Evaluates gastroesophageal reflux disease.

Harvard.text: A method of cataract removal. It uses ultrasound waves to break up the clouded lens of the eye so it can be suctioned out with a needle.

LLM.text: A cataract-surgery technique that uses ultrasound to break up and remove the cloudy lens through a small incision. An intraocular lens is usually implanted to restore focusing ability.

Harvard.text: Cells that can ingest other cells, bacteria, and foreign particles.

LLM.text: Immune cells that engulf and digest microorganisms, dead cells, and other particles.

Harvard.text: Sleep problem that results when a person's internal clock becomes out of sync with external time. This can be a problem for people who work the night shift.

LLM.text: A circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorder in which the timing of sleep is persistently shifted earlier or later than desired or required by social schedules.

Harvard.text: A helpful enzyme that seems to clear toxins and help prevent cancer-causing substances from binding to DNA.

LLM.text: An enzyme that catalyzes a conjugation reaction in the metabolism and detoxification of drugs and other compounds, such as glucuronidation, sulfation, acetylation, or glutathione conjugation.

Harvard.text: Powerful tranquilizing drugs used to treat schizophrenia and, sometimes, severe nausea.

LLM.text: Phenothiazines are medicines that chiefly block dopamine receptors and are used for selected psychotic, behavioral, or nausea-related conditions.

Harvard.text: A decongestant drug used to treat nasal congestion and sometimes mild incontinence.

LLM.text: A sympathomimetic decongestant formerly used in some products; it can raise blood pressure and has been restricted because of safety concerns.

Harvard.text: A rare adrenal gland tumor that secretes hormones that narrow blood vessels and increase blood pressure.

LLM.text: Pheochromocytoma is a catecholamine-producing tumor of chromaffin tissue, usually in the adrenal gland, causing episodic or sustained hypertension, headache, sweating, and palpitations. extra-adrenal paraganglia. Approximately ten percent are bilateral, ten percent are extra-adrenal, and ten percent are malignant. Classic presentation includes episodic headache, sweating, and palpitations with sustained or paroxysmal hypertension.

Harvard.text: Thick, sticky mucus secreted by mucous membranes, such as the sinuses.

LLM.text: Phlegm is thick mucus produced in the lower airways and expelled by coughing; its amount, color, blood, and accompanying symptoms can help assess respiratory disease.

Harvard.text: Sensitivity to noise, often experienced during a migraine attack.

LLM.text: Abnormal sensitivity to or fear of sound, often associated with migraine.

Harvard.text: An enzyme that breaks down substances that help the penis become erect and maintain an erection.

LLM.text: An enzyme that degrades cyclic guanosine monophosphate in smooth muscle; its inhibitors are used for erectile dysfunction, pulmonary hypertension, and selected other conditions.

Harvard.text: Use of a laser to seal off blood vessels.

LLM.text: Coagulation of tissue by intense light, often laser light, to treat lesions such as abnormal retinal vessels.

Harvard.text: A medical treatment that uses a light source to activate a photosensitizing drug (one that becomes activated by light exposure). Often used in oncology, dermatology, and cosmetic surgery.

LLM.text: A treatment that combines a photosensitizing agent with light to generate reactive oxygen species and destroy cancer cells, used for actinic keratosis, superficial skin cancers, and selected visceral tumors.

Harvard.text: Sensitivity to light, often experienced during a migraine attack.

LLM.text: Death of a fetus before delivery; medical and legal definitions vary according to gestational age and local regulations.

Harvard.text: A sensation of sparks or flashes of light across the visual field.

LLM.text: The perception of flashes, sparks, or other lights without an external light source; sudden onset may indicate vitreoretinal disease and requires prompt eye assessment.

Harvard.text: Laser surgery used to reshape the cornea in order to correct vision problems.

LLM.text: Laser eye surgery that reshapes the cornea to correct refractive errors.

Harvard.text: A cosmetic procedure that uses intense pulsed light to remove wrinkles and improve skin tone and texture.

LLM.text: A dermatologic treatment using controlled light or laser energy to reduce selected pigment changes, superficial vascular lesions, or signs of photoaging; results and risks depend on the device and skin type.

Harvard.text: A physician who specializes in physical medicine, pain, and rehabilitation. These doctors diagnose and treat sports injuries and degenerative conditions like arthritis or low back pain, and oversee rehab for patients with severe impairments resulting from trauma, stroke, and other conditions.

LLM.text: Physician specialty focusing on function, quality of life for patients with impairment, disability. See rehabilitation medicine.

Harvard.text: Any voluntary body movements that burn calories, including walking up stairs, vacuuming a floor, going for a brisk stroll, or engaging in a structured program of exercise.

LLM.text: Any movement produced by skeletal muscles that increases energy expenditure, including occupational, household, transportation, and recreational movement. Regular activity supports cardiovascular, metabolic, musculoskeletal, and mental health.

Harvard.text: The process through which the body becomes accustomed to a psychoactive drug or rewarding behavior and misses it if it’s taken away. People with physical dependence who stop or cut down on their substance or activity of choice might develop uncomfortable withdrawal symptoms.

LLM.text: A state in which the body adapts to a substance or medication and develops withdrawal symptoms when it is reduced or stopped.

Harvard.text: A state of being physically sound and healthy; having the ability to perform physical activity well.

LLM.text: The capacity to perform physical activity safely and effectively, including cardiorespiratory endurance, muscular strength, flexibility, and body-composition components.

Harvard.text: Substances made by plants that have biological effects in the human body. Examples include isoflavones, lycopene, lutein, and zeaxanthin.

LLM.text: Biologically active chemical compounds produced by plants; some may affect human physiology, but their clinical effects and evidence vary widely.

Harvard.text: A plant component that mimics the effects of estrogen hormones in the body.

LLM.text: A plant-derived compound with structural or functional similarity to estrogen that can interact with estrogen receptors, with effects dependent on the compound, dose, and tissue.

Harvard.text: A brain disorder that causes dementia, neurotic behavior, and gradual changes in personality and emotional control.

LLM.text: A form of frontotemporal dementia characterized by progressive changes in behavior, language, and personality.

Harvard.text: A gland located in the middle of the brain, between the brain’s two hemispheres, that produces melatonin in response to declining light.

LLM.text: A small endocrine gland in the brain that secretes melatonin and helps regulate circadian rhythms.

Harvard.text: A substance that binds to amyloid proteins in the brain (markers for Alzheimer’s disease), making them visible under positron emission tomography (PET) scanning.

LLM.text: A radiolabeled tracer used with positron-emission tomography to bind fibrillar amyloid-beta deposits in the brain during research or specialized evaluation of Alzheimer disease.

Harvard.text: The so-called master gland, located at the base of the brain. It controls and regulates the thyroid and other glands throughout the endocrine system.

LLM.text: Pea-sized "master gland" in the sella turcica, connected to hypothalamus by infundibulum. Anterior pituitary (adenohypophysis): GH, TSH, ACTH, FSH, LH, prolactin. Posterior pituitary (neurohypophysis): ADH (vasopressin), oxytocin (from hypothalamus). Regulates other endocrine glands and bodily functions.

Harvard.text: A false or inactive medication or treatment that may still offer relief despite being ineffective. In clinical trials, the effectiveness of a new drug is often tested against a placebo.

LLM.text: Inactive substance used as control in trials. Placebo effect: improvement from expectation.

Harvard.text: A change or improvement in symptoms that is due to a dummy medication or treatment (placebo) rather than a real drug or treatment.

LLM.text: A psychological and physiological phenomenon where a patient experiences a real improvement in health or symptoms after receiving an inactive treatment (like a sugar pill) due to their expectations of healing.

Harvard.text: Connective tissue in the foot which joins the heel bone to the ball of the foot.

LLM.text: A thick band of connective tissue along the sole of the foot that supports the arch and helps transmit forces during walking.

Harvard.text: An inflammation of the plantar fascia; the leading cause of heel pain.

LLM.text: The most common cause of heel pain, caused by degeneration and microtears of the plantar fascia at its calcaneal origin. Presents with sharp, stabbing heel pain with the first steps in the morning (post-static dyskinesia), improving after a few minutes but worsening with prolonged standing or activity.

Harvard.text: A wart on the sole of the foot, caused by a virus.

LLM.text: A lung infection caused by recently inhaled Histoplasma spores; it may cause fever, cough, chest discomfort, and fatigue, or no symptoms.

Harvard.text: 1) A layer of bacteria that forms on the surface of a tooth and can cause dental disease. 2) A fatty deposit in or on the walls of an artery, as part of atherosclerosis.

LLM.text: A raised, palpable lesion greater than approximately 1 cm, often formed by the coalescence of papules. Plaques are characteristic of several inflammatory, infectious, and neoplastic skin disorders.

Harvard.text: The fluid in which blood cells are suspended.

LLM.text: The liquid portion of blood in which blood cells and dissolved substances circulate.

Harvard.text: White blood cells that produce large quantities of antibodies as part of an immune system response.

LLM.text: Mature B lymphocytes that produce antibodies.

Harvard.text: An enzyme that breaks down the protein involved in clotting blood (fibrin), dissolving the clot.

LLM.text: A proteolytic enzyme that breaks down fibrin and helps dissolve blood clots.

Harvard.text: A colorless, disk-shaped cell in the blood that is necessary for clotting.

LLM.text: A small blood component that helps form clots and stop bleeding.

Harvard.text: A physician who specializes in the medical, surgical, and orthopedic management of foot and ankle disorders.

LLM.text: A podiatrist is a clinician specializing in assessment and treatment of the feet, ankles, and related lower-limb problems within the scope of local practice.

Harvard.text: A localized patch of gray or white hair on the scalp, eyebrows, or eyelashes.

LLM.text: A localized patch of white or depigmented hair caused by reduced melanin in follicles, occurring in vitiligo, alopecia areata, inflammatory disease, genetic syndromes, or after injury.

Harvard.text: An inherited disorder characterized by the formation of abnormal cysts in enlarged ovaries; a leading cause of female infertility and a common cause of hirsutism.

LLM.text: Common endocrine disorder affecting six to twelve percent of reproductive-aged women characterized by hyperandrogenism, ovulatory dysfunction, and polycystic ovarian morphology on ultrasound.

Harvard.text: Excessive thirst.

LLM.text: Excessive, unquenchable thirst. A classic symptom of hyperosmolar states and endocrine disorders.

Harvard.text: A rare disease in which the muscles become inflamed and weak.

LLM.text: An idiopathic inflammatory myopathy characterized by symmetric, proximal muscle weakness (shoulders, hips) with elevated muscle enzymes (CK, aldolase, LDH). More common in women, peaks at 30-50 years.

Harvard.text: An abnormal, noncancerous growth that protrudes from mucous membranes, like those found in the sinuses and colon lining.

LLM.text: A growth projecting from a mucous membrane; it may be benign, precancerous, or rarely cancerous.

Harvard.text: A sleep study that examines brain waves and other measures of physiological functioning.

LLM.text: An overnight sleep study that records brain activity, eye movements, muscle activity, heart rhythm, airflow, breathing effort, and blood oxygen. It helps evaluate sleep apnea, movement disorders, parasomnias, and other sleep conditions.

Harvard.text: A type of fat that is abundant in soybean, corn, cottonseed, safflower, and sunflower oils, as well as in fatty fish. One type, omega-3 fats, are especially important for cardiovascular health.

LLM.text: Liquid at room temperature. Sources: fish, vegetable oils, nuts. Essential fatty acids.

Harvard.text: Excessive urination.

LLM.text: Excessive urine output, defined as >3 L/day in adults. Causes are divided into water diuresis and solute diuresis. Water diuresis: central diabetes insipidus (ADH deficiency), nephrogenic diabetes insipidus (ADH resistance from lithium, hypercalcemia, hypokalemia, genetic causes), and primary polydipsia (psychogenic or dipsogenic).

Harvard.text: A branch of psychology that studies mental health rather than illness, focusing on how life can be more happy and fulfilling.

LLM.text: The study of well-being, strengths, resilience, and factors that help people thrive.

Harvard.text: A medical imaging test that uses a radioactive substance to assess organ and tissue function in the body and to look for disease. Commonly called a PET scan.

LLM.text: Functional imaging modality using positron-emitting radionuclides. Common isotope: fluorine-18 (110 min half-life). Detection: annihilation photons (511 keV) detected in coincidence. Tracers: FDG (metabolism), florbetapir (amyloid), flortaucipir (tau), PSMA (prostate cancer).

Harvard.text: The part of the eye behind the iris and in front of the lens that is filled with aqueous humor.

LLM.text: The part of the eye between the iris and lens, containing aqueous humor.

Harvard.text: An inflammation of the bursa sac surrounding the joint in the heel of the foot, causing swelling and pain.

LLM.text: Inflammation of a bursa near the back of the heel, causing pain and swelling.

Harvard.text: A minimally invasive surgical procedure that is sometimes an option for repairing a herniated disk.

LLM.text: A minimally invasive operation that enlarges a spinal nerve opening to relieve compression.

Harvard.text: Heart attack involving the rear wall of the heart muscle.

LLM.text: A heart attack involving the back wall of the heart.

Harvard.text: Nerve pain caused by the herpes zoster virus, also known as shingles.

LLM.text: Persistent nerve pain in an area affected by shingles after the rash has healed.

Harvard.text: Bone loss caused by lower estrogen levels associated with menopause. Sometimes called type I osteoporosis.

LLM.text: Bone loss caused by lower estrogen levels associated with menopause. Sometimes called type I osteoporosis.

Harvard.text: The period in a woman's life lasting from the end of perimenopause until the end of life.

LLM.text: The period in a woman’s life lasting from the end of perimenopause until the end of life.

Harvard.text: Pertaining to the period after giving birth.

LLM.text: Relating to the period after childbirth.

Harvard.text: A persistent headache resulting from a head or neck injury, sometimes lasting for a year or more.

LLM.text: A headache that begins or persists after a head or neck injury.

Harvard.text: A prolonged reaction to a traumatic event. Post-traumatic stress disorder can cause crippling anxiety and leading to other problems, such as sleep disturbances, depression, and substance abuse. Often referred to as PTSD.

LLM.text: A disorder that may develop after exposure to actual or threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violence, causing persistent re-experiencing, avoidance, negative mood or cognition, and heightened arousal.

Harvard.text: The amount of urine left in the bladder after urinating.

LLM.text: The amount of urine remaining in the bladder after urination, measured by ultrasound or catheterization. A persistently high residual may indicate incomplete emptying, but its significance depends on the volume, timing, symptoms, and clinical context.

Harvard.text: Force times speed of movement. It reflects how quickly a given force is exerted.

LLM.text: The rate at which work is performed; in exercise, it combines force and movement speed.

Harvard.text: An emerging field of physical medicine aimed at boosting the ability to exert strength quickly, especially in relation to practical, day-to-day tasks.

LLM.text: Exercise designed to improve the ability to produce force rapidly.

Harvard.text: A member of a class of drugs called alpha blockers. Prazosin eases the symptoms of benign prostatic hyperplasia by relaxing smooth muscle tissue in the capsule that surrounds the prostate.

LLM.text: An alpha-1 blocker that relaxes blood vessels and smooth muscle.

Harvard.text: A substance that the body can convert into the active form of a vitamin. One example is beta carotene, which the body can convert into vitamin A as needed.

LLM.text: A substance that can be converted into another biologically active substance.

Harvard.text: A fasting blood sugar level above a healthy level, but still below the level used to diagnose diabetes. An individual with prediabetes is at increased risk for developing diabetes.

LLM.text: Blood glucose higher than normal but below the diagnostic threshold for diabetes, usually identified by A1C, fasting glucose, or an oral glucose-tolerance test; it increases future diabetes and cardiovascular risk.

Harvard.text: High blood pressure during pregnancy accompanied by such signs as protein in the urine and swelling of the hands and feet; can progress to eclampsia, characterized by seizures.

LLM.text: Preeclampsia is pregnancy-related hypertension with proteinuria or other maternal organ dysfunction after midpregnancy and can progress to seizures, stroke, liver injury, or placental complications. pressure 140/90 mmHg or higher) after 20 weeks gestation with proteinuria or other end-organ damage.

Harvard.text: Blood pressure that is above normal but not high enough to qualify as hypertension. An individual with prehypertension is at increased risk for developing hypertension.

LLM.text: Blood pressure above normal but below the former threshold for hypertension.

Harvard.text: A method of reducing cardiac workload by decreasing the pressure of blood entering the heart.

LLM.text: Lowering the amount of blood returning to the heart to reduce cardiac workload.

Harvard.text: An early beat in an atria that feels like the heart skipped a beat.

LLM.text: A premature beat arising from an ectopic focus in the atria, producing an early P wave (often abnormal morphology) followed by a normal QRS; common and usually benign, increasing with age and caffeine/stress. ECG: early abnormal P wave, normal PR and QRS, followed by a compensatory pause.

Harvard.text: Ejaculation that occurs before or immediately after penetration; this can interfere with a couple having a mutually satisfying sexual experience.

LLM.text: Ejaculation occurring sooner than desired. Most common sexual dysfunction in men. Treatment: behavioral techniques, topical anesthetics, SSRIs, counseling.

Harvard.text: An early beat in a ventricle that feels like the heart skipped a beat.

LLM.text: An early heartbeat arising from the ventricles.

Harvard.text: Age-related hearing loss caused by the death of hair cells in the inner ear.

LLM.text: Bilateral, usually symmetric age-related sensorineural hearing loss, initially affecting high frequencies and speech discrimination in noise. Management includes hearing rehabilitation, hearing aids, communication strategies, and cochlear implantation in selected severe cases.

Harvard.text: Age-related difficulty focusing the eyes at close range, as the flexible lens of the eye becomes less elastic.

LLM.text: A disease, structural abnormality, or developmental problem affecting a fetus before birth.

Harvard.text: An erection that lasts longer than three hours. Emergency medical treatment is required to prevent permanent damage to the penis.

LLM.text: Prolonged, painful erection lasting longer than 4 hours, occurring independently of sexual desire or stimulation. Medical emergency categorized into two types: ischemic (low-flow, veno-occlusive) and non-ischemic (high-flow, arterial).

Harvard.text: A commonly used skin test to confirm hypersensitivity to a broad range of allergens.

LLM.text: A skin test in which small amounts of suspected allergens are introduced into the skin.

Harvard.text: Use of angioplasty as the first treatment to open a blocked artery that is causing a heart attack, rather than using clot-busting (thrombolytic) drugs.

LLM.text: Angioplasty used as the initial treatment to reopen an artery during an acute heart attack.

Harvard.text: High blood pressure with no known cause. Also known as essential hypertension.

LLM.text: High blood pressure without an identifiable single underlying cause.

Harvard.text: Bone loss that results from a normal physiological process, such as menopause or aging.

LLM.text: Bone loss due to aging, menopause, or other normal physiological processes rather than another disease.

Harvard.text: The smallest known infectious agent; unlike a virus or bacterium it is made entirely of protein and contains no nucleic acid or chromosomes.

LLM.text: An infectious agent composed solely of misfolded protein (PrPSc) that propagates by converting normal cellular prion protein (PrPC) into the abnormal conformation; contains no nucleic acid, resistant to standard sterilization (heat, radiation, formaldehyde).

Harvard.text: Live microorganisms used to benefit health, such as the L. acidophilus bacteria found in yogurt.

LLM.text: Live microorganisms administered in adequate amounts to confer a health benefit by modulating the microbiome and immune responses.

Harvard.text: The long-term memory of skills and procedures, or how-to knowledge. Also called implicit memory.

LLM.text: Long-term memory for learned skills and procedures.

Harvard.text: A group of early symptoms preceding a given disease or condition. For example, a migraine prodrome (fatigue, hunger, nervousness) may occur hours or days before the headache strikes.

LLM.text: An early symptom or group of symptoms that precedes a disease episode.

Harvard.text: A female steroid hormone produced by the ovaries that prepares the uterine lining for pregnancy.

LLM.text: A natural steroid hormone produced mainly by the corpus luteum after ovulation and by the placenta during pregnancy. It transforms and maintains the endometrium for implantation, reduces uterine contractility during pregnancy, supports breast glandular development, and contributes to regulation of the menstrual cycle.

Harvard.text: A synthetic compound that produces effects similar to those of the hormone progesterone.

LLM.text: A progestin is a synthetic progesterone-like hormone used in contraception, hormone therapy, and treatment of selected gynecologic conditions.

Harvard.text: Any hormone having the same effect as progesterone in the body; refers to both natural progesterone and synthetic progestin.

LLM.text: A synthetic form of progesterone, the hormone that maintains the uterine lining in the secretory phase of the menstrual cycle and supports early pregnancy.

Harvard.text: A prediction on how a person's disease will progress in the future.

LLM.text: Predicted outcome of cancer. Factors: stage, grade, molecular features, patient status. Survivability statistics.

Harvard.text: A mind/body technique for inducing the relaxation response that involves isolating, tensing, and relaxing specific sets of muscles in sequence.

LLM.text: A behavioral technique that alternately tenses and relaxes muscle groups to reduce physical tension and promote relaxation.

Harvard.text: A condition in which an organ or other body part drops from its normal position.

LLM.text: Downward displacement or protrusion of an organ or tissue from its normal position, often through a supporting structure or body opening.

Harvard.text: When part of a spinal disk bulges out of a tear or weak spot in the disk’s tough outer shell. Also known as herniated disk.

LLM.text: A spinal disk that bulges or ruptures and may compress a nearby nerve; also called a herniated disk.

Harvard.text: An advanced stage of diabetic eye disease characterized by the development of new blood vessels that grow into the vitreous cavity; they are fragile and may bleed and cause loss of vision.

LLM.text: Advanced retinal disease in which abnormal new blood vessels grow and may bleed or impair vision.

Harvard.text: Steps taken to prevent a particular disease or condition, such as taking nitroglycerin to prevent angina.

LLM.text: Preventive administration of a vaccine, antimicrobial, or immune globulin to prevent infection in exposed or at-risk individuals. Examples: post-exposure prophylaxis for rabies, HIV, and hepatitis B; perioperative antibiotic prophylaxis; and chemoprophylaxis for malaria. See also Endocarditis Prophylaxis.

Harvard.text: The ability to sense the position of one’s body in space, in relation to other objects.

LLM.text: The sense of body position, movement, and joint position arising from mechanoreceptors in muscles (muscle spindles), tendons (Golgi tendon organs), and joints, as well as skin receptors. Signals ascend via the dorsal column-medial lemniscal pathway (conscious proprioception) and the spinocerebellar tract (unconscious).

Harvard.text: Forward bulging or displacement of an organ, especially of an eye. See exophthalmos.

LLM.text: Forward displacement or bulging of an eye.

Harvard.text: A type of research method that collects data on a group of people at the start of the study and then follows them into the future, gathering data over time.

LLM.text: An observational or interventional study that enrolls participants and follows them forward in time to record exposures, interventions, and outcomes.

Harvard.text: A group of chemicals that have hormone-like actions; prostaglandins help regulate blood pressure and contraction of smooth-muscle cells (for example, those in the lining of the blood vessels).

LLM.text: Lipid compounds involved in labor initiation and cervical ripening. Endogenous prostaglandins (PGE2, PGF2alpha) stimulate uterine contractions and promote cervical softening. Synthetic analogs used clinically: misoprostol (PGE1) and dinoprostone (PGE2 gel or insert) for cervical ripening and labor induction.

Harvard.text: Cancer of the prostate gland.

LLM.text: Most common non-cutaneous cancer in men. Risk factors: age, family history, African American race, high red meat intake. Screening: PSA testing, DRE. Diagnosis: transrectal ultrasound-guided biopsy. Staging: TNM system, Gleason score.

Harvard.text: A walnut-shaped gland at the base of the male bladder. It produces a fluid that forms part of semen.

LLM.text: Prostate gland refers to an anatomical structure, biological substance, or physiologic concept used in describing the human body and its function.

Harvard.text: A protein produced by the prostate. Elevated levels may indicate the presence of cancer, benign prostatic hyperplasia, or prostatitis. Often referred to as PSA.

LLM.text: A serine protease produced mainly by prostate epithelial cells and secreted into seminal fluid. PSA can be measured in blood, where levels may rise with benign enlargement, inflammation, infection, or prostate cancer. Interpretation depends on age, prostate size, medicines, symptoms, and changes over time.

Harvard.text: Another name for prostate cancer.

LLM.text: A malignant tumor arising from the prostate gland, most commonly adenocarcinoma; evaluation includes clinical assessment, prostate-specific antigen testing, imaging, and biopsy when indicated.

Harvard.text: A small, springlike cylinder, designed to relieve pressure from an enlarged prostate and improve urine flow by widening a narrowed urethra.

LLM.text: A small device placed in the prostatic urethra to help maintain urine flow when the prostate obstructs it.

Harvard.text: A blockage at the base of the bladder that reduces or prevents the flow of urine into the urethra, the tube that carries urine out of the body (also known as bladder outlet obstruction). Typical symptoms include feeling the need to urinate right away yet having to strain to do so, having a weak urinary stream, dribbling after urinating, feeling as though the bladder has not been emptied completely, needing to urinate frequently, or experiencing urinary incontinence.

LLM.text: Lower urinary-tract symptoms traditionally attributed to prostate enlargement, including weak stream, hesitancy, frequency, urgency, nocturia, and incomplete emptying; causes are not limited to the prostate.

Harvard.text: An inflammation of the prostate gland, sometimes caused by a bacterial infection, which may result in painful or difficult urination.

LLM.text: Inflammation or infection of the prostate that may cause pelvic or urinary pain, difficulty urinating, fever, or recurrent urinary infections. It can be acute, chronic bacterial, or chronic pelvic pain syndrome.

Harvard.text: An artificial device such as a hearing aid, artificial joint, or dentures that substitutes for a missing body part.

LLM.text: A prosthesis is an artificial device that replaces or supports a missing or impaired body part, such as a limb, joint, tooth, heart valve, or eye.

Harvard.text: A class of drugs that help fight retrovirus infections; commonly prescribed to treat human immunodeficiency virus (HIV).

LLM.text: A class of antiretroviral drugs that block the viral protease enzyme responsible for cleaving polyprotein precursors into functional proteins during HIV replication, preventing the formation of mature, infectious virions. Used in combination antiretroviral therapy for HIV infection.

Harvard.text: One of the three major nutrients (along with carbohydrates and fats). It is used by the body for building and repairing tissues. Protein is derived primarily from animal sources but can be obtained from nuts and seed, some grains, and other plant sources.

LLM.text: Polymer of amino acids linked by peptide bonds. Structure: primary (sequence), secondary (alpha helix, beta sheet), tertiary (3D folding), quaternary (multiple subunits). Functions: enzymes, structural, transport, signaling, immune defense, movement. Folding determined by amino acid sequence (Anfinsen's dogma). Chaperones assist folding.

Harvard.text: A plan that lays out the procedures that will be followed in conducting a physical examination, a research study, or the treatment of a disease.

LLM.text: A predefined plan specifying procedures for a clinical study, examination, or treatment.

Harvard.text: Itching.

LLM.text: Itching: an unpleasant sensation provoking scratching, a common symptom of skin and systemic disease.

Harvard.text: Abbreviation for prostate-specific antigen, a protein produced by the prostate. Elevated levels may indicate the presence of cancer, benign prostatic hyperplasia, or prostatitis.

LLM.text: Prostate-specific antigen, a protein measured in blood to help evaluate prostate conditions.

Harvard.text: The rate at which a man’s PSA level increases over time.

LLM.text: The rate at which PSA concentration changes over time.

Harvard.text: A decongestant drug that may also relieve mild incontinence.

LLM.text: A sympathomimetic (alpha-1 agonist, some beta effects) oral decongestant used for nasal congestion in colds and sinusitis. Increases nasal mucosal vasoconstriction.

Harvard.text: Arthritis caused by crystals of calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate in the joints. Also known as calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate disease.

LLM.text: Calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease (CPPD): deposition of calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate crystals in joints, causing acute arthritis resembling gout (pseudogout) or chronic osteoarthritis-like disease.

Harvard.text: A common skin disease characterized by thickened patches of inflamed red skin; sometimes accompanied by painful joint swelling and stiffness.

LLM.text: Psoriasis is a chronic immune-mediated inflammatory disease producing sharply demarcated scaly plaques and possible nail, joint, eye, or systemic involvement. joints, and its severity and distribution vary among individuals.

Harvard.text: A form of therapy that focuses on how life events, desires, and close relationships lead to conflict, symptoms such as anxiety or depression, and difficulty in managing life’s tasks.

LLM.text: A form of depth psychology that explores how unconscious processes, early life experiences, and internal conflicts influence current thoughts, feelings, and behaviors. It involves exploration of transference and countertransference, defense mechanisms, and the therapeutic relationship as a vehicle for change.

Harvard.text: Symptoms and illnesses that have a psychological cause, rather than a physical one.

LLM.text: Caused or substantially influenced by psychological factors.

Harvard.text: Difficulty in getting or maintaining erections because of a psychological cause, such as stress or depression.

LLM.text: Erectile difficulty primarily related to psychological factors rather than a structural disease.

Harvard.text: Symptoms and illnesses that involve both the mind and the body, in which psychological stress may result in physical illness.

LLM.text: Relating to physical symptoms influenced by psychological processes or stress.

Harvard.text: Abbreviation for percutaneous transluminal coronary angioplasty, a procedure used to open blocked coronary arteries.

LLM.text: Percutaneous transluminal coronary angioplasty, a procedure that opens a narrowed coronary artery.

Harvard.text: A drooping of the eyelid attributed to weakened muscles.

LLM.text: The drooping of the upper eyelid, which can be congenital or acquired, and can range from mild drooping that is primarily a cosmetic concern to severe drooping that obstructs the visual axis and causes amblyopia in children or visual impairment in adults.

Harvard.text: Abbreviation for post-traumatic stress disorder, a prolonged reaction to a traumatic event. PTSD can cause crippling anxiety and leading to other problems, such as sleep disturbances, depression, and substance abuse.

LLM.text: Post-traumatic stress disorder, a condition involving persistent trauma-related memories, avoidance, negative mood or cognition, and heightened arousal after a severe traumatic event.

Harvard.text: A pelvic floor muscle that forms a sling around the rectum and helps maintain fecal continence.

LLM.text: A pelvic-floor muscle sling around the rectum that helps maintain continence.

Harvard.text: Arteries supplying blood to the genital area.

LLM.text: Arteries supplying blood to the external genital and perineal region.

Harvard.text: The nerve that carries sensation from the genital area to the central nervous system.

LLM.text: The nerve carrying sensation and motor signals to much of the perineum and pelvic floor.

Harvard.text: Pertaining to the lungs.

LLM.text: Relating to the lungs.

Harvard.text: A condition caused by excess fluid accumulating in the lungs, making breathing difficult.

LLM.text: Accumulation of fluid in the pulmonary interstitium and alveoli, most commonly due to left-sided heart failure (cardiogenic). Causes increased hydrostatic pressure leads to transudation. Presents with acute dyspnea, orthopnea, crackles, and S3 gallop. Non-cardiogenic causes include ARDS, renal failure, and high altitude.

Harvard.text: Blockage of one or more arteries in the lungs by a blood clot that formed elsewhere, often in the legs. Typically accompanied by sudden shortness of breath, chest pain, and cough.

LLM.text: Occlusion of the pulmonary arterial bed by a thrombus, tumor, air, or fat, most commonly originating as a deep vein thrombosis (DVT) from the lower extremities. Presents with acute onset of dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, cough, hemoptysis, tachycardia, and hypoxemia.

Harvard.text: The veins that carry blood from the lungs to the left atrium.

LLM.text: Veins carrying oxygen-rich blood from the lungs to the left atrium.

Harvard.text: Tissue containing nerves and blood vessels that fills the chamber at the center of the tooth.

LLM.text: Soft connective tissue central to tooth containing blood vessels, nerves, connective tissue. Responds to injury with inflammation, necrosis, calcification. Root canal therapy removes infected pulp.

Harvard.text: The difference between systolic blood pressure and diastolic blood pressure (systolic pressure minus diastolic pressure = pulse pressure). Pulse pressure may help predict heart disease risk.

LLM.text: The difference between systolic and diastolic blood pressure.

Harvard.text: When the heart muscle becomes so weak that it can no longer pump enough blood to the rest of the body.

LLM.text: Severe weakening of the heart’s pumping ability, causing inadequate blood flow to organs.

Harvard.text: The dark, circular opening in the middle of the iris of the eye.

LLM.text: Central round iris aperture for light entry, size controlled by sphincter pupillae (CN III parasympathetic, constricts to 2-3 mm) and dilator pupillae (sympathetic, dilates to 8 mm). The pupillary light reflex tests CN II (afferent) and CN III (efferent): light in one eye causes bilateral constrination (direct and consensual).

Harvard.text: Formed of or containing pus.

LLM.text: Containing or producing pus.

Harvard.text: A thick, yellow or green liquid that is composed of dead cells and bacteria, most often found at the site of a bacterial infection.

LLM.text: A thick, yellow or green liquid that is composed of dead cells and bacteria, most often found at the site of a bacterial infection.

Harvard.text: A muscular valve at the lower end of the stomach that opens to the duodenum.

LLM.text: A muscular valve regulating passage of stomach contents into the duodenum.

Harvard.text: A form of vitamin B6.

LLM.text: A form of vitamin B6 involved in metabolism and nervous-system function.

Harvard.text: Paralysis of all limbs, often caused by a severe neck injury.

LLM.text: Paralysis of all four limbs and trunk, resulting from a spinal cord lesion at the cervical level or a bilateral brainstem lesion. Common causes include traumatic spinal cord injury, stroke, multiple sclerosis, spinal cord tumors, and demyelinating disease.

Harvard.text: A modification of computed tomography that provides measurements of bone mass as well as an image.

LLM.text: CT-based imaging that measures bone mineral density as well as showing bone structure.

Harvard.text: A period of time in which a sick person is kept away from others to prevent the spread of disease.

LLM.text: Separation or restriction of movement of people who have been exposed to an infectious disease while monitoring whether they become ill. It differs from isolation of people who are already infected.

Harvard.text: Medications that quickly open the bronchial tubes by relaxing the muscles surrounding these airways.

LLM.text: Fast-acting medicines that relax airway muscle and rapidly ease bronchoconstriction.

Harvard.text: Any sleep other than REM sleep, in which thinking and most physiological activities slow, but movement still occurs. Also called non-REM sleep.

LLM.text: Non-REM sleep, during which brain and body activity generally slow.

Harvard.text: A condition in which the radial nerve is compressed at the elbow, causing pain, numbness, tingling, and muscle weakness in the hand and arm.

LLM.text: Compression of the radial nerve near the elbow, causing arm pain, tingling, or weakness.

Harvard.text: Energy in the form of particles or waves, such as x-rays and gamma rays. Radiation is often used to help make a diagnosis, as in x-rays, or as a treatment for cancer.

LLM.text: Energy transmitted as particles or electromagnetic waves, including X-rays and gamma rays.

Harvard.text: Treatment with high-energy rays (from x-rays or other sources) designed to control disease and destroy cancer cells.

LLM.text: Use of ionizing radiation to kill cancer cells. Types: external beam, brachytherapy, stereotactic. Mechanisms: DNA damage, cell death. Side effects: fatigue, skin reactions, site-specific effects.

Harvard.text: Surgery to remove the entire prostate.

LLM.text: Surgery that removes the entire prostate, usually with nearby seminal vesicles.

Harvard.text: Pain caused by irritation of a nerve as it exits the spinal cord.

LLM.text: Dysfunction of a spinal nerve root, usually from disc herniation, narrowing, or inflammation. It may cause shooting pain, tingling, numbness, weakness, or altered reflexes along the affected nerve pathway.

Harvard.text: A radioactive form of iodine that can be used as a tracer during a radioactive iodine uptake test or a radioactive thyroid scan. Much larger amounts are used in the treatment of hyperthyroidism.

LLM.text: Used for thyroid imaging and treatment. I-131 emits beta particles (therapy) and gamma rays (imaging). Half-life: 8 days. Used for hyperthyroidism (Graves, toxic nodules) and thyroid cancer ablation. I-123 for diagnostics (shorter half-life, pure gamma).

Harvard.text: A blood test used for identifying allergens.

LLM.text: A blood test used to detect allergen-specific IgE antibodies.

Harvard.text: A non-surgical technique using an electromagnetic current to penetrate deep into the body’s tissues, which can be used to treat pain, cancer, and heart rhythm disorders, among other conditions.

LLM.text: Electromagnetic energy used in some diagnostic and therapeutic medical procedures.

Harvard.text: Another name for an x-ray.

LLM.text: An image produced using X-rays.

Harvard.text: Another name for nuclear tests: tests that use tiny amounts of short-lived radioactive substances that can target particular organs or cell receptors to diagnose disease.

LLM.text: Imaging that detects radiation from a tracer administered to the patient.

common_names: nuclear tests: tests that use tiny amounts of short-lived radioactive substances that can target particular organs or cell receptors to diagnose disease

Harvard.text: Short-lived radioactive chemicals that are used in nuclear imaging tests.

LLM.text: Radioactive atoms used as tracers in nuclear medicine imaging or treatment.

Harvard.text: Abnormal lung sounds that might be a sign of fluid buildup congestion in the lungs.

LLM.text: Crackling or bubbling sounds heard in the lungs, often caused by fluid or narrowed airways.

Harvard.text: A study in which researchers choose a study population at random; one group receives the intervention (such as a nutritional supplement) and another group receives a placebo. Often referred to as an RCT.

LLM.text: An experimental study in which participants are assigned by chance to different interventions or a control condition and followed for specified outcomes.

Harvard.text: The extent of movement—and thus flexibility—in a joint, measured in the degrees of a circle.

LLM.text: ROM: joint movement capacity. Goniometer measurement. Restrictions from contracture, pain, swelling.

Harvard.text: A period of intense brain activity during sleep, often associated with dreams; named for the rapid eye movements that occur during this time. Also called dreaming sleep.

LLM.text: A sleep stage marked by rapid eye movements, vivid dreaming, and high brain activity.

Harvard.text: Abbreviation for radioallergosorbent test, a blood test used for identifying allergens.

LLM.text: A blood test for allergen-specific IgE antibodies.

Harvard.text: A condition in which the blood vessels in the fingers and other extremities narrow in response to cold or stress, causing them to turn white or blue.

LLM.text: Episodic narrowing of small arteries in the fingers or toes, triggered by cold or stress and causing sequential color changes, numbness, or pain.

Harvard.text: Abbreviation for randomized controlled trial, a study in which researchers choose a study population at random; one group receives the intervention (such as a nutritional supplement) and another group receives a placebo.

LLM.text: Randomized controlled trial, a study comparing randomly assigned intervention and control groups.

Harvard.text: Abbreviation for recommended dietary allowance, the average daily amount of a nutrient that will meet the nutritional needs of almost all (97%–98%) healthy people at specific stages of their lives.

LLM.text: Recommended dietary allowance, the daily nutrient intake sufficient for nearly all healthy people in a defined group.

Harvard.text: Joint problems triggered by bacterial or viral infection elsewhere in the body.

LLM.text: An inflammatory arthritis that develops after certain genitourinary or gastrointestinal infections. It may involve the joints, eyes, skin, or urinary tract; not every person has all of these features.

Harvard.text: Insomnia caused by withdrawal from sleep medication; usually it is at least as serious as before the medication was used.

LLM.text: Return or worsening of insomnia after stopping a sleep medicine.

Harvard.text: Structures on the outside of a cell membrane that permit attachment of specific chemicals.

LLM.text: Cell proteins or structures that bind specific signaling molecules and trigger a response.

Harvard.text: A gene that will not be expressed in the offspring unless it is inherited from both the mother and father. A recessive gene from one parent that is paired with a dominant gene from the other parent will be overridden by the dominant gene.

LLM.text: Allele whose phenotype is masked in heterozygotes. Autosomal recessive disorders: cystic fibrosis, sickle cell anemia, Tay-Sachs disease. Requires two copies for expression.

Harvard.text: A thrombolytic (clot-dissolving) drug made using recombinant DNA technology; used to dissolve blood clots causing an ischemic stroke, pulmonary embolism, or myocardial infarction.

LLM.text: A laboratory-produced clot-dissolving medicine used in selected emergencies.

Harvard.text: The average daily amount of a nutrient that will meet the nutritional needs of almost all (97%–98%) healthy people at specific stages of their lives.

LLM.text: The average daily intake expected to meet the nutrient needs of nearly all healthy people in a defined group.

Harvard.text: A process of overcoming addiction to alcohol, other psychoactive substance, or addictive behavior. Often this involves a commitment to abstinence, but sometimes it involves reduced use rather than complete abstinence.

LLM.text: The process of regaining health, function, or stability after illness, injury, surgery, substance use, or another health problem; its course varies by cause and individual factors.

Harvard.text: A weakening of the vaginal wall that allows the rectum to bulge into the vagina.

LLM.text: A weakening of the vaginal wall that allows the rectum to bulge into the vagina.

Harvard.text: The last 12 centimeters of the colon, through which waste is eliminated from the body.

LLM.text: The final straight section of the large intestine, approximately 12-15 cm long, extending from the sigmoid colon to the anal canal. The rectum stores feces before defecation.

Harvard.text: The deflection of light as it passes through one medium to another of different density; also refers an eye test to evaluate the eye’s ability to focus.

LLM.text: The bending of light as it passes through the cornea, aqueous humour, lens, and vitreous humour. In an eye examination, refraction determines the optical power needed to focus a clear image on the retina; refractive power is measured in dioptres.

Harvard.text: Leakage of blood back into a heart chamber that occurs when a heart valve doesn't close properly

LLM.text: The backward flow of blood through a heart valve that fails to close properly (valvular incompetence or insufficiency).

Harvard.text: A professional trained to evaluate driving skills and, when appropriate, suggest equipment and adaptations to make driving safer for people with certain physical or mental limitations.

LLM.text: An occupational-therapy or rehabilitation professional who evaluates driving ability and helps people adapt skills, equipment, or habits after illness or injury.

Harvard.text: A reaction that occurs when a person’s immune system recognizes a transplanted organ as a threatening substance and tries to rid the body of it.

LLM.text: An immune response in which the body attacks transplanted tissue or an organ.

Harvard.text: The return of symptoms and disease after a person seems to have recovered.

LLM.text: Return or worsening of a disease after a period of improvement or remission. The term is used for cancer and many noncancerous disorders.

Harvard.text: The physical effects of meditation and certain other techniques that are opposite to those of the stress response. Effects include marked drops in oxygen consumption, carbon dioxide expiration, heartbeat, and respiration, as well as stabilization or lowering of blood pressure.

LLM.text: Physiological changes produced by relaxation practices that counter the stress response.

Harvard.text: Abbreviation for rapid eye movement, which occurs during a period of sleep characterized by intense brain activity, often associated with dreams.

LLM.text: Rapid eye movement, a sleep stage associated with vivid dreams and intense brain activity.

Harvard.text: A sleep disorder marked by movement during REM sleep, when muscles are normally paralyzed.

LLM.text: A sleep disorder in which a person acts out dreams during REM sleep.

Harvard.text: An increase in REM sleep, often with nightmares, that occurs after deprivation of REM sleep or the withdrawal of REM-suppressing medications.

LLM.text: Increased REM sleep after REM deprivation or withdrawal of a REM-suppressing medicine.

Harvard.text: A lessening in the severity of a disease and its symptoms. In cancer, a reduction in the size of a tumor and its symptoms.

LLM.text: Decrease or disappearance of cancer signs. Complete remission: no detectable disease. Partial remission: significant reduction but not complete.

Harvard.text: Altering a body part. Bone is constantly being remodeled in response to exercise or inactivity. Heart tissue is remodeled in response to a heart attack or high blood pressure.

LLM.text: Bone adaptation to implant stress. Wolff's law: bone remodels along lines of stress.

Harvard.text: Pertaining to the kidneys.

LLM.text: Renal means relating to the kidneys, which filter blood, regulate fluid and electrolytes, produce hormones, and excrete urine.

Harvard.text: Narrowing of an artery that supplies blood to the kidney.

LLM.text: Narrowing of renal artery causing renovascular hypertension. Atherosclerotic most common in elderly at ostium. Fibromuscular dysplasia in young women causing mid-distal stenosis with string-of-beads appearance. Flash pulmonary edema and declining function on ACE inhibitors indicate intervention.

Harvard.text: An enzyme released by the kidney that stimulates production of angiotensin and aldosterone, two substances in the body that affect blood pressure.

LLM.text: An enzyme released mainly by juxtaglomerular cells of the kidney. It initiates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system and helps regulate blood pressure and fluid balance.

Harvard.text: Re-establishing blood flow, such as when a blockage in a coronary artery that is causing a heart attack is cleared.

LLM.text: Restoration of blood flow to tissue after an interruption.

Harvard.text: Techniques used to restart circulation to part of the heart or brain that has been cut off from blood flow during a heart attack or stroke. Reperfusion may entail clot-dissolving drugs, balloon angioplasty, or surgery.

LLM.text: Treatment that restores circulation to tissue deprived of blood, such as clot-dissolving treatment or angioplasty.

Harvard.text: Number of times an exercise calls for a muscle to be worked and released (usually eight to 12). Often referred to as reps.

LLM.text: The number of times an exercise movement is performed consecutively or within a prescribed set.

Harvard.text: The surgical removal of a lesion or part or all of an organ or other body structure.

LLM.text: Surgical removal of part or all of an organ, tissue, or lesion.

Harvard.text: An instrument that permits a surgeon to view the inside of a body cavity in order to remove a part of an organ or structure.

LLM.text: An endoscopic surgical instrument with a viewing system and working loop used to remove or cauterize tissue, especially during prostate or bladder procedures.

Harvard.text: The habitat in which an infectious agent normally lives, grows, and multiplies. Reservoirs include human, animal, and environmental reservoirs.

LLM.text: A human, animal, or environmental habitat in which an infectious agent normally lives, multiplies, and persists. A reservoir may serve as the source from which the agent is transmitted to a susceptible host.

Harvard.text: The ability of a pathogen to withstand drugs previously effective against them. Usually the result of genetic mutation.

LLM.text: The ability of a microorganism to withstand a medicine that previously inhibited or killed it.

Harvard.text: High blood pressure that does not respond to drug therapy and lifestyle changes.

LLM.text: High blood pressure that remains above goal despite appropriate treatment with multiple medicines.

Harvard.text: The removal of bone tissue, both mineral and protein, by osteoclasts.

LLM.text: The removal and absorption of tissue, especially the breakdown of bone by osteoclasts.

Harvard.text: The process by which gases enter the body, including external respiration (breathing), and internal respiration, in which oxygen taken in by the lungs is carried by the blood to tissues and carbon dioxide is removed.

LLM.text: The process of exchanging oxygen and carbon dioxide between an organism and its environment, including ventilation and gas exchange in the lungs.

Harvard.text: Renarrowing of a blood vessel that has been widened with angioplasty.

LLM.text: Re-narrowing of a blood vessel after it has been opened by angioplasty or another procedure.

Harvard.text: The rate at which the body burns calories while at rest. Resting energy expenditure accounts for 60%–75% of the daily calories burned.

LLM.text: The calories the body uses at rest to maintain essential functions.

Harvard.text: Achy or unpleasant feelings in the legs associated with a need to move. Most prominent at night, making it hard to fall asleep or stay asleep.

LLM.text: An urge to move the legs, usually accompanied by uncomfortable sensations, that begins or worsens during rest, is relieved by movement, and occurs predominantly in the evening or night. The condition causes significant distress or impairment. It is associated with iron deficiency, renal failure, pregnancy, and peripheral neuropathy.

Harvard.text: The process of reviving a person who is not breathing or whose heart is not beating using techniques such as artificial respiration and heart massage.

LLM.text: Emergency measures used to restore breathing and circulation.

Harvard.text: The innermost layer of the eye, which converts light energy to electrical energy and sends visual images to the brain via the optic nerve.

LLM.text: Retina concerns retina, a body structure, substance, or clinical concept whose meaning depends on location, function, and patient context. globe for phototransduction (light to neural signals). Ten layers, with photoreceptors (rods for low-light vision, cones for color vision) in the outer nuclear layer.

Harvard.text: A condition in which the retina separates from the choroid (the back of the eye) and leads to a loss of vision.

LLM.text: An eye emergency in which the light-sensitive neurosensory retina separates from the underlying retinal pigment epithelium. The main types are rhegmatogenous detachment caused by a retinal tear, tractional detachment caused by scar tissue pulling on the retina, and exudative detachment caused by fluid collecting beneath it without a tear. Sudden new floaters, flashes of light, a curtain or shadow in the field of vision, or reduced vision require urgent eye assessment because untreated detachment can cause permanent vision loss.

Harvard.text: A synthetic, vitamin A-like compound.

LLM.text: A vitamin-A-related compound used in some skin treatments and other medical applications.

Harvard.text: The act of recalling previously learned information, involving the reactivation of particular nerve-cell pathways in the brain related to that piece of information.

LLM.text: Process of organ or tissue recovery from a donor for transplantation; also called procurement.

Harvard.text: An adverse effect of both prostate surgery and some medications that causes semen to flow back into the bladder rather than out through the penis.

LLM.text: Semen enters bladder instead of exiting urethra. Causes: diabetes, surgery, medications. Dry orgasm. Treatment: medications, sperm retrieval for fertility.

Harvard.text: A research method that looks for possible causes for a current disease by examining a study population's past habits.

LLM.text: A study that examines past records or exposures to investigate disease causes or outcomes.

Harvard.text: Restoration of blood flow to areas of heart muscle affected by coronary artery disease by means of coronary artery bypass surgery or angioplasty.

LLM.text: Restoration of blood flow to an area through bypass surgery, angioplasty, or another procedure.

Harvard.text: An interrelated set of brain regions that are all involved in recognizing, experiencing, and remembering pleasurable or rewarding events.

LLM.text: A group of interconnected brain circuits, including dopaminergic pathways, that assigns motivational value to stimuli and helps regulate reinforcement and goal-directed behavior.

Harvard.text: Any one of over 100 disorders that cause inflammation in connective tissues.

LLM.text: A broad group of disorders affecting joints, muscles, bones, connective tissue, or immune function, including arthritis and lupus.

Harvard.text: Pain and stiffness of soft tissues in and around joints.

LLM.text: Pain, stiffness, or discomfort in joints and surrounding soft tissues.
