Harvard.text: An inflammatory autoimmune disease that typically attacks the connective tissue of the joints, causing them to become painful, inflamed, and sometimes deformed.

LLM.text: A chronic autoimmune inflammatory disease that commonly causes symmetric pain, swelling, and progressive damage in the small joints of the hands and feet. It may also affect other organs.

Harvard.text: An antibody found in about 85% of people with rheumatoid arthritis; also appears in other diseases and sometimes in healthy people.

LLM.text: An autoantibody, usually of the IgM class, directed against part of IgG. It may support a diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis but can also occur in other autoimmune diseases, infections, and healthy people.

Harvard.text: A medical doctor trained to diagnose and treat disorders involving inflammation of the joints and other parts of the musculoskeletal system.

LLM.text: A physician specializing in inflammatory and autoimmune diseases of joints and connective tissue.

Harvard.text: The branch of medicine devoted to the study and treatment of diseases marked by inflammation, degeneration, or metabolic problems of the connective tissues (particularly the joints and related structures).

LLM.text: The medical specialty concerned with musculoskeletal disorders and systemic autoimmune and inflammatory diseases.

Harvard.text: Reshaping the cartilage and bone of the nose to achieve the desired profile. Commonly known as a nose job.

LLM.text: Rhinoplasty is surgery that changes nasal shape or function for cosmetic, structural, or reconstructive reasons, with risks involving breathing, bleeding, infection, and appearance. cosmetic reasons (aesthetic rhinoplasty—improving nasal appearance) or functional reasons (functional rhinoplasty—improving nasal airflow by correcting internal/external nasal valve collapse, deviated septum, or turbinate hypertrophy).

Harvard.text: A surgical procedure that involves removing excess skin and tightening the underlying muscle to correct sagging around the jaws, jowls, and neck. Does not include work on the eyes or forehead. Commonly known as a face lift.

LLM.text: Cosmetic surgery that removes excess facial skin and tightens supporting tissues.

Harvard.text: The right upper chamber of the heart; it receives partially deoxygenated blood as it returns from the body's tissues and moves it into the right ventricle for distribution to the lungs.

LLM.text: Receives deoxygenated blood from superior vena cava, inferior vena cava, and coronary sinus. Smooth posterior part (sinus venosus) and rough anterior auricle with pectinate muscles. The fossa ovalis is the fetal foramen ovale remnant. The SA node pacemaker is near the superior vena cava opening.

Harvard.text: One of the principal coronary arteries that supplies blood to the heart; this vessel supplies the right and lower part of the heart.

LLM.text: Arises from the right aortic sinus and travels in the right atrioventricular groove. It supplies the right atrium, right ventricle, SA node (60\% of individuals), AV node (85\% of individuals), and the inferior wall of the left ventricle.

Harvard.text: The right lower chamber of the heart; it receives blood from the right atrium for distribution to the lungs.

LLM.text: Receives deoxygenated blood from the right atrium through the tricuspid valve, pumping into the pulmonary trunk via the pulmonary valve. Thinner walls (3-5 mm) than the left ventricle due to low pulmonary resistance.

Harvard.text: An itchy condition of the scalp caused by a fungal infection. Also known as tinea capitis.

LLM.text: Ringworm is a contagious superficial dermatophyte infection of skin, hair, or nails that produces scaly annular lesions, itching, or localized hair loss. by dermatophytes (Trichophyton, Microsporum, Epidermophyton). See Tinea.

Harvard.text: A simple hearing test that uses a tuning fork to determine what type of hearing loss a person has.

LLM.text: The Rinne test is a screening test that compares air conduction and bone conduction hearing using a vibrating tuning fork (typically 512 Hz) to help differentiate between conductive and sensorineural hearing loss.

Harvard.text: Any factor that can cause a person to be more likely to develop a disease. For example, smoking is a risk factor for lung cancer.

LLM.text: A risk factor is a characteristic, exposure, behavior, or condition associated with increased likelihood of a disease or adverse outcome.

Harvard.text: Drinking that increases the chances of adverse consequences; drinking more than guidelines on moderate drinking suggest.

LLM.text: Alcohol use that increases the likelihood of health, safety, or social consequences.

Harvard.text: Abbreviation for restless legs syndrome, an achy or unpleasant feelings in the legs associated with a need to move. Most prominent at night, making it hard to fall asleep or stay asleep.

LLM.text: Restless legs syndrome, an urge to move the legs with uncomfortable sensations, especially at night.

Harvard.text: Light-sensitive cells in the retina that respond best in darkness and dim light.

LLM.text: Retinal photoreceptor cells that provide vision in dim light and contribute to peripheral vision but do not detect color.

Harvard.text: The portion of the tooth below the gum line.

LLM.text: The part of a tooth below the gum line.

Harvard.text: A channel in the root of the tooth that contains the pulp.

LLM.text: The channel inside a tooth root containing the pulp and its nerves and blood vessels.

Harvard.text: A procedure in which diseased pulp tissue is removed from the pulp chamber and root canal and the area is sealed off.

LLM.text: Dental treatment in which infected or inflamed pulp is removed from a tooth, the canal is cleaned and sealed, and the tooth is restored.

Harvard.text: A skin condition that enlarges blood vessels in the face, causing redness of the nose and other parts of the face.

LLM.text: Rosacea is a chronic inflammatory facial skin disorder with flushing, persistent redness, papules, pustules, visible vessels, and sometimes ocular or nasal changes. erythema, flushing, telangiectasia, inflammatory papules or pustules, phymatous change, or ocular involvement. It is classified by phenotype rather than by obligatory subtypes.

Harvard.text: A group of tendons and muscles used to raise the arm from the side and rotating the shoulder.

LLM.text: A group of four muscles and their tendons that stabilize the glenohumeral (shoulder) joint and allow a wide range of motion. The muscles are the supraspinatus (abduction), infraspinatus (external rotation), teres minor (external rotation), and subscapularis (internal rotation)—collectively remembered by the acronym SITS.

Harvard.text: Indigestible dietary fiber found in grains, fruits, vegetables, and other foods. Roughage is thought to help prevent conditions such as constipation.

LLM.text: Dietary fiber, especially the indigestible plant material that adds bulk to stool and supports normal bowel function.

Harvard.text: A tear or break in an organ or tissue. Tissue that protrudes through the rupture is known as a hernia.

LLM.text: A tear or complete break in an organ, vessel, muscle, or other tissue.

Harvard.text: When part of a spinal disk bulges out of a tear or weak spot in the disk’s tough outer shell. Also known as prolapsed disk or herniated disk.

LLM.text: A spinal disk whose outer layer has torn, allowing inner material to bulge outward.

Harvard.text: Inflammation of the sacroiliac joints, which connect the lower spine to the pelvis.

LLM.text: Inflammation of one or both sacroiliac joints, causing pain in the lower back, buttock, or posterior thigh that may worsen with prolonged rest. Causes include axial spondyloarthritis, psoriatic or enteropathic arthritis, infection, trauma, and degenerative disease.

Harvard.text: The larger triangular bone at the base of the spine.

LLM.text: Large triangular bone from 5 fused sacral vertebrae between the hip bones. Articulates with L5 superiorly and coccyx inferiorly. The sacral promontory is an obstetric landmark. Contains 4 pairs of sacral foramina. Forms the posterior pelvic wall.

Harvard.text: Abbreviation for seasonal affective disorder, sadness and depression brought on by a lack of exposure to sunlight. SAD usually appears in the fall or winter and subsides in the spring.

LLM.text: Seasonal affective disorder, a recurring mood disorder linked to seasonal changes and reduced daylight.

Harvard.text: A watery solution that contains a small amount of salt and is often used to administer drugs or as a substitute for plasma.

LLM.text: A sterile water solution containing sodium chloride, commonly used for fluids, irrigation, or drug delivery.

Harvard.text: One of three pairs of glands that pour lubricating fluids and digestive enzymes into the mouth.

LLM.text: Any exocrine gland that secretes saliva into the oral cavity. The major paired glands are the parotid, submandibular, and sublingual glands; numerous minor glands occur throughout the oral mucosa.

Harvard.text: A superficial blood vessel that extends from the thigh to the calf; it can be removed and used as a coronary bypass graft.

LLM.text: A superficial vein of the lower limb that drains the foot and leg. The great and small saphenous veins are clinically important in venous disease and may be used as graft material in selected vascular or cardiac bypass procedures.

Harvard.text: A membrane that covers the muscle fiber and ties the end of it to a tendon.

LLM.text: The specialized cell membrane surrounding a muscle fiber.

Harvard.text: A cancer that arises in the soft tissues of the body that connect, support, and separate other tissues or organs. Sarcomas can occur almost anywhere in the body.

LLM.text: A malignant tumor arising from connective or supporting tissues, including bone, cartilage, fat, muscle, and blood vessels. Examples include osteosarcoma, liposarcoma, and rhabdomyosarcoma.

Harvard.text: A person who can make a choice and be satisfied with it when presented with an option that meets his or her standards, without needing to examine all options or find the absolute best.

LLM.text: A person who chooses an option that meets acceptable criteria without seeking the absolute best option.

Harvard.text: A type of fat found in animal foods such as meat, poultry skin, butter, and whole-milk dairy products, as well in as palm and coconut oils. A diet high in saturated fat tends to raise blood levels of unhealthy low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol.

LLM.text: A dietary fat whose fatty-acid chains contain no carbon-carbon double bonds. It is found in foods such as fatty meat, butter, full-fat dairy, coconut oil, and palm oil; replacing some saturated fat with unsaturated fat can help lower LDL cholesterol and cardiovascular risk.

Harvard.text: A toe or finger swollen and red along its entire length.

LLM.text: Diffuse swelling of an entire finger or toe, often seen with inflammatory arthritis.

Harvard.text: A shoulder joint that connects the scapula to the ribs at the back of the chest.

LLM.text: The functional gliding connection between the scapula and the back of the chest wall.

Harvard.text: A circular drainage system in the eye located where the clear cornea, white sclera, and colored iris meet to form an angle.

LLM.text: A circular endothelial-lined channel at the junction of the cornea and sclera that drains aqueous humor from the anterior chamber into the venous circulation.

Harvard.text: Pain along the course of the sciatic nerve (which runs from the buttock, down the back and side of the leg, and into the foot and toes), often because of a herniated disk.

LLM.text: Sciatica is radiating leg pain or sensory symptoms along a lumbosacral nerve-root distribution, commonly from disk herniation or spinal narrowing. through the buttock and down the posterior thigh to the foot. Most commonly caused by lumbar disc herniation compressing the nerve root (L4-L5 or L5-S1). Other causes: spinal stenosis, spondylolisthesis, piriformis syndrome, and epidural abscess.

Harvard.text: A diagnostic technique based on the detection of energy emitted by radioactive substances injected into the body; also called radionuclide scanning.

LLM.text: Nuclear medicine imaging in which a radiotracer is administered and its distribution is recorded to evaluate the structure or function of an organ.

Harvard.text: The perception of flashing lights or lines that sometimes occurs during the aura of a migraine headache.

LLM.text: Perceived flashes or zigzag lines, often occurring during a migraine aura.

Harvard.text: The white of the eye; a tough, protective coating of collagen and elastic tissue that, with the cornea, makes up the outer layer of the eyeball.

LLM.text: The sclera is the tough white outer coat of the eye that protects the globe and provides attachment for eye muscles.

Harvard.text: A surgical technique that indents the sclera and choroid to reattach the retina.

LLM.text: A retinal-detachment repair procedure in which a silicone band or buckle is placed around the outside of the eye to support the retinal break and reduce traction.

Harvard.text: An autoimmune disease in which the skin thickens and hardens; sometimes other parts of the body are affected, and joint pain may result.

LLM.text: Scleroderma is an autoimmune connective-tissue disease causing skin thickening and variable fibrosis or vascular injury in the gastrointestinal tract, lungs, kidneys, or heart.

Harvard.text: An abnormal lateral, or sideways, curvature of the spine.

LLM.text: Scoliosis is a three-dimensional sideways curvature and rotation of the spine, which may be idiopathic, congenital, neuromuscular, or degenerative.

Harvard.text: A blank spot in the visual field that is sometimes evident during the aura of a migraine headache.

LLM.text: A focal area of diminished or absent vision within an otherwise intact visual field, classified by location and morphology.

Harvard.text: A disease caused by vitamin C deficiency, characterized by bruising, poor wound healing, bleeding of the gums, and loosened teeth.

LLM.text: Vitamin C deficiency causing impaired collagen formation, with bleeding gums, easy bruising, petechiae, poor wound healing, anemia, bone pain, and fatigue.

Harvard.text: Sadness and depression brought on by a lack of exposure to sunlight. Seasonal affective disorder usually appears in the fall or winter and subsides in the spring. sometimes referred to as SAD.

LLM.text: A specifier of recurrent major depressive episodes that occur at a specific time of year, most commonly winter (with remission in spring/summer). Symptoms: hypersomnia, hyperphagia with carbohydrate craving, weight gain, fatigue, and low energy.

Harvard.text: A gland that opens into a terminal hair follicle; it secretes sebum, the natural oily conditioner of hair.

LLM.text: A small gland in the skin that secretes sebum (oil) into hair follicles to lubricate and waterproof the skin and hair.

Harvard.text: A mild and common condition that is characterized by an itchy, flaky scalp and that may extend to the ears, face, and chest. Also known as dandruff.

LLM.text: A chronic inflammatory skin condition affecting sebum-rich areas: scalp, face (nasolabial folds, eyebrows), chest, and intertriginous areas. Presents with erythematous patches with greasy, yellowish scales. Dandruff is a mild form. More common and severe in Parkinson disease, HIV/AIDS, and Down syndrome.

Harvard.text: High blood pressure that has an identifiable, often correctable, cause such as kidney disease, hyperthyroidism, sleep apnea and other conditions.

LLM.text: High blood pressure caused by another medical condition or by a medication.

Harvard.text: Bone loss associated with an identifiable medical condition, treatment with certain drugs, or immobility.

LLM.text: Bone loss caused by another illness, medication, or prolonged immobility.

Harvard.text: The release of chemical substances produced by the body; or the substance that is produced.

LLM.text: Active movement of a substance from cells into a body fluid, lumen, or external environment. In toxicokinetics, renal tubular or biliary secretion can contribute to elimination of a toxin or metabolite.

Harvard.text: Shorthand for erythrocyte sedimentation rate—a test involving red blood cells used to check for different infections, inflammations, and cancers.

LLM.text: A blood test measuring how quickly red blood cells settle, used as a nonspecific marker of inflammation.

Harvard.text: A drug or a procedure that has a calming effect and relieves anxiety and tension.

LLM.text: A medication that reduces central nervous system activity, producing calming effects, drowsiness, and sleep at higher doses. Sedatives are used for anxiety, procedural sedation, insomnia, and as adjuncts in anesthesia.

Harvard.text: A sudden, involuntary contraction of muscles that results in rhythmic contortions of the body, often accompanied by a loss of consciousness. Also called a convulsion.

LLM.text: A transient occurrence of signs and/or symptoms due to abnormal, excessive, or synchronous neuronal activity in the brain. Provoked seizures have an identifiable acute cause (fever, electrolyte disturbance, drug toxicity, withdrawal). Unprovoked seizures occur without an acute trigger.

Harvard.text: Chemically synthesized drugs that mimic estrogen in some tissues but act to block estrogen’s effects in others.

LLM.text: Medicines that activate estrogen receptors in some tissues and block them in others.

Harvard.text: Antidepressants that block the reuptake of serotonin into the neurons that released it, leaving more serotonin available to nerve cell receptors. Commonly used to treat depression and other mood disorders.

LLM.text: Antidepressants that increase serotonin signaling by reducing its reuptake into nerve cells.

Harvard.text: A group of people who meet to discuss and offer assistance to one another with the goal of providing social support for changing troubling behavior patterns.

LLM.text: A peer group in which members support one another while changing a harmful behavior or coping with a problem.

Harvard.text: Structures surrounding the prostate gland involved in storing secretions made by the gland.

LLM.text: Glands behind the bladder that produce much of the fluid in semen.

Harvard.text: Gradual loss of body functions caused by the biological aging process, which increases risk of disease, disability, and death.

LLM.text: Gradual biological decline associated with aging.

Harvard.text: Diagnosis once given to people over 65 with dementia.

LLM.text: An outdated term formerly used for dementia in older adults.

Harvard.text: A set of structured exercises that sex therapists use to help couples focus on the sensual aspects of physical contact without pressure to achieve orgasm.

LLM.text: Structured touch exercises used in sex therapy to reduce performance pressure and improve intimacy.

Harvard.text: Permanent hearing loss caused by damage to the cochlea, hair cells, or auditory nerve.

LLM.text: Hearing loss from pathology of the cochlea or auditory (eighth cranial) nerve, characterized on pure-tone audiometry by elevated bone conduction thresholds and no air-bone gap.

Harvard.text: The destruction or infection of tissues by disease-causing organisms, usually accompanied by a fever.

LLM.text: Sepsis is life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated response to infection, with possible shock, respiratory failure, kidney injury, coagulation abnormalities, or altered consciousness. Sepsis-3 definition: infection + SOFA score increase >= 2. Septic shock: sepsis with vasopressor requirement and lactate >2 mmol/L.

Harvard.text: A condition in which disease-causing organisms have spread to the bloodstream from an infection elsewhere in the body. Also known as blood poisoning.

LLM.text: Septicemia is an older term for serious bloodstream infection; modern assessment distinguishes bacteremia from sepsis, which is life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by infection.

Harvard.text: A wall or other structure that divides one cavity from another. For example, in the heart the muscular septum separates the right side of the heart from the left side.

LLM.text: A wall or partition separating two spaces, such as the nasal septum between the nasal cavities or the cardiac septum between heart chambers.

Harvard.text: Abbreviation for selective estrogen receptor modulators, chemically synthesized drugs that mimic estrogen in some tissues but act to block estrogen’s effects in others.

LLM.text: Selective estrogen receptor modulators that have estrogen-like effects in some tissues and blocking effects in others.

Harvard.text: A pocket of lymphatic fluid that builds up at an incision after surgery.

LLM.text: A pocket of clear fluid that develops near a surgical incision or injured tissue.

Harvard.text: A neurotransmitter that helps regulate sleep and appetite, mediate moods, and inhibit pain.

LLM.text: A neurotransmitter involved in mood, sleep, appetite, and pain regulation.

Harvard.text: Antidepressants that slow the reuptake of both serotonin and norepinephrine into the neurons that released these substances, leaving more serotonin and norepinephrine available to nerve cell receptors. Commonly used to treat depression and other mood disorders.

LLM.text: Antidepressants that block the reuptake of both serotonin and norepinephrine. They include venlafaxine, duloxetine, desvenlafaxine, and levomilnacipran. SNRIs are used for major depressive disorder, generalized anxiety disorder, diabetic neuropathy, fibromyalgia, and chronic pain.

Harvard.text: A painful inflammation in and around two small bones known as sesamoids, located beneath the base of the big toe, at the ball of the foot.

LLM.text: Inflammation and pain around a small sesamoid bone, often beneath the big toe.

Harvard.text: A specific number of repetitions of an exercise done as a group.

LLM.text: A group of consecutive repetitions of an exercise.

Harvard.text: A problem with any area of a person’s sexual response that causes distress.

LLM.text: Persistent difficulty in sexual activity causing distress. In women: low sexual desire (hypoactive), arousal disorder, orgasmic disorder (anorgasmia), and genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder (dyspareunia, vaginismus). In men, it may involve erectile dysfunction, delayed or premature ejaculation, or reduced sexual desire. Causes include medical and psychological conditions, relationship factors, and adverse effects of substances or medicines.

Harvard.text: A serious medical condition in which there too little blood flows to the outer portions of the body, resulting in cold, sweaty skin; a weak pulse; irregular breathing; and dilated pupils. Shock can be caused by a loss of blood, severe heart problems, severe infections, allergic reactions, or drug overdoses.

LLM.text: Shock is inadequate tissue perfusion and oxygen delivery, caused by hypovolemia, pump failure, obstruction, or abnormal vascular tone and leading to cellular and organ injury. failure, and severe loss of vascular tone.

Harvard.text: Information the brain stores temporarily, from milliseconds to minutes.

LLM.text: The temporary storage and use of information over seconds to minutes.

Harvard.text: A device inserted into the body to redirect the flow of blood or other fluid from one area to another.

LLM.text: Tube diverting fluid. Types: ventriculoperitoneal (CSF), ventriculoatrial, lumboperitoneal, ventriculopleural. Indications: hydrocephalus. Complications: obstruction, infection, overdrainage, migration. Valves regulate pressure.

Harvard.text: An unwanted, and sometimes dangerous, reaction caused by medication or other treatment.

LLM.text: An unintended pharmacological effect of a drug occurring at therapeutic doses, usually predictable from the drug's mechanism of action (a Type A reaction).

Harvard.text: Section of the colon leading to the rectum that makes an S-shaped curve.

LLM.text: S-shaped segment from descending colon to rectum in the left iliac fossa, approximately 40-50 cm, with complete mesentery (intraperitoneal, mobile). Most common diverticular disease site from narrow lumen and high pressure. Common volvulus site, particularly in elderly/institutionalized patients. Second most common colorectal cancer site.

Harvard.text: Internal examination of the rectum and sigmoid colon using a flexible viewing tube inserted through the anus.

LLM.text: Endoscopic examination of the rectum and lower colon using a flexible or rigid sigmoidoscope. It can identify inflammation, bleeding, polyps, or tumors and may allow biopsy or treatment.

Harvard.text: Character strengths such as curiosity, integrity, and modesty that people identify with, appreciate having, and enjoy using.

LLM.text: Personal character strengths that a person values and naturally uses.

Harvard.text: The active ingredient in Viagra. It blocks the breakdown of cyclic guanosine monophosphate, a chemical necessary for an erection.

LLM.text: The citrate salt of sildenafil, a phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor used for erectile dysfunction and pulmonary arterial hypertension.

Harvard.text: Heart attack that occurs without pain or symptoms; occurs most commonly in the elderly or in people with diabetes.

LLM.text: A myocardial infarction without recognized pain or typical warning symptoms.

Harvard.text: Shortage of oxygen delivery to the heart muscle that causes no symptoms.

LLM.text: Inadequate blood flow to heart muscle without noticeable symptoms.

Harvard.text: A test using gamma rays to measure bone density, usually in the forearm.

LLM.text: An older technique using gamma rays to measure bone density, usually in an arm or peripheral bone.

Harvard.text: The natural pacemaker of the heart. Located in the right atrium, the sinoatrial node, sometimes called the sinus node, initiates the heart's electrical activity.

LLM.text: The heart's natural pacemaker, located at the junction of the superior vena cava and right atrium. It consists of specialized cells that spontaneously depolarize at a rate of 60-100 beats per minute, setting the normal sinus rhythm.

common_names: sinus node, initiates the heart's electrical activity

Harvard.text: A specialized group of heart cells in the right atrium that generate the electrical impulses that cause the heart muscle to contract. Also called the heart's natural pacemaker.

LLM.text: The heart’s natural pacemaker, located in the right atrium.

Harvard.text: The heart's normal rate and rhythm.

LLM.text: The normal heart rhythm generated by electrical impulses from the sinoatrial node.

Harvard.text: Muscles attached to bones throughout the body that allow voluntary movement to occur.

LLM.text: Muscles attached to bones that produce voluntary movement.

Harvard.text: Any of several approaches to improve skin texture, tone, wrinkle appearance, and discolorations by promoting new collagen and epidermal growth. Chemical peels, dermabrasion, microdermabrasion, and laser procedures are skin-resurfacing techniques.

LLM.text: Procedures that improve skin texture or pigmentation by removing or remodeling superficial skin layers.

Harvard.text: Temporary pause in breathing during sleep, lasting at least 10 seconds and associated with a fall in blood oxygen or arousal from sleep. Obstructive sleep apnea is caused by an obstruction in the airway blocking air flow; central sleep apnea occurs when the brain temporarily stops sending signals to the muscles that control breathing.

LLM.text: Repeated pauses or reductions in breathing during sleep. It may be obstructive, central, or mixed and can disturb sleep and oxygenation.

Harvard.text: The pattern made when sleep stages are charted on a hypnogram.

LLM.text: The pattern and organization of sleep stages across a sleep period.

Harvard.text: A feeling of paralysis that may occur during the transition between wakefulness and sleep if the REM sleep stage begins before a person is fully asleep; classically associated with narcolepsy.

LLM.text: Temporary inability to move or speak when falling asleep or waking, while awareness is partly or fully preserved. Episodes usually last seconds to minutes and may include frightening hallucinations. Recurrent episodes can be associated with sleep deprivation, irregular sleep, narcolepsy, or other sleep disorders.

Harvard.text: On an electroencephalogram (EEG), brief rhythmic bursts of activity that appear during stage 2 sleep.

LLM.text: Brief bursts of rhythmic brain activity during stage 2 non-REM sleep.

Harvard.text: A slender piece of material surgically inserted under the urethra or bladder neck to provide support and improve continence.

LLM.text: A supportive device or surgically placed strip used to support an injured limb or urinary structures.

Harvard.text: See herniated disk.

LLM.text: A spinal disk that bulges or herniates through a tear in its outer layer.

Harvard.text: Forward displacement of a vertebra in relation to the vertebra immediately below; also called spondylolisthesis.

LLM.text: Forward displacement of one vertebra relative to the one below it.

Harvard.text: An instrument that magnifies internal structures of the eye with the aid of a thin beam of light. Also called a biomicroscope.

LLM.text: An instrument using magnification and a narrow beam of light to examine the eye.

Harvard.text: One of two main types of skeletal muscle fibers. Slow-twitch fibers are recruited most heavily for endurance (aerobic) exercises. See also fast-twitch fiber.

LLM.text: A muscle fiber adapted for sustained, aerobic activity and fatigue resistance.

Harvard.text: Sleep stages 3 and 4; during slow-wave sleep the brain becomes less responsive to external stimuli.

LLM.text: Deep non-REM sleep characterized by slow brain waves and reduced responsiveness.

Harvard.text: A section of the digestive system that includes the duodenum, jejunum, and ileum and plays the major role in absorbing nutrients for the body.

LLM.text: Longest GI segment (approximately 6 meters) from pylorus to ileocecal valve. Primary nutrient digestion and absorption site. Three segments: duodenum (25 cm, chyme/bile/pancreatic enzymes), jejunum (2.5 m, prominent folds/villi for absorption), ileum (3.5 m, Peyer's patches for immunity).

Harvard.text: An acronym for an approach to setting goals for behavioral change: set a very Specific goal; find a way to Measure progress; make sure it’s Achievable; make sure it’s Realistic; and set Time commitments.

LLM.text: A goal-setting framework emphasizing specific, measurable, achievable, realistic, and time-bound goals.

Harvard.text: The conventional eye chart used to test vision with lines of block letters in progressively smaller sizes.

LLM.text: An eye chart used to measure distance visual acuity by testing the smallest line of letters a person can identify at a standard distance.

Harvard.text: Bodily symptoms that have no clear physical cause or are out of proportion to a given ailment, and may stem from psychological causes.

LLM.text: Expression of psychological distress through physical symptoms.

Harvard.text: Sleepwalking.

LLM.text: Sleepwalking; a parasomnia involving complex behaviors that arise during partial arousal from non-rapid-eye-movement sleep.

Harvard.text: Talking in one’s sleep.

LLM.text: Talking during sleep.

Harvard.text: A crystalline sugar alcohol used as a sweetening agent.

LLM.text: A sugar alcohol used as a sweetener and, in larger amounts, as an osmotic laxative.

Harvard.text: A hollow chamber into which inhaled medicines can be squirted before inhalation. Spacers are used with metered-dose inhalers to help deliver medicine effectively to the bronchial tubes and to reduce the amount of medicine left behind on the tongue and throat.

LLM.text: A chamber used with a metered-dose inhaler to improve delivery of medicine to the lungs.

Harvard.text: An involuntary muscle contraction.

LLM.text: A sudden, involuntary, sustained or repetitive contraction of a muscle or group of muscles.

Harvard.text: A ring of muscle that surrounds an opening and can be contracted to close the opening. For example, the muscles found at the anus and the opening of the bladder are sphincters.

LLM.text: A ring-shaped muscle that regulates an opening by contracting and relaxing.

Harvard.text: A device for measuring blood pressure.

LLM.text: An instrument used to measure arterial blood pressure, typically consisting of an inflatable cuff and a pressure-measuring system. Manual devices use Korotkoff sounds, while automated devices generally use oscillometric sensing. Correct cuff size and technique are essential for reliable measurements.

Harvard.text: A congenital defect in which part of the spinal column fails to develop completely, leaving part of the spinal cord exposed.

LLM.text: A neural tube defect: incomplete closure of the neural tube (days 22-28), causing spinal cord/meningeal malformation.

Harvard.text: A procedure to attach two or more vertebrae with a bone graft in order to eliminate motion and relieve pain.

LLM.text: Surgical union of two or more vertebrae using bone graft or bone graft substitutes with instrumentation (rods, screws, cages). Approaches: posterior (posterolateral fusion, transforaminal lumbar interbody fusion TLIF), anterior (anterior lumbar interbody fusion ALIF), and lateral (extreme lateral interbody fusion XLIF).

Harvard.text: A narrowing of the spinal canal, which can result in compression of nerve roots.

LLM.text: Narrowing of the spinal canal causing compression of the spinal cord or nerve roots. Lumbar stenosis (most common): neurogenic claudication (leg pain/weakness with walking, relieved by sitting/leaning forward), often bilateral.

Harvard.text: Use of a hollow needle to withdraw fluid from the lower part of the spinal canal for testing. Also called a lumbar puncture.

LLM.text: A procedure that withdraws cerebrospinal fluid from the lower spinal canal for testing.

Harvard.text: The lever-like backward projection extending off each vertebra, to which muscles and ligaments are attached.

LLM.text: The posterior bony projection of a vertebra to which muscles and ligaments attach.

Harvard.text: A device that measures airway obstruction, used to diagnose asthma and determine the severity of the condition.

LLM.text: An instrument that measures the volume and flow of air inhaled and exhaled during pulmonary function testing.

Harvard.text: A simple, painless breathing test performed in a physician’s office or pulmonary function laboratory that measures how fast air can be forced from the lungs and the total amount of air that can be emptied from the lungs.

LLM.text: Most common PFT measuring air volume and flow during forced breathing. Key measurements: FVC, FEV1, FEV1/FVC ratio. Used to diagnose and classify obstructive and restrictive diseases.

Harvard.text: A painful spasm in the left upper abdomen below the rib cage, produced by areas of trapped gas in the colon.

LLM.text: Left-upper-abdominal pain caused by gas trapped at the bend between the transverse and descending colon.

Harvard.text: Forward displacement of a vertebra in relation to the vertebra immediately below.

LLM.text: Spondylolisthesis is forward or backward displacement of one vertebra relative to another, potentially causing back pain, nerve compression, or spinal instability.

Harvard.text: A general term for degeneration of the spine that causes narrowing of the spinal canal and the small openings (intervertebral foramina) through which spinal nerves exit the canal.

LLM.text: Degenerative changes of the spine, including disc degeneration and bony overgrowth, commonly associated with aging.

Harvard.text: Porous bone, also called trabecular bone, often found at the center of long bones.

LLM.text: Porous trabecular bone found inside many bones, especially near joints.

common_names: trabecular bone, often found at the center of long bones

Harvard.text: A stretched or torn ligament.

LLM.text: An injury to a ligament (connective tissue connecting bone to bone) caused by excessive stretching or tearing. Grading: Grade I (mild stretching, microscopic tears), Grade II (partial tear with laxity), Grade III (complete tear with instability).

Harvard.text: A mixture of saliva and mucus that is coughed up from the respiratory tract. Sputum may be examined in a laboratory for signs of disease.

LLM.text: Mucus or phlegm produced in the lower airways and expelled by coughing. Its amount, color, odor, or blood content may provide clues to infection, inflammation, or bleeding, but appearance alone does not establish a diagnosis.

Harvard.text: Flat, scaly epithelial cell.

LLM.text: A thin, flat epithelial cell.

Harvard.text: Abbreviation for selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, antidepressants that block the reuptake of serotonin into the neurons that released it, leaving more serotonin available to nerve cell receptors. Commonly used to treat depression and other mood disorders.

LLM.text: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors are a class of antidepressant drugs that selectively inhibit the reuptake of serotonin from the synaptic cleft into the presynaptic neuron by blocking the serotonin transporter, increasing serotonergic neurotransmission.

Harvard.text: Angina pectoris (chest pain with exertion or stress) that is well-controlled with medicines and lifestyle changes.

LLM.text: Predictable exertional chest pain caused by temporary inadequate coronary blood flow.

Harvard.text: Narrowings in the heart arteries that cause angina pectoris in a predictable and stable pattern over time (for example, after walking a certain distance).

LLM.text: Coronary artery narrowing causing a consistent, predictable pattern of angina.

Harvard.text: A model for how people make changes in their lives. According to this model, changes in behavior are made gradually and in relatively distinct stages.

LLM.text: A model describing gradual phases people pass through while changing behavior.

Harvard.text: The process of determining how far cancer has progressed. Staging is often used to determine the best course of treatment.

LLM.text: Assessment of the extent of cancer, including the size of the primary tumor, lymph-node involvement, and distant metastases.

Harvard.text: An herbal product in which what is believed to be the active ingredient meets an established standard of strength.

LLM.text: An herbal extract adjusted to contain a specified amount of a selected constituent.

Harvard.text: Cholesterol-lowering medications that interfere with the enzyme 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-coenzyme A reductase; also known as HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors. Statins work by changing the way the liver processes lipids.

LLM.text: Cholesterol-lowering medicines that inhibit HMG-CoA reductase.

Harvard.text: An abnormal narrowing of a passageway, such as a blood vessel, or other type of opening in the body.

LLM.text: Narrowing of vessel lumen. Causes: atherosclerosis, thrombosis, dissection, external compression. Symptoms depend on location and severity. Treatment: medical, angioplasty, stenting, bypass.

Harvard.text: A wire mesh device inserted into an artery to prop it open once a blockage has been cleared by angioplasty.

LLM.text: A stent is a tube or scaffold placed inside a narrowed or obstructed vessel, duct, or other passage to keep it open.

Harvard.text: 1) A surgical procedure or other method that results in a person being unable to reproduce. 2) The process by which materials are thoroughly cleaned of all organisms that could cause disease or infection.

LLM.text: A process eliminating all microbial life including spores, achieving a sterility assurance level of at least $10^-6$.

Harvard.text: Another term for corticosteroids—steroid medications made to mimic hormones produced naturally by the adrenal glands. They are used to treat a wide range of health problems.

LLM.text: Hormone-like medicines or compounds with a four-ring chemical structure; corticosteroids are used to reduce inflammation.

Harvard.text: A substance that speeds up chemical reactions inside cells and provides a boost of energy. Examples include caffeine and amphetamine.

LLM.text: A substance that increases activity of the central nervous system or other body systems.

Harvard.text: The sac-like organ of the digestive system between the esophagus and the duodenum which breaks down food and moves it along to the small intestine to be digested.

LLM.text: J-shaped muscular organ in the left upper quadrant, connecting esophagus to duodenum. Regions: cardia, fundus, body, antrum, pylorus. Functions: food storage, mechanical churning, chemical digestion (pepsin, HCl), intrinsic factor secretion (B12 absorption). Mucosa has rugae (folds) allowing expansion.

Harvard.text: A stretched or torn muscle or tendon, usually caused by accident, misuse, or overuse.

LLM.text: An injury to a muscle or tendon (connective tissue connecting muscle to bone) caused by excessive stretching, contraction, or overload. Grading: Grade I (mild stretching with few muscle fibers torn), Grade II (moderate partial tear), Grade III (complete muscle/tendon rupture).

Harvard.text: The most superficial layer of the epidermis.

LLM.text: The outermost layer of the epidermis, composed mainly of dead keratinized cells.

Harvard.text: The ability of muscles to exert force.

LLM.text: The ability of a muscle or muscle group to exert force.

Harvard.text: Popular term for exercises that harness resistance supplied by body weight, free weights such as dumbbells or weighted cuffs, resistance bands, or specialized machines; also known as resistance training or weight training.

LLM.text: Exercise using resistance to increase muscle strength and capacity.

Harvard.text: A thrombolytic (clot-dissolving) agent designed to dissolve the blood clots that block an artery during a heart attack or stroke.

LLM.text: A thrombolytic agent that forms a plasminogen activator complex, converting plasminogen to plasmin and lysing fibrin clots. Used for STEMI, massive pulmonary embolism, and deep vein thrombosis (largely replaced by tissue plasminogen activator, which is more fibrin-specific and less antigenic).

Harvard.text: An innate survival response in which certain hormones are released, increasing blood flow to the brain or heart. The stress response leads to an energy surge, enabling a person to flee dangerous situations. Ongoing stress, however, can sap energy and damage health.

LLM.text: A physiological and psychological response to perceived threats or demands that activates the sympathetic nervous system and the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis.

Harvard.text: A hairline crack in a bone that usually occurs from overuse; left untreated, this may lead to displacement of the bones.

LLM.text: A bone injury caused by repetitive submaximal loading that exceeds the rate of remodeling and repair. It often presents with gradually increasing, localized activity-related pain and may progress to a complete fracture if loading continues.

Harvard.text: Physiological changes, such as quickened breathing and heartbeat and increased blood pressure, brought on by stress hormones released in response to a real or perceived threat to safety. Also called the fight-or-flight response.

LLM.text: Physiological changes that prepare the body to respond to a perceived threat.

Harvard.text: A diagnostic test in which cardiovascular measurements such as heart rate, blood pressure, and electrical activity are recorded while the heart is being stressed (usually by having the person exercise on a treadmill or bicycle).

LLM.text: A cardiovascular test that records symptoms, heart rhythm, and other responses while the heart is stressed by exercise or medication; it helps evaluate ischemia and exercise capacity.

Harvard.text: Stressful events or circumstances that may be real or perceived threats to equilibrium and well-being.

LLM.text: Events, conditions, or circumstances that trigger a stress response.

Harvard.text: A line, streak, or band, such as the stretch marks that occur in pregnancy.

LLM.text: A line, streak, or band in tissue, such as a stretch mark.

Harvard.text: The abnormal narrowing of a hollow passage in the body, such as the esophagus or the urethra.

LLM.text: Abnormal narrowing of a hollow body passage.

Harvard.text: Blockage or rupture of a blood vessel supplying the brain; often leads to impaired brain function or death.

LLM.text: Stroke is sudden neurologic dysfunction from interrupted cerebral blood flow or bleeding, causing focal deficits and requiring urgent evaluation for reperfusion or hemorrhage management. neuronal death and neurological deficits.

Harvard.text: A state of lethargy and unresponsiveness.

LLM.text: A state of reduced consciousness in which the patient is unresponsive to most environmental stimuli but can be temporarily aroused by vigorous, repeated stimulation (painful stimuli, loud shouting).

Harvard.text: A disease or condition that progresses slower than an acute condition but faster than a chronic condition.

LLM.text: Between acute and chronic. Examples: subacute thyroiditis.

Harvard.text: A painful version of thyroid inflammation caused by viral infection. Symptoms are flu-like and include fever, muscle aches and pains, and a painful, swollen thyroid gland. Also known as de Quervain’s thyroiditis.

LLM.text: Inflammatory condition of the thyroid most likely viral in etiology presenting with painful tender thyroid enlargement, fever, and malaise. Associated with elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein.

Harvard.text: A hemorrhagic stroke that occurs when a blood vessel on the surface of the brain bursts and bleeds into the space between the brain and the skull; usually caused by an aneurysm or other blood vessel malformation.

LLM.text: Bleeding into the subarachnoid space, the area between the arachnoid membrane and the pia mater surrounding the brain, most commonly caused by rupture of a cerebral (berry) aneurysm.

Harvard.text: Space inside the brain where cerebrospinal fluid circulates.

LLM.text: The space between the arachnoid and pia mater containing cerebrospinal fluid.

Harvard.text: Beneath the skin.

LLM.text: Subcutaneous means beneath the skin; injections by this route deliver medicine into the fatty tissue between skin and muscle.

Harvard.text: Deepest layer of skin, which consists of connective tissue and fat.

LLM.text: Subcutaneous tissue (hypodermis, superficial fascia) lies beneath the dermis and connects skin to underlying structures. It contains adipose tissue (fat), blood vessels, nerves, and the superficial muscular aponeurotic system (SMAS). Subcutaneous fat provides insulation, cushioning, and energy storage.

Harvard.text: A blood clot in the brain between the cerebral cortex and the dura.

LLM.text: A collection of blood between the dura mater and the arachnoid mater, caused by tearing of bridging veins that traverse the subdural space.

Harvard.text: Heart-muscle cells on the inside of the heart chambers; these cells are highly susceptible to damage from blockages of the major coronary arteries.

LLM.text: Heart-muscle cells in the inner layer of the myocardium, which are especially vulnerable to reduced blood flow.

Harvard.text: Continued substance use despite substance-related social or interpersonal problems.

LLM.text: An older, nonspecific term for harmful or problematic substance use. Current clinical language generally uses substance-use disorder.

Harvard.text: A condition characterized by excessive and often compulsive substance use, impaired control over substance use, continued use of substances despite adverse consequences, and withdrawal symptoms that emerge when the substance use is discontinued.

LLM.text: A state in which repeated substance use produces physiologic adaptation, so that reducing or stopping the substance may cause withdrawal. It is distinct from, but may occur with, substance-use disorder.

Harvard.text: Vaccines using only part of a microbe—the antigens—to elicit an immune response; these vaccines tend to cause fewer adverse reactions than vaccines which contain the whole microbe.

LLM.text: Vaccines containing selected antigenic components of a microorganism rather than the whole organism; they cannot cause infection from replication of the pathogen.

Harvard.text: The V-shaped hollow at the margin of the tooth and gum.

LLM.text: A sulcus is a groove or furrow, such as a groove on the brain surface or a groove between structures in an organ.

Harvard.text: A class of medications that works by stimulating the pancreas to produce more insulin.

LLM.text: Oral antidiabetic agents that stimulate insulin secretion from pancreatic beta cells by blocking ATP-sensitive potassium channels on the beta cell membrane. This causes membrane depolarization, opening of voltage-gated calcium channels, calcium influx, and exocytosis of insulin-containing granules.

Harvard.text: Confusion or disorientation beginning at the end of the day and continuing into the night; often occurs in people with Alzheimer's disease or vascular dementia.

LLM.text: Late-day or evening worsening of confusion, agitation, wandering, or behavioral symptoms in some people with dementia or delirium, influenced by fatigue, light, routines, and unmet needs.

Harvard.text: The major vein that carries deoxygenated blood from the upper body to the heart.

LLM.text: Formed by brachiocephalic vein junction at the first right costal cartilage, returning upper body deoxygenated blood to the right atrium. Approximately 7 cm, valveless. Related to right lung/pleura, right phrenic nerve, and azygos vein.

Harvard.text: A solid form of medication that is inserted in the rectum or vagina and absorbed into the bloodstream.

LLM.text: A solid, single-dose dosage form designed to be inserted into a body orifice (rectum, vagina, or urethra) where it melts, softens, or dissolves, releasing the active pharmaceutical ingredient for local or systemic effects.

Harvard.text: A small group of nerve cells located in the hypothalamus that controls the sleep/wake cycle.

LLM.text: A paired group of neurons in the anterior hypothalamus that functions as the principal circadian clock and coordinates daily rhythms using light-related signals from the retina.

Harvard.text: An abnormally fast heartbeat originating in heart tissue above the ventricles.

LLM.text: A rapid rhythm (150-250 bpm) originating above the ventricles, characterized by narrow QRS complexes. Most common forms are AV nodal reentrant tachycardia (AVNRT) and AV reentrant tachycardia (AVRT). Episodes are typically paroxysmal with sudden onset and offset. Vagal maneuvers and adenosine are diagnostic and therapeutic.

Harvard.text: The process of sewing tissues together after surgery; or the stitch itself.

LLM.text: A thread or strand of material used to approximate tissues (bring wound edges together) and hold them in place until healing occurs.

Harvard.text: An offshoot of the autonomic nervous system; it sends signals to prepare the body for action when stress hormones are released in response to perceived or real dangers.

LLM.text: The division of the autonomic nervous system responsible for the 'fight or flight' response, preparing the body for intense physical activity or stress. Sympathetic preganglionic neurons originate in the intermediolateral column of the spinal cord gray matter (T1--L2), making it the thoracolumbar system.

Harvard.text: Exercise test, usually using a treadmill or bicycle, that increases in difficulty at set stages and is stopped when the person develops chest pain, breathlessness, or extreme fatigue.

LLM.text: An exercise stress test continued until symptoms, physiologic limits, diagnostic endpoints, or safety concerns require stopping, while cardiovascular responses are monitored.

Harvard.text: The junction between two neurons, across which chemical neurotransmitters carry messages.

LLM.text: The specialized junction between a neuron and another neuron (or effector cell—muscle, gland) where information is transmitted from one cell to another.

Harvard.text: Fainting or loss of consciousness caused by a temporary shortage of oxygen in the brain.

LLM.text: A transient loss of consciousness caused by temporary global cerebral hypoperfusion. See Fainting.

Harvard.text: Surgical removal of the synovial membrane that lines the joints.

LLM.text: synovectomy is used in relation to synovectomy during assessment, diagnosis, treatment, monitoring, or patient support.

Harvard.text: A thick liquid that lubricates the joints and tendons.

LLM.text: A viscous fluid within a synovial joint that lubricates articular surfaces and helps nourish cartilage.

Harvard.text: The most mobile type of joint; found in the shoulders, wrists, fingers, hips, etc.

LLM.text: A freely movable joint in which the articulating bones are separated by a fluid-filled joint cavity enclosed by a capsule.

Harvard.text: Inflammation of the synovium.

LLM.text: Inflammation of the synovial membrane lining a joint, causing swelling, pain, warmth, and joint effusion. Causes: inflammatory arthritis (RA, psoriatic, gout, reactive, septic), autoimmune (SLE), and trauma/overuse.

Harvard.text: A thin membrane that lines joint capsules and produces synovial fluid.

LLM.text: The inner layer of the joint capsule in synovial joints, composed of synovial lining cells (type A macrophage-like, type B fibroblast-like) on a vascularized connective tissue base. Produces synovial fluid (hyaluronic acid, lubricin, proteinases) for lubrication and chondrocyte nutrition.

Harvard.text: Pertaining to something that affects the whole body rather than separate organs or parts.

LLM.text: Systemic means involving the whole body or multiple organ systems rather than being limited to one local site.

Harvard.text: A connective tissue disease that can affect internal organs, nervous system, skin, and joints.

LLM.text: Multisystem autoimmune disease, more common in women. Features: malar rash, photosensitivity, oral ulcers, arthritis, serositis, renal disorder, neurologic disorder, hematologic disorder, immunologic disorder. Diagnosis: ANA positive plus clinical/immunologic criteria.
The absence of detectable hepatitis C virus RNA in the blood 12 or more weeks after completing antiviral treatment, indicating virologic cure. Reinfection remains possible.

Harvard.text: The brief period during which the heart contracts during a normal heartbeat, pumping blood into the aorta and the pulmonary artery.

LLM.text: The phase of the cardiac cycle during which the ventricles contract and eject blood into the pulmonary artery and aorta.

Harvard.text: The first or top number in a blood pressure reading; a measure of the pressure blood exerts against arterial walls when the heart contracts.

LLM.text: The highest arterial pressure during ventricular contraction, reported as the upper number of a blood-pressure measurement.

Harvard.text: The inability of the heart to pump blood efficiently due to weakening and enlargement of the ventricles. Systolic heart failure is usually caused by coronary artery disease, high blood pressure, and valvular heart disease.

LLM.text: Heart failure with reduced ability of the left ventricle to contract and eject blood, commonly reflected by a reduced ejection fraction.

Harvard.text: Abbreviation for T lymphocyte, a type of white blood cell that is produced in the bone marrow and is part of the body’s immune system.

LLM.text: An anatomical structure, tissue, or physiologic process with the location or function indicated by the term; disease or injury changes its expected findings.

Harvard.text: A type of white blood cell that is produced in the bone marrow and is part of the body’s immune system. Also called a T cell.

LLM.text: A lymphocyte that develops in the thymus and mediates cellular immunity, including immune regulation, cytotoxicity, and help for antibody responses.

Harvard.text: An abnormally fast heartbeat, usually above 100 beats per minute.

LLM.text: A faster-than-expected heart rate that may be a normal response or a sign of disease. See Fast Heart Rate.

Harvard.text: A drug used by women to prevent breast cancer or its recurrence.

LLM.text: tamoxifen is a medicine or pharmacologic agent; its indication, dosing, contraindications, interactions, and adverse effects depend on the specific product and patient.

Harvard.text: A drug used to treat symptoms of an enlarged prostate gland. It relieves constriction of the urethra and improves urine flow by relaxing the smooth muscle tissues in the capsule that surrounds the prostate. Unlike other drugs in this class, tamsulosin does not decrease blood pressure.

LLM.text: tamsulosin is a medicine or pharmacologic agent; its indication, dosing, contraindications, interactions, and adverse effects depend on the specific product and patient.

Harvard.text: Also called neurofibrillary tangles—twisted strands of proteins that are found inside the dead or dying nerve cells of people with Alzheimer's disease.

LLM.text: Abnormal intracellular aggregates of hyperphosphorylated tau protein, also called neurofibrillary tangles, found in Alzheimer disease and some other tauopathies.

Harvard.text: Involuntary writhing movements of the arms, legs, and tongue caused by high doses of antipsychotic drugs over long periods of time.

LLM.text: Involuntary, repetitive, purposeless movements caused by prolonged use of antipsychotic medications, typically developing after months to years of exposure. Movements include choreoathetoid movements of the tongue, face, and extremities (lip smacking, tongue protrusion, grimacing, choreiform movements of limbs).

Harvard.text: An inherited condition in which two bones of the foot are fused together; can result in rigid flat feet.

LLM.text: An abnormal connection between two bones in the rear or middle foot, usually present from birth. It can cause a stiff, painful flatfoot, recurrent ankle sprains, and limited foot motion, often becoming more noticeable during adolescence.

Harvard.text: A hardened layer of plaque that builds up on teeth. Also called calculus.

LLM.text: Tartar, or dental calculus, is mineralized plaque firmly attached to teeth and capable of contributing to gingivitis, periodontitis, and bad breath.

Harvard.text: Also called cranial arteritis and giant cell arteritis—inflammation and damage to blood vessels supplying blood to the head and neck.

LLM.text: A vasculitic disorder affecting medium and large arteries, particularly the temporal artery, predominantly occurring in adults over 50 years of age.

common_names: cranial arteritis and giant cell arteritis&mdash

Harvard.text: One of the four major subdivisions of the two hemispheres of the brain’s cerebral cortex. The temporal lobe plays a role in hearing, long-term memory, and behavior.

LLM.text: One of the four major lobes of the cerebral hemisphere, located beneath the lateral fissure (Sylvian fissure) on the lateral surface of the brain, extending medially to the parahippocampal gyrus. The temporal lobe is involved in auditory processing, language comprehension, memory, and emotion.

Harvard.text: Inflammation of a tendon, usually caused by injury; may cause pain and restrict movement of the muscle attached to the tendon.

LLM.text: Tendinitis is painful inflammation or degeneration of a tendon, often from repetitive loading, causing localized tenderness and pain with movement.

Harvard.text: A cord of collagen fibers that connect a muscle to a bone.

LLM.text: Dense regular connective tissue connecting muscle to bone, composed primarily of type I collagen fibers arranged in parallel bundles. Transmits muscle force to bone to produce movement. Poor vascularity (slower healing). Enclosed in tendon sheath (synovial) at friction points.

Harvard.text: Alternative spelling of tendinitis—inflammation of a tendon, usually caused by injury; may cause pain and restrict movement of the muscle attached to the tendon.

LLM.text: Tendinopathy: inflammation or degeneration of a tendon from overuse, repetitive strain, or trauma, causing localized pain, swelling, and tenderness with activity. Common sites: rotator cuff (supraspinatus), lateral elbow (tennis elbow), medial elbow (golfer's elbow), Achilles, patellar (jumper's knee), biceps, and De Quervain.

Harvard.text: Swelling and inflammation of the protective sheath covering the tendons, which decreases the sheath’s production of synovial fluid.

LLM.text: Tenosynovitis is inflammation of the sheath surrounding a tendon, producing pain, swelling, and restricted gliding, commonly in the hand or wrist.

Harvard.text: A headache, usually mild or moderate in intensity, not accompanied by other symptoms; pain is usually felt throughout the head, across the forehead, or in the back of the head. Also known as a muscle-contraction headache.

LLM.text: The most common headache type, characterized by bilateral, pressing/tightening head pain of mild-moderate intensity (like a band around the head), lasting 30 min to days, without nausea or vomiting; photophobia or phonophobia may be present but not both.

Harvard.text: A drug used to treat symptoms of an enlarged prostate gland. It relieves constriction of the urethra and improves urine flow by relaxing the smooth muscle tissue in the capsule that surrounds the prostate.

LLM.text: terazosin is a medicine or pharmacologic agent; its indication, dosing, contraindications, interactions, and adverse effects depend on the specific product and patient.

Harvard.text: A male hormone that stimulates bone and muscle growth and sexual development in men; also produced in lesser amounts in women, promoting sex drive and muscle growth.

LLM.text: A steroid sex hormone produced mainly by the testes and, in smaller amounts, by the ovaries and adrenal glands. It supports reproductive development, muscle and bone maintenance, red-blood-cell production, libido, and other physiologic functions; levels vary with age, sex, time of day, illness, and medicines.

Harvard.text: A brain structure that relays sensory information to other parts of the brain; also plays a role in memory consolidation.

LLM.text: Bilateral ovoid gray matter structure forming the third ventricle's lateral walls, the brain's relay station for nearly all sensory (except olfaction), motor, and limbic information to the cortex. Numerous nuclei: VPL (spinothalamic, dorsal column), VPM (trigeminal), LGN (visual), MGN (auditory), VL/VA (motor).

Harvard.text: A pattern of brain waves on an electroencephalogram (EEG) characteristic of light, stage 1 sleep.

LLM.text: Electroencephalographic oscillations commonly defined as approximately 4–7 hertz, seen prominently during drowsiness and some sleep stages and also in certain waking states.

Harvard.text: A class of oral medication that improves sensitivity to insulin.

LLM.text: Insulin sensitizers activating peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors primarily in adipose tissue and skeletal muscle. Agents include pioglitazone and rosiglitazone. Mechanisms include enhanced insulin-mediated glucose uptake, altered adipokine secretion, and reduced hepatic glucose output.

Harvard.text: Pertaining to the chest.

LLM.text: Thoracic means relating to the chest, the thoracic spine, or structures within the thorax such as the heart and lungs.

Harvard.text: Breaking up a blood clot.

LLM.text: The dissolution of a blood clot using a medicine such as a fibrinolytic agent. It is used only in selected conditions because it can cause serious bleeding.

Harvard.text: Agents or medications that dissolve blood clots and restore blood flow through a blocked artery; used to treat myocardial infarction, ischemic stroke, and pulmonary embolism. Also called clot busters. Examples include tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) and streptokinase.

LLM.text: Medicines that activate fibrinolysis and dissolve an established blood clot; they are used selectively for time-critical conditions because they can cause serious bleeding.

Harvard.text: Formation of a blood clot (called a thrombus) in a blood vessel or chamber of the heart.

LLM.text: The formation of a blood clot within the cardiovascular system during life, potentially obstructing blood flow and causing tissue ischemia or infarction. Arterial thrombi typically form on ruptured atherosclerotic plaques, are composed primarily of platelets and fibrin, and appear pale and grossly attached to the vessel wall.

Harvard.text: A blood clot that forms inside a blood vessel or chamber of the heart.

LLM.text: A blood clot that forms within a blood vessel or heart and remains attached at its site of formation, potentially obstructing blood flow or embolizing.

Harvard.text: A sudden, excruciating headache that may be the result of bleeding in the head.

LLM.text: A sudden, severe headache that reaches maximum intensity within seconds to minutes; it is a medical emergency until dangerous causes such as subarachnoid hemorrhage are excluded.

Harvard.text: A specialized organ of the immune system located in the upper-middle chest where T cells mature.

LLM.text: Primary lymphoid organ in the anterior mediastinum, largest in childhood, involutes with age. Site of T-cell maturation (thymopoiesis): thymocytes undergo positive and negative selection to produce self-tolerant, MHC-restricted T cells. Epithelial cells produce thymic hormones (thymosin, thymopoietin).

Harvard.text: A two-lobed gland located in the front of the neck below the larynx (voice box). It secretes hormones that help regulate the body's metabolism and calcium balance.

LLM.text: An endocrine gland located in the anterior neck, consisting of two lobes (right and left) connected by an isthmus, lying anterior to the trachea between the cricoid cartilage and the suprasternal notch.

Harvard.text: Two iodine-containing hormones called thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3). They help regulate the body's metabolism and calcium balance.

LLM.text: T3 and T4. Increase basal metabolic rate. Required for normal development.

Harvard.text: A surgical procedure to remove all or part of the thyroid.

LLM.text: thyroidectomy is used in relation to thyroidectomy during assessment, diagnosis, treatment, monitoring, or patient support.

Harvard.text: Inflammation of the thyroid gland. Types of thyroiditis include Hashimoto’s thyroiditis, subacute thyroiditis, and postpartum or silent thyroiditis.

LLM.text: Inflammation of the thyroid gland with various etiologies. Hashimoto thyroiditis: autoimmune, most common cause of hypothyroidism in iodine-sufficient areas. Subacute (De Quervain) thyroiditis: post-viral, presents with painful thyroid and transient hyperthyroidism followed by hypothyroidism.

Harvard.text: A hormone secreted into the bloodstream by the pituitary gland that stimulates the thyroid gland. Doctors measure levels of TSH to determine whether a person’s thyroid hormone levels are normal.

LLM.text: A pituitary hormone that stimulates the thyroid to produce thyroid hormones.

Harvard.text: The presence of too much thyroid hormone in the body. This may be caused by an overproductive thyroid, inflammation of the thyroid, or taking too much thyroid hormone.

LLM.text: A clinical state caused by excessive thyroid hormone activity in the body.

Harvard.text: One of two types of major thyroid hormone manufactured by the thyroid gland. It contains four iodine atoms. Also known as T4.

LLM.text: The main thyroid hormone containing four iodine atoms.

Harvard.text: Abbreviation for transient ischemic attack, a brain attack that resolves on its own within 24 hours. Sometimes called a mini-stroke, a TIA is often an early warning sign of an impending stroke.

LLM.text: A transient ischemic attack, a temporary episode of neurological dysfunction from reduced brain blood flow.

common_names: mini-stroke, a TIA is often an early warning sign of an impending stroke

Harvard.text: The large bone of the calf, or shinbone.

LLM.text: Tibia concerns tibia, a body structure, substance, or clinical concept whose meaning depends on location, function, and patient context. Proximal: tibial plateau (medial/lateral condyles) and tibial tuberosity (patellar ligament insertion). Shaft: sharp subcutaneous anterior border. Distal: medial malleolus articulating with the talus at the ankle.

Harvard.text: Pain from a disorder of the trigeminal nerve, the chief sensory nerve of the face. Also called trigeminal neuralgia.

LLM.text: A chronic pain condition characterized by recurrent, sudden, severe, electric shock-like pain in the distribution of the trigeminal nerve (typically V2/V3). See Trigeminal Neuralgia.

Harvard.text: An antiplatelet drug that prevents the formation of blood clots.

LLM.text: An antiplatelet medicine that reduces platelet aggregation and clot formation.

Harvard.text: An herbal product made by soaking an herb or other plant material in a mixture of water and alcohol to extract certain ingredients believed to be medicinal or beneficial.

LLM.text: Alcohol extract of plant or chemical substance. Common concentration: 10-40\% alcohol. Examples: tincture of iodine (antiseptic), tincture of benzoin (skin protector). Also used for liquid medications.

Harvard.text: An itchy condition of the scalp caused by a fungal infection. Also known as ringworm.

LLM.text: A dermatophyte infection of the scalp and hair shafts, most common in children. It may cause scaling, alopecia, broken hairs, black dots, or an inflammatory kerion.

Harvard.text: Athlete’s foot.

LLM.text: A dermatophyte infection of the feet presenting in interdigital, moccasin, vesiculobullous, or ulcerative patterns. It may coexist with tinea unguium. Diagnosis is clinical or mycologic when uncertain; treatment uses topical antifungals for limited disease and oral therapy for extensive, refractory, or nail-associated infection.

Harvard.text: A ringing in the ears or some other sound that has no external cause.

LLM.text: Tinnitus is perception of sound without an external source, often related to hearing loss, noise exposure, ear disease, medications, vascular causes, or neurologic factors.

Harvard.text: A group of cells that are specialized to do a certain job and are joined together to form a body structure, such as muscle or kidney.

LLM.text: A group of similar cells and their surrounding materials that work together to perform a specific function.

Harvard.text: A clot-dissolving enzyme produced naturally in the blood vessels and artificially produced as a medication. Tissue plasminogen activator (commonly known as tPA) is used to break down blood clots in the treatment of heart attack, ischemic stroke, and pulmonary embolism. tPA must be used within a few hours after symptoms begin.

LLM.text: An enzyme that converts plasminogen to plasmin, helping dissolve fibrin in blood clots. Recombinant forms are used as thrombolytic medicines in selected emergencies.

Harvard.text: The highest amount of a nutrient deemed likely to have no harmful health effects for almost all healthy people when taken consistently.

LLM.text: The highest usual daily nutrient intake unlikely to cause harm in nearly all healthy people.

Harvard.text: The process through which the body becomes less responsive to a psychoactive substance or rewarding behavior. Over time, people who develop tolerance need larger doses to get the same effect they first got with smaller doses.

LLM.text: A decreased response to a drug after repeated administration, requiring dose escalation to achieve the same effect. Unlike tachyphylaxis, tolerance develops over weeks to months of chronic use.

Harvard.text: One class of pattern-recognition receptors, found on the surfaces of the cells of the innate immune system.

LLM.text: Innate-immune receptors that detect characteristic microbial or tissue-danger signals.

Harvard.text: An agent believed to invigorate a specific body organ.

LLM.text: A substance or preparation traditionally believed to invigorate or strengthen the body.

Harvard.text: A glaucoma screening test that measures pressure inside the eye.

LLM.text: Measurement of pressure inside the eye, usually to assess for glaucoma or monitor its treatment. Methods include applanation, noncontact air-puff, rebound, and electronic devices; results must be interpreted with corneal thickness and the clinical context.

Harvard.text: Infectious disease that attacks the teeth. Also called dental caries.

LLM.text: Destruction of tooth structure caused by acids produced by bacteria.

Harvard.text: Pertaining to an external surface of the body, such as the skin, mouth, vagina, or anus; often used to describe the administration of medicine that is applied directly to such a surface.

LLM.text: Applied directly to a body surface, usually the skin or a mucous membrane.

Harvard.text: Pertaining to something that is poisonous.

LLM.text: Poisonous or capable of causing injury to living tissue.

Harvard.text: An enlarged thyroid gland with nodules that produce excess thyroid hormone. This type of goiter is to blame for hyperthyroidism in many people over 60.

LLM.text: An enlarged thyroid with nodules that produce excessive thyroid hormone.

Harvard.text: A poison, usually one produced by a living organism.

LLM.text: A poisonous substance produced by a living organism.

Harvard.text: Vaccines that protect against harmful bacterial toxins. These vaccines contain toxins that have been detoxified and rendered inactive.

LLM.text: Vaccines that protect against harmful bacterial toxins. These vaccines contain toxins that have been detoxified and rendered inactive.

Harvard.text: Abbreviation for tissue plasminogen activator, a clot-dissolving enzyme produced naturally in the blood vessels and artificially produced as a medication. tPA is used to break down blood clots in the treatment of heart attack, ischemic stroke, and pulmonary embolism. tPA must be used within a few hours after symptoms begin.

LLM.text: Tissue plasminogen activator, a clot-dissolving enzyme or medicine.

Harvard.text: Bone tissue arranged in a meshwork of thin plates or beams that is commonly found at the center of long bones and that composes a large part of the hip and vertebrae. Also called cancellous bone or spongy bone.

LLM.text: Porous, lattice-like bone tissue found inside bones and near many joints.

Harvard.text: A system of fine, mesh-like tissue in the anterior chamber of the eye through which aqueous humor drains; located in the angle where the clear cornea, white sclera, and colored iris join.

LLM.text: A porous tissue in the eye through which aqueous humor drains.

Harvard.text: A standard surgical procedure for glaucoma that creates a new channel for fluid drainage from the anterior chamber to the sub-conjunctival space.

LLM.text: A conventional glaucoma filtration surgery that creates a new drainage pathway for aqueous humor by removing a small piece of the trabecular meshwork and creating a partial-thickness scleral flap under which aqueous humor filters from the anterior chamber into the subconjunctival space, forming a filtering bleb.

Harvard.text: A laser procedure that burns small holes on the eye's trabecular meshwork to ease the flow of aqueous humor from the eye.

LLM.text: Laser treatment that improves aqueous-humor drainage through the trabecular meshwork.

Harvard.text: A mineral that is required only in tiny amounts in the diet to maintain health; the principal trace minerals are chromium, copper, selenium, sulfur, and zinc.

LLM.text: A mineral required by the body in very small amounts.

Harvard.text: A hole created through the front of the neck and into the windpipe (trachea). It provides an air passage when the usual route for breathing is obstructed, such as after a traumatic injury to the face or neck, or when long-term use of a breathing machine (ventilator) is needed.

LLM.text: A surgically created opening through the neck into the trachea, usually with insertion of a tube.

Harvard.text: The procedure used to create a tracheostomy.

LLM.text: An operation that creates an opening through the neck into the trachea. The opening is called a tracheostomy.

Rough, thin, ridged nails with many tiny pits, sometimes called twenty-nail dystrophy when most or all nails are affected. It may occur on its own or with psoriasis, alopecia areata, eczema, or lichen planus.

Harvard.text: The process of putting a bone or other body part under a pulling tension by applying weights and pulleys to help healing.

LLM.text: A pulling force used to align, immobilize, or relieve pressure on tissue or a fracture.

Harvard.text: A type of fat made during hydrogenation of liquid vegetable oil. Trans fats are found in many solid margarines, commercially prepared baked goods, and fried foods in many restaurants. Trans fats increase harmful low-density lipoprotein, decrease protective high-density lipoprotein, and promote blood clotting and inflammation. Also known as trans fat.

LLM.text: An unsaturated fatty acid with trans configuration, often formed during industrial oil processing.

Harvard.text: An ultrasound technique that makes images of the major arteries at the base of the brain.

LLM.text: Ultrasound measurement of blood flow through major arteries at the base of the brain.

Harvard.text: The use of low-voltage electrical current (through electrodes placed on the skin) to provide pain-suppressing stimulation.

LLM.text: Low-voltage electrical stimulation delivered through skin electrodes to reduce pain.

Harvard.text: Through the skin.

LLM.text: A route of drug administration delivering drug through intact skin into the systemic circulation via a patch or gel, bypassing first-pass metabolism and providing steady plasma concentrations over hours to days. Examples: nitroglycerin, fentanyl, nicotine, estrogen, clonidine, rotigotine.

Harvard.text: A measure of iron circulating in the blood.

LLM.text: The percentage of transferrin iron-binding sites occupied by iron.

Harvard.text: The process of taking blood from a healthy person and infusing it into a person whose own blood has been depleted during surgery or an accident, or is for some reason not functioning correctly. Transfusions of whole blood or of specific blood cells (such as red cells, white cells, or platelets) are possible.

LLM.text: Administration of donated blood or blood components into a person’s circulation.

Harvard.text: A brain attack that resolves on its own within 24 hours. Sometimes called a mini-stroke or TIA, a transient ischemic attack is often an early warning sign of an impending stroke.

LLM.text: A transient ischemic attack (TIA) is a temporary episode of neurological dysfunction caused by focal brain, spinal cord, or retinal ischemia without acute infarction.

common_names: mini-stroke or TIA, a transient ischemic attack is often an early warning sign of an impending stroke

Harvard.text: Minor, fleeting pain.

LLM.text: Pain that is brief and resolves rather than persisting.

Harvard.text: Heart attack that destroys the entire thickness of a section of heart muscle.

LLM.text: A heart attack involving the full thickness of part of the heart wall.

Harvard.text: The process of removing an organ or other donated body part from one person and implanting it in another person.

LLM.text: Transfer of an organ, tissue, or cells from a donor to a recipient.
