Harvard.text: A procedure that uses sound waves to create an image of the prostate gland as a means of detecting cancer. Sound waves are directed to the prostate from a probe inserted in the rectum.

LLM.text: Ultrasound imaging of the prostate or nearby structures using a rectal probe.

Harvard.text: An operation used to treat benign prostatic hyperplasia (enlarged prostate gland) in which incisions are made in prostate tissue to relieve pressure on the urethra and ease urinary difficulties.

LLM.text: An operation using small prostate incisions to relieve obstruction of urine flow.

Harvard.text: A heat therapy for benign prostatic hyperplasia (enlarged prostate gland) that uses microwaves to destroy prostate tissue that obstructs urine flow.

LLM.text: Heat treatment using microwaves to destroy prostate tissue obstructing urine flow.

Harvard.text: A procedure that uses radio waves to heat and destroy cells in the prostate gland that are obstructing the urethra.

LLM.text: Treatment using radiofrequency heat delivered by needles to destroy obstructing prostate tissue.

Harvard.text: An operation used to treat benign prostatic hyperplasia (enlarged prostate gland) in which excess prostate tissue is surgically removed.

LLM.text: An endoscopic operation that removes obstructing prostate tissue to improve urine flow in selected people with benign prostatic enlargement. Alternatives and indications depend on symptoms, prostate size, complications, and patient preference.

Harvard.text: The ringlike projection on each side of a vertebra to which muscles and ligaments are attached and, in the chest area, to which the ribs are connected.

LLM.text: Bony projections extending laterally from vertebrae that provide attachment sites for muscles and ligaments and, in the thoracic spine, articulate with ribs.

Harvard.text: A prolonged, intense reaction to bereavement that affects one in 10 people who lose a loved one. Key signs are inability to accept the death; frequent nightmares and intrusive, upsetting memories; detachment from others; constant yearning for the deceased; and excessive loneliness. Also known as complicated grief or chronic grief.

LLM.text: Alternate index label; see Complicated grief.

Harvard.text: A rhythmic, quivering movement of muscles that can be caused by diseases such as Parkinson disease, side effects of medication, or old age.

LLM.text: A tremor is involuntary rhythmic shaking caused by alternating muscle activity, occurring at rest, with posture, or during movement.

Harvard.text: A three-flap valve that sits between the right atrium and the right ventricle.

LLM.text: Right atrioventricular valve with anterior, posterior, and septal cusps supported by chordae tendineae and three papillary muscles. Largest cardiac valve. Most commonly affected in IV drug use-associated endocarditis. Tricuspid regurgitation from right ventricular dilation, endocarditis, or carcinoid. Stenosis is rare, mostly rheumatic.

Harvard.text: A class of medications that relieve depression by interfering with the reuptake of serotonin and norepinephrine by neurons in the brain and spinal cord. At low doses, they are effective as pain medicines.

LLM.text: An antidepressant that inhibits reuptake of norepinephrine and serotonin; it can treat depression and some pain syndromes but may cause anticholinergic, cardiac, and toxic effects.

Harvard.text: Pain from a disorder of the trigeminal nerve, the chief sensory nerve of the face. Also called tic douloureux.

LLM.text: A chronic pain condition characterized by recurrent, sudden, severe, electric shock-like pain in the distribution of the trigeminal nerve (typically V2/V3). Often triggered by light touch, chewing, or brushing teeth. Most cases are caused by vascular compression of the trigeminal nerve root.

Harvard.text: Anything that can set off symptoms.

LLM.text: A trigger is an event, exposure, stimulus, or condition that initiates or worsens a symptom, disease episode, behavior, or physiologic response.

Harvard.text: A tender area that, when stimulated, also elicits pain elsewhere in the body.

LLM.text: A localized hyperirritable spot in a taut band of skeletal muscle that can produce characteristic local or referred pain when compressed.

Harvard.text: The primary type of fat in the body and in the diet, formed from three fatty-acid molecules and one glycerol molecule. This fat can raise the risk for heart disease when elevated.

LLM.text: A blood lipid consisting of three fatty acids attached to glycerol. Persistently high levels increase the risk of pancreatitis and contribute to cardiovascular risk.

Harvard.text: One of two types of major thyroid hormone manufactured by the thyroid gland. It contains three iodine atoms. Also known as T3.

LLM.text: The thyroid hormone T3, the more biologically active thyroid hormone, produced mainly by peripheral conversion of thyroxine and important in regulating metabolism and growth.

Harvard.text: A class of medications that work by constricting blood vessels in the head and perhaps by inhibiting inflammation.

LLM.text: Selective serotonin-receptor agonists used to abort migraine attacks by constricting certain cranial vessels and reducing trigeminal signaling; contraindications include some vascular diseases.

Harvard.text: A groove in front of the femur where the patella moves as the knee bends and straightens.

LLM.text: A pulley-shaped anatomical structure; examples include the humeral trochlea at the elbow and the trochlea of the superior oblique muscle in the orbit.

Harvard.text: Proteins found in heart muscle that leak into the circulation during a heart attack or other heart injury.

LLM.text: Regulatory proteins released into blood when cardiac muscle is injured; cardiac troponin is the preferred biomarker for detecting myocardial injury and diagnosing myocardial infarction in context.

Harvard.text: An enzyme secreted by the pancreas that helps digest proteins.

LLM.text: A pancreatic proteolytic enzyme secreted as trypsinogen and activated in the small intestine, where it helps digest dietary proteins and activates other pancreatic enzymes.

Harvard.text: Abbreviation for thyroid-stimulating hormone, a hormone secreted into the bloodstream by the pituitary gland that stimulates the thyroid gland. Doctors measure levels of TSH to determine whether a person’s thyroid hormone levels are normal.

LLM.text: Thyroid-stimulating hormone, a pituitary hormone that stimulates thyroid hormone production; its blood concentration is the main initial test for many thyroid disorders.

Harvard.text: Any type of swelling or enlargement of tissues; most often used to describe an abnormal growth of tissue, which can be cancerous or noncancerous.

LLM.text: A tumor is an abnormal mass of cells caused by excessive or uncontrolled growth; it may be benign or malignant.

Harvard.text: The dense fibrous membrane surrounding each corpus cavernosum and the corpus spongiosum in the penis.

LLM.text: A dense fibrous connective-tissue capsule surrounding an organ, especially the testis, where it supports the seminiferous tissue and forms septa.

Harvard.text: The eardrum.

LLM.text: The tympanic membrane (eardrum) is a thin, cone-shaped, translucent membrane at the medial end of the external auditory canal that separates the external ear from the middle ear and serves as the interface for sound transmission by converting acoustic energy into mechanical vibrations of the ossicular chain.

Harvard.text: A test of the eardrum's motion and pressure in the middle ear. Also known as impedance testing.

LLM.text: An objective test that varies air pressure in the ear canal while measuring movement of the tympanic membrane and middle-ear pressure. It helps assess middle-ear fluid, eustachian-tube dysfunction, perforation, and ossicular or tympanic-membrane abnormalities.

Harvard.text: A type of diabetes, a chronic condition that affects the way the body's tissues use sugar (glucose), their main source of fuel. Once called juvenile-onset diabetes and insulin-dependent diabetes. People with this form of diabetes don't make enough insulin, a hormone that controls the movement of glucose into cells. They must rely on insulin injections.

LLM.text: Type 1 diabetes is autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells causing absolute insulin deficiency, hyperglycemia, and risk of diabetic ketoacidosis without insulin replacement.

Harvard.text: Bone loss due to estrogen decline associated with menopause.

LLM.text: An older classification referring mainly to postmenopausal osteoporosis, in which accelerated trabecular bone loss increases fracture risk, particularly at the vertebrae and wrist.

Harvard.text: A type of diabetes, a chronic condition that affects the way the body's tissues use sugar (glucose), their main source of fuel. Once called adult -onset diabetes and non-insulin-dependent diabetes. People with this form of the disease have tissues that either resist the effects of insulin (a hormone that control the movement of sugar into cells) or the body doesn't produce enough insulin. It is initially treated with diet, exercise, weight-loss if needed, and oral medications.

LLM.text: Type 2 diabetes is chronic hyperglycemia caused by insulin resistance and progressive beta-cell dysfunction, with risks to the eyes, kidneys, nerves, heart, and blood vessels.

Harvard.text: Bone loss due to aging.

LLM.text: An older classification referring mainly to age-related osteoporosis, involving cortical and trabecular bone loss and increased risk of hip and vertebral fractures.

Harvard.text: A break in the skin or other surface that often occurs along with inflammation, infection, or cancerous growth.

LLM.text: Full-thickness loss of epidermis extending into the dermis or deeper tissue, often healing with a scar. Causes include vascular disease, pressure, infection, neuropathy, inflammatory disease, trauma, and malignancy.

Harvard.text: A painless, noninvasive imaging method that uses high-frequency sound waves.

LLM.text: Ultrasound uses high-frequency sound waves to create images of organs, vessels, tissues, or a developing fetus without ionizing radiation. quadrant (RUQ): gallbladder (gallstones, cholecystitis), liver (steatosis, cysts), kidneys, and pancreas. Pelvic: uterus, ovaries, adnexa. Renal: hydronephrosis, stones, cysts, tumors. Scrotal: testicular torsion, epididymitis, varicocele, hydrocele.

Harvard.text: Estrogen taken without an accompanying progestogen.

LLM.text: Estrogen therapy given without a progestogen in a person with a uterus.

Harvard.text: Personal losses that are not acknowledged and mourned. Many mental health experts believe that reactions to these losses crop up later, often skewing a person’s response to an entirely different loss.

LLM.text: Significant losses that have not been fully acknowledged or emotionally processed.

Harvard.text: Healthy dietary fats from plant sources such as vegetable oils, nuts, and whole grains, as well as from fatty fish. Includes monounsaturated fat and polyunsaturated fat.

LLM.text: A dietary fat whose fatty-acid chains contain one or more carbon-carbon double bonds. Monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fats are common in vegetable oils, nuts, seeds, and fish; replacing saturated fat with unsaturated fat generally supports healthier LDL cholesterol levels.

Harvard.text: Chest pain that occurs or worsens in frequency, severity, or duration when a person is at rest or engaging in mild activity.

LLM.text: Myocardial ischemia at rest, new-onset severe angina, or a crescendo pattern (more frequent, longer, lower-threshold) without evidence of myocardial necrosis (normal troponin). Pathophysiology: acute plaque rupture with thrombosis causing transient severe coronary obstruction.

Harvard.text: Inhalation that requires undue extra exertion; this extra work may cause insomnia and daytime sleepiness.

LLM.text: Increased effort to breathe through a narrowed upper airway, often causing sleep disruption and daytime sleepiness.

Harvard.text: Muscular valve located at the upper portion of the esophagus that opens to allow food or liquid to enter the digestive system.

LLM.text: A muscular valve at the top of the esophagus that opens during swallowing.

Harvard.text: A waste product of protein digestion and metabolism.

LLM.text: The principal nitrogen-containing waste product of protein metabolism, formed in the liver and excreted mainly by the kidneys.

Harvard.text: The tube that connects each kidney to the bladder.

LLM.text: The paired muscular tubes (25-30 cm) conveying urine from the renal pelvis to the urinary bladder, crossing the pelvic brim at the pelvic inlet. Three anatomical narrowings (pelviureteric junction, pelvic brim, vesicoureteric junction) are common sites of ureteric stone impaction.

Harvard.text: The tube leading from the bladder through which urine is carried from the body.

LLM.text: The tube conveying urine from the bladder to the exterior. Male urethra (18-20 cm): prostatic, membranous, and spongy (penile) parts; carries urine and semen; longer and more tortuous than female. Female urethra (3-4 cm): short, straight, predisposing to ascending urinary tract infections.

Harvard.text: Movement of the urethra out of place when abdominal pressure increases, leading to stress incontinence.

LLM.text: Excessive movement of the urethra during increased abdominal pressure, contributing to stress incontinence.

Harvard.text: Inflammation of the urethra.

LLM.text: Urethritis is inflammation of the urethra, commonly from sexually transmitted infection, causing dysuria, irritation, or discharge and requiring evaluation of partners and complications. (Chlamydia trachomatis, Neisseria gonorrhoeae) or non-infectious causes. Presents with dysuria, urethral discharge, and meatal itching. Diagnosis: urine nucleic acid amplification testing (NAAT).

Harvard.text: The sudden and uncontrollable need to urinate or defecate.

LLM.text: A sudden, compelling desire to urinate that is difficult to defer—a lower urinary tract symptom. Causes: overactive bladder (detrusor overactivity, often idiopathic), urinary tract infection (urgency + dysuria), bladder outlet obstruction (BPH), neurogenic bladder, interstitial cystitis, and pelvic floor disorders.

Harvard.text: Routinely needing to urinate more than eight times during the day or more than twice at night.

LLM.text: The need to urinate more often than usual, which may result from infection, bladder irritation, increased urine production, or other urinary disorders.

Harvard.text: Inability to control urine flow, resulting in involuntary discharge or leakage.

LLM.text: Involuntary leakage of urine, significantly affecting psychological, social, and physical well-being.

Harvard.text: Part of the body that produces and excretes urine. It consists of the kidneys, ureters, bladder, and urethra.

LLM.text: The kidneys, ureters, bladder, and urethra, which produce, transport, store, and excrete urine.

Harvard.text: A specialist who deals with the urinary tract and male reproductive system.

LLM.text: A physician specializing in urinary-tract disorders and the male reproductive system.

Harvard.text: An itchy rash of usually short duration. Also known as hives.

LLM.text: A skin reaction causing transient, itchy raised welts that change location and usually resolve within 24 hours. It may occur with angioedema, which is deeper swelling often affecting the lips, eyelids, tongue, or extremities.

Harvard.text: Inflammation of the pigmented part of the eye (the iris); may seriously affect vision.

LLM.text: Inflammation of the uveal tract—the iris, ciliary body, and choroid—and sometimes nearby eye tissues. It may result from infection, autoimmune or other inflammatory disease, trauma, or an unknown cause. Symptoms can include eye pain, redness, light sensitivity, floaters, blurred vision, or reduced vision; prompt eye assessment is important because untreated inflammation can damage vision.

Harvard.text: A small, fleshy flap of tissue that hangs from the back of the throat over the root of the tongue.

LLM.text: A small, fleshy flap of tissue that hangs from the back of the throat over the root of the tongue.

Harvard.text: A surgical treatment for obstructive sleep apnea that involves removing the uvula, the tonsils, and a rim of loose tissue at the back of the soft palate.

LLM.text: Surgery that removes or reshapes the uvula, tonsils, and soft-palate tissue to treat obstructive sleep apnea.

Harvard.text: A method of protecting the body against disease by injecting parts or all of a microorganism that will cause the body to develop antibodies against the microorganism and later fight off disease.

LLM.text: Administration of a vaccine to stimulate immune response and provide protection against infectious disease. Types: live attenuated, inactivated, subunit, mRNA, viral vector. Schedule varies by country. Herd immunity achieved when sufficient proportion immune.

Harvard.text: Various manual or battery-operated pumps that a man can use to draw blood into the penis to create an erection.

LLM.text: Pumps that draw blood into the penis to produce an erection.

Harvard.text: Spasms of the muscles around the vaginal opening that prevent penile penetration.

LLM.text: Involuntary tightening of the muscles around the vaginal opening that can make penetration painful or impossible. It may be associated with pelvic-floor dysfunction, fear, prior pain, or other factors and is treatable with a tailored multidisciplinary approach.

Harvard.text: Structures consisting of leaflets that divide the chambers of the heart and prevent the backflow of blood from one chamber to another during contraction of the heart.

LLM.text: Structures that permit fluid or blood to move predominantly in one direction and prevent backward flow; cardiac valves and venous valves are important examples.

Harvard.text: Also called Prinzmetal's angina, these are attacks of chest pain caused by spasms of one or more coronary arteries almost always while a person is at rest.

LLM.text: Chest pain caused by temporary coronary-artery spasm, often occurring at rest.

common_names: Prinzmetal's angina, these are attacks of chest pain caused by spasms of one or more coronary arteries almost always while a person is at rest

Harvard.text: Having to do with blood vessels and circulation.

LLM.text: Relating to blood vessels.

Harvard.text: Dementia caused by narrowing or blockage of blood vessels in the brain or by a stroke or series of tiny strokes. Also called multi-infarct dementia.

LLM.text: Cognitive impairment caused by cerebrovascular disease, such as strokes or chronic small-vessel injury. Symptoms may develop suddenly or gradually and can include problems with attention, executive function, memory, or walking. Management addresses the underlying vascular risks and functional needs.

Harvard.text: An operation to improve blood flow either by repairing leaks in blood vessels or by rerouting arteries to bypass blockages.

LLM.text: Surgery that repairs or reroutes blood vessels to improve circulation.

Harvard.text: Inflammation of blood vessels.

LLM.text: Inflammation of blood vessels causing tissue ischemia and necrosis. Classification by vessel size. Large vessel: giant cell arteritis, Takayasu arteritis. Medium vessel: polyarteritis nodosa (PAN), Kawasaki disease.

Harvard.text: An operation that ties off or cuts the tubes through which sperm travel from the testicles to the urethra; used as a form of birth control.

LLM.text: A permanent contraceptive procedure in which the vas deferens are divided or occluded to prevent sperm from entering the ejaculate. It does not immediately provide sterility and does not protect against sexually transmitted infections.

Harvard.text: A substance or condition, such as drugs, cold, fear, and nicotine, that causes blood vessels to narrow and thus de­creases the flow of blood.

LLM.text: A substance that narrows blood vessels.

Harvard.text: A widening of the blood vessels that results in increased blood flow.

LLM.text: The widening of blood vessels during inflammation, resulting in increased blood flow to the affected area. This process is mediated primarily by histamine released from mast cell granules acting on H1 receptors, nitric oxide produced by endothelial nitric oxide synthase, and prostaglandins particularly PGE2.

Harvard.text: A substance or condition that causes blood vessels to open wider and increase the flow of blood.

LLM.text: A substance that widens blood vessels.

Harvard.text: Uncontrollable contraction or spasm of a blood vessel.

LLM.text: Sudden involuntary narrowing caused by contraction of a blood vessel.

Harvard.text: An animal or insect that transmits an infectious disease from a reservoir to a susceptible host.

LLM.text: A living carrier, commonly an arthropod, that transmits an infectious agent between hosts. Biological vectors support replication or development of the agent; mechanical vectors transfer it without such biologic change.

Harvard.text: A vessel that carries blood back to the heart.

LLM.text: A blood vessel that carries deoxygenated blood toward the heart (except pulmonary veins, which carry oxygenated blood). Veins have thinner walls and larger lumens than arteries, with less smooth muscle and elastic tissue.

Harvard.text: Pertaining to a vein.

LLM.text: Relating to veins.

Harvard.text: Seepage of blood out of a vein.

LLM.text: Inadequate retention of blood in the penis during erection because blood escapes through veins.

Harvard.text: Machine that inflates the lungs with oxygen.

LLM.text: Mechanical device providing ventilatory support. Modes: assist-control, SIMV, CPAP, PRVC. Parameters: tidal volume, respiratory rate, FiO2, PEEP.

Harvard.text: One of the two lower chambers of the heart. The right ventricle pumps blood to the lungs; the left ventricle pumps blood to the rest of the body.

LLM.text: One of the two lower, thicker-walled chambers of the heart that pump blood out of the heart. The right ventricle pumps deoxygenated blood into the pulmonary artery (low-pressure system); the left ventricle pumps oxygenated blood into the aorta (high-pressure system, generating systemic blood pressure).

Harvard.text: Abnormal heart rhythm that starts in the lower chambers of the heart; this rhythm disturbance can occur as a complication of a heart attack and impairs the heart's pumping ability.

LLM.text: An abnormal heart rhythm arising from the ventricles. It may cause palpitations, dizziness, fainting, chest discomfort, or sudden cardiac arrest; fainting or severe symptoms require emergency care.

Harvard.text: A deadly heart rhythm in which the ventricles contract independently of the atria and in a chaotic manner.

LLM.text: Chaotic electrical activity in ventricles, causing no cardiac output. Immediate defibrillation is treatment. Causes: coronary artery disease, cardiomyopathy, electrolyte disturbances, drug toxicity. Post-resuscitation care: targeted temperature management, coronary angiography, ICU admission.

Harvard.text: Heart muscle that makes up the lower chambers of the heart.

LLM.text: Heart muscle forming the walls of the ventricles.

Harvard.text: Break in the heart muscle that allows blood to escape into the pericardial sac.

LLM.text: A tear in a ventricular wall, often a life-threatening complication of myocardial infarction.

Harvard.text: One or more holes in the septum, the muscular wall separating the right and left sides of the heart.

LLM.text: An opening in the wall between the ventricles that can allow blood to flow from the left ventricle to the right. The effects depend on the size and location of the defect and may range from no symptoms to heart failure or pulmonary vascular disease.

Harvard.text: A very fast heartbeat that starts in the ventricles. Ventricular tachycardia can be deadly if it renders the heart unable to pump enough blood to the body.

LLM.text: A wide-complex tachycardia (QRS >0.12 s) originating from the ventricles, with a rate of 100-250 bpm. Monomorphic VT has uniform QRS complexes; polymorphic VT has varying QRS morphology. VT is life-threatening and may degenerate to ventricular fibrillation.

Harvard.text: Small veins.

LLM.text: Very small veins that collect blood from capillaries.

Harvard.text: One of the cylindrical bones that form the spine (plural: vertebrae).

LLM.text: The individual bone of the vertebral column (33 vertebrae: 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral fused, 4 coccygeal). Parts: vertebral body, vertebral arch (pedicles, laminae), spinous and transverse processes, articular processes/facets, and vertebral foramen (spinal canal).

Harvard.text: One of two blood vessels that run up the back of the neck and join at the base of the skull to form the basilar artery. The vertebral arteries carry blood from the heart to the brain.

LLM.text: An artery ascending through the neck that supplies blood to the brainstem and posterior brain.

Harvard.text: A minimally invasive procedure to stabilize compressed vertebrae and alleviate pain. A needle is inserted into the compressed portion of a vertebra and surgical cement is injected to support the vertebra and prevent further collapse.

LLM.text: A minimally invasive procedure that injects bone cement into a collapsed vertebral body to stabilize selected painful compression fractures.

Harvard.text: Dizziness; often a spinning sensation or a feeling that the ground is tilting.

LLM.text: A false sensation of rotational or linear movement of the self or the environment, and it is a symptom rather than a disease, requiring differentiation from dizziness, disequilibrium, and presyncope.

Harvard.text: A weight-loss diet that allows 800 or fewer calories per day (usually followed under medical supervision).

LLM.text: A medically supervised diet providing about 800 or fewer calories per day.

Harvard.text: A lipoprotein that transports triglyceride manufactured in the liver to fat tissue in the body. VLDL eventually becomes low-density lipoprotein (LDL) after the triglyceride has been removed.

LLM.text: A lipoprotein that transports liver-produced triglycerides and can become LDL.

Harvard.text: The balance organs, located in the labyrinth in the inner ear.

LLM.text: Inner-ear and brain structures responsible for balance and spatial orientation.

Harvard.text: Pertaining to or caused by a virus.

LLM.text: Caused by or relating to a virus.

Harvard.text: A disease or condition that is highly infectious or dangerous or rapidly progressing.

LLM.text: Highly harmful, severe, or capable of causing serious disease.

Harvard.text: The internal organs, especially those found in the abdomen.

LLM.text: The internal organs of the body, particularly those within the thoracic and abdominal cavities. The thoracic viscera include the heart, lungs, esophagus, trachea, and thymus.

Harvard.text: Fat that lies beneath the abdominal wall, in the spaces surrounding the liver, intestines, and other organs. Sometimes called belly fat or abdominal adiposity.

LLM.text: Fat stored within the abdominal cavity around internal organs; excess visceral fat is associated with insulin resistance, dyslipidemia, and cardiovascular risk.

Harvard.text: The eye's ability to see sharply, usually measured in comparison to what a normal eye would see from 20 feet. Problems in visual acuity can usually be corrected with eyeglasses.

LLM.text: The resolving power of the eye, defined as the ability to distinguish two points as distinct, and the most common clinical measure of visual function.

Harvard.text: The part of the occipital lobe in the brain that processes visual stimuli.

LLM.text: The region of the occipital cerebral cortex that receives and processes visual information from the eyes through the visual pathways.

Harvard.text: The full scope of what the eye sees; includes central and peripheral vision.

LLM.text: The entire area that can be seen while the eyes remain fixed in one position. Visual-field loss may result from retinal, optic-nerve, or brain lesions and is assessed by perimetry.

Harvard.text: A technique used to treat benign prostatic hyperplasia (enlarged prostate gland) that allows the surgeon to view the prostate directly while it is being shrunk by a laser beam.

LLM.text: Laser prostate surgery performed with direct visualization to remove obstructing tissue.

Harvard.text: Measurements that indicate how well the body is functioning, including pulse rate, respiration (breathing rate), temperature, and blood pressure.

LLM.text: Basic measurements of physiologic status, commonly including temperature, pulse, respiratory rate, blood pressure, and oxygen saturation. Values vary with age, activity, illness, and measurement conditions; trends and clinical context are important.

Harvard.text: A hormone that plays a key role in ensuring the absorption of calcium from the intestines.

LLM.text: Vitamin D supports calcium and phosphate balance, bone mineralization, muscle function, and immune processes; deficiency causes rickets in children and osteomalacia or bone loss in adults.

Harvard.text: A microsurgical procedure in which part of the vitreous humor of the eye is removed and then replaced with sterile saline or some other fluid.

LLM.text: Surgical removal of the vitreous gel, typically via the pars plana approach, using a cutting probe under microscopic visualization. Indications include vitreous hemorrhage, complicated retinal detachment, macular holes, epiretinal membranes, intraocular foreign bodies, and endophthalmitis.

Harvard.text: The clear, gel-like substance that fills the space behind the lens of the eye and supports the shape of the rear portion of the eye.

LLM.text: The clear gel that fills the space between the lens and retina. It helps maintain the shape of the eye and transmits light to the retina.

Harvard.text: Abbreviation for very-low-density lipoprotein, a lipoprotein that transports triglyceride manufactured in the liver to fat tissue in the body. VLDL eventually becomes low-density lipoprotein (LDL) after the triglyceride has been removed.

LLM.text: Very low-density lipoprotein. Transports endogenous triglycerides.

Harvard.text: The body’s maximum capacity for oxygen consumption during peak exertion. Also known as aerobic power, maximal oxygen consumption, or cardiorespiratory endurance capacity.

LLM.text: The maximum rate at which the body can use oxygen during intense exercise.

common_names: aerobic power, maximal oxygen consumption, or cardiorespiratory endurance capacity

Harvard.text: Unstable components of a preparation that evaporate easily.

LLM.text: Plant oils containing compounds that evaporate readily at room temperature.

Harvard.text: Abbreviation for ventricular septal defect—one or more holes in the septum, the muscular wall separating the right and left sides of the heart.

LLM.text: Ventricular septal defect, a hole in the wall separating the heart’s ventricles.

Harvard.text: An agent that is believed to aid in wound healing.

LLM.text: A substance traditionally believed to promote wound healing.

Harvard.text: Inflammation of the tissue around the opening of the vagina that makes sexual activity painful.

LLM.text: An older term for localized provoked vulvodynia, characterized by pain or burning at the vulvar vestibule, often triggered by touch or attempted penetration.

Harvard.text: Pain in the vulva that may or may not be brought on by touch or pressure.

LLM.text: Vulvodynia is chronic vulvar pain without an identifiable specific cause, often described as burning or rawness and triggered by touch, pressure, or occurring spontaneously.

Harvard.text: Force on the wall of the heart muscle caused by pressure inside the heart's pumping chamber; excessive wall stress can impair the heart's ability to pump and increase the heart's need for oxygen.

LLM.text: Force exerted on a heart chamber wall by pressure inside the chamber.

Harvard.text: An anticoagulant drug that prevents blood clotting; people taking it must have regular blood tests to determine that their blood does not clot too readily or too slowly.

LLM.text: An anticoagulant that reduces blood clot formation by inhibiting vitamin-K-dependent clotting factors.

Harvard.text: An abnormal fibrous growth caused by a viral infection.

LLM.text: A benign skin growth caused by infection with human papillomavirus.

Harvard.text: Salty-tasting salivary secretions stimulated by gastroesophageal reflux.

LLM.text: A sudden increase in salty saliva associated with acid reflux.

Harvard.text: A hearing test that uses a tuning fork to diagnose one-sided hearing loss.

LLM.text: The Weber test is a screening test for lateralization of hearing that uses a vibrating tuning fork (typically 512 Hz) placed on the midline of the skull (vertex or forehead) to determine whether the sound is heard equally in both ears or louder in one ear, providing information about the type and side of hearing loss.

Harvard.text: An irreversible state of acute confusion and amnesia that develops in alcoholics as a result of malnutrition-related thiamine deficiency.

LLM.text: A neurologic disorder caused by thiamine deficiency, combining acute or previous Wernicke encephalopathy with persistent memory impairment and confabulation in some patients. Causes include alcohol-use disorder, malnutrition, and prolonged vomiting.

Harvard.text: The brain region responsible for the comprehension of speech.

LLM.text: A language-related region, usually in the dominant posterior superior temporal cortex, important for comprehension of spoken and written language.

Harvard.text: The popular term for muscle and ligament damage resulting from rapid and extreme extension and flexion of the neck. The term is also used for the accident causing the injury, most often a rear-end motor vehicle accident.

LLM.text: A neck injury caused by a rapid back-and-forth movement of the head.

Harvard.text: The inner portion of the brain, composed primarily of axons, each surrounded by a myelin sheath that insulates the nerve fibers (and appears white). Messages are sent between different regions of the brain (gray matter) via these nerve fibers.

LLM.text: Regions of the brain and spinal cord composed primarily of myelinated nerve fibers, responsible for transmitting signals between brain regions.

Harvard.text: Blood pressure that is elevated in a doctor’s office but is normal at home.

LLM.text: High blood pressure in a medical setting with normal readings outside it.

Harvard.text: A response to danger or stress characterized by apathy, lethargy, and depression; or the physical or psychological response to a sudden lack of an addictive substance such as alcohol or nicotine.

LLM.text: Physical or psychological symptoms that occur when an addictive substance is reduced or stopped.

Harvard.text: A type of short-term memory process that involves temporarily storing and manipulating information.

LLM.text: The short-term holding and manipulation of information during a task.

Harvard.text: A xanthoma on the eyelid.

LLM.text: Xanthelasma palpebrarum are soft, yellow, lipid-filled papules or plaques on the medial canthus of the eyelids (upper more commonly than lower), the most common form of cutaneous xanthoma. They are composed of foam cells (lipid-laden macrophages) in the superficial dermis.

Harvard.text: A yellow, lipid-laden deposit in the skin or on a tendon.

LLM.text: A xanthoma is a yellowish deposit of lipid-laden macrophages in the skin, subcutaneous tissue, or tendons. It may occur with hyperlipidemia, diabetes, cholestatic liver disease, or an inherited lipid disorder and warrants assessment of the underlying cause. presenting as yellow-orange papules, nodules, or plaques.

Harvard.text: A laser technique to correct blurred vision caused by cloudiness that may develop in the skin of the cataract left in the eye after cataract surgery; a laser is used to create a hole in the membrane to allow light to enter clearly focused onto the retina.

LLM.text: A laser procedure that creates an opening in an opaque posterior lens capsule after cataract surgery. It can improve vision when posterior capsule opacification is causing visual symptoms.

Harvard.text: An extract of the bark of a West African tree sometimes used in treating erectile dysfunction. Yohimbine appears to increase blood flow to the penis and prevent blood from leaving it too quickly.

LLM.text: An alpha-2 adrenergic antagonist derived from yohimbe-related compounds and studied for erectile dysfunction; evidence is limited and adverse effects may include anxiety, high blood pressure, palpitations, and seizures.

Harvard.text: Thin, gelatinous ligaments that attach the lens to the ciliary body and support the lens centrally behind the pupil.

LLM.text: The plural of zonule; in ophthalmology, usually the suspensory fibers that support the crystalline lens. Weak or disrupted zonules can contribute to lens subluxation and complicate cataract surgery.

Harvard.text: An infectious disease that is transmissible under normal conditions from animals to humans.

LLM.text: An infectious disease that can be naturally transmitted between vertebrate animals and humans. Transmission may occur through direct contact, contaminated food or water, animal products, or arthropod vectors.
A1C test measures glycated hemoglobin, the fraction of hemoglobin with glucose attached, to estimate average blood glucose over roughly the preceding 2 to 3 months.
A rare inherited disorder affecting growth, facial development, the skeleton, and sometimes the genitals.
Aase syndrome is a rare inherited disorder characterized by congenital hypoplastic anemia and distinctive skeletal abnormalities.
Abdomen - swollen is the presentation described by abdomen - swollen; onset, severity, associated findings, causes, and need for care guide assessment.
A localized enlargement of the abdominal aorta, usually defined as an aortic diameter of at least 3 cm or more than 50 percent above normal. Enlargement can progress to rupture.
Abdominal aortic aneurysm repair - open treats or supports abdominal aortic aneurysm repair - open; indication, preparation, complications, and recovery depend on the procedure and patient.

A sensation of fullness or visible enlargement of the abdomen, commonly caused by intestinal gas, constipation, food intolerance, or functional gastrointestinal disorders. Persistent or severe bloating may require evaluation for organic disease.
A computed tomography study that produces cross-sectional images of the abdomen using X-rays. It can identify structural abnormalities, injury, inflammation, bleeding, or masses.
Surgical inspection of the abdominal cavity to identify or treat a suspected source of pain, bleeding, infection, obstruction, or other disease.
The circumference of the abdomen measured at a standardized level. It is used to monitor abdominal distention, fetal growth, obesity, ascites, and changes in intra-abdominal volume.

A palpable or imaging-detected abnormal collection, enlargement, or lesion within the abdomen. Causes include distended bowel or bladder, organ enlargement, hernia, inflammatory collection, benign tumour, and malignancy; assessment depends on location, mobility, tenderness, systemic features, and appropriate imaging.
A magnetic resonance imaging study that produces detailed images of the abdomen using magnetic fields and radiofrequency energy.
Discomfort within the abdomen classified as visceral (dull, midline, poorly localized), parietal (sharp, well localized, worsened by movement), or referred from a distant source.
Abdominal pain - children under age 12 is the presentation described by abdominal pain - children under age 12; onset, severity, associated findings, causes, and need for care guide assessment.

Involuntary tensing of the abdominal wall, usually caused by irritation of the peritoneum. It may occur with peritonitis, perforation, severe infection, or intra-abdominal bleeding and requires clinical assessment.
Sounds produced by movement of gas and fluid through the intestines; changes in frequency or character may support, but do not establish, a diagnosis.
A procedure in which a needle or catheter is inserted into the abdominal cavity to remove or test ascitic fluid. It is also called paracentesis.
First-aid maneuver used for severe choking in a conscious person, intended to expel an obstructing object from the airway.
An ultrasound examination that uses sound waves to produce images of the abdomen and assess its structure and blood flow when applicable.
Abdominal wall fat pad biopsy evaluates abdominal wall fat pad biopsy; interpretation uses the method, specimen or body region, reference range, and clinical question.
Abdominal wall surgery treats or supports abdominal wall surgery; indication, preparation, complications, and recovery depend on the procedure and patient.
A plain radiograph of the abdomen used to assess selected causes of pain, obstruction, perforation, foreign bodies, or urinary stones. It has limited sensitivity for many abdominal disorders.
Abnormal hemoglobins testing evaluates abnormal hemoglobins testing; interpretation uses the method, specimen or body region, reference range, and clinical question.
Uterine bleeding that is abnormal in frequency, regularity, duration, or volume, occurring outside of normal menstruation or in women who are not pregnant.
Abnormally dark or light skin is the presentation described by abnormally dark or light skin; onset, severity, associated findings, causes, and need for care guide assessment.

An immune reaction caused by transfusion or pregnancy involving incompatible A, B, or O blood-group antigens. It can cause acute hemolysis, transfusion reactions, or hemolytic disease of the newborn. See also Hemolytic Disease of the Newborn.

Medication abortion uses prescribed medicines, commonly mifepristone followed by misoprostol or misoprostol alone, to end an early intrauterine pregnancy; confirmation of completion and assessment for ectopic pregnancy are important.
Abortion - procedure treats or supports abortion - procedure; indication, preparation, complications, and recovery depend on the procedure and patient.

A localized collection of pus within the abdominal or pelvic cavity, usually caused by infection or leakage from an injured or inflamed organ. It may cause pain, fever, and sepsis and often requires antimicrobial treatment and drainage.
Absence of sweating is the presentation described by absence of sweating; onset, severity, associated findings, causes, and need for care guide assessment.

A brief generalized seizure causing sudden impaired awareness and behavioral arrest, usually followed by rapid recovery. Electroencephalography commonly shows generalized three-hertz spike-and-wave activity.

Primary amenorrhea, meaning failure to have the first menstrual period by the expected age. Causes include chromosomal or reproductive-tract abnormalities, endocrine disorders, chronic disease, and inadequate energy availability.

Secondary amenorrhea, meaning absence of menstrual periods for an extended interval in a person who previously menstruated. Pregnancy is considered first; other causes include endocrine disease, medications, stress, weight change, and ovarian dysfunction.
Absent pulmonary valve is a congenital heart defect in which the pulmonary valve is missing or severely underdeveloped, often causing pulmonary-artery enlargement and respiratory symptoms.
Hyperpigmented, velvety, thickened plaques typically in skin flexures (neck, axillae, groin) and often associated with insulin resistance, obesity, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and metabolic syndrome.
ACE blood test measures angiotensin-converting enzyme in serum; it may support evaluation of sarcoidosis and selected granulomatous or liver disorders but is not diagnostic alone.
ACE inhibitors block formation of angiotensin II and are used for hypertension, heart failure, diabetic kidney protection, and selected cardiovascular conditions.
Acetaminophen and codeine overdose involves toxic exposure to acetaminophen and codeine overdose; dose, route, timing, symptoms, and antidote availability guide the clinical response.
Weight-based dosing guidance for acetaminophen in children; the total daily dose must account for all combination products to avoid liver toxicity.
Acetaminophen overdose involves toxic exposure to acetaminophen overdose; dose, route, timing, symptoms, and antidote availability guide the clinical response.
Toxic effects caused by excessive exposure to acetone. Severity depends on the dose, route, timing, coexisting conditions, and clinical findings; suspected poisoning requires prompt assessment.
Acetylcholine receptor antibody testing detects antibodies associated with autoimmune myasthenia gravis and is interpreted with the neurologic examination and other studies.
A disorder in which the lower esophageal sphincter fails to relax normally and esophageal peristalsis is impaired, causing difficulty swallowing and regurgitation.
Aches and pains during pregnancy is the presentation described by aches and pains during pregnancy; onset, severity, associated findings, causes, and need for care guide assessment.
Painful inflammation or degeneration of the Achilles tendon, usually caused by repeated loading.
Achilles tendon repair reconnects a ruptured Achilles tendon, followed by immobilization and graduated rehabilitation to restore plantar-flexion strength.
A group of severe inherited disorders in which cartilage and bone development are profoundly impaired.

Autosomal dominant skeletal dysplasia (FGFR3 gene). Most common form of dwarfism. Features: short limbs, macrocephaly, frontal bossing, trident hand, spinal stenosis. Homozygous form lethal. Normal intelligence.
A test of the kidney’s ability to excrete acid after an acid load, used in evaluating renal tubular acidification disorders.

An older term for glycosaminoglycans, long carbohydrate chains in connective-tissue substances such as cartilage, skin, and synovial fluid. Abnormal degradation or storage can cause mucopolysaccharidoses.

Toxic effects caused by excessive exposure to acid soldering flux. Severity depends on the dose, route, timing, coexisting conditions, and clinical findings; suspected poisoning requires prompt assessment.
Acid-fast stain uses dyes that remain in the cell wall of mycobacteria and some related organisms, helping identify them in clinical specimens.
An acid-base disturbance in which the concentration of hydrogen ions increases, tending to lower arterial blood pH below 7.35.

Surgical reconstruction of the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) following rupture, one of the most common knee ligament injuries. The ACL is a primary restraint to anterior tibial translation and rotatory instability, and its rupture frequently occurs during non-contact pivoting sports activities ( skiing, soccer, basketball).
A benign, slow-growing tumor of the vestibular portion of the vestibulocochlear nerve. It may cause hearing loss, tinnitus, or balance problems.

Acute damage to the auditory system from a brief, intense sound such as an explosion or firearm. It may cause tinnitus, temporary or permanent sensorineural hearing loss, and tympanic or ossicular injury; urgent audiologic assessment is indicated when hearing loss is sudden.

Impaired platelet adhesion or aggregation that develops after birth. Causes include antiplatelet medicines, kidney failure, hematologic disease, and other systemic disorders; platelet counts may remain normal, but mucocutaneous bleeding can occur.

A rare genetic skeletal dysplasia characterized by short, broad fingers and toes, nasal and midface hypoplasia, short stature, and variable intellectual disability. Some patients have resistance to parathyroid or other hormones.
Chronic growth hormone (GH) excess in adulthood, typically from a pituitary somatotroph adenoma.
ACTH blood test evaluates acth blood test; interpretation uses the method, specimen or body region, reference range, and clinical question.

A dynamic test of adrenal cortisol reserve using synthetic adrenocorticotropic hormone, usually cosyntropin. An inadequate cortisol rise supports adrenal insufficiency, although interpretation depends on timing, assay, recent glucocorticoid exposure, and whether disease is acute or chronic.

A chronic infection caused by branching, gram-positive anaerobic bacteria of the genus Actinomyces, which normally colonize the mouth, gastrointestinal tract, and genital tract. It can form infiltrative masses and draining sinuses containing sulfur granules.

Acute adrenal crisis is life-threatening cortisol deficiency causing hypotension, vomiting, abdominal pain, electrolyte disturbance, hypoglycemia, or shock; urgent glucocorticoid and fluid treatment is required.
Acute arterial occlusion of the kidney abruptly reduces renal blood flow and may cause flank pain, hematuria, hypertension, or acute kidney injury.
Acute inflammation of the tracheobronchial tree, usually caused by a viral respiratory infection and characterized by cough, with or without sputum production, lasting up to several weeks.

Sudden or rapidly developing incoordination caused by cerebellar dysfunction. In children it may follow an infection, but stroke, intoxication, inflammation, tumor, and other urgent causes must be considered.

Acute inflammation of the gallbladder, most often caused by persistent cystic-duct obstruction by a gallstone. It commonly causes sustained right-upper-quadrant pain, fever, nausea, and a positive Murphy sign; ultrasound and timely antimicrobial and surgical assessment are standard.

A clinical spectrum caused by acute myocardial ischemia from plaque disruption, thrombosis, or less commonly coronary spasm. It includes unstable angina, NSTEMI, and STEMI and requires rapid assessment with symptoms, serial ECGs, and cardiac troponin testing.

A rare but serious inflammatory disorder of the spinal cord, usually affecting the gray matter and causing sudden flaccid limb weakness, reduced reflexes, and sometimes cranial-nerve or respiratory involvement. MRI and cerebrospinal-fluid studies support the diagnosis; urgent neurologic and respiratory monitoring is required.
A sudden decline in kidney function that causes waste products and fluid to accumulate in the body.
Acute lymphoblastic leukemia is a rapidly progressive cancer of immature lymphoid precursor cells that crowds the bone marrow and can involve blood, lymph nodes, or the central nervous system.

A mild altitude illness caused by rapid ascent, usually producing headache with nausea, fatigue, dizziness, or sleep disturbance. Prevention and treatment include gradual acclimatization, descent when symptoms worsen, oxygen, and appropriate medical therapy.
Childhood acute myeloid leukemia is a marrow and blood cancer caused by uncontrolled proliferation of immature myeloid cells, producing anemia, infection, and bleeding risk.
A clinical syndrome of glomerular inflammation marked by hematuria, variable proteinuria, edema, hypertension, and reduced kidney function.

Sudden inflammation of the pancreas, most often caused by gallstones or alcohol. It causes upper-abdominal pain and may cause vomiting or systemic complications; severity ranges from mild to life-threatening.

A severe inflammatory lung injury causing acute hypoxemic respiratory failure and diffuse lung opacities not fully explained by heart failure. Common triggers include sepsis, pneumonia, aspiration, trauma, and pancreatitis.

Most common cause of intrinsic AKI resulting from ischemic or nephrotoxic injury to tubular epithelial cells. Ischemic ATN develops from prolonged prerenal states. Nephrotoxic ATN results from direct injury by aminoglycosides, amphotericin B, cisplatin, contrast, and myoglobin.
Primary adrenal insufficiency resulting from destruction or dysfunction of the adrenal cortex, leading to deficiency of cortisol, aldosterone, and adrenal androgens.
Adenoid removal treats or supports adenoid removal; indication, preparation, complications, and recovery depend on the procedure and patient.

A condition in which endometrial glands and stroma are present within the myometrium (uterine muscle). Most common in multiparous women in their 40s and 50s. Presents with heavy menstrual bleeding (menorrhagia), severe dysmenorrhea, chronic pelvic pain, and uterine enlargement.

Emotional or behavioral symptoms in response to an identifiable stressor occurring within three months of the onset of the stressor. The symptoms are disproportionate to the severity of the stressor and cause significant distress or impairment. It resolves within six months of the termination of the stressor.
The physical, cognitive, emotional, and social changes that occur as a person develops from childhood into adulthood, including puberty and the development of greater independence.
Adolescent test or procedure preparation treats or supports adolescent test or procedure preparation; indication, preparation, complications, and recovery depend on the procedure and patient.
Adrenal gland removal treats or supports adrenal gland removal; indication, preparation, complications, and recovery depend on the procedure and patient.
Adrenergic bronchodilator overdose involves toxic exposure to adrenergic bronchodilator overdose; dose, route, timing, symptoms, and antidote availability guide the clinical response.

A rare malignant tumor of the adrenal cortex that may secrete cortisol, androgens, or aldosterone or be non-functional. Often large at diagnosis; treatment is en bloc resection, with mitotane for advanced disease.
An inherited disorder causing abnormal buildup of very-long-chain fatty acids and progressive nervous-system or adrenal damage.

A malignant tumor arising from connective or supporting tissues, such as muscle, fat, fibrous tissue, blood vessels, or peripheral nerves. It often presents as a painless enlarging mass and requires imaging and biopsy for diagnosis.
A systemic inflammatory disorder characterized by fever, joint pain or arthritis, and a transient salmon-colored rash.
Documents and instructions that state a person’s healthcare preferences and designate a surrogate decision-maker if the person later lacks decision-making capacity.
Bacteria that grow using oxygen or tolerate oxygen, although individual species differ in their exact oxygen requirements.
Aflatoxin is a toxin produced by certain Aspergillus molds in contaminated foods; chronic exposure can injure the liver and increase hepatocellular-carcinoma risk.

Toxic effects caused by excessive exposure to aftershave products. Severity depends on the dose, route, timing, coexisting conditions, and clinical findings; suspected poisoning requires prompt assessment.
A severe deficiency or absence of immunoglobulins, causing recurrent infections.
Age-related hearing loss is the presentation described by age-related hearing loss; onset, severity, associated findings, causes, and need for care guide assessment.
A state of excessive motor activity, emotional excitement, and restlessness. In psychiatric settings, it may be a symptom of mania, psychosis, delirium, substance intoxication, or withdrawal.

A severe reduction or near-absence of circulating neutrophils, usually defined as an absolute neutrophil count below $0.510^9/L$. It may be caused by medications, chemotherapy, autoimmune disease, infections, or bone-marrow disorders and presents with fever, sore throat, oral ulcers, or recurrent serious infections.
Aicardi syndrome is a rare developmental brain disorder classically involving agenesis of the corpus callosum, chorioretinal lacunae, and infantile seizures.
Alanine transaminase (ALT) blood test evaluates alanine transaminase (alt) blood test; interpretation uses the method, specimen or body region, reference range, and clinical question.
Albumin blood (serum) test evaluates albumin blood (serum) test; interpretation uses the method, specimen or body region, reference range, and clinical question.
A problematic pattern of alcohol use leading to significant impairment or distress. Severity is classified as mild (2--3 criteria), moderate (4--5 criteria), or severe (6 or more criteria).

A syndrome that may occur after abrupt cessation or substantial reduction of prolonged heavy alcohol use. Symptoms can include tremor, anxiety, sweating, nausea, hallucinations, seizures, or delirium; onset and severity vary, and severe withdrawal requires urgent medical care.

A high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis caused by prolonged heavy alcohol use, poor nutritional intake, and vomiting. It typically presents with abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, dehydration, and tachypnea, often with a normal or low blood glucose concentration.
Alcoholic liver disease includes steatosis, alcohol-associated hepatitis, and cirrhosis caused by sustained alcohol exposure.

A length-dependent peripheral neuropathy associated with chronic excessive alcohol use and nutritional deficiency, especially thiamine deficiency. It causes burning pain, numbness, paraesthesia, and weakness, most prominently in the feet and lower legs.
Aldolase blood test evaluates aldolase blood test; interpretation uses the method, specimen or body region, reference range, and clinical question.
Aldosterone blood test evaluates aldosterone blood test; interpretation uses the method, specimen or body region, reference range, and clinical question.

A metabolic (elevated bicarbonate) or respiratory (low PaCO2) disturbance that raises arterial pH above 7.45. Metabolic alkalosis: vomiting/NG suction (HCl loss), diuretics, mineralocorticoid excess, hypokalemia, and alkali ingestion—compensated by hypoventilation; chloride-responsive vs. chloride-resistant distinguishes causes.
An inherited disorder of tyrosine metabolism causing homogentisic-acid accumulation and darkening of urine or tissues.

An inflammatory condition of the conjunctiva mediated by IgE-dependent mast cell degranulation in response to environmental allergens, characterized by bilateral ocular itching, tearing, conjunctival injection, and eyelid edema.
Immune reactions to substances that are usually harmless, such as foods, medicines, pollens, or insect venom. They may be immediate or delayed and can range from localized symptoms to anaphylaxis.

Immune reactions to normally harmless substances such as foods, pollens, medicines, insect venom, or animal dander. Reactions range from localized rhinitis or dermatitis to life-threatening anaphylaxis.
Subcutaneous allergen immunotherapy involving gradually increasing doses of selected allergens to reduce allergic sensitivity; administration requires monitoring for systemic reactions.
Allergy testing - skin evaluates allergy testing - skin; interpretation uses the method, specimen or body region, reference range, and clinical question.

A plant-derived substance used in some topical products and supplements; topical preparations may soothe minor irritation, while oral latex-containing products can cause cramps, diarrhea, and electrolyte problems.
ALP - blood test evaluates alp - blood test; interpretation uses the method, specimen or body region, reference range, and clinical question.
ALP isoenzyme test evaluates alp isoenzyme test; interpretation uses the method, specimen or body region, reference range, and clinical question.
A fetal plasma protein produced mainly by the yolk sac and liver; maternal or blood AFP measurement is used in selected prenatal screening and evaluation of liver or germ-cell tumors.
Alpha-1 antitrypsin blood test evaluates alpha-1 antitrypsin blood test; interpretation uses the method, specimen or body region, reference range, and clinical question.

An autosomal codominant genetic disorder caused by mutations in the SERPINA1 gene. It predisposes to early-onset panlobular emphysema (lower lobes), liver disease, and panniculitis. PiZZ genotype is most severe. Treatment includes AAT augmentation therapy and smoking avoidance.

Hereditary nephritis caused by mutations in type four collagen genes leading to progressive sensorineural hearing loss, ocular anomalies, and renal failure. X-linked form from COL4A5 mutations is the most common. Autosomal recessive and dominant forms exist.
A rare autosomal-recessive disorder caused by ALMS1 variants, associated with cone-rod dystrophy, hearing loss, obesity, insulin resistance, cardiomyopathy, and progressive kidney or liver disease.
Structural or functional changes in the lung alveoli that can impair gas exchange and occur with infection, edema, emphysema, interstitial disease, or developmental disorders.

A progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized pathologically by amyloid-beta plaques, tau neurofibrillary pathology, and neuronal loss. It most commonly presents with insidious impairment of episodic memory followed by broader cognitive and functional decline.
Transient monocular vision loss lasting seconds to minutes, classically described as a curtain descending over the field, caused by retinal or optic nerve ischemia.

External genital anatomy that does not have typical male or female features, usually because of a difference in sex development. Evaluation includes examination, chromosome and hormone testing, pelvic or abdominal imaging, and assessment for congenital adrenal hyperplasia.

A developmental reduction in vision caused by abnormal visual input during early childhood, without a sufficient structural explanation. It commonly results from misalignment, unequal focusing power, or obstruction of vision in one eye.

Infection with the protozoan parasite Entamoeba histolytica, acquired mainly by ingestion of faecally contaminated food or water. It may be asymptomatic or cause amoebic colitis with abdominal pain, diarrhoea, or dysentery, and can spread through the portal circulation to produce a liver abscess.

A focal collection of necrotic material in the liver caused by Entamoeba histolytica, usually following intestinal infection. It commonly causes fever, right-upper-quadrant pain, and tender hepatomegaly; diagnosis is supported by imaging and serology.
A group of inherited disorders in which enamel formation is abnormal, causing enamel that may be thin, poorly mineralized, weak, or easily worn on most or all teeth.
Amino acids are organic molecules that form proteins and also serve as precursors or fuels in human metabolism.
Aminoaciduria is abnormal urinary loss of amino acids caused by renal tubular transport defects, inherited metabolic disease, or generalized tubular injury.
Aminophylline overdose involves toxic exposure to aminophylline overdose; dose, route, timing, symptoms, and antidote availability guide the clinical response.
Amitriptyline and perphenazine overdose involves toxic exposure to amitriptyline and perphenazine overdose; dose, route, timing, symptoms, and antidote availability guide the clinical response.
Amitriptyline hydrochloride overdose involves toxic exposure to amitriptyline hydrochloride overdose; dose, route, timing, symptoms, and antidote availability guide the clinical response.
Ammonia blood test evaluates ammonia blood test; interpretation uses the method, specimen or body region, reference range, and clinical question.
Toxic effects caused by excessive exposure to ammonia. Severity depends on the dose, route, timing, coexisting conditions, and clinical findings; suspected poisoning requires prompt assessment.

Toxic effects caused by excessive exposure to ammonium hydroxide. Severity depends on the dose, route, timing, coexisting conditions, and clinical findings; suspected poisoning requires prompt assessment.

A procedure in which a needle is used to obtain amniotic fluid for genetic, chromosomal, infectious, or other prenatal testing. It is usually performed after the first trimester when clinically indicated; risks and benefits depend on the reason for testing and gestational age.
Amniotic band sequence results when fibrous amniotic strands entangle developing fetal parts, producing constriction rings, limb defects, or craniofacial and body-wall abnormalities.

The clear to pale-yellow fluid surrounding the fetus within the amniotic sac. Early in pregnancy it is derived largely from maternal plasma; later, fetal urine and lung fluid are major sources, and the fetus continuously swallows and recycles it.
A blood test measuring amylase, an enzyme produced mainly by the pancreas and salivary glands; elevated values may occur in pancreatitis and other conditions.
A urine test measuring amylase excretion, sometimes used with blood amylase when evaluating pancreatic or salivary-gland disease.
A progressive neurodegenerative disease that damages motor neurons, causing muscle weakness, loss of movement, speech or swallowing difficulty, and eventually respiratory failure.
Bacteria that grow without oxygen; some are harmed by oxygen.

Linear tear in the distal anal mucosa usually posterior in the midline. Presents with painful defecation and bright red blood on wiping or in the toilet. Associated with constipation, hard stools, and chronic diarrhea. The internal anal sphincter spasm perpetuates the fissure by reducing blood flow to the posterior midline.

Chronic tubulointerstitial renal injury associated with prolonged or excessive use of analgesic medicines. It may cause impaired urinary concentration, sterile pyuria, haematuria, papillary necrosis, hypertension, and progressive chronic kidney disease.
A rare, rapidly growing, and highly aggressive thyroid cancer that often presents as a large fixed neck mass with dysphagia or airway compromise. Prognosis is poor; management is usually palliative.
A natural or surgically created connection between two tubular structures, such as blood vessels or segments of the intestine.

terms.term: Anemia Caused By Low Iron - Children

LLM.text: Iron-deficiency anemia in a child caused by insufficient iron intake, increased requirements, blood loss, or impaired absorption. It reduces hemoglobin production and may cause pallor, fatigue, irritability, or impaired development.

terms.normalized_term: anemia caused by low iron - children

terms.term: Anemia Caused By Low Iron - Infants And Toddlers

LLM.text: Iron-deficiency anemia in an infant or toddler, commonly related to inadequate dietary iron, excessive cow's milk intake, increased growth requirements, or blood loss. It may cause pallor, fatigue, irritability, and developmental effects.

terms.normalized_term: anemia caused by low iron - infants and toddlers

LLM.text: Anemia of inflammation. Normocytic or microcytic. Low iron, low TIBC, normal/high ferritin.
A brain aneurysm is a focal weakness and ballooning of a cerebral-artery wall; rupture causes subarachnoid hemorrhage and sudden severe headache.

A genetic disorder caused by loss of function of the UBE3A gene on chromosome 15 (maternal deletion or paternal uniparental disomy). Features: severe intellectual disability, absent speech, seizures, ataxia, and frequent laughter. Characteristic happy demeanor with hand-flapping movements.
Chest discomfort caused by inadequate oxygen-rich blood flow to the heart muscle, usually from coronary artery disease.

A degenerative abnormality of small blood vessels in the colon that can cause intermittent or recurrent lower gastrointestinal bleeding, often without pain. Diagnosis and treatment depend on the bleeding pattern and endoscopic findings.

Rapid swelling of the deep dermis/subcutaneous and submucosal tissues (lips, eyelids, tongue, throat, hands, GI tract) due to mast cell mediator release (histamine—allergic/idiopathic, urticaria associated) or bradykinin-mediated (hereditary angioedema—C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency; ACE-inhibitor-induced).

terms.term: Angioplasty And Stent Placement - Carotid Artery

LLM.text: Angioplasty and stent placement - carotid artery is a treatment, procedure, or care topic; indications, benefits, risks, and follow-up depend on the patient and clinical goal.

terms.normalized_term: angioplasty and stent placement - carotid artery

LLM.text: A catheter-based procedure that widens a narrowed coronary artery, usually with an inflatable balloon, and may place a stent to help keep the artery open and improve blood flow to the heart muscle.

terms.term: Angioplasty And Stent Placement - Peripheral Arteries

LLM.text: A catheter-based procedure that widens a narrowed peripheral artery, usually with an inflatable balloon, and may place a stent to improve blood flow to an affected limb or organ.

terms.normalized_term: angioplasty and stent placement - peripheral arteries

LLM.text: Unequal pupil size. It may be physiologic or caused by disorders of the eye, autonomic nerves, or brain; sudden anisocoria with headache, eye pain, or neurologic symptoms requires urgent assessment.
Ankle arthroscopy treats or supports ankle arthroscopy; indication, preparation, complications, and recovery depend on the procedure and patient.

Pain in or around the ankle, commonly caused by sprain, fracture, tendinitis, arthritis, bursitis, or infection. Inability to bear weight, deformity, marked swelling, or fever requires prompt assessment.
Ankle replacement treats or supports ankle replacement; indication, preparation, complications, and recovery depend on the procedure and patient.

A congenital anomaly where a ring of pancreatic tissue completely or partially encircles the second portion of the duodenum, causing duodenal obstruction. It results from failure of the ventral pancreatic bud to completely rotate around the duodenum during embryogenesis.

terms.term: Anomalous Left Coronary Artery From The Pulmonary Artery

LLM.text: A rare congenital anomaly in which the left coronary artery arises from the pulmonary artery instead of the aorta. It can cause myocardial ischemia, heart failure, arrhythmia, or sudden death, particularly in infancy or exertion.

terms.normalized_term: anomalous left coronary artery from the pulmonary artery

LLM.text: Complete absence of testicular tissue, present from birth or caused by loss of previously formed testes. It results in absent or severely reduced testosterone production and infertility unless treated with appropriate hormone replacement.

A localized collection of pus in the tissues around the anus or rectum, usually caused by infection of an anal gland. It commonly causes severe anal pain, swelling, fever, and difficulty sitting. Prompt incision and drainage is the standard treatment.

Measurement of pressures in the anal canal and rectum to assess sphincter function and rectal sensation. A pressure-sensing catheter is inserted into the rectum and slowly withdrawn through the anal canal. Measures resting and squeeze pressures reflecting internal and external sphincter function respectively.
Anoscopy and high-resolution anoscopy evaluates anoscopy and high-resolution anoscopy; interpretation uses the method, specimen or body region, reference range, and clinical question.
Relating to the front of the body or positioned closer to the front.

A sprain or tear of the ligament that limits forward movement and rotation of the tibia relative to the femur. It commonly occurs during sudden stopping, pivoting, or landing and may cause a pop, rapid swelling, pain, and knee instability.
Anterior knee pain is the presentation described by anterior knee pain; onset, severity, associated findings, causes, and need for care guide assessment.
Anterior vaginal wall repair treats or supports anterior vaginal wall repair; indication, preparation, complications, and recovery depend on the procedure and patient.

A serious infectious disease caused by the gram-positive bacterium Bacillus anthracis, which forms highly resistant spores that can persist in the environment for decades, and it is primarily a zoonotic disease of herbivores (cattle, sheep, goats) that can be transmitted to humans through contact with infected animals or their products.
Anthrax blood test evaluates anthrax blood test; interpretation uses the method, specimen or body region, reference range, and clinical question.
Anti-DNase B blood test evaluates anti-dnase b blood test; interpretation uses the method, specimen or body region, reference range, and clinical question.
Anti-glomerular basement membrane blood test evaluates anti-glomerular basement membrane blood test; interpretation uses the method, specimen or body region, reference range, and clinical question.

An autoimmune disease in which antibodies target basement-membrane components in the kidney and sometimes the lungs. It can cause rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, pulmonary hemorrhage, or both and requires urgent treatment.
Anti-insulin antibody test evaluates anti-insulin antibody test; interpretation uses the method, specimen or body region, reference range, and clinical question.

An operation intended to reduce reflux of stomach contents into the esophagus, usually by reinforcing the gastroesophageal junction. It may be considered for selected patients with gastroesophageal reflux disease or a hiatal hernia.
Anti-reflux surgery - children treats or supports anti-reflux surgery - children; indication, preparation, complications, and recovery depend on the procedure and patient.

Toxic effects caused by excessive exposure to anti-rust products. Severity depends on the dose, route, timing, coexisting conditions, and clinical findings; suspected poisoning requires prompt assessment.
An autoantibody associated especially with autoimmune hepatitis, although low levels can occur in other autoimmune or infectious conditions.
Bacteria resisting antibiotic effects. Mechanisms: enzymatic degradation, target modification, efflux pumps, membrane permeability. Driven by antibiotic overuse.
Antibody titer blood test evaluates antibody titer blood test; interpretation uses the method, specimen or body region, reference range, and clinical question.
Anticoagulant rodenticides poisoning involves toxic exposure to anticoagulant rodenticides poisoning; dose, route, timing, symptoms, and antidote availability guide the clinical response.
Antidiarrheal medicine overdose involves toxic exposure to antidiarrheal medicine overdose; dose, route, timing, symptoms, and antidote availability guide the clinical response.
Antidiuretic hormone blood test evaluates antidiuretic hormone blood test; interpretation uses the method, specimen or body region, reference range, and clinical question.

Toxic effects caused by excessive exposure to antifreeze, usually products containing ethylene glycol or propylene glycol. Severity depends on the substance, dose, route, timing, coexisting conditions, and clinical findings; suspected poisoning requires prompt assessment.
Medicines that block histamine effects and reduce symptoms such as itching, sneezing, and runny nose; sedation and interactions vary by agent.
An autoantibody strongly associated with primary biliary cholangitis, interpreted with cholestatic liver tests and clinical findings.
Antinuclear antibody panel evaluates antinuclear antibody panel; interpretation uses the method, specimen or body region, reference range, and clinical question.
Antiparietal cell antibody test evaluates antiparietal cell antibody test; interpretation uses the method, specimen or body region, reference range, and clinical question.
Antiphospholipid syndrome is an autoimmune thrombophilia associated with venous or arterial clots and pregnancy morbidity in the presence of persistent antiphospholipid antibodies.
Antiplatelet drugs such as clopidogrel, prasugrel, and ticagrelor that reduce ADP-mediated platelet activation and thrombosis risk, with bleeding as a major adverse effect.

A pattern of disregard for and violation of the rights of others occurring since age 15 years. At least three of seven criteria: failure to conform to social norms, deceitfulness, impulsivity, irritability and aggressiveness, reckless disregard for safety, consistent irresponsibility, and lack of remorse.

A blood test that measures antibodies against streptolysin O, a toxin produced by group A streptococci. Rising or elevated titers support recent streptococcal infection and help evaluate suspected rheumatic fever or poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis, although a single value does not prove active infection.
Antithrombin III blood test evaluates antithrombin iii blood test; interpretation uses the method, specimen or body region, reference range, and clinical question.
Antithyroglobulin antibody test evaluates antithyroglobulin antibody test; interpretation uses the method, specimen or body region, reference range, and clinical question.
Aortic aneurysm repair - endovascular treats or supports aortic aneurysm repair - endovascular; indication, preparation, complications, and recovery depend on the procedure and patient.
Aortic angiography evaluates aortic angiography; interpretation uses the method, specimen or body region, reference range, and clinical question.

Symptoms and signs caused by narrowing or blockage of the aorta or its major branches. Causes include large-vessel vasculitis, atherosclerosis, thrombosis, and congenital disease; findings may include unequal pulses, limb claudication, or neurologic symptoms.

A tear in the inner layer of the aorta that allows blood to enter the wall and form a false channel. Stanford type A involves the ascending aorta; type B does not. Treatment depends on the type, symptoms, complications, and overall clinical condition.

Incomplete closure of the aortic valve allowing blood to flow backward from the aorta to the left ventricle during diastole. Causes include bicuspid aortic valve, endocarditis, aortic root dilation, hypertension, and connective tissue disorders. Murmur: early diastolic decrescendo murmur at the left sternal border.

Narrowing of the aortic valve opening, obstructing left ventricular outflow. It is the most common valvular disease in developed countries, usually caused by calcific degeneration. Symptoms include angina, syncope, and heart failure (SAD triad).
Aortic valve surgery - minimally invasive treats or supports aortic valve surgery - minimally invasive; indication, preparation, complications, and recovery depend on the procedure and patient.
Aortic valve surgery - open treats or supports aortic valve surgery - open; indication, preparation, complications, and recovery depend on the procedure and patient.
A congenital opening between the ascending aorta and pulmonary artery.
An autosomal dominant craniosynostosis syndrome caused by FGFR2 mutations (most commonly Ser252Trp or Pro253Arg).

A scoring system developed by Virginia Apgar in 1952 to assess the newborn's immediate condition at 1 and 5 minutes after birth. Five components (each scored 0, 1, or 2): Appearance (skin color), Pulse (heart rate), Grimace (reflex irritability), Activity (muscle tone), and Respiration (breathing effort).
Describing failure of a tissue, especially bone marrow, to produce adequate cells; aplastic anemia causes pancytopenia from marrow failure.

A bone marrow failure syndrome characterized by pancytopenia (anemia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia) and a hypocellular bone marrow with replacement by fat cells, resulting from immune-mediated destruction of hematopoietic stem cells.

Recurrent pauses in breathing in a premature infant, sometimes accompanied by bradycardia or oxygen desaturation. It may be central, obstructive, or mixed. Management includes monitoring and, when needed, respiratory stimulation or support.
